News.title: Hundreds more prisoners to be freed in second phase of early release scheme
News.content:
About 650 more offenders will leave jails in England and Wales early on Tuesday in the second phase of the government's plan to tackle the prison population crisis.

The group will include offenders serving up to two and a half years for crimes.

Under the new rules, they are leaving jail after serving a third of their sentence behind bars, rather than half.

The second wave of releases comes as the government takes its plan to radically overhaul criminal courts back to Parliament - but also as probation officers prepare to vote in a ballot that could lead to a strike over pay and workload.

Some 700 offenders left jail early on 1 October - all of whom were serving terms of less than 19 months.

Monday's second stage begins the process of releasing batches of offenders serving increasingly long sentences - culminating next June with those serving more than 12 years.

Napo, the probation service union, said the releases have put enormous strain on its members, who are charged with monitoring the offenders in the community.

Typically, those being released should expect to be electronically tagged and subject to other monitoring conditions for the second third of their sentence.

On Tuesday, the union's members will meet to discuss next week's vote, which could lead to strike action. Probation officers have been offered a 5% pay rise by the Ministry of Justice (MoJ), while it had demanded 12% as part of a plan to make up for loss of earnings caused by cuts from 2010.

The MoJ says the offer is fair and has been accepted by two other unions and is twinned with a Â£700m investment in probation to recruit 1,300 extra officers and the roll-out of AI tools to cut the workload of monitoring offenders.

News.title: Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again
News.content:
The Brexit debate is back.

For years, it felt like the only thing Westminster talked about.

I have had a ringside seat at it all, from the Conservative election victory in 2015, with the party's promise in its manifesto that year to offer "a straight in-out referendum on our membership of the European Union by the end of 2017."

Then there was the then Prime Minister David Cameron's negotiation with the European Union to try to secure what he saw as a better deal and then the referendum itself on Thursday, 23 June 2016.

And that, you will remember, was merely the start, as years of wrangling began. Two general elections came and went in 2017 and 2019 and it took the two prime ministers after David Cameron, first Theresa May and then Boris Johnson, before the UK left the European Union at 23:00 on Friday, 31 January 2020.

Little wonder perhaps that by that point, almost irrespective of someone's views on the topic, there was an appetite to talk about something else. Anything else. Political parties picked up that vibe and while their long standing instincts on the EU were there to see if you scratched the surface, there was minimal desire to extemporise about them any time soon.

With the arrival of Andy Burnham as prime minister, that has changed, despite what he said just a few months before he arrived in Downing Street.

He has been happy to repeatedly lean into an argument claiming that it is time to "face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good" and "the status quo is not good enough for Britain." First he made this case at the Labour Party Conference last month and now he has made it again in the House of Commons.

Burnham is attempting to make a two-pronged case.

First, in the short term, he wants to "deepen" the UK's relationship with the EU at a summit in Brussels at the end of next month. He insists such a deepening would be within the promise made by Labour at the last general election that the UK would say no to the customs union, the single market and freedom of movement.

Which brings us onto the second element of his case, in the medium term. What might Labour promise in its next general election manifesto? The prime minister told me a fortnight ago the manifesto could promise an in-out referendum.

In the Commons, he sought to reassure you, whatever your view on Brexit.

"This country in the next decade needs to know where it's going. There are no assumptions here, and as I said, the British public will be the boss of whatever is decided," he said.

Hang on, say critics, it was decided by voters a decade ago.

"They weighed the arguments and made a decision. The least they are owed is politicians willing to defend it," argues Lord Frost, external, a former Brexit minister and chief Brexit negotiator in the Telegraph.

The focus of the next five weeks, ahead of a UK-EU Summit in Brussels on Friday 20 November, is what Downing Street sees as short term wins on youth mobility, food and drink, and energy.

Andy Burnham hopes to make an argument that what he will portray as a sensible, pragmatic deepening of the relationship with Brussels can help cut illegal immigration and boost economic growth.

He sought to goad the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch for seeking to oppose a plan he thinks can contribute to growth. She argued it risked regurgitating yesterday's arguments with little prospect of success.

And, strikingly, his attempt at goading his opponents went further still. He told The Rest Is Politics podcast that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there was Russian interference in the Brexit referendum.

"I've had a clear answer that, yes, there was," he claimed, without saying who provided that clear answer or what the evidence for that suggested clarity was.

In the Commons, his language appeared a little softer. He told MPs it was "inconceivable" to think that Russia did not try to interfere. A double negative deployed this time, about alleged attempts at interference.

His political opponents were already pouncing. The Reform UK leader Nigel Farage was blunt â calling the prime minister "a liar."

The former Prime Minister Boris Johnson added that he had asked the same question as Andy Burnham did when he became Foreign Secretary, external "and they replied that there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".

News.title: Government expands police support to political figures who are not MPs
News.content:
Political figures who are not currently MPs will be given police support, the home secretary has announced.

Shabana Mahmood told MPs there was "insufficient protection" for those serving in public life and that the new announcement will cover peers, former MPs and party spokespeople.

She also announced an urgent, independent review of security arrangements for high-profile figures including politicians and royals.

It comes three months after Reform UK spokeswoman and former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home in Devon, having been hit on the head with a hammer 21 times as she ate lunch.

Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with her murder, and he was also charged with preparing acts of terror against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Kerry is alleged to have carried out research on prominent targets over a period of two years, including trying to gain entry into Farage's London home.

Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Mahmood said that "robust debate and criticism are part of this job - threats, abuse and violence are not."

She did not elaborate on what the support would involve, but told MPs it would include access to a named police officer and help with wider security measures.

The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years, following the murders of Conservative MP Sir David Amess in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox in 2016.

"We owe it to them and to everyone who believes in a fair and open country to ensure that those who serve at all levels receive the protection they deserve," Mahmood added.

The "root and branch" independent review into security arrangements will be led by former national security advisor Stephen Lovegrove, and will look into "physical threats, online risks and the dangers posed within our more polarised society".

Mahmood confirmed that the review will report within six months, and build on the existing work of Sir Robert Buckland, who is leading a separate review into the murder of Sir David.

In response, shadow home secretary Chris Philp welcomed the extension of protective measures, saying threats to elected representatives are threats to democracy.

Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf welcomed the review, but added: "It is disappointing that it took the murder of one of our colleagues, countless threats towards our party spokespeople and months of campaigning from Reform UK to make this government take action."

Reform has in recent months accused the government of a "dereliction of duty" over Farage's taxpayer-funded security, claiming it had previously been "downgraded" - a charge that the Home Office has said is "categorically untrue".

Decisions over the security of current MPs and members of the House of Lords are made by the House of Parliament's security team.

There is a separate, independent committee, the Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec), to deal with high-profile political candidates, which is staffed by officials from the Home Office, the Cabinet Office, and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.

The Jo Cox Foundation welcomed the home secretary's announcement but said "strengthening physical security" alone was not enough.

"We must also tackle the root causes - including online harms and education - to prevent future attacks," its chief executive Olivia Field said in a statement on X.

According to data released to the BBC in April, the number of alleged offences against MPs have increased year-on-year, with 976 recorded in 2025, compared to 364 in 2019.

MPs reported 4,064 crimes to the Met's Parliamentary Liaison Team between 2019 and 2025. Most offences were related to malicious communications followed by harassment, and criminal damage to a building.

In 2025, there were 50 death threats reported - up from 31 the previous year.

News.title: Heating oil customers face tough winter despite shake-up promise
News.content:
Heating oil customers facing soaring bills have been promised better regulation of the sector by the government.

Ministers say they will tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed.

With prices close to having doubled in the past year, some campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from the same cap as regular, variable gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales.

But there is no sign of the government proposing such a change, nor when the stricter rules will take effect.

Ministers said they would work with industry to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition".

In the meantime, oil users have been offered discounts on heat pumps, a code of practice is in place, and industry practices setting minimum order volumes at 500 litres for some consumers will be reviewed. Domestic tanks typically hold between 1,000 and 2,000 litres.

The government said this had left some people having to pay for more heating oil than they might need.

News.title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
News.content:
The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt.

Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night.

This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers.

Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after.

Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working.

Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership.

News.title: Abramovich's close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest
News.content:
One of Roman Abramovich's closest associates misled a UK court to help secure ownership of Siberian oil fields, leaked documents seen by the BBC suggest.

Eugene Tenenbaum, a former director of Chelsea Football Club, helped to manage the billionaire's wealth at the time of the case in 2008, which Abramovich won.

Tenenbaum was giving evidence during proceedings taken against Abramovich by a company owned by another Russian billionaire, who was claiming the oil fields had been stolen from him and other investors.

The leaked documents now suggest there was a premeditated attempt by Abramovich to reduce the value of the other investors' stake in the Siberian venture.

Roman Abramovich's lawyers say their "client denies all the allegations made against him".

Lawyers for Eugene Tenenbaum say he "denies in the strongest terms any suggestion that he committed perjury or contempt of court".

The 2008 court case centred on the ownership of Siberian oil fields being developed jointly between Abramovich's company, Sibneft, and the Russian subsidiary of the British company, Sibir Energy PLC, owned by Russian billionaire Chalva Tchigirinsky.

Sibneft contributed money, while the subsidiary Yugraneft provided the licences for the oil fields.

Their partnership - which became known as Sibneft-Yugra - ended acrimoniously.

Sibir's 50% interest in the joint venture had been diluted, or reduced, to less than 1%. It said this had been done without its knowledge.

Unsuccessful attempts to sue Sibneft in both Russia and the British Virgin Islands led to the court proceedings in London.

At court in 2008, Yugraneft claimed "to have been the victim of a massive fraud directed by Mr Abramovich", as a result of which it had suffered a loss of "not less that $2 billion", which in 2008 was worth about Â£1bn.

But Abramovich's team claimed that Yugraneft had been unable to repay loans of more than $30m, so lost its right over the shares.

News.title: On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged
News.content:
It was a journey at high speed through the desert - in a pick-up truck with armed fighters in the back. We were travelling with Yemen's pro-government forces, catching glimpses of the Arabian Sea, and forbidding mountain peaks in the distance. Houthi rebels were dislodged from here just days ago, we were told.

When you are battling over expanses of empty desert, progress can be hard to see. But these soldiers, in Shaab-al-Jinn in Lahj governorate, showed us new sandbagged defences - new lines in the sand.

"There was heavy fighting," said Tawfiq Al Haboun, a bearded commander in camouflage uniform.

"They have snipers, artillery and ballistic missile launchers."

Here in the far corners of the Middle East, a war is being waged with global implications.

Yemen's entrenched civil war is now impossible to ignore. It's part of a wider conflict, stretching from Tehran to Riyadh, where missiles slammed into the international airport this weekend. Yemen's Houthi fighters â already a threat to global shipping â are an increasing threat to Saudi Arabia. And they provide leverage for their backers in Iran, Saudi's regional rival.

Tawfiq Al Haboun pointed to shards of fibre glass and bits of metal at his feet â part of a downed Houthi drone that he said was carrying C4 explosives.

Commander Al Haboun is from the Southern Forces, part of the loose â very loose â alliance of groups fighting for Yemen's government, which is internationally recognised, and backed by Saudi Arabia and its air strikes.

The Houthis swept into the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, ousting the government. A year later a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened, trying to dislodge the Houthis. Despite years of devastating air strikes, that hasn't worked.

News.title: Britain won't tolerate threats on our soil, Miliband says as he summons Iran ambassador
News.content:
The foreign secretary has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil" following last month's incident at RAF Fairford.

Ed Miliband said attempts by Iran to undermine the UK's security "through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs the incident in Gloucestershire was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard", while the home secretary said the likely coordinator was a "known individual based in Iran".

Iran's ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said Tehran was not involved and was willing to cooperate with British authorities.

The Foreign Office has also sanctioned two Iranians, including the head of the regime's counterespionage operations - with both men subjected to travel bans and asset freezes.

Burnham also indicated Iran could be hit with further sanctions over its suspected role.

It comes as the UK and 28 other countries - including the US, Canada, Australia, France and Germany - issued a joint statement condemning "in the strongest terms" violent attacks by Iran.

The statement accuses Tehran of carrying out "lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities" and also recognises the UK's attribution of Iranian involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.

A huge police operation began after officers were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base in the early hours of 27 September.

Dozens of homes were evacuated in the nearby village of Whelford and a large cordon was put in place around the site.

So far, a total of seven men - all in their 20s - have been arrested and later bailed in connection with the incident. No one has been charged.

Last week, Downing Street insisted the airbase was safe after the US withdrew all of its bombers â about a dozen B-1s from the base â back to their home stations on American soil.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

RAF Fairford, in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved an American request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

A US state department spokesman confirmed that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had a call with Miliband on Monday where they discussed "holding Iran to account for its actions and of continued collaboration to secure US assets in the United Kingdom".

News.title: Burnham to push for new post-Brexit deals at EU summit
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told MPs he will push for new post-Brexit deals with the EU at a summit next month.

He said "deeper cooperation" on some key issues - including youth mobility, food and drink, and energy - would help drive economic growth in the UK.

In a statement to MPs, Burnham also warned the EU's Made In Europe plans posed "a risk to UK manufacturing" and said he was in talks to get "an arrangement" that worked for the UK. The EU proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors but could impact British industry and supply chains.

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister was "unpicking" the deal the UK signed with the EU.

Although he said he was keen to negotiate a closer relationship with the EU, Burnham made clear Labour's manifesto commitments not to return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement, would stay in place until the next election.

Burnham said the "immediate priority" was securing a successful outcome at the November summit, adding: "I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.

"At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach like the one I am suggesting."

While the prime minister has committed to the current Labour manifesto's red lines about Brexit, in interviews after Labour conference, he did not rule out a new manifesto, which could include re-joining the EU.

It is increasingly clear that economic growth, and cooperation on illegal immigration, are going to be at the centre of No 10's arguments when it comes to selling a closer relationship both at - and beyond - next month's summit.

The Brexit withdrawal agreement in 2020 agreed the UK's "divorce bill" payments to the EU, and allowed the rules and regulations in the UK to start to diverge from those in the EU, which was necessary in order to negotiate trade deal with other countries.

But the divergence in food standards caused problems for UK food exports to its largest market, a problem that Sir Keir Starmer started to try to fix by renegotiating some common rules to reduce red tape.

In May 2025, this resulted in a post-Brexit deal agreeing continued access to UK waters for EU fishing boats until 2038, in return for a deal to reduce checks on food exports to the EU, which meant the UK was able to sell raw burgers and sausages back into the EU for the first time since Brexit.

The summit next month will see a series of deals with the EU on the table, Burnham told MPs, including food and drink, energy trading, and coordinating on immigration.

Burnham claimed these agreements could add the equivalent of Â£10bn per year to the economy by 2040, arguing that it would be a "dereliction of duty" to turn away from the chance to cut bureaucracy.

"At present entire truckloads of plants or fresh produce can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or a minor paperwork delay," he said.

"Fresh meat and fish spoil while waiting in trucks, and tonnes of exports have to be written off. Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around Â£100m in lost exports.

"British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU, seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned - this is having a real impact on businesses and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage."

The prime minister said a fresh agreement at the EU summit would also "ease the pressure on prices in the supermarket".

He said securing an energy deal, involving emissions trading, could "lower energy costs for households and businesses alike", adding this could cut wholesale energy costs by 20% in Northern Ireland.

Burnham said he also hoped to rebuild links with EU police and security agencies to boost information-sharing and help tackle smuggling gangs.

And he said being open about a new relationship with the EU was necessary to get a good deal on all these things: "If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have.

"Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain."

News.title: Healey faces £35bn Budget challenge to meet spending pledges, says think tank
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey faces having to find Â£35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said that if the government wants to raise defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030 and lift health spending without squeezing other departments, it will need a "top-up" of billions of pounds.

Higher inflation, caused by the Iran war, could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the IFS said.

The Treasury declined to comment.

The government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.

The IFS said that Healey must set out "credible" spending plans in the Budget, which will take place on 28 October.

"A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller.

"Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course.

"Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.

Speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home.

"But Britain and our alliesâ¯can face up to these challenges together."

He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".

Miller told the BBC's Today programme that Healey had inherited spending plans for government departments where spending growth would slow in the coming years.

"[It] already looked likely that he would have to make spending cuts just to live within those," she said. "Now, along comes the Middle East war, inflation goes up and those spending plans look very tight indeed."

Added to that, the chancellor has said he wants to get defence spending up to 3% of national income. Under Keir Starmer's leadership, Healey resigned as defence secretary in June in a battle with the Treasury over military spending.

Miller said: "You put all that together, if he wanted to do all of that within current spending plans he's looking at having to cut some other services by something like Â£35bn."

She said the government would have a "tough time" if it wanted to raise taxes to stop cuts to departments and fund defence spending.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced billions of pounds in tax rises. Meanwhile, Labour pledged in its manifesto "not increase taxes on working people", ruling out rises to National Insurance, income tax or VAT. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will stick to that promise.

Miller said: "You'd really have to be scaping around and doing lots of small things to get up to big sums."

News.title: Health and safety inquiry after fatal tiger attack
News.content:
A health and safety investigation has been launched into the death of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park was closed over the weekend following reports of a man climbing down into the enclosure from a walkway on Saturday afternoon.

An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. South Yorkshire Police confirmed he was visiting the park on his own.

"I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation," a City of Doncaster Council spokesperson said.

Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to the man's family and those who were at the scene.

"We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident," he said.

"At this time, we won't be commenting further on the individual or the investigation and we ask that the privacy of those involved is respected at this difficult time."

The wildlife park remains closed for third day as investigations continue.

A park spokesperson said: "Due to the events over the weekend, the park will remain closed today. Thank you for your understanding."

News.title: Reform pledges to suspend UK's asylum system for up to five years
News.content:
Reform UK has announced plans to effectively close down the UK's asylum system for a full parliamentary term if elected.

The party said all new asylum applications would be rejected and existing applications voided, with all claimants marked for deportation. It said no grants of humanitarian protection or refugee status would be made, while legal refugee routes and resettlement schemes would end.

Reform said it would also scrap the asylum tribunal system and deport 90,000 people currently with appeal cases, with home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf saying "Britain is full".

Labour called the proposals a "clear sign of desperation and weakness" and the Refugee Council branded them "unworkable".

Reform said its existing plans to make migrants who have entered the UK illegally, overstayed a visa or originated from a safe country ineligible for asylum would effectively prevent any current asylum claimant "from ever having their case heard".

The party said it would therefore "suspend the asylum system entirely for a full parliamentary term".

A parliamentary term usually lasts five years unless an early UK general election is called.

Under further proposals, Reform said it would pull the UK out of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), repeal the Human Rights Act 1998 and disapply the 1951 Refugee Convention to prevent legal challenges to its plans.

The party said it would ban British visas for countries such as Pakistan, Somalia, Eritrea, Syria, Afghanistan and Sudan if they refuse to allow deportation flights to land in their country.

News.title: Normandy veteran Henry Rice dies aged 100
News.content:
World War Two veteran Henry Rice, who survived a near-miss when a torpedo was fired at the boat he was on, has died at the age of 100.

Rice, from Cranleigh in Surrey, was a signalman aboard HMS Eastway as part of the Normandy landings, arriving at Juno Beach five days after D-Day.

He received the Legion d'honneur from the French government and had called for schools to teach children more about the Normandy landings because the "world is dangerous at the moment".

A spokesperson from the Spirit of Normandy Trust, a charity for veterans, said: "Henry was a great character, with a cheeky smile that endeared him to everyone he met."

Rice previously told the BBC that revisiting Normandy for a remembrance service in June this year meant "everything" to him.

"I've had a super lifetime," he said.

When thinking about veterans who had died, he added: "I find it too easy to wipe a tear away, so I don't let myself think too deeply. But when I'm on my own, then I do."

News.title: Public inquiry over Manchester synagogue attack deaths
News.content:
A public inquiry will examine the deaths of two men killed during an attack at a synagogue in Manchester.

Melvin Cravitz, 66, died from multiple stab wounds and fellow worshipper Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a bullet fired by armed police as he blocked the synagogue doors when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, tried to get in the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue on 2 October 2025.

Announcing the inquiry, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "What happened that day must be fully understood."

Syrian-born UK citizen Al-Shamie was shot dead by police while he carried out his attack.

Police had already seized Al-Shamie's mobile phone containing details of his extremist mindset but did not analyse the contents until after he had attacked the synagogue.

It took place on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year for Jews.

Mahmood said: "In recent days, we marked the first anniversary of the terror attack at the Heaton Park synagogue.

"On that awful day in October of last year, as our Jewish community celebrated Yom Kippur, two brave men â Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby â lost their lives, and three others were seriously injured.

"What happened that day must be fully understood. So, as requested by the coroner, I can today announce a public inquiry into the deaths of Mr Cravitz and Mr Daulby.

"This will ensure that all evidence can be heard, including any sensitive national security material that could not otherwise be fully heard in the coroner's court."

News.title: PC thought murderer was making 'empty threats' before arson attack
News.content:
The court heard Quinn and PC Mike Grundy went to the scene in Walkden around 01:25 GMT after Michelle Pearson called 999 because Bolland and three others were outside her house.

Bolland had been heard shouting "I'm going to break Kyle's jaw" and threatened to "boot the door down".

Quinn, as the senior officer, told the court she knew Bolland, two weeks earlier, had threatened to set fire to Michelle Pearson's house and smashed windows with a hammer.

There were also markers on databases about his drug use, firearms and violence.

Yet she chose not to arrest Bolland as she believed it was an "empty threat".

"As a police officer, you get to see the worst side of a community and unfortunately, Salford and what I saw in 14 yearsâ¦.individuals make threats like that, quite often."

She left Jackson Street around 02:30.

Her shift was not due to end until 05:00, the inquest heard.

Bolland's last known address was close by, but Quinn chose to go back to the police station.

When asked whether she should have tried to arrest him immediately, Quinn said "In hindsight, yes".

She told the court: "It's not that we had stopped dealing with the job, we had write-ups to do.

The family's barrister, Anna Morris KC asked if that work was more important than questioning Bolland - to which Quinn replied: "No".

Quinn said: "As a police officer, you get to see the worst side of a community and unfortunately in Salford and what I saw in 14 years, individuals make threats like that quite often.

"We didn't believe we needed to make an arrest, there and then, that night."

In his statement, Grundy had told Michelle he expected Bolland to be arrested.

It was suggested in the inquest that this was likely to have made Michelle feel she was not in any danger.

The inquest also heard that despite asking Michelle if she felt safe in the house, she sought not to try and move the family immediately to a secure location.

Quinn said she did not see the point in calling Michelle's housing provider, City West, because it was out of hours.

The inquest continues.

News.title: Russell Brand appears in court for start of rape trial
News.content:
There are six female complainants in the case.

During the selection process, potential jurors were asked a number of questions by the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan.

"Many of you will have heard of him", the judge said, adding that Brand had been on television "a great deal a couple of years ago.

The judge said: "About three years ago there was a television programme and a long article in the Times newspaper in which some allegations were made against him of sexual misconduct. They were allegations he firmly denied."

He asked potential jurors to tell him if they remembered watching the Channel 4 documentary or reading the article. Six put their hands up.

The judge also told them that the trial is expected to take about six weeks, but jurors might need to be available until 11 December.

The potential jurors were whittled down to 20.

Those jurors were told a smaller group of them would be chosen on Tuesday and sworn in for the trial before being sent home.

Before leaving court Bennathan warned them they must not carry out any research about Brand.

The actor and broadcaster rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

Brand went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States.

News.title: UK households to face sharper rise in inflation than previously thought, IMF warns
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

British households face a steeper increase in inflation than earlier predictions suggested, driven by escalating energy and food costs linked to conflict in the Middle East, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.

Updated projections also indicate that Prime Minister Andy Burnham will see UK economic growth slow down over the coming year.

The global financial institution stated that price pressures will continue to gather pace internationally into next year as war disrupts energy supplies.

An extended stalemate or worsening crisis in the Middle East could "keep energy and food prices elevated and volatile", dampening expansion and weakening government fiscal positions, the IMF said.

It added that these risks could be compounded by extreme weather, cyber attacks, and targeted strikes on energy infrastructure.

The warnings were echoed by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), which said the most pressing problem for Chancellor John Healey identified ahead of the Budget on October 28 is that inflation will erode the budgets of government departments, creating the need for either large cuts to some public services or potential top ups to spending plans totalling tens of billions of pounds.

The latest world economic outlook showed that UK consumers are set to witness faster-than-expected inflation for this year and 2027.

Consumer prices are set to have increased by 3.3% in 2026, up from a previous prediction of 3.2%. This would mark the joint second-highest rate among the G7 group of countries.

An extended stalemate or worsening crisis in the Middle East could "keep energy and food prices elevated and volatile", the IMF said. ( PA )

Meanwhile, inflation is expected to slow to 2.8% for next year, but this is significantly higher than the 2.4% rate previously forecast by the IMF.

Most recent figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed that inflation increased to 3.1% in August and is expected to tick higher over the coming months, amid pressure from higher household energy bills.

The Bank of England has said it expects UK inflation to lift to “slightly above 4%” in the first quarter of 2027, partly linked to another increase in the household energy price cap in January.

However, inflation is then expected to swing back lower throughout the year.

The IMF said it expects core UK inflation to fall back to target levels by the end of this year, later than it had previously forecast.

Globally, inflation is expected to lift to 4.7% in 2026 and then slow to 4.1% in 2027, although this would be 0.2 percentage points higher than its previous predictions.

The report, which was released alongside annual meetings from the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok, also pointed to stronger-than-expected UK growth for this year.

UK gross domestic product (GDP) is set to grow 1.3% this year, having previously predicted a 1% rise.

However, growth for next year is set to slow to 1.2%, down from a previous forecast of 1.3%.

An upwards boost from the adoption of AI technology has helped to boost many economies globally this year.

However, the IMF indicated that accelerating prices and further disruption linked to the Middle East conflict are likely to weigh on growth.

The latest report also indicated that the shock to the labour market has been shallower than expected, with UK unemployment set to strike 5.3% this year, down from a prediction of 5.6%.

“We are determined to drive good growth in every postcode, provide some breathing space for today, and fresh hope for the future.”

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: “John Healey must tackle both problems in the Budget by getting Britain drilling and dealing with out of control welfare spending.

“If the Chancellor reaches for more tax rises instead, he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it.”

News.title: Pennsylvania reports its sixth measles death this year. RFK Jr’s CDC still says it’s two
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A sixth person infected with measles has died in Pennsylvania after the worst outbreak of the virus in the state in over 35 years.

The 39-year-old woman had underlying health conditions and had previously been treated for measles, the Franklin County Coroner’s Office said Monday.

“This is the first death in Franklin County in many years with a patient with a recent history of a measles diagnosis and meets the definition set forth by the Pennsylvania Department of Health for a measles-associated death,” the coroner’s office wrote in a statement, shared to Facebook.

The office said it would not release any additional details about the case.

Measles is spreading across Pennsylvania and in other parts of the U.S. The state’s Department of Health reported 1,136 cases since the start of the year and 157 in the last week alone.

open image in gallery A county coroner in Pennsylvania has reported the state’s sixth measles death ( Getty Images/iStock )

Pennsylvania’s measles tracker showed five deaths Monday but a note explained the next update would be Wednesday due to the Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples’ Day holiday.

The state’s Health Department told The Independent it is aware of the death reported by the Franklin County coroner.

“Our team has reached out to the coroner’s office and is conducting a thorough review of the reported death. We will update the public after our investigation is finished,” Press Secretary Neil Ruhland said via email.

As part of the investigation, the department will rely on its definition for a measles-associated death, he noted.

The department defines a measles-associated death as one that occurs within 30 days of the start of symptoms of infection, with clinical evidence of an infection, a positive lab test for measles and no other unrelated causes.

Why is the CDC count different?

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention only reports two deaths from measles in Pennsylvania.

There have been no updates to the federal death count since late September. A note above the data states the total is subject to change as more information becomes available and “relevant reviews are completed.”

Pennsylvania’s first measles death was reported in late August. It was also the first measles death of the year in the U.S.

open image in gallery This map, updated last Friday, from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows where measles cases are the highest in the U.S. The states with the fewest cases are in the lightest blue. States with the highest cases are in the darkest blue ( CDC )

Health Sec. Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro have traded shots at each other on social media over the numbers.

Shapiro blasted what he called the Trump administration’s “incompetence” in responding to the virus and Kennedy initially claimed that Pennsylvania’s measles deaths were “fabricated.”

The CDC previously told The Independent that the agency had "mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks across the country.”

“We are saddened to learn of this death in Pennsylvania. The CDC remains committed to supporting the state as it responds to the ongoing measles outbreak,” HHS Press Sec. Grace Davis Jamison said in an email to The Independent responding to a request for comment on the death count.

Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to recommend the MMR vaccine as the most effective way to prevent measles infection, she added.

How is measles spreading nationally?

There are 4,080 confirmed measles cases this year in the District of Columbia and 46 states. There have also been 42 new outbreaks in 2026.

Last year, there were 2,289 confirmed measles cases. Some outbreaks from 2025 continued into the beginning of this year, including in Utah and South Carolina.

Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause life-threatening brain-swelling and high fever, especially in those who have not received two doses of the MMR vaccine.

open image in gallery Getting two doses of the vaccine that targets measles, mumps and rubella infections offers lifelong protection against severe infection - but vaccine hesitancy has helped cases rise since last year, according to doctors ( Reuters )

Vaccination provides lifelong protection against infection and severe illness. But rising vaccine hesitancy and misinformation has led cases to reach the worst levels since the 1990s, doctors previously told The Independent.

The U.S. is now at risk of losing its long-held elimination status, medical experts say, because there has been continuous spread of measles for more than a year.

News.title: Colombia's new government: 2016 deal with rebel group has not brought peace — but 132,000 killings
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Colombia’s new government told the United Nations on Monday that over 132,000 people have been killed and armed group membership has increased from 6,000 to almost 30,000 in the decade since the country signed a highly touted peace agreement with its largest rebel group.

Addressing the Security Council for the first time, Foreign Minister Omar Bula said “the ideological and international promotion of the peace agreement as an exemplary event worthy of emulation is not borne out by the figures” — and said lasting peace remains elusive and a challenge for conservative President Abelardo de la Espriella, who was inaugurated in August.

The government's figures could not be independently verified.

The peace agreement between the government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, ended more than 50 years of war in which more than 220,000 people died and nearly 6 million were displaced. In the aftermath, an estimated 14,000 fighters laid down their weapons.

But Bula said that in addition to the 132,930 people “murdered in Colombia” between the July 2016 signing and August 2026, nearly 100,000 cases of extortion and more than 2,750 kidnappings have been recorded throughout the country.

Today, he said, Colombia is facing not only its largest remaining rebel group, the National Liberation Army, but also the Clan del Golfo cartel, dozens of factions of the former FARC rebels and regional and transnational criminal networks.

The groups have also expanded their fights for territorial control, “subjugating communities and controlling strategic corridors through violence, extortion, and illicit economies,” Bula said. Drug trafficking, a key driver of the criminal activity, has also reached “unprecedented levels worldwide,” and in 2023 coca production in Colombia surged by over 50%.

De la Espriella, a Colombian-American citizen who calls himself “The Tiger” and supports U.S. President Donald Trump, has pledged to tackle the persistent violence in Colombia by breaking with leftist former President Gustavo Petro’s policy of negotiating with armed groups, arguing that the peace process has failed.

In the 60 days since de la Espriella became president, Bula said, security forces reported 32,029 arrests, the seizure of over 135 tons of narcotic drugs and the removal of 3,414 firearms from circulation.

The president also signed 119 extradition orders aimed at dismantling international drug rings and transnational organized crime in Colombia. He has also been dealing with a 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck on Aug. 13, five days after his inauguration.

“The aim of these actions is to regain control over land, to weaken armed groups and their sources of financing, and to restore the presence and authority of the state in areas where criminal organizations have sought to substitute it,” he said.

Colombia’s top diplomat said these efforts underscore the government’s commitment to restore state control, a key policy that — along with ensuring security and justice — is a precondition to build sustainable peace.

The Security Council has been monitoring the 2016 peace accord at the government’s request and Bula said its implementation remains a commitment. The mandate for the U.N. verification mission expires Oct. 31.

News.title: A 6.1 earthquake jolts southern Panama after Friday’s destructive tremors
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A preliminary magnitude 6.1 earthquake hit southern Panama Monday evening, according to the U.S. Geological Survey, but there were no immediate reports of casualties or property damage.

The quake struck around 6:20 p.m. at a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles) about 18 kilometers (11 miles) west of Río Grande in the country's south.

The quake comes after two powerful 7.7 and 6.6 magnitude earthquakes and a series of aftershocks roiled southern Panama on Friday afternoon. They collapsed buildings near the epicenter and prompted evacuations across the country.

News.title: Trump gushes about how attractive, athletic Sen. Jon Husted is: ‘I looked at his a**’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Donald Trump oddly gushed about Sen. Jon Husted’s attractiveness and athleticism during a rally in Ohio — all to boost Republican candidates ahead of the midterms.

The president said Ohioans had to vote for Husted to keep his seat amid a challenge from Sherrod Brown, a former Democratic senator from Ohio. Jon Gruden, a former Super Bowl-winning coach, introduced the president at Monday’s rally and mentioned to Trump that he and the senator played ball together in college.

“I'm standing over here, and I don't do this with men very often. I started examining [Husted’s] body because I didn't know he was a great athlete, and I looked, and I watched up and down,” Trump told his supporters Monday night in Youngstown with Husted in the crowd. “I looked at his a**, and I looked at the whole, and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He's got these like claws.”

Husted was an All-American defensive back at the University of Dayton, where he got his bachelor’s and master’s degrees.

Trump said that Gruden told him about Husted’s athletic prowess. Gruden was on the Dayton Flyers with Husted in 1985.

open image in gallery Donald Trump has gushed about Sen. Jon Husted’s attractiveness and athleticism during a rally in Ohio to boost Republican candidates ahead of the midterms ( Getty Images )

“I said, ‘John, what are you doing here?’ I thought he was going to say, ‘I'm here for you, sir. I have such respect for you.’ But he didn't say that. He said, ‘I'm here for my teammate.’ I said, ‘Who's your teammate?’ He said, ‘It's John Husted,’” Trump told the crowd.

The president recalled asking Gruden if Husted was “any good,” to which Gruden replied, “He was the best player on the team.”

Later in his speech, Trump baselessly claimed Brown “wants to have men playing in women’s sports” and then went on a rant about female kickers in football.

“John Gruden is a great coach on a lot of championship teams. John, did you ever have a woman that you were desperate to have on one of your championship teams?” Trump said. “How about every once in a while I'll see a kicker — they have a kicker who's a female because they put them on.”

open image in gallery ‘I'm standing over here, and I don't do this with men very often. I started examining [Husted’s] body because I didn't know he was a great athlete...I looked at his a**, and I looked at the whole, and then I looked at his hands,’ Trump told his supporters Monday night in Youngstown ( Getty Images )

Trump then suggested Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham be placed on a men’s team.

“Let's put her on. I like Sophie. Yeah, you'd have a lot of men wanting to go and watch her. She's beautiful. You're not allowed to say that anymore. However, as a politician, please, please let me take it back,” the president said.

Trump’s speech was repeatedly interrupted by protesters, which the president insulted with “your mom” and fat jokes, as he did at a recent Texas rally.

During the first disturbance, Trump said there were paid protesters in the crowd.

“They get paid by the lefties in order to destroy our country. They're scum, but he's going back home to mom...He's got to go on a diet. He's a fat guy,” Trump said. “What he doesn't know is that his mother and father voted for me.”

Later on, another protester with a Palestinian flag interrupted Trump’s speech, reminiscent of a protester waving a Mexican and a Palestinian flag during Vice President JD Vance’s speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas last month.

open image in gallery Jon Gruden, a former NFL and Super Bowl-winning coach, introduced the president at Monday’s rally and mentioned to Trump that he and Husted played together in college ( Getty Images )

In a recent CNN poll conducted by research firm SSRS, Brown — who served in the Senate from 2007 to 2025 — led Husted — a former lieutenant governor who was appointed to fill Vance’s vacated Senate seat — by six points among likely Ohio voters, 49 to 43 percent.

Trump, who’s seen record-low approval ratings, has been campaigning in red states as if he were on the ballot; in fact, he’s told his supporters to vote for Republicans whom he’s endorsed as if he were on the ballot. Meanwhile, Democrats in Texas, Alaska, Iowa and Kansas are gaining ground in states that Republicans typically win easily, according to recent New York Times/Siena University polls.

Husted later joined Trump on stage Monday night, telling the crowd, “Mr. President, you've helped bring this region back and this state to prominence. And I tell you what, we are going to do everything that we can to win on November 3, and you're going to bring it home with us, aren't you?”

“Wow, he's really changed since you all learned how great an athlete he was,” Trump said following Husted’s remarks. “I just hit him on the back, and I hurt my hand a little bit. He's like a piece of steel.”

Later on, influencer and boxer Jake Paul went on stage and spoke out against the protesters.

“I get confused by the left, the protesters. Do they not have jobs? That's all they do — just carry signs around while we're doing the work,” the Ohio native said. “We have to protect this state because Washington doesn't belong to celebrities like me. It doesn't belong to the politicians. It belongs to you guys and us, the American people.”

News.title: The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is being filled again after repeated repair blunders
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool began refilling Monday after months of construction delays, peeling paint and dropped vandalism charges.

A partially filled, navy blue basin was visible behind security fencing surrounding the pool. A sign posted at the perimeter by the National Park Service informed visitors: “The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is being refilled as the National Park Service and contractors put the final touches on a historic effort to clean, repair, and beautify this iconic national landmark. As part of the normal refilling process, the water may temporarily appear cloudy before clearing.”

Contractor Atlantic Industrial Coatings, which received a no-bid contract for the project, updated its website on October 5 to announce: “All warranty repairs were completed Friday, 10/2/2026! It has been an honor to serve our great nation!”

However, journalists from The Washington Post observed workers at the site as recently as October 7 — a day after Trump stated the project was complete and four days after the contractor announced warranty repairs had wrapped up. Crews were seen spraying material onto two interior sections of the pool, while grates for the central drain remained uninstalled.

The refilling follows a second round of repair work necessitated by the flaking of the pool's new “American flag blue” coating, an issue the Justice Department attributed to a “botched” initial application.

open image in gallery Months after peeling paint, construction delays and federal court dismissals stalled progress, the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool began refilling on Monday ( Reuters )

Internal reports submitted by Atlantic Industrial Coatings to the Trump administration admitted its own implementation had fallen short, noting that workers applied too little primer due to “human oversight” and used two incompatible chemicals during application.

President Donald Trump had announced the restoration initiative in the spring ahead of America 250 events planned for the National Mall. Initial estimates set the renovation cost at $2 million, but spending has since surpassed $16 million.

Shortly after work began, the pool experienced a large algae bloom followed by the structural coating failure.

open image in gallery The refilling follows a second round of repair work necessitated by the flaking of the pool's new ‘American flag blue’ coating, an issue the Justice Department attributed to a ‘botched’ initial application ( Getty )

Though the site has faced recurring algae issues for decades, Trump claimed on Truth Social in July that the green blooms were caused by vandals who “dumped fertilizer in the water” and suggested the pool’s coating was “cut and powerfully lifted off the surface” with a box cutter.

Police records confirmed blade cuts along the pool’s foam layer. However, critics say the security fence — which could remain until early next year under federal contracts — is mainly being used to hide construction errors.

Federal agents were recently observed at the drained basin using laser-scanning and measuring equipment on the grimy floor. A spokesperson for the FBI Washington Field Office Evidence Response Team told The Independent that agents were “assisting the U.S. Park Police in its investigation of damage to the Reflecting Pool.”

open image in gallery Atlantic Industrial Coatings announced that all warranty repairs were completed on October 2 following the pool’s coating failure. However, crews were still observed working at the site days later ( Reuters )

Meanwhile, ethics experts have questioned the ongoing security measures, with Craig Holman of Public Citizen telling The Independent that the chain-link enclosure represented an effort “to prevent curious citizens from gathering and displaying the fraying paint flakes.”

Despite contractor issues, Trump maintained that illegal activity contributed to the site’s complications, as reported by The Washington Post.

“The Reflecting Pool is totally complete, and we changed the old pipes,” Trump told reporters on October 6. “We wanted to get open for July Fourth, and now we went and got rid of all of the old pipes, which we were going to do later during the winter. We did it, and I think it’s almost complete. I’m going to visit.”

Addressing the site's history over the summer, Trump added: “We had vandalism there, and we have it about as vandal-proof as you can get. But only sick people do that, and we have their pictures.”

open image in gallery President Donald Trump insisted that illegal activity caused the pool’s structural failures, citing alleged fertilizer dumping and razor blade cuts along the lining ( AFP/Getty )

Federal officials initially attributed the damage to intentional destruction. Several people were arrested, including former Olympian David Hearn after U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro alleged at a press conference that he had “forcefully and violently” pulled at the lining.

Hearn denied damaging the site, stating he only touched a loose flap of coating. Federal prosecutors dropped the case in July, and a judge ruled on October 1 that charges against Hearn could not be refiled.

Visitors at the National Mall on Monday offered mixed reactions to the project's execution and oversight.

Jerad Johnson, a 46-year-old pastor visiting from Georgia, told The Washington Post that any alleged damage to the monument was “a disgrace.”

open image in gallery Visitors at the National Mall expressed mixed reactions to the project’s execution, with some lamenting the rapid timeline and others calling the rising costs a waste of taxpayer money ( Getty )

“The things that we’re trying to honor here are about more than an individual,” Johnson said. “Whether they appreciate or don’t appreciate our president, still respect the fact that this isn’t just about a person; it’s about our entire country and our country’s history.”

Regarding the structural flaws and rapid timeline of the repairs, Johnson added: “When you’re trying to rush to get a project done by a certain date, that happens.”

Other tourists criticized the cost and the management of public space in the capital.

“I think it’s a complete waste of taxpayer money,” Andrea Meisgeier, 53, of San Diego, told the publication.

Her son, 19-year-old college student Maxwell Meisgeier, reflected on the atmosphere around the National Mall.

“You feel like it’s his city when you’re walking around in it,” he said. “It’s not your city. It’s not the same.”

“It’s our city,” his mother added. “The citizens’.”

News.title: One person is dead, several others injured in incident involving Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags roller coaster Monday afternoon in Georgia, according to police.

The incident took place at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Atlanta, according to the Cobb County Police Department. Detectives with department's major crimes unit will investigate the incident.

Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured.

A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully cooperating with local authorities as they investigate the incident.

“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said.

Last month, Six Flags Magic Mountain, in Southern California, announced that it was retiring its famous X2 roller coaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. Six Flags recently settled a wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022, and three more lawsuits alleging traumatic brain injuries were filed last week.

Last year, a 32-year-old man died after riding a high-speed roller coaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. He died from blunt impact injuries and his death was ruled accidental.

News.title: Coventry hammer Newcastle to show why they belong – and Jaissle may not
News.content:
You can get a sense of what sort of mode a team are in within the first few passages of play and Newcastle were not sharp or precise. It was sloppy.

That was certainly true of goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who was off his line in no-man’s-land trying to snuff out a through ball that he was not going to get. He stood up to deflect it away, but then rashly chased after it, diving at full stretch at the feet of Coventry’s Sidiki Cherif and failing to get the ball. Jack Rudoni coolly sent the Czech goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot.

Newcastle had been awful in their last away game at Leeds, another 4-1 thrashing, and there were many of the same faults on display.

It was not a good first half for Fernandez-Pardo up top. They are mystified in Belgium why he believes he is a centre-forward rather than a winger and he did not do himself any favours here. Newcastle’s best move of the game resulted in Lewis Miley playing in Jacob Murphy down the left. His cutback was perfect for Fernandez-Pardo to sweep home at the near post but instead of trying to make contact, he dummied it, thinking Harvey Barnes was better placed. He wasn’t. It was a baffling piece of centre-forward play.

It had been the easiest 40 minutes Lampard’s side have had since they were promoted, but Newcastle still should have scored before the break.

Nico González spotted the run of Fernandez-Pardo through the middle. He wriggled clear of Bobby Thomas and sat down goalkeeper Carl Rushworth, but the Coventry centre-back got back to block his shot.

Newcastle pressed the self-destruct button early in the second half. A long throw into the box was half cleared. There was a half-hearted attempt to close Cherif down from Yoane Wissa and then a shot that somehow went through a crowd of three Newcastle defenders, including the legs of Botman, and nestled in the bottom corner.

News.title: AI cuts diagnosis for eye disease from 23 days to just 30 seconds
News.content:
Patients whose eye scans were read by an AI programme got results in 30 seconds, compared to facing an average waiting time of 23 days for results from a doctor, a study in Tanzania has shown.

Millions of people around the world have diabetic retinopathy, a condition where high blood sugar levels damage the tiny blood vessels in the retina.

It can lead to irreversible blindness if left untreated. Around a third of the 23 million people with diabetes in Africa have the complication.

In its early stages, diabetic retinopathy can have no symptoms, and the World Health Organization recommends that people living with diabetes undergo regular screening to check their eye health, so that they can be treated if necessary.

For the new study, published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers randomly assigned over 2,000 patients with diabetes visiting clinics in Tanzania’s Kilimanjaro and Arusha regions to either receive usual screening care, or to have a new type of AI-assisted screening.

Two fifths of the participants had changes in their eyes that needed referral to specialist care. In the half screened using AI, 36 per cent attended the central ophthalmology clinic within eight weeks, compared to 18 per cent in the standard care group.

Most of the people working in the regions where the study was based are farmers, said Dr Jestus Rwiza of the Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre, co-author on the paper. “They depend on vision.”

The economic effects of blindness are felt by the whole family, he said, recalling how the daughter of one patient “had to stop schooling to help the mother”.

News.title: WHO probes ‘unanswered questions’ over Russian plague worker
News.content:
The World Health Organization has said it still does not have enough information to rule out a lab accident after the death of a worker in a Russian plague lab.

Last week reports emerged that Darya Shipilova, a lab worker in Irkutsk, Siberia, had died of pneumonic plague after dropping a test tube containing samples of the pathogen Yersinia pestis, which causes the disease.

Some 200 people were quarantined and there were reports of a further case. Shipilova was working at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk.

Russian authorities have insisted that there was no lab accident and Shipilova’s mother, Svetlana, has also disputed that her daughter dropped a test tube.

“It’s impossible to break a test tube like that,” she said. “Even if you fling it at the wall. Only an amateur could say something like that,” she said.

News.title: El Nino, hunger and fuel threaten ‘perfect storm’, says UN
News.content:
A triple shock of rising energy prices, spiralling borrowing costs and a turbocharged El Niño could push “tens if not hundreds of millions of people” into poverty, the UN has warned.

The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) said the three “compounding crises” are hitting developing economies especially hard, with governments running out of resources to shield people from the fallout, in a new report.

“We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty,” said Alexander De Croo, the UNDP administrator, warning that surging oil and food prices mean families across the world have “no safety margin”.

“Governments of developing countries are left with impossible choices: cut support to their poorest citizens or risk their entire development agenda,” he added.

The report was published ahead of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings, which kicked off in Bangkok on Monday. Debt pressures, energy prices and geopolitical tensions are high on the agenda.

But UNDP stressed that the meetings were taking place as three shocks converge, and the crisis morphs from a regional to a global one that’s affecting roughly 100 countries.

Seven months ago, when the war in Iran broke out, the UN agency warned that the conflict had triggered the “most severe oil supply shock in history”. That continues today – after a brief respite, oil prices have been pushed back beyond $100 a barrel, as hostilities have resumed in the Middle East.

But two more threats now “challenge the capacity of developing countries to manage the energy shock”, meaning developing economies “will have trouble funding their policy responses in the months ahead”.

News.title: Max Verstappen is back and Mercedes are already worried
News.content:
Kimi Antonelli, third: “It was a very tough race out there but really happy with a podium at the end, I managed to take advantage of the fight between Lewis and Lando. To take P3 is a great result from the team, very happy with that.”

He is told that he can clinch the title at the next race:

“Can I, really? Let’s not worry about that. Let’s try to do the best weekend possible and finish the job.”

Charles Leclerc, second: “We were quite strong at the beginning of the race and then we started degrading at the end of the first stint. I pushed a lot at the beginning of the last stint and then degraded a bit more than the others. I gave it all and I don’t regret anything.

“I don’t think there’s anything more we could do but be a bit more aggressive at the start. It’s true that we brought some small new parts to the car which maybe helped us to do a little step forward but it’s enough. Today I think we had a good pace overall.”

Max Verstappen, winner: “It’s taken a while but I think this race was very good. We had pace when we needed to have it on the soft tyre and the medium. Very happy to win here. You always try to do your best and luckily [the start] it was just good enough.

“I think the last few races have been really positive for us. It’s great to see and we have a lot of motivation in the team to try to deliver even more results... hopefully we can have a bit more fun until the end of the year.”

News.title: The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool
News.content:
Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

News.title: Three tasks to get your home ready for autumn, according to a professional cleaner
News.content:
When I was sweating away this summer, I never thought the weather would turn, but it’s almost time to crank up our radiators and crack out the big duvet.

They’re the tasks no one likes doing, but luckily for you, I’ve worked as a cleaner for more than a decade. I’ve discovered some shortcuts to make the hated jobs that bit easier.

Tip one: Keep your summer duvet fresh in storage

If, like me, you want to get your winter duvet out, your summer one needs to be cleaned and packed away to keep it fresh come spring.

Start by spot cleaning any stains. You can just use a standard household fabric stain remover for this. If you want to wash your duvet, most domestic washing machines aren’t big enough to fit a double, let alone a king or a super king. Your best bet is to take them down to the laundrette and follow the care instructions on the label.

Sports.title: Emotional Coventry ace Jack Rudoni lifts lid on nan’s heart attack after incredible shirt tribute in Newcastle thrashing

JACK RUDONI dedicated Coventry City’s first goal at home in the Premier League for 25 years to his ill nan, who is recovering after a heart attack.

The Englishman, 25, was not born when Coventry last scored and won in the top-flight – that a 1-0 win over Sunderland in April 2001 at Highfield Road.



Rudoni scored from the penalty spot on six minutes, even though he is not the first team’s regular taker from 12 yards.

When he sent Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek the wrong way with a cool finish, he ran over to the corner flag and showed off a message on the white T-shirt underneath his Sky Blues top.



It read “GET WELL SOON NAN” and hinted at what an emotional time it has been for him and his family.

The Carshalton-born midfielder later revealed on Sky Sports that his beloved nan was recovering in hospital – and he hoped she had the football on the TV in the ward.



Rudoni, a former AFC Wimbledon star, said: “Last week, unfortunately, my nan had a heart attack. So she will be watching this from hospital.

“She is stable, which is good. She is a strong woman. She will definitely come through.

“That was for you, nan. I want to dedicate that to her from where she is watching it in hospital.”

Head coach Frank Lampard praised Rudoni for the strength he has shown over the last week.

He said: “It happened a week ago and is still ongoing. I saw his T-shirt.

“I have been there for him. I have an understanding of those types of situations.

“He has had a tough period for different reasons with his injury and being out.

Rudoni will go down as the answer to a quiz question for generations to come – who scored the first Premier League goal at the Coventry Building Society Arena, which was opened in 2005?
