In the dark, one of the pledges, Mortimer M Leggett, and two fraternity members stumbled over a cliff and plunged into the gorge of Six Mile Creek. The two fraternity members survived. Leggett, however, did not.

Secret initiation rituals can forge an “informal psychological social contract in which members feel obligated to protect the organisation”, according to Pietro Sasso, who studies college student experience at Old Dominion University.



Some members may feel the need to rally around the fraternity even when “doing so conflicts with their personal values or responsibilities to others”, Sasso added.

“My research on fraternity cultures suggests that organisational socialisation can normalise behaviours that individuals might otherwise question, making the environment itself an important part of prevention,” he explained.

Inside Doe’s lawsuit against Chi Phi

Doe’s case cites some of the social pressures and incentives that lead young men and women to Greek life on campus.

“She was drawn to the sorority and its promises of sisterhood and lifelong friendships, the status it conferred on its members, and the community it provided on campus when she was over 1,000 miles away from home,” the lawsuit said of Doe.

But Doe said she joined Cornell’s Greek community without being fully aware of the pattern of sexual assault associated with the local fraternities.

During Doe’s first semester, in 2022, there were at least five reported cases of victims at Cornell being drugged, and two alleged cases of sexual assault. All of those cases, according to her lawsuit, took place at fraternities.

Two years later, on the night of the alleged gang rape, Doe claims she was pressured by fraternity members to take drugs like ketamine, marijuana and alcohol. After agreeing to a threesome, she said she found herself in a “room full of predatory, fraternity men” who raped her while she was incapacitated.

A photo of a group chat included in her lawsuit shows one Chi Phi member informing his fellow fraternity brothers that there was “free pussy” in an upstairs alumni room. A member of the chat replies, “I f***ing love chi phi.” Another chimes in, “Like you can walk in and whip it out.”

Several of the men have denied any wrongdoing.

But the case has sparked questions about whether the culture of Greek life contributes to a high rate of sexual assault in fraternities and sororities.

One 2021 survey published by the American Psychological Association tracked male students from high school through their second year of college. It found that fraternity members were 62 percent more likely to report sexual aggression during their first two years of college.

Separately, a 2009 study published in the journal Violence Against Women estimated that 29 percent of sorority members reported suffering sexual assault during college, roughly four times the rate of non-members.

Reforming Greek life

After the alleged gang rape in 2024, Cornell’s Chi Phi chapter was closed, and the fraternity remains barred from campus. Two male defendants in Doe’s lawsuit were expelled, while another two were suspended.

But some student activists say too little is being done to reform Greek life in the wake of Doe’s case. They want stronger measures to enforce accountability within private, members-only groups where secrecy often reigns.

CJ Barles, a junior at the University of California, Davis, is one of the students across the US organising protests in support of Doe. She told Al Jazeera she understands the appeal of the fraternity and sorority systems.

“Affiliated students say it looks good on their resume,” Barles explained. “They see it as a built-in cult, a seat at the table and a crew to call their own.”

But Barles said she has heard troubling reports. Some fraternities, she explained, hold parties “requiring every man” to arrive with several women in tow. That requirement says “a lot about the culture some of these spaces cultivate”, she added.

At a rally last week, Barles and other protesters called on the University of California system to implement new measures to hold fraternities accountable for sexual assault, including enshrining students’ right to withdraw consent during sexual encounters.



But Barles said she left feeling dumbstruck by the accounts of sexual violence shared by women on campus, many of whom spoke from personal experience.

“It’s unbelievably upsetting, the amount of stories I heard,” said Barles. The litany of grievances has fanned her scepticism of the Greek system: “I wouldn’t step within a mile of most of them.”

World.title: Canada’s Carney calls for unity as Alberta prepares for secession vote
World.content:
Share Canada’s Carney calls for unity as Alberta prepares for secession vote on social media

Prime Minister Mark Carney has used his Thanksgiving message to Canadians to call for national unity, a week before the oil-rich province of Alberta is set to vote on a proposal to secede from Canada.

“We can’t build big things on fault lines,” Carney said in his video message on Monday, warning that Canada faces threats to its economy, security and way of life.

“We have to be strong, and we are stronger together.”

His comments come as Albertans head to the polls on October 19 to decide whether to begin the process of seeking independence. The initial referendum is non-binding, but it proposes to hold a binding vote in the future to decide whether Alberta should secede.

The question facing voters is: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

The vote follows a growing push by a vocal group of separatists, fuelled by longstanding grievances over federal energy and environmental policies.

The secessionist movement has accused the Canadian government of unfairly targeting Alberta’s oil and gas industry, the cornerstone of the province’s economy.

The movement is also being watched south of the border, as Canada’s relationship with the United States under President Donald Trump has become strained.

An investigation by The Globe and Mail earlier this month revealed that US Republican operatives met with secession organisers in Alberta to talk about campaign strategies. Separatist leaders had reportedly offered access to the province’s water and oil royalties in exchange for US support for independence. Separatist leaders have disputed those claims.



Carney’s comments also come after another secessionist movement, the Parti Quebecois, won the most seats in a provincial election in Quebec last week, allowing it to return to power after more than a decade.

The Parti Quebecois, however, only won 59 seats out of a total of 129 in Quebec’s National Assembly, leaving it short of a majority government.

Still, following that victory, US tech entrepreneur Elon Musk, considered the richest man on the planet, applauded the results. He has been known to use his wealth and influence to support political causes, particularly on the far right.

“Good. Quebec should separate,” Musk wrote on social media. “They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too.”

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, said he was filming the message from a classroom at his former school, St Francis Xavier High School in Edmonton.

“I’m back home a lot these days because we are building big things again in Alberta: thousands of new homes, high-speed rail, a new pipeline to the West Coast that will create lasting opportunity and prosperity for hundreds of thousands of people in this province and across the country,” he said.

Despite the secessionist movement’s growing visibility, polls suggest most Albertans oppose independence.

World.title: Conflict, drought increasing risk of famine in Sudan: Monitor
World.content:
Conflict and drought are increasing the risk of famine across Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, warns a global food crisis monitor.

“An El Nino-induced drought, affecting roughly half of the country, is compounding the impacts of conflict and displacement, reducing food availability, driving up prices and affecting livelihoods,” the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said on Monday in a statement.

“Healthcare is extremely limited, often entirely inaccessible, while clean water is becoming increasingly scarce, leaving a poorly nourished population highly vulnerable to disease and death,” it added.

The IPC is an initiative aimed at enhancing food security and consists of 21 organisations and intergovernmental institutions, including the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the World Bank, the World Food Programme (WFP) and the World Health Organization (WHO).

‘Food insecurity, acute malnutrition and excess mortality’

Farmers’ livelihoods have deteriorated and dependence on food assistance is on the rise, said the IPC. “Food insecurity, acute malnutrition and excess mortality will likely intensify,” it warned.

Poor vegetation growth affects nearly two-thirds of cropland in North Darfur and about half in South Darfur, West Kordofan and South Kordofan, where severe water shortages and limited opportunity for agricultural recovery threaten livelihoods.

The IPC reported worsening acute malnutrition in additional areas, including Nyala, where the proportion of children accessing nutrition services who were admitted for severe acute malnutrition doubled from approximately 5% to 11% between January and August. Two displacement camps in South Darfur also recorded global acute malnutrition above famine thresholds.



In North Darfur, delayed rains that impacted crop cultivation and “critically low” food stocks have worsened food insecurity, it added. Western Kordofan is suffering one of its worst droughts since 2004 amid poor rainfall.

The lasting effect as conflict persists

In May, nearly 19.5 million people, over 40% of the population, were facing high levels of acute food insecurity, according to an IPC assessment. Of those, 135,000 were in Phase 5, the most severe classification, characterised by extreme food shortages, starvation, very high levels of malnutrition and deaths from disease or acute malnutrition.

Sudan’s war erupted in April 2023 when tensions between the military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), escalated into open fighting in the capital, Khartoum, before spreading across the country. The conflict has killed at least 150,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, though aid groups say the actual toll is likely higher. About 13 million people have been displaced.

The army holds sway in Sudan’s central and eastern regions, while the Darfur region in the west and parts of the south are under control of the rival RSF.

The arid Darfur region, which is about the size of Spain, has faced some of the worst violence, with displacement camps invaded and ethnic cleansing killing thousands at a time.

World.title: Why do Iran’s oil ‘intermediaries’ owe the government billions?
World.content:
Iran says intermediaries handling its oil sales owe it billions of dollars, but how did the debts accumulate?

As the United States maintains a naval blockade of Iran’s ports and imposes more sanctions on its oil exports, Tehran is confronting another problem: billions of dollars in revenue from previous oil sales that it says have gone missing.

A spokesperson for Iran’s judiciary said in September that a network of oil intermediaries known as “trustees” owed the Iranian government between 10 billion euros ($11bn) and 11 billion euros ($12bn). That figure was equivalent to half of the total oil revenue projected in Iran’s government budget for the current fiscal year.

US officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, have tied Iran’s struggles to access oil revenues as evidence that its economic pressure campaign is having an effect. In August, Bessent said that “Iran’s shadow banking system was buckling” under pressure from the US campaign against the country, which has been ramped up as Washington seeks a way to force Tehran to capitulate in the war between the two countries, launched by the US and Israel in late February.

So who are the oil intermediaries, why does Iran depend on them, and what has happened to the billions of dollars they owe? Let’s take a closer look.

Who are Iran’s oil intermediaries?

The debt, and the crisis it has created for the Iranian government, both stem from an oil-sales arrangement Tehran adopted in 2012 in response to US sanctions targeting Iranian oil exports.

American and European sanctions targeting Iranian oil sales and revenue collection began in 2012. The stated rationale behind both sets of measures was that revenue from oil sales helped finance Iran’s nuclear programme and that restricting Iranian oil exports could prevent the programme from advancing.



In response, the Iranian government devised a way to circumvent international sanctions on its oil sales. Unable to sell oil through the Oil Ministry and receive the proceeds through the Central Bank, it began selling oil to domestic buyers or using it to settle outstanding obligations to institutions and organisations owed money by the state.

This arrangement gave rise to a network of oil intermediaries often referred to in Iran as the “trustee network”. Rather than selling all its oil through official government channels, the state entrusted crude oil to institutions, individuals and companies to sell on its behalf. The proceeds were supposed to be transferred to the government’s treasury, with the sellers or recipient institutions subsequently recovering their agreed costs and outstanding claims. Some institutions sold the oil themselves, while others contracted private trading companies to handle the sales.

The Oil Industry Pension Fund, established for retired Oil Ministry employees familiar with the oil-sales process, was among the first institutions to receive crude oil for sale. Other recipients included Khatam al-Anbiya Construction Base, a major hub for large-scale infrastructure projects. Even the municipal police received payments owed to them by the government in the form of crude oil.

Effect of the nuclear deal

Even in those early experiments, discrepancies emerged between the revenue expected from oil sales and the amounts sellers actually deposited into the government’s treasury. These discrepancies eventually gave rise to some of Iran’s largest economic corruption cases.

The accounting discrepancies and the government’s inability to recover money from private sellers entrusted with Iranian oil persisted until 2016, when the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) nuclear deal was signed and when sanctions on Iranian oil sales were lifted. The government was subsequently able to regain control over oil sales.

Individuals who had sold Iranian oil but failed to return the proceeds were imprisoned. With the ability to sell oil again through legal and transparent channels, the government was able, for a time, to manage its oil revenues and spending with greater control.

How did money from oil sales go unreturned?

After US President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from the JCPOA in 2018 during his first presidential term, the Iranian government once again had to rely on private oil traders to sell its oil. But the problems associated with selling oil through intermediaries rather than official state channels, including delays in returning revenues, accounting discrepancies, debts owed by oil sellers to the government, and the occasional seizure of Iranian oil shipments at sea, once again constrained the government’s ability to manage its oil revenues.



Moreover, the US expanded its sanctions beyond Iranian government institutions and interests, adding bank accounts involved in transactions with the Iranian government, currency-exchange offices, companies, and individuals to its sanctions lists. As a result, the time between individuals participating in Iran’s oil-trading network and being sanctioned themselves, along with their assets and companies, and having their accounts blocked or frozen grew progressively shorter.

This contributed to an accumulation of debts owed by sanctioned oil traders – no longer able to access their accounts – to the government. It also left Iran with little choice but to expand its private oil-sales network. That meant increasing the number of people involved in trading Iranian oil, reducing the volume of oil allocated to each individual or company and, ultimately, increasing the risk that the proceeds would not be returned.

Iranian officials have also accused trustees of exploiting the sanctions workarounds to enrich themselves.

The billions of dollars owed by private oil sellers to the Iranian government are a combination of outstanding payments, disputed financial obligations and allegations of corruption. Iran’s judiciary chief recently addressed the issue, warning that oil sellers who refuse to return the proceeds from oil sales will face legal action. But such warnings do not change the sanctions environment or remove the obstacles that prevent some oil sellers from returning the money.

World.title: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
World.content:
Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities".

There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.

On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

World.title: Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire
World.content:
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure "effective immediately". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggested it was "news for me", while Russia has not commented publicly.

So who is saying what?

Donald Trump says an energy ceasefire has been agreed.

Kyiv asks: Has it? It is willing to sign up â if Russia does.

Russia is saying: Very little.

Russian President Vladimir Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked whether such a ceasefire had been agreed during his daily conference call with journalists.

"Contacts are continuing," Peskov replied.

"As soon as we have anything to say about this, we will definitely inform you."

Peskov may not have had much to say on the matter, but the pro-Kremlin media has.

It has dubbed President Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire "a gift" for Moscow.

"Of course we benefit," pro-government news outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets concluded.

"It means that all Russia has to do is not destroy Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery.

"That has already been attacked several times. It's barely functioning anyway.

"But Kyiv won't be allowed to hit the multitude of refineries we have.

"In effect it's a one-way deal that benefits us. That's why no one here has officially rejected it."

In other words, Moscow believes Trump's announcement ties Ukraine's hands, not Russia's.

In recent months, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities have caused extensive damage, as well as fuel shortages across the country.

Should such attacks continue, expect the Russians to claim that Kyiv is harming US economic interests â as well as the Republican Party's chances in the midterm elections in November.

Russian officials will argue that the strikes undermine the recent Trump-Putin fuel deal for the US to import Russian diesel.

Trump has claimed the agreement will benefit US consumers, although there is widespread scepticism that the volumes involved will do much to lower fuel prices.

World.title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds
World.content:
The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.

Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (Â£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.

Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.

Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".

Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.

Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".

The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.

For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.

Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, Â£5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.

The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".

Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.

World.title: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
World.content:
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.

On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.

Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".

Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.

UN Secretary General AntÃ³nio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.

President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.

Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.

Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.

They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.

Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

World.title: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies aged 34
World.content:
US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34.

"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," his representative told the BBC.

He died in Brownsville, Texas. No immediate cause of death was provided.

Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role as Walter White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series starring Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. He earned a Screen Actors Guild Award in 2014 for his work on the series.

"Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," his representative Sean Reilly said in a statement to the BBC.

Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's.

He created The Mitte Foundation as well, to support philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, using his platform "to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities", Reilly said.

The Brownsville Police Department confirmed the actor's passing in a statement to the BBC, saying the cause and manner of death have not been determined and the investigation remains ongoing. No "foul play" was suspected, according to police.

The actor was declared dead on 12 October at what was believed to be his home, Cameron County Justice of the Peace, Cyndi Hinojosa, told the Associated Press, adding that an autopsy would be performed.

World.title: South Africa's deputy police chief resigns after being charged with sexual offences
World.content:
South Africa's deputy police chief has resigned three weeks after he was charged with sexual offences.

A lawyer representing Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya submitted his resignation letter at his disciplinary hearing on Monday, a police spokesperson said.

Sibiya, 59, is also accused of having links to organised crime bosses - allegations which led to him being suspended last year.

He denies those allegations, as well as charges that he sexually groomed a 16-year-old girl and raped an 18-year-old woman. He also faces a charge of human trafficking.

Sibiya says he did have sex with the 18-year-old but that it was consensual.

He has been in custody since he was arrested three weeks ago.

Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said in a post on X that his departure from the police force was regarded as a dishonourable discharge, external because he was still facing a disciplinary case when he resigned.

The accusations that Sibiya was linked to crime bosses emerged at a major public inquiry over allegations of police corruption and collusion with criminals, known as the Madlanga Commission.

Sibiya was accused of interfering with investigations into political killings in KwaZulu-Natal province.

He was also accused of receiving a gift of cash, as well as 20 impalas, from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract.

He denied the allegation.

The Madlanga Commission has transfixed South Africa over the past year and unearthed widespread allegations of links between police officers and crime bosses.

It was set up by President Cyril Ramaphosa after the KwaZulu-Natal police chief held a press briefing where he accused the then Police Minister Senzo Mchunu of working with criminal gangs.

Mchunu denies the allegations against him but has been suspended.

World.title: Immigration agents search congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
World.content:
"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said in a statement.

"This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said he had "nothing to do" with the justice department's investigation into Omar, while describing her as a "complainer" and a "terrible person".

The Republican president said of the Somali-born congresswoman: "She comes from a country that is a non-country.

"And then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution."

Omar's communications director Jacklyn Rogers called Monday morning's raid "an outrageous abuse of power" by the Trump administration, adding: "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."

The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear.

A BBC crew saw several agents at Omar's home, some carrying boxes to a van.

News of the search was first reported by Fox News, which said the investigation was about immigration paperwork filed by her late father when Omar was a child.

The timing of the raid - 22 days before the November midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years - raised concerns from Omar's fellow Democrats.

The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it was being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or to disadvantage a candidate.

The US House of Representatives Democratic Party leadership said in a statement that Omar had long been targeted with "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations" by Trump.

"Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," it said.

Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena for her records.

Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", making allegations of marital fraud against Omar.

Separately, White House border tsar Tom Homan told Fox News that Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.

Omar denied these allegations last month.

"I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email.

World.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
World.content:
Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected.

The chief executive of CoopÃ©rative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.

More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while 180 stores from IntermarchÃ© and its Netto brand were affected, with a spokesman saying that another 100 shops were urgently disconnected from the internet to prevent the same thing happening to them.

Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.

The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.

Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process.

Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified.

The firm added in s statement that it had "long advised" businesses to keep supported systems up to date.

"Reliable refrigeration is critical to our customers' operations, and we remain committed to supporting our customers and helping them maintain secure and reliable systems they are used to."

The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France.

Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed.

In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns IntermarchÃ© and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon.

The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible".

IntermarchÃ© said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.

As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires.

French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.

Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of â¬270,000 (Â£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.

French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".

European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."

In a post on X, CoopÃ©rative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".

He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable".

Have you been affected by this cyber attack? Share your experience.

World.title: Nigeria records 268 Lassa fever deaths as fatality rate rises to 23.6% – NCDC
World.content:
Nigeria has recorded 268 deaths from Lassa fever in 2026, with the case fatality rate rising to 23.6 per cent, compared with 18.6 per cent during the same period in 2025, according to the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC).

The deaths were recorded among 1,138 confirmed cases reported between epidemiological weeks one and 40, covering 28 September to 4 October 2026.

The NCDC’s latest situation report shows that confirmed cases have increased from 924 during the corresponding period in 2025 to 1,138 this year, while deaths have risen from 172 to 268.

The figures highlight the continued burden of the disease despite a sharp decline in newly confirmed infections in the latest reporting week.

In week 40, the number of new confirmed cases fell to three from 13 in the previous week. The latest cases were reported in Bauchi and Benue states.

One death was recorded among the three confirmed cases during the week, giving a weekly case fatality rate of 33.3 per cent.

The NCDC attributed the persistently high fatality rate partly to late presentation of cases at health facilities, alongside the high cost of treatment and poor health-seeking behaviour in affected communities.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Five states account for 88% of cases

The NCDC said 24 states had reported at least one confirmed Lassa fever case across 119 local government areas (LGAs) as of week 40.

Five states, Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue, accounted for 88 per cent of all confirmed cases recorded in 2026.

Ondo accounted for 36 per cent of confirmed cases, followed by Bauchi with 23 per cent, Taraba with 12 per cent, Edo with 11 per cent and Benue with six per cent.

The remaining 12 per cent of cases were reported across 19 other states.

People aged 21 to 30 years remained the most affected age group, although the report showed that confirmed cases ranged from one to 93 years.

No new healthcare worker infection was recorded during week 40. However, the cumulative number of healthcare workers affected by the disease in 2026 stood at 54.

Response

In response to the outbreak, the NCDC said it had developed a 30-day healthcare worker protection plan, with support from the World Health Organisation (WHO) and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, to curb infections among frontline health workers in endemic states.

The agency also reported training healthcare workers in infection prevention and control, distributing personal protective equipment to health facilities and strengthening case management in affected states.

It said incident management systems had been activated in Benue, Plateau, Kebbi, Kano and Gombe states, while national rapid response teams had been deployed to seven high-burden states.

The agency also conducted community engagement activities with religious and traditional leaders in Edo and Ondo states and sensitised farmers and market women in Ondo in collaboration with the National Orientation Agency.

Despite these activities, the NCDC identified late presentation of cases, poor environmental sanitation, inadequate awareness and the high cost of treatment as continuing challenges in communities with high case burdens.

The agency urged states to sustain community engagement on Lassa fever prevention throughout the year.

It also advised healthcare workers to maintain a high index of suspicion for the disease, ensure timely referral and treatment, and adhere to standard infection prevention and control procedures.

Lassa fever

Lassa fever is an acute viral haemorrhagic illness transmitted to humans primarily through contact with food or household items contaminated by the urine or faeces of infected rats.

Human-to-human transmission can also occur, particularly in healthcare settings where infection prevention and control measures are inadequate.

The NCDC recommends keeping food in rodent-proof containers, maintaining good environmental sanitation and avoiding contact with rodents.

People who develop symptoms consistent with Lassa fever, particularly after possible exposure, should seek prompt medical attention.

World.title: Gov Mbah tasks SEDC on gas pipeline, regional railways, support for industrial programme
World.content:
Enugu State Governor, Dr Peter Mbah, has urged the South East Development Commission (SEDC) to prioritise the development of a regional gas pipeline, railway network and initiatives to accelerate industrialisation in the region.

Mbah said the proposed infrastructure would boost economic activities, improve connectivity among the five South East states and strengthen regional integration.

He also urged the National Assembly to ensure adequate funding for the Commission, describing it as a strategic platform for addressing the region’s development needs.

The governor made the calls on Monday when he received the Senate Committee on the South East Development Commission led by its Chairman, Senator Orji Uzor Kalu.

The delegation, which paid a courtesy call to the governor on the sidelines of its oversight visit to have a firsthand assessment of the projects and programmes of the SEDC, was also accompanied by the management of the Commission, led by its Managing Director, Mr Mark Okoye.

“For us in the South East, this Committee is one of the most important committees of the National Assembly, given the immense development prospects it holds for our people,” he said.

The governor identified a high-pressure gas pipeline connecting major cities across the South East as a critical intervention that could provide industries with reliable access to gas and stimulate large-scale industrial development.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He argued that the region should benefit from gas resources produced within the wider southern part of the country, noting that pipeline infrastructure already transports gas to other parts of Nigeria.

“If we are able to have a high-pressure gas pipeline across all the major cities in the South East, I know that the SEDC is a veritable platform that can essentially execute a project of that scale,” Mbah said.

Mbah also proposed an inter-state railway network linking major cities across the five South East states to facilitate trade, improve transportation and reduce pressure on the region’s road network, urging the states to work together on a common design for the proposed railway system, with the SEDC providing a platform for coordination and regional collaboration.

“We are hoping that, given the coming into effect of the SEDC, we will be able to use it as a platform to bring all the other states together to have a common design on the South East railway line,” he said.

The governor further highlighted the commission’s role in supporting agriculture and technology-driven enterprises, citing the flag-off of a 200-hectare integrated Agro Development Programme at Nomeh Unateze, Enugu State, as one of its interventions in the agricultural sector.

He assured the commission of the state government’s support in providing an enabling environment for the project.

Mbah also stressed the need for the SEDC to provide funding opportunities for young entrepreneurs whose businesses had attained the minimum viable product stage, enabling them to expand their operations and contribute to economic growth.

He called on the senators to support the Commission in securing the funding required to undertake the project, describing it as a potential catalyst for an industrial revolution in the region.

Earlier, Kalu commended the Mbah administration for its interventions in infrastructure, education, healthcare, water supply and transportation.

He cited the development of Smart Green Schools, more than 7,000 classrooms, Type II primary healthcare centres across the state’s 260 electoral wards, and the state’s multimodal transportation system.

The senator also acknowledged Mbah’s efforts to strengthen engagement between the South East and the Federal Government, expressing appreciation to President Bola Tinubu for facilitating the establishment of the SEDC.

Kalu disclosed that the issue surrounding the location of the Commission’s headquarters had been resolved, following the Enugu State Government’s provision of temporary office accommodation and a site for its permanent headquarters.

“We wanted to make sure that the commission locates to Enugu State as soon as possible, and this has been a subject of disagreement. But today, I can assure you that the issue is settled,” he said.

He thanked the governor for the support provided to facilitate the commission’s take-off and assured him of the committee’s continued support for its activities.

World.title: FG to invest $3bn into health sector by 2030
World.content:
The federal government has announced plans to invest an additional $3 billion in Nigeria’s health sector by 2030 as part of efforts to reduce dependence on foreign assistance and strengthen domestic health financing.

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, said this on Monday in Abuja at a media conference announcing the fifth Global High-Level Ministerial Conference on AMR, scheduled for 6 -8 December, 2026.

Mr Pate said the conference, the first to be hosted on African soil, would focus on translating global commitments into practical actions with the theme, “One Health: Advancing Global AMR Commitment through Local Action”.

He was responding to questions on the health Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between Nigeria and the United States.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Nigeria and the United States signed a five-year bilateral health MoU on 19 December 2025, under the US America First Global Health Strategy.

Mr Pate said the planned investment was part of a transition arrangement under which both countries would work towards Nigeria fully financing its health sector by 2030.

“From now until 2030, the expectation is that the federal government will put in $3 billion into health, which is more than what the US government will contribute as it ramps down its contribution,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the arrangement reflected Nigeria’s position that long-term dependence on external assistance was not in the country’s national interest.

“Our position is that dependency in the long run is not in our national interest on external support,” he said.

“We articulated that we want Nigeria to exit from dependency from other entities over time.”

Health financing

Mr Pate acknowledged that achieving self-sustaining health financing would require increased domestic investment, noting that Nigeria was not yet in a position to fully fund its health sector.

He said 15 Nigerian government institutions, including the ministries of Foreign Affairs, Finance, and Health and Social Welfare, participated in articulating Nigeria’s position during negotiations with the United States.

According to him, the US had supported health programmes in Nigeria for about 25 years, including interventions for HIV, tuberculosis and malaria, benefiting millions of Nigerians.

However, following a shift in US government policy in 2025, Nigeria decided to assume greater responsibility for financing its health programmes.

“How do we own it responsibly? So, with the US government, we agreed that we will have a transition. By 2030, they exit and we exit. That means we fully fund our health sector,” he said.

Mr Pate said President Bola Tinubu had increased domestic health allocations, including providing six per cent of the government budget for health, as part of efforts to strengthen Nigeria’s contribution.

He emphasised that sustainable financing would require all three tiers of government to increase spending on citizens’ health.

Mr Pate said the transition was intended to strengthen Nigeria’s ownership of health programmes and reduce reliance on funding decisions made by other countries.

“We cannot rely on somebody else’s taxpayers funding for the health of Nigerians,” he said.

On concerns surrounding the MoU, Mr Pate described it as a non-binding framework for cooperation, anchored on Nigeria’s national policies and laws.

“The MoU that was signed with the US government is a non-binding MoU. It is anchored on Nigerian policy, national policies and laws, does not subvert our sovereignty or subvert US government sovereignty over their resources.

“It’s also one that either party can walk away at any time,” he said.

Mr Pate said the Attorney-General of the Federation had also confirmed that the agreement contained nothing that subverted Nigeria’s national interest.

He added that the MoU was publicly available and interested parties could request a copy from the ministry through the Freedom of Information process.

The minister said the agreement aligned with the government’s Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative, which prioritises improved governance, stronger primary healthcare, expanded health insurance coverage, domestic production and increased health security.

He said the cooperation would support public health and laboratory capacity, including the detection of antimicrobial resistance, while promoting local capacity to produce essential health commodities.

Mr Pate said strengthening domestic production and ensuring local markets could supply essential medicines, including antimicrobials, were important steps towards reducing external dependence.

He said the transition would require sustained efforts and domestic investment to ensure Nigeria could finance its health priorities as external contributions declined.

Mr Pate urged Nigerians to examine the agreement and its provisions, saying the government’s objective was to strengthen national ownership of health financing and service delivery.

(NAN)

World.title: Lagos govt water privatisation will deepen inequality, coalition warns
World.content:
A collation of development-focussed groups and individuals has warned that privatising water services in Lagos could make water less affordable for poor residents, urging the state government to invest more in public water infrastructure.

Rufus Olusesan, president of the Precision, Electrical and Related Equipment Senior Staff Association (PERESSA), gave the warning on Monday during the Africa Week of Action Against Water Privatisation 2026, organised by the Our Water, Our Right Africa Coalition (OWORAC) in Lagos.

He stated that private operators could prioritise profitable areas at the expense of underserved communities such as Ajegunle and Makoko.

“Water is not a commodity. It is a human right,” Mr Olusesan said.

Speaking on the theme, Reclaiming Africa’s Water Future: Public Water for All, he called on the Lagos State Government to allocate at least five per cent of its annual budget to water infrastructure.

He noted that the current allocation was less than one per cent, although the figure could not be independently verified.

He also called for the rehabilitation of the Iju, Adiyan and Ishasi waterworks, completion of the Adiyan II project and investigations into contractors handling water projects that had failed to deliver the expected results.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Coalition warns against commercialisation of water

In a joint statement read by Geoffrey Occansey of Ghana’s Water Citizens Network/Revenue Mobilisation Africa, OWORAC noted that inadequate public investment, population growth, urbanisation and climate pressures had worsened water supply challenges across Africa.

The coalition urged governments to strengthen public water systems rather than use their shortcomings to justify transferring services to private operators.

The statement cited global figures showing that 2.1 billion people lacked safely managed drinking water in 2024, while 3.4 billion lacked safely managed sanitation. In sub-Saharan Africa, it said, 167 million people relied on limited drinking-water services that year.

The coalition stated that households without reliable public water supplies often depended on vendors, tankers and private boreholes, leaving poorer residents to pay more for an essential service.

Citing research on urban water access in sub-Saharan Africa, it explained that low-income households relying on vendors could pay between 10 and 20 times more per unit of water than households connected to public networks.

“This is a poverty penalty in which those with the lowest incomes can end up paying the highest prices for an essential service,” the statement said.

It warned that commercial tariffs, concessions, public-private partnerships and prepaid water meters could worsen inequality if access increasingly depended on households’ ability to pay.

The statement also cited a 2025 Global Witness investigation into a Veolia-managed landfill in Colombia, alongside concerns about Veolia’s operations in Gabon and Suez’s involvement in Senegal’s urban water system. The coalition argued that private-sector involvement required effective public oversight and did not automatically resolve infrastructure and sanitation problems.

It called on African governments to publish water-related contracts, financing arrangements, tariffs and expenditure, while involving workers and affected communities in decisions about water management.

Lagos water policy faces opposition

Opposition to private-sector participation in Lagos water services predates the latest campaign.

PREMIUM TIMES previously reported that the Amalgamated Union of Public Corporations, Civil Service, Technical and Recreational Service Employees (AUPCTRE) opposed the Lagos State Government’s plan to operate its waterworks through a public-private partnership (PPP) arrangement.

The union accused the management of the Lagos Water Corporation of using water scarcity to persuade residents that private-sector participation was the only sustainable way to improve supply.

“It is disheartening to state here that at this critical period when countries throughout the world are embracing re-municipalisation, Lagos State is spearheading privatisation,” the union said.

The Lagos State Government had maintained that it is not privatising its waterworks but adopting a PPP model to meet the state’s growing demand for water.

The Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa (CAPPA) had also opposed the proposed arrangement, insisting that water supply should remain publicly managed and affordable.

At Monday’s event, Mr Olusesan proposed a water board comprising government representatives, workers, community groups and civil society organisations. He said the board should publish its budgets and expenditure quarterly to enable residents to monitor public spending.

He also alleged that the Lagos Water Corporation disengaged more than 800 workers in 2024 to make the corporation more attractive to investors. He warned that replacing permanent staff with casual workers could undermine job security, pension entitlements and the technical capacity required to maintain water infrastructure.

A report had stated that the Lagos State Public Service Joint Negotiating Council (Trade Union) condemned the reported dismissal of more than 370 workers from the corporation.

In a petition to the state government, the council’s chairperson, Olusegun Balogun, alleged that the dismissals were carried out under the guise of restructuring and redundancy without adequate communication or negotiations with union representatives.

Mr Balogun urged the government to suspend the process and engage the affected unions, including AUPCTRE and the Senior Staff Association of Statutory Corporations, Government-Owned Companies and Associated Organisations.

He also called for an investigation into the corporation’s management and the use of World Bank loans allocated to improve its operations.

The Renevlyn Development Initiative (RDI) separately alleged that the dismissals were part of an attempt to privatise water services in Lagos. The group urged the state government to reverse the disengagement and improve water supply across the state.

The reported dismissal of more than 370 workers and Mr Olusesan’s claim concerning over 800 workers in 2024 relate to separate accounts. The corporation and the state government should clarify the figures and circumstances surrounding the reported job losses.

OWORAC proposes continental funding target

At the event, Holiness Olufemi, programme officer for water campaigns at CAPPA, unveiled OWORAC’s position paper on implementing the Africa Water Vision 2063.

Titled “Implementing the Africa Water Vision 2063: An OWORAC Coalition Position on Water Justice, Public Control and Democratic Water Governance”, the paper calls for stronger public water systems, adequate government funding and greater community participation in water management.

Ms Olufemi said the vision could improve access to water and sanitation across Africa, but its success would depend on governments committing sufficient resources and ensuring that public spending produced measurable results.

One of the paper’s central proposals is a continental financing benchmark for water and sanitation, supported by national funding targets and transparent reporting.

Ms Olufemi cited the 2001 Abuja Declaration, under which African leaders committed to allocating at least 15 per cent of their annual budgets to health, as a precedent for establishing a similar benchmark for water and sanitation.

Under the proposal, governments would be assessed not only on their budget allocations but also on the funds released and spent, the infrastructure delivered and the resulting improvements in access to safe and affordable water.

The paper also proposes an African Water Accountability and Monitoring Mechanism to track progress and hold institutions accountable.

Mr Olusesan called for legislation recognising access to water as a human right and prohibiting water privatisation.

“Government must fund water corporation as it funds roads and airports,” she said.

The campaign comes as the African Union marks 2026 as the Year of Assuring Sustainable Water Availability and Safe Sanitation Systems to Achieve the Goals of Agenda 2063.

OWORAC urged African governments to use the Africa Water Vision 2063 and the 2026 United Nations Water Conference to advance public financing and strengthen community participation in water governance.

“Public Water for All is not a slogan. It is possible, it is affordable, it is our right,” Ms Olusesan said.

The joint statement was endorsed by water justice and civil society organisations from Nigeria, Ghana, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Zimbabwe and Kenya, as well as the international organisation Corporate Accountability.

World.title: 120,000 vehicles converted under Tinubu’s CNG initiative – Minister
World.content:
Nigeria’s Presidential Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) and Electric Vehicle Initiative has attracted about $2.5 billion in private investment, alongside approximately N250 billion in government funding and commitments, the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, has said.

Mr Idris said more than 120,000 vehicles had been converted under the initiative, with over 400 certified conversion centres and more than 90 refuelling stations established nationwide. Another 180 refuelling stations are in development, he said.

He said the initiative was creating jobs and business opportunities in host communities as the federal government pursues efforts to reduce transportation costs and diversify the economy.

The CNG programme was introduced after President Bola Tinubu removed the petrol subsidy in May 2023, a decision that contributed to higher transport costs and intensified economic pressure on Nigerians. The government subsequently promoted CNG as a cheaper alternative to petrol, particularly for commercial transport operators.

However, the cost of converting vehicles has presented a barrier for many motorists, even as they seek to reduce their fuel expenses.

The cost of converting petrol-powered vehicles to run on CNG could cost between N750,000 and N2.5 million, depending on the vehicle and engine. The upfront expense makes the transition difficult for motorists already grappling with higher operating costs.

In September, Nairametrics documented challenges facing motorists who had made the switch, including inadequate refuelling infrastructure, long queues and lost working hours.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The minister disclosed the initiative’s investment figures during a media chat with senior editors and journalists on Monday, where he highlighted the government’s economic reforms and their impact on key indicators.

He said Nigeria’s inflation rate had fallen from about 27 per cent in January 2025 to around 15 per cent, while the country’s external reserves exceeded $54 billion in September, the highest level in almost two decades.

The economy is also projected to grow by more than 4 per cent in 2026, while Nigeria’s current account surplus rose to $12 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $8.6 billion in the corresponding period of 2025, according to the minister.

Mr Idris attributed the improvements to the government’s economic policies, saying the reforms were helping to stabilise the economy, restore confidence and create conditions for sustained growth.

“The macroeconomic numbers have turned the corner, and I would ask that we always look at what they mean beyond the headlines,” he said.

However, he acknowledged that many households continued to face cost-of-living pressures, saying the government’s priority was to ensure that improvements in economic indicators translated into better living conditions.

“Our commitment is to ensure that stronger economic indicators translate into more jobs, more productive businesses, more affordable essential services and greater purchasing power for Nigerian families,” he said.

“The reforms are strengthening our economic fundamentals, rebuilding confidence and creating the conditions for broader prosperity. We are determined to consolidate these gains and accelerate their impact across the country.”

Infrastructure, agriculture

Mr Idris said infrastructure projects were creating economic opportunities for contractors, suppliers, engineers, artisans, transporters and other businesses.

He said the government’s four Legacy Projects covered about 3,000 kilometres across the country’s six geopolitical zones, alongside hundreds of other projects in road, rail, port, power, health and education infrastructure.

He also cited a recently approved highway project worth approximately N1.5 trillion in Niger State, which he said would improve connectivity along an important agricultural and commercial corridor.

On agriculture, the minister said the government had placed food security at the centre of its economic policy, with support for mechanisation, access to inputs, irrigation and agricultural financing intended to increase domestic production, improve farmers’ incomes and reduce food costs.

Healthcare, education and jobs

The minister said the federal government had commissioned two additional cancer treatment centres, bringing the total number of commissioned centres to five, as it works towards making 10 available nationwide.

He said the investments, alongside the revitalisation of primary healthcare, were expected to expand access to treatment and strengthen the health system.

On education, Mr Idris said the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) had supported more than 1.6 million students, paying over N192 billion in tuition fees and N180 billion in upkeep allowances.

He said the funding provided relief for students, parents and guardians who would otherwise struggle to meet the cost of higher education.

He also said the Three Million Technical Talent programme was expanding opportunities for young Nigerians to acquire digital skills in software development, data science, cybersecurity and emerging technologies.

The minister said investments in domestic refining, solid minerals, industrial production and innovation were also part of the government’s efforts to diversify the economy and create sustainable employment.

World.title: Kaduna has mainstreamed mental health, says Uba Sani
World.content:
Governor Uba Sani has disclosed that Kaduna State is the only sub national in Nigeria that has integrated mental health into the primary and secondary health systems.

The governor made this known at the Federal Neuro-Psychiatric Hospital (FNPH), Barnawa, Kaduna on Friday, during the 2026 World Mental Health Day, themed “Lived Experiences Heard: Real Voices, Real Change.’’

Represented by the Commissioner of Health, Mrs Umma K Ahmad, Uba Sani further disclosed that Kaduna State’s ‘’ first cohort of 100 doctors, nurses and pharmacists, from 10 of our General Hospitals, has been certified under the World Health Organization’s mhGAP programme.’’

According to Governor Uba Sani, mental health screening is now part of the normal maternal and child health services in Kaduna State.

‘’We are extending services to all 30 General Hospitals and to primary health care facilities in all 23 Local Government Areas, while strengthening and expanding access at the tertiary level,’’ he added.

The Governor pointed out that the result of integrating mental health into primary and secondary health systems is a model of care that is human rights-focused, evidence-based and decentralised.

Describing the model as a global standard, he said that it was built on partnership between a Federal institution and a State Government working as one.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Governor Uba Sani commended the Medical Director of the Federal Neuro-Psychiatric Hospital, Professor Aishatu Yusha’u Armiya’u, who has ‘’gone above and beyond the call of duty in service to the people of Kaduna State.’’

He said that under her leadership, this hospital’s Dialysis Centre has become the only facility in Kaduna State that attends to septic patients who too often had nowhere else to go.

Uba Sani disclosed that the hospital recently launched the Telepsychiatry Programme, which allows patients to receive care wherever they may be.

‘’For families in the hard-to-reach rural communities of Kaduna State, that means fewer long journeys, lower costs and care that arrives in time. It also lets this hospital’s specialists to support health workers in our primary and secondary facilities, strengthening the very system we are building together,’’ he added.

In her speech, Prof Armiyau noted that although mental health conditions are generally not communicable diseases in the medical sense, she argued that some mental-health-related behaviors, emotions, or symptoms can spread socially.

‘’Let us also remember that mental health is not only an individual responsibility. It is a shared responsibility. During this Mental Health Week, I encourage each one of us to take practical steps.

‘’Check on a families, friends and colleagues. Listen to someone who needs to talk. Take care of yourself. Seek professional help when necessary. And, most importantly, treat others with kindness and understanding,’’ she counselled.

The Medical Director commended Governor Uba Sani for his administration’s huge investment in the health sector and other critical areas in Kaduna State.

‘’Under your leadership, Kaduna State has taken important steps towards strengthening the mental health system and promoting a more humane and rights-based approach to mental healthcare.

‘’ The enactment of the Kaduna State Mental Health Law in September 2025 represents an important institutional step towards protecting the rights and dignity of persons living with mental health conditions. I salute you for this!’’, she added.

Prof Armiyau noted that FNPH has collaborated with the Kaduna State Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Agency (KADSAMHSA), by training and the certification of multidisciplinary health workers drawn from PHCs across all 23 Local Government Areas, under the WHO Mental Health Gap Action Programme (MHGAP).

She further said that the hospital has also unveiled a Smart Digital Patient Card, to provide patients with easier access to essential information, including biodata, medical history, treatment records and appointments.

According to the Medical Director of FNPH, the Smart Digital Patient Card also supports electronic payments and contributes towards the hospital’s transition to a more efficient, increasingly paperless system.

World.title: Minister defends NNPC petrol discount, says it’s not return to subsidy
World.content:
The Minister of Information, Mohammed Idris, has defended the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited’s (NNPC) 30-day petrol discount initiative, saying it is intended to provide temporary relief to Nigerians amid rising global energy costs.

Mr Idris said the decision did not represent a return to fuel subsidy, explaining that the NNPC had opted to forgo some of its profits to cushion the impact of higher petrol prices on consumers.

“The NNPC has looked at it and said we are making this much profit. Why can’t we forgo some of the profit that we are making, so that Nigerians will have some form of cushioning?” he said.

The minister made this point during a media chat with senior editors and journalists on Monday, where he highlighted the government’s economic reforms and their impact on key indicators.

The NNPC’s discount has attracted criticism from opposition politicians, labour leaders and other stakeholders, who have questioned its duration, reach and potential impact on households struggling with the cost of living.

Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar has criticised the initiative, describing it as a politically motivated measure that would offer only temporary relief ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Atiku also questioned the decision to make NNPC Limited bear the cost of the discount, asking whether the company’s board approved the arrangement and how the financial implications would be reflected in its accounts.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He questioned the government’s handling of the state-owned oil company, which operates as a commercial entity under the Petroleum Industry Act.

He also challenged the government to explain the cost of the discount and how it would benefit motorists outside the NNPC retail network, which is less than half of the total filling stations across the country.

The president of the Trade Union Congress, Festus Osifo, and Social Democratic Party presidential candidate Adewole Adeboye have also questioned the policy. The TUC’s concerns include its implementation and whether the arrangement amounts to a form of subsidy despite the government’s position.

In his remarks, the minister acknowledged the pressure of rising energy costs on households and businesses, adding that the federal government remained committed to expanding access to affordable energy alternatives and strengthening domestic production.

Mr Idris said rising energy costs were a global challenge, with governments adopting different approaches to protect their economies and cushion the impact on citizens.

He said President Bola Tinubu remained committed to economic reforms while prioritising the welfare of Nigerians.

“Our approach is to consolidate the gains of these reforms, expand affordable energy alternatives, strengthen domestic production and create the conditions for sustainable reductions in the cost of living,” he said.

According to the minister, the administration is working to ensure that the benefits of economic recovery translate into greater affordability, improved purchasing power and better living conditions.

Reforms

Mr Idris said the achievements of the Renewed Hope Agenda over the last three years were evident across the eight presidential priority areas, including economic growth, national security, agriculture, energy, infrastructure, education, healthcare, industrialisation and governance.

He said the administration’s economic reforms were restoring stability and confidence, while investments in infrastructure were opening new opportunities and agricultural initiatives were strengthening food production.

He added that security operations were addressing threats to lives and livelihoods, while investments in education and healthcare were expanding access to essential services.

The minister said the government intended to consolidate these gains and ensure that the benefits of its reforms reached more Nigerians.

“There is certainly more work to be done, but there is equally substantial progress to build upon,” he said.

Oil production, exports

Mr Idris said the decline in oil theft and a significant increase in crude oil production had boosted revenue for the federal, state and local governments.

He also said Nigeria earned more than $6 billion from non-oil exports in 2025, describing it as the highest amount in the country’s history.

According to him, the earnings supported businesses in agriculture, mining, petrochemicals, manufacturing, processing and logistics.

He added that the foreign exchange market had stabilised, allowing businesses and investors to plan with greater confidence.

Mr Idris said the government’s next task was to ensure that the gains from the economic recovery reached more households and improved their purchasing power.

He said the government welcomed scrutiny from journalists but urged them to provide context when reporting the economic difficulties Nigerians face, alongside the government’s reported achievements and the challenges that remain.

“Finally, my dear colleagues, we are not asking you to stop scrutinising the government. Your scrutiny makes us better. What I ask for is clarity and context: that the pressures Nigerians feel are reported alongside their causes, the progress being made and the work that remains,” he said.

“Our shared interest is an informed public and a stronger Nigeria.”

World.title: Edo youths quit cults en masse
World.content:
Several youths in Edo State have publicly renounced their membership of various cult groups in a mass exercise.

The exercise, themed “Restitution, Rehabilitation and Safer Edo State,” was organised by the Edo State Government as part of efforts to tackle cultism and other violent crimes.

At the event, Governor Monday Okpebholo commended the youths for renouncing cultism.

Mr Okpebholo, however, warned others still involved in the practice to follow suit or face the full weight of the law.

The governor said his administration would sustain its campaign against cultism and criminality, stressing that the government is determined to make the state safe for residents.

“We are not afraid to go after cultists and criminal elements in Edo.

“Please take the message back to those that have not changed; they still have the power to renounce because if they are caught, there will be no mercy,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Okpebholo said the government is providing opportunities for rehabilitation and reintegration for those willing to abandon criminal activities and turn their lives around.

He warned that the government would not hesitate to order the demolition of buildings used for cult-related activities.

The governor said Edo recorded more than 300 cult-related killings annually before his administration assumed office in 2024, adding that the figure had since dropped to almost zero.

He did not, however, provide statistics to back his claim.

Earlier, the Coordinator of the State Special Security Squad, Operation Flush Out Kidnapping and Cultists, Noah Idemudia, commended the governor for establishing the squad and supporting its collaboration with security agencies.

Mr Idemudia said the squad had contributed to the state’s efforts to combat kidnapping and cult-related activities.

The Commissioner of Police in Edo, Patrick Daaor, also commended the administration’s efforts to tackle crime, particularly cultism.

Mr Daaor said the programme was designed to save young lives and encourage former cult members to become productive members of society.

The Edo State Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Roland Otaru, SAN, said cult-related activities had destroyed lives and property across the state.

READ ALSO: Police commissioner in Bayelsa orders crackdown on cult groups

Mr Otaru said the government’s initiatives demonstrated its commitment to restoring peace.

He added that establishing a Special Criminal Court had strengthened the state’s criminal justice system.

He urged cult members to take advantage of the renunciation programme, abandon criminal activities and embrace lawful means of livelihood.

(NAN)

World.title: FRSC ​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍​‍​⁠​‌​⁠‌​confirms female NYSC member dead in Ibadan auto crash
World.content:
FILE IMAGE

The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC), Oyo Sector Command, has confirmed the death of a female corps member in a road crash on Monday in Ibadan.

The Sector Commander in Oyo State, Corps Commander Kehinde Dahunsi, disclosed this in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN).

Dahunsi said that the crash involved a motorcycle and an articulated truck.

According to him, the female corps member lost her life in the accident while the motorcycle rider sustained a fracture in his leg.

He said that while the body of the corps member had been deposited at the State Hospital morgue, the motorcyclist was rushed to the University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan, for medical attention.

The sector commander noted that details of the late corps member could not be ascertained at the time of the rescue operation.

“We recorded a traffic crash today around Agodi Gardens within the Ibadan metropolis. It involved a truck and a motorcycle carrying a corps member.

“Unfortunately, we lost the corps member, and the rider also sustained a fracture in his leg.

“We carried out emergency rescue operations; we conveyed the body of the late corps member to the State Hospital morgue, while the injured rider was rushed to the University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan,” he said.

Meanwhile, Mrs Abimbola Faniyi, the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) Public Relations Officer in the state, said efforts were underway to obtain the deceased’s details, including her Place of Primary Assignment (PPA).

(NAN)

World.title: Ronaldo Asian Champions League match delayed due to missile alert
World.content:
Nassr’s Portuguese forward #07 Cristiano Ronaldo and Neftchi Fergana’s defender Koffi Kouao react during the AFC Champions League group B football match between Al-Nassr and Neftchi Fergana at the Alawwal Park stadium in Riyadh on October 12, 2026. (Photo by Fayez NURELDINE / AFP)

Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr saw their Asian Champions League match against Neftchi Fergana delayed by an hour on Monday after the Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia has recently come under a series of attacks from the Iran-backed group, including strikes on oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs — including a string of lethal hits on Riyadh’s international airport.

There was a sparse crowd in the stands of Al-Awal Park for the game which was scheduled for 9:15 pm local time (1815 GMT).

The stadium announcer said the situation was safe, that the match would be played, and asked spectators to remain in their seats.

However, the television channel broadcasting the match announced a one-hour delay.

Shortly before, AFP correspondents reported hearing explosions in Riyadh.
