World.title: Shock and surprise after FBI arrests Canadian cybersecurity expert in ShinyHunters hacking case
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadians in the cybersecurity world say they were shocked to hear that a prominent ransomware negotiator had been arrested by the FBI over suspected connections to criminal hacking group ShinyHunters.

FBI Director Kash Patel on Friday confirmed the arrest of a "suspected co-conspirator" in the recent ShinyHunters cyberattack on FBIjobs.gov which exposed a trove of sensitive data about FBI staff.

"We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what's left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate," Patel said on social media.

Reuters reported Sunday that sources familiar with the matter identified the arrested suspect as Ed Dubrovsky, a Canadian cybersecurity executive whose career has focused on helping clients negotiate with ransomware attackers.

Court documents from the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania show Dubrovsky is facing two criminal charges: conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money, and interference with commerce by threats.

The allegations have not been proven in court.

FBI Director Kash Patel testifies during a Senate Judiciary hearing on Oversight of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, in September 2026 in Washington. Patel confirmed the arrest of a suspected co-conspirator in the ShinyHunters investigation. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)

'A sense of shock'

"For the cybersecurity community in general, I think that there's a sense of shock," Toronto-based tech and cybersecurity analyst Ritesh Kotak told CBC News on Monday.

Kotak says Dubrovsky is "very popular" and has spoken at numerous conferences, but stressed that the charges "are clearly just allegations" and that it is not yet known "what exactly has happened."

"This is an individual that was for the most part respected when it came to ransomware negotiations," he said. "A lot of people are familiar with his work as well."

The ​court records, which are partially sealed, provide conflicting spellings of the suspect's last ⁠name — "Dobrovsky" or "Dobrosky" — and do not identify his age, profession or employer.

Prison records show a 54-year-old named Edward Dubrovsky is being held at a federal detention centre in Philadelphia.

Reuters reported that electronic wallet records leaked in 2010 and preserved by dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs identify Dubrovsky as a 54-year-old resident of Richmond Hill, a suburb of Toronto.

Long history in cybersecurity

Dubrovsky's LinkedIn profile describes him as a specialist in ‌negotiating with cybercriminals over ransom payments, as well as a "globally recognized cybersecurity expert, business leader, speaker, author and educator."

According to his profile, Dubrovsky has held senior positions in cybersecurity for decades.

He wrote on LinkedIn last month that he would be attending the NetDilligence conference in Philadelphia in October with cybersecurity firm CyberSteward. The company posted photos of Dubrovsky at the conference a week ago and said he was signing copies of a book he recently published about handling cyber extortion.

WATCH | Experts say AI will drive future cybercrime: AI can make cyberattacks faster and smarter | Duration closed caption 1:29 A new EY report suggests AI will become a major force behind cybercrime in 2026 as programs help attackers hone their scamming skills.

In the book's introduction, Dubrovsky writes: "I have negotiated with criminals who viewed themselves as martyrs, criminal masterminds, and patriots of their own countries even after deploying malware against critical infrastructure and causing billions of dollars in damage. Such people could still look in the mirror and see goodness."

CBC News reached out to CyberSteward by phone, email and in person at its Toronto address, but did not get a response Monday.

The FBI's national press office declined to comment directly on Dubrovsky's arrest and referred CBC News to Patel's statement.

RCMP spokesperson Ian Lordon told The Canadian Press on Friday that "the RCMP is aware of the arrest of a Canadian in the U.S. in connection with the ShinyHunters hack," but directed all further questions to the FBI.

ShinyHunters 'poked the bear': expert

ShinyHunters is known as one of the world's most prolific data theft and extortion groups, typically demanding ransom payments in exchange for not releasing the sensitive data it has obtained.

The hacking group caused chaos at universities around the world in May, including in Canada, with a cyberattack on Canvas, an online learning-management system that connects millions of students with their instructors.

ShinyHunters has also been associated with high-profile cyberattacks affecting companies including Telus, Microsoft, Ticketmaster , Pornhub and Rockstar Games.

Last month, the group claimed responsibility for stealing a massive trove of data from the FBI — including officials' job assignments, addresses and social security numbers — in what it said was retaliation for the law enforcement agency making false claims about the group.

ShinyHunters later told CBC News they would not release the data.

David Shipley, a cybersecurity expert and CEO of Fredericton-based Beauceron Security, said the stunt "poked the bear" and has "literally unleashed the most powerful law enforcement agency in the world on them."

WATCH | Canvas strikes deal with hackers: Online learning platform strikes deal with hackers that targeted schools | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 6:25 The parent company behind Canvas, a widely used learning management platform connecting students with their schools or universities, has struck a deal with the hacking group claiming responsibility for last week's massive cybersecurity breach.

Shipley said surprise was the first thing that came to mind when he heard of the latest arrest.

"I knew the ShinyHunters investigation was going to go in interesting places because it's already the stuff of Hollywood movies," he told CBC News.

"I don't think anyone saw this twist coming."

Shipley said Dubrovsky was well regarded and worked for "top-tier" cybersecurity firms.

"I feel terrible for his former colleagues, both at his current firm and his past firms, who have been dragged through these awful headlines," he said.

World.title: RJ Mitte, Breaking Bad star and disability rights advocate, dead at 34
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Actor and disability rights advocate RJ Mitte, who brought a lifetime of experience with cerebral palsy to fictional family struggles in an essential role on Breaking Bad, died Monday at age 34, authorities and his representatives said.

Cameron County Justice of the Peace Cyndi Hinojosa told The Associated Press that she declared Mitte dead at about 1:30 p.m. at what she believed was his home in Brownsville, Texas.

She said she was unable to provide a cause, but an autopsy will be performed.

Mitte played Walter White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston's chemistry teacher-turned-meth dealer Walter White on nearly every episode of the five seasons of the AMC show, which recently ranked as the best of the 21st century in a New York Times poll.

Diagnosed at age three, Mitte told The Associated Press in 2014 that his disability and the surrounding struggles with physical therapy, family problems and exorbitant medical bills — all key subjects on the show — made him better at his job.

WATCH | Mitte talks disability, bullying and Breaking Bad at 2014 Ottawa event: Breaking Bad star gives anti-bullying speech | Duration 2:27 RJ Mitte, known as Walt Jr. of Breaking Bad, was in Ottawa to speak out against bullying.

"You develop a different mentality and you develop a different look at how the world sees you and how you see the world," he said. "You're able to use that. And I think it's an asset instead of something that would hinder."

Mitte was born and raised in Jackson, Miss.

He landed small guest roles on sitcoms after moving to Los Angeles to act in 2006. Like his character, he was in his mid-teens when he began his work on Breaking Bad, starting in 2007. The show ran from 2008 to 2013.

"Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," the actor's representatives said in a statement announcing his death. The statement said he used "his platform to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation."

His later credits included the ABC Family series Switched at Birth and the superhero satire series Guardians of Justice.

He was also a producer of several independent films.

As an advocate, he served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's. He was also president of his own Mitte Foundation supporting philanthropic and community initiatives around disabilities.

World.title: Emergency medical help for Christa Pike was delayed due to confusion, 911 tapes reveal
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials following her failed lethal injection last month, according to 911 dispatch recordings reviewed by The Associated Press.

The recordings show that precious minutes elapsed as officials and responders tried to figure out whether a request for emergency help in the execution chamber was legitimate.

The first call came in at 8:40 p.m. local time on Sept. 30, and it was about half an hour before prison officials affirmed it was legitimate and began letting responders through the prison gates.

"Per supervisors here at the DEC [Department of Emergency Communications], we have been informed it is a false call," one unidentified person says at 9:03 p.m. "There is no medical assistance needed at Riverbend Prison."

It wasn't until 9:11 p.m. that prison officials affirmed the call for help was legitimate, the calls show.

No protocol for failed injections

Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed Slemmer, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death.

State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn't result in death, but it doesn't spell out what to do if an inmate survives the second injection.

The first 911 call, released only as a written transcript, reported that Pike was unconscious and not breathing normally.

After being taken to hospital, Pike was on a ventilator for several days, and her lawyers did not expect her to survive.

However, they said Pike woke up last Tuesday and began talking and walking with assistance, and she has since been discharged and is back at the women's prison where she was housed for 30 years.

WATCH | Push for answers over failed execution: Christa Pike's lawyers demand answers, transparency over botched execution | Duration closed caption 2:17 Lawyers for convicted murderer Christa Pike are pushing for answers and transparency after she survived several lethal injection attempts last week. A Tennessee judge also ordered the court to preserve all evidence connected to the botched execution.

Details of 1st call

The initial 911 call came from a person whose name and title were redacted. The caller told a dispatcher that they were at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, where they had tried to execute someone, but she was still alive.

As emergency responders worked to verify the call, they were in touch with representatives of the prison's Central Control, who said they "would have been the ones to call in and they did not make that call," according to a recording time-stamped at 9:07 p.m.

Around the same time, a first responder could be heard over the radio saying, "Somebody is outside the gate at the prison telling us that it's real and demanding us to go in. They say they are some sort of state official. I need somebody to get out to the gate and talk to those people."

Central Control confirmed the call was legitimate a few minutes later, clearing the way for responders to enter through the gates at about 9:11 p.m. An Associated Press reporter witnessed an ambulance and fire trucks pull up to the building inside the prison campus at 9:14 p.m.

At 9:34 p.m., as medics were transporting Pike to hospital, one asked dispatch to make sure the prison knew where they were taking her.

"Just 'cause there's been so much other confusion, I want to make sure they are aware of this," the responder said.

Two other calls were made

The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications released with some redactions a batch of audio recordings, including radio traffic and calls with emergency dispatchers. Police said the audio from the first 911 call was exempt from public disclosure under state law.

Two subsequent emergency calls were made, including one at 9:08 p.m. by one of Pike's lawyers, Kelly Gleason.

"My client, Christa Gail Pike, is undergoing a state execution. She has completed the stages of the protocol and last we knew from the attorney who is present, she is still alive and breathing and needs immediate life-saving care," Gleason said on the call.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong in the attempted execution. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream.

Before the execution attempt, Pike's lawyers told courts and prison officials that she had a blood disorder that could cause clotting at injection sites.

World.title: Ukraine caught between escalating war and growing pressure from Trump administration
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed global leaders and military officials at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Ukraine's president found himself in a familiar position: trying to shore up international support for his country while managing an increasingly fractious relationship with Washington.

Zelenskyy is caught between an escalating war at home and a Trump administration that appears to be increasing pressure on Kyiv to halt its attacks on Russian refineries while simultaneously pursuing fuel deals with Moscow.

Several media outlets, including the Financial Times and CNN , have reported that U.S. officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine if Kyiv does not halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

"We need American pressure on Russia, not sanctions relief, not concessions," Zelenskyy said in a virtual address to the forum.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, met with U.S. President Donald Trump during the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York City on Sept. 22. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

Ceasefire? What ceasefire?

Zelenskyy spoke a day after U.S. President Donald Trump appeared to unilaterally declare an energy ceasefire in a social media post, catching Kyiv and its European allies off guard.

Although Zelenskyy said he had not been aware of the agreement, he indicated that Kyiv would support it if Moscow did the same.

But by Monday, it was clear that no such ceasefire was in place.

When asked Monday morning about the supposed agreement, the Kremlin said "contacts" were ongoing, but it declined to comment on any specifics. Later that evening, Zelenskyy said Russia had struck six energy facilities in Ukraine.

WATCH | Russia still bombing energy infrastructure after 'ceasefire,' Ukraine says: Ukraine accuses Russia of violating 'energy ceasefire' shortly after Trump announces deal | Duration closed caption 4:27 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Russia violated a recent so-called 'energy ceasefire' announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, claiming Russian attacks on energy infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv. Trump made a brief social media post on Sunday announcing the purported agreement to mutually cease attacks on energy sites, saying the ceasefire took effect immediately and warning: 'Do not break it!'

If the announcement of an energy ceasefire came as a surprise to Ukraine, Trump's declaration on Friday that the United States would begin importing Russian diesel was seen as a betrayal.

Less than a month earlier, Trump had signed a sweeping sanctions package into law that would authorize him to impose hefty tariffs on major importers of Russian oil and gas.

While Trump's relationship with Zelenskyy has often been tumultuous, with the U.S. president repeatedly accusing Ukraine of prolonging the war, Washington's latest threats come as Trump faces growing political pressure at home over surging fuel prices .

In recent months, fuel prices, including for diesel, have surged because of the blockage in the Strait of Hormuz and Ukraine's attacks on Russia's refineries. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images)

The politics of fuel prices

Trump has blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries for driving up diesel prices, which have risen by 70 per cent since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February, disrupting shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

"Trump is deflecting blame for high energy prices and the price at the pump onto Zelenskyy," said Timothy Ash, an associate fellow in the Russia and Eurasia program at Chatham House.

"His war on Iran is the main reason why energy prices are higher," Ash said.

In an interview with CBC News, Ash said he believes Trump's diesel deal with Russia also reflects a desire to return to "business as normal" and pursue commercial deals with Moscow.

However, energy analysts doubt the agreement will have much impact on U.S. prices, in part because Russia's ability to supply additional fuel is constrained by sustained Ukrainian attacks on its energy infrastructure . Kyiv claims it has destroyed about half of Russia's refining capacity.

Trump has said Russia will immediately export more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the U.S. and global markets. That amounts to about 2.25 million barrels, less than the nearly three million barrels the U.S. transport sector consumes each day, according to government data.

"It's a perfectly Trumpian deal. It's very short on details, and yet it's announced and being sold very, very loudly," said Tamas Varga, a London-based analyst with PVM Oil Associates.

"It looks like the whole deal is not going to have a significant impact on mitigating the rise in retail diesel prices in the U.S."

Black smoke rises from the area of the Russian oil producer Gazprom Neft's Moscow oil refinery on the southeastern outskirts of Moscow on June 18. (AFP/Getty Images)

Trump's track record on Ukraine

The diesel agreement is another reminder of Trump's transactional approach to foreign policy, further eroding whatever trust Ukrainians may still have in Washington's ability to steer negotiations and help secure a workable peace.

Trump's social media post about the so-called energy ceasefire on Sunday marked the second time in less than a month that he had claimed Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure. Neither announcement appeared to be rooted in reality.

Zelenskyy has not publicly confirmed reports that Washington has threatened to cut off intelligence sharing or prevent Ukraine's allies from purchasing U.S.-made weapons, including Patriot air defence missiles. However, the Trump administration has taken similar steps before.

In March 2025, days after a tense, televised meeting between Trump and Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, the U.S. briefly suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

Oleksandr Kraiev, an international relations expert at the Kyiv-based think-tank Ukrainian Prism, said the pressure from Washington currently amounts to threats. But he said Ukraine must be prepared for the possibility that Trump could follow through, given his unpredictability.

"When you are being played by a cynical leader, you have to become cynical yourself," Kraiev said in a phone interview with CBC News from Kyiv.

"We have to play the game with them … but we should always be relying on ourselves and on our European allies more than on our American allies."

A family walks past an apartment building that was hit by a Russian drone in Kharkiv, Ukraine, on Monday. (Thomas Peter/Reuters)

Threats to cut off intelligence

Despite Trump's impulsive whims, Kraiev said Kyiv cannot abandon diplomacy with Washington and simply wait for the "hotheads" to cool down. He said even though European countries are increasing their supplies of weapons and ammunition, Ukraine remains heavily dependent on the U.S.

"The Americans provide less than 15 per cent of all of our munitions and all of our armaments, but this 15 per cent cannot be duplicated anywhere else," Kraiev said, pointing to Lockheed Martin's PAC-3 air defence interceptor as an example.

Experts say European countries also cannot easily replicate the satellite imagery the U.S. provides to Ukraine, which helps Kyiv plan attacks and defend against Russian strikes.

Robert Tollast, a research fellow in land warfare at the Royal United Services Institute, said U.S. spy satellites help Ukraine identify targets in occupied areas of eastern Ukraine, particularly those more than 80 kilometres from the front line.

"The U.S. have basically a repository of satellite intelligence imagery that their partner nations have access to," he said, adding that in some cases the requested images are delivered in as little as 15 minutes.

He says the images can show Ukraine Russian military positions and whether it is moving weaponry or troops around.

"If Ukraine loses access to this, it would complicate their targeting efforts."

World.title: Selma Blair accused of assaulting and injuring flight attendants, police officer and nurse
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Actor Selma Blair was arrested after she was accused of injuring two flight attendants on a trip from Los Angeles to New York. She was also charged Monday with assaulting a police officer who was taking her to the hospital and a nurse after she arrived there.

Blair, 54, was taken into custody at about 11 p.m. ET on Sunday when the Delta Air Lines plane was parked at the gate at New York's John F. Kennedy Airport, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said in a statement.

Blair and one of the flight attendants were taken to hospital for evaluation, the port authority said.

A police officer taking her to Jamaica Hospital Medical Center said in charging documents that while she was securing Blair to a stretcher, Blair pulled a leg from the straps and kicked her repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling. Later, a nurse moving Blair said the actor kicked her in the chest, causing substantial pain.

She was arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault late Monday at a court in Queens, where a judge set her bail at $20,000 US cash or $60,000 US bond and set the next hearing for January.

Blair was taken into custody late Sunday night after her plane landed at New York's John F. Kennedy Airport, shown on June 24. (Bruce Bennett/Getty Images)

A representative for Blair told The Associated Press that the actor had a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct.

Details of what happened aboard the aircraft weren't immediately disclosed by the airline, police or the FBI, which was investigating, but Delta said in a statement it "has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first."

In air traffic communications, the Delta pilot asks the tower to have medical personnel waiting at the gate to treat bite marks and a bloody nose, but says ambulances were not necessary.

"It sounds like the disruptive passenger also bashed her head on the bulkhead or something like that," the pilot told the tower, according to audio posted on the ATC app. "So we'll obviously have to get her potentially checked out as well as involved with law enforcement."

Previous in-flight incident

It's not the first time Blair — who had major roles in such films as 1999's Cruel Intentions, 2001's Legally Blonde and 2004's Hellboy — has had issues aboard a plane.

In 2016, Blair apologized for making statements she regretted on a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles, saying that she mixed alcohol with medication, which made her black out.

In recent years, Blair, who was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018, has been an advocate for disability rights. In 2023, she joined then-president Joe Biden at the White House to celebrate the anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act.

World.title: Prominent U.S. archbishop compares planned livestream of firing squad execution to terrorist practices
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Catholics serving in the U.S. army should not participate in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood ‌shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to livestream in December, a prominent U.S. archbishop said on Monday.

In an unusually strongly worded statement, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the U.S. armed forces, raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to ​broadcast the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort ​Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree.

Broglio said he presided at the funeral of one of Hasan's victims, and lamented the shooting. But the Ohio-born archbishop asked whether the U.S. ​wanted to "imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically ⁠killing our adversaries."

"I oblige any Catholics ⁠assigned to the firing squad to request to be ‌excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church," Broglio said.

U.S. army regulations do allow for soldiers to request religious exemptions or accommodations, and the army has yet to say how it intends to select members of the firing squad.

The Pentagon says Nidal Hasan will be executed by firing squad in a livestreamed broadcast in December. (Bell County Sheriff's Office/Handout/Reuters)

Backlash from Republicans, international observers

U.S. War Secretary Pete ⁠Hegseth announced plans to livestream the shooting last week, triggering a backlash among Republicans in Congress, religious leaders and international observers. U.S. President Donald Trump approved Hasan's execution by firing squad but has said he is still deciding whether to allow the ‌livestreaming to proceed.

The event would be extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the U.S. military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945. Hasan, now 56, requires a wheelchair, having been ​shot by police during his arrest.

Hegseth said last week he wants U.S. soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and ⁠location of Hasan's shooting spree. Hegseth has argued that making the event public will help serve as a deterrent.

Broglio ⁠questioned whether the effect of a livestreamed execution on young viewers had been considered. He said the U.S. military ⁠had ⁠a good reputation and asked if there ​was "really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of ​a man in a wheelchair to ⁠the whole world."

Broglio's statement was issued shortly after he met on Monday in Rome with Pope Leo, who has clashed with Trump and his Pentagon over issues including the Iran war. Leo on Saturday condemned the death penalty, without mentioning the Hasan case specifically.

U.S. Vice-President JD Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has said that if it does ultimately get livestreamed, he would ⁠not watch it.

World.title: Carney’s Thanksgiving message directed at Alberta ahead of separation referendum
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In a video released on social media on Thanksgiving Monday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said this year's holiday is different as Albertans prepare to vote next week in a referendum on the province's future in Canada. 'Canada is facing real threats to our economy, to our security, to our way of life. We have to be strong and we are stronger together,' he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the nation from a classroom in Alberta on Thanksgiving morning, addressing the non-binding question tied to Alberta’s potential separation from Canada in the upcoming referendum.

“A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future,” Carney said as he sat at a desk in his alma mater, St. Francis Xavier High School, in west Edmonton.

“Now, I have some perspectives on this choice. I grew up in Alberta.”

Albertans are preparing to go to the polls on Oct. 19 for a 10-question referendum. The final question asks whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada, or hold a second, binding referendum on separating from the country.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: What conversations are you having about the Alberta referendum with friends and family? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for this Sunday's show.

“I'm back home a lot these days because we are building big things again in Alberta,” Carney said, referencing the federal government’s housing initiatives, a proposed high-speed rail route from Edmonton to Calgary and the newly proposed pipeline stretching from Alberta’s oilfield to the West Coast.

“We can't achieve any of this if we're divided. You can't build big things on fault lines.”

Carney continued, referencing recent threats to Canada’s economy and security.

“Generations of Albertans helped build this country,” he said. “It's yours, it's ours, and it's worth fighting for.”

Lori Williams, associate professor of policy studies at Calgary's Mount Royal University, said the prime minister's statement could boost his popularity in Alberta.

"[Carney] is the most popular politician in the province right now," Williams said. "That idea of inspiring people about the future of Canada might have some resonance.

"On the other hand, [Premier] Danielle Smith has scrupulously avoided saying too much about the referendum questions."

CBC News requested comment from Smith's office on the prime minister's address.

“We encourage Albertans to visit albertareferendum2026.ca where they can view the 10 ballot questions and access information on these important issues to inform their vote,” Sam Blackett, Smith's press secretary, wrote in an emailed statement.
