This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Pays for the Bridge and Who Builds It

The money comes from the International Development Association, the World Bank fund that gives grants and cheap loans to the poorest countries. It flows through the Transport Sector Development and Coastal Protection Project, a World Bank programme for the islands’ roads and coastline.

A World Bank notice says the Lembá bridge works were awarded on 16 December 2024 for US$8,230,273. The winner, Consortium China JK & SUCI, lists an address in São Tomé and had 18 months to build.

The same consortium won the smaller Brigoma bridge nearby for US$3,160,007. Téla Nón puts the World Bank financing for both bridges at about US$11.3 million, close to the two contracts combined.

Cardoso now speaks of a “financial gap”, because the first design of the Lembá bridge included no concrete piles at all. The 2024 tender described a girder bridge with three spans of 34 metres, 106.1 metres long and 10.6 metres wide.

The award notice lists one other evaluated bidder for the Lembá job, the Portuguese builder ACA Alberto Couto Alves. The 2024 tender specified semi-deep foundations for every support, a design now replaced by 30-metre piles.

A Farming Region Cut Off Since 2021

The old Lembá bridge collapsed in a storm in December 2021, and the Brigoma bridge also fell. Together, the losses cut the far north of Lembá district off from the rest of the island.

Lembá district lies in the north-west of São Tomé island, and its capital is the small town of Neves. Farms in the region once supplied bananas, cocoyam and breadfruit to the market in Neves and to the capital.

Farmer Linda da Silva told Téla Nón, in a report published on 7 October, that the temporary crossing floods whenever it rains. “The government is the one that should explain,” she said, as she carried a bucket of cocoa on her head.

At Ponta Furada, a cocoa estate on the far side of the river, only 4 people remain where more than 200 once farmed. The paper links the isolation to higher prices for bananas and other local food in the capital.

Gilson Sacramento, a motorcycle taxi rider who ferried farmers and palm-wine tappers across the river, criticised the roads institute, the builders and the site supervisors. Cardoso conceded that residents were right to complain, saying, “Communication was lacking here.”

The New Timeline for the Lembá Bridge

Cardoso said the World Bank, as the financier, has already approved the new design, and that work will start immediately. “Initially we planned 24 months, but that will not be met,” he said.

He said the bridge would be finished in 12 months, now that the new design is approved. “I give my guarantee, in 2027 we will have the bridge completed,” he told Téla Nón.

Warning signs were public in August 2025, when infrastructure minister Nelson Cardoso visited the bridge works in Lembá. Téla Nón reported then that the project rested on a conceptual study, with soil surveys still pending.

The contractor has started building homes to resettle families living near the site. As part of setting up the works yard, 4 classrooms were built for the Lembá community school.

What It Means for US Readers

The US State Department rates São Tomé and Príncipe at Level 2, “exercise increased caution”, in an advisory issued on 4 September 2026. It warns that secondary roads are often damaged and that driving gets harder in the rainy months from September to May.

Americans who need help are served by the US Embassy in Luanda, Angola, which also covers São Tomé and Príncipe. Visitors heading to the island’s north should plan for slow, weather-dependent travel until the new Lembá bridge opens.

For investors and builders, the case is a lesson in World Bank-funded tenders that go out before the ground is surveyed. Here the redesign has already cost a year and needed fresh approval from the lender.

The World Bank says growth in São Tomé and Príncipe has relied on externally financed public spending, a model it calls increasingly unsustainable. It expects growth of only 0.4% in 2026, while the islands also cope with a shortage of petrol.

What Is Not Known

Neither the roads institute nor the World Bank has published the new cost of the redesigned Lembá bridge. It is also unclear whether the government, the lender or the contractor will cover the extra concrete piles.

No firm restart date has been announced beyond the roads chief’s promise that work begins immediately. It is also unclear whether the smaller Brigoma bridge, tendered in the same package, needs a similar redesign.

The MLSTP, the main opposition party that led the islands to independence in 1975, won 24 of 55 seats in the 27 September parliamentary election. A new government has yet to be named, so it is unclear whether the next cabinet will keep the 2027 deadline.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is the Lembá bridge in São Tomé delayed?

The project went to tender without a detailed geotechnical study of the riverbed. When the contractor drilled, it found 13 metres of mud, so the bridge had to be redesigned on concrete piles 30 metres deep.

Who is paying for the Lembá bridge?

The World Bank’s International Development Association finances the works under a transport and coastal protection project. The Lembá works contract, awarded in December 2024, is worth US$8,230,273.

Who is building the Lembá bridge?

World Bank records show the contract went to Consortium China JK & SUCI, which lists an address in São Tomé. The same consortium won the nearby Brigoma bridge.

When will the Lembá bridge be finished?

Adelino Cardoso, director of the National Roads Institute, promised completion within 12 months, in 2027. The original plan was a 24-month build after the June 2025 launch.

Is it safe for Americans to travel to São Tomé and Príncipe?

The US State Department rates the country at Level 2, exercise increased caution. It warns that secondary roads are often damaged and that rain makes driving harder from September to May.

World.content:

MALI · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Mali is a landlocked Sahel country in West Africa, ruled by a military government since coups in 2020 and 2021.

— What happened On Monday 12 October, the Malian newspaper Le Challenger reported that the 2027 draft budget cuts the Rural Support Programme by about 41.4%.

— The numbers The programme falls from 64.40 billion CFA francs (about US$110 million) in 2026 to 37.73 billion CFA francs (about US$64 million) in 2027.

— Where money goes Rural land development and equipment rises about 24.7% to 69.87 billion CFA francs (about US$119 million), now the agriculture ministry’s largest line.

— The whole budget The government adopted the draft on Friday 18 September, with spending of 4,462.6 billion CFA francs (about US$7.6 billion), up 11.75% on 2026.

— Why it matters to Americans Washington rates Mali at Level 4, Do Not Travel, and the budget shows how a military government backed by Russian partners sets its priorities.

— Still open The National Transitional Council, Mali’s appointed parliament, must still examine and vote on the draft before the budget year starts.

Mali’s draft budget for 2027 cuts the agriculture ministry’s rural support programme by about 41%, Malian newspaper Le Challenger reported on Monday 12 October. The programme falls from 64.40 billion CFA francs (about US$110 million) to 37.73 billion CFA francs (about US$64 million).

For foreign readers, the figures show where a military government that relies on Russian partners puts its money while its army fights armed groups. The US State Department rates Mali at Level 4, Do Not Travel, citing terrorism, kidnapping, crime and unrest.

What the 2027 Draft Cuts and What It Adds

Total payment credits for the agriculture ministry fall to about 127.92 billion CFA francs (about US$218 million) in 2027. That is about 6.3% below the 136.58 billion CFA francs (about US$233 million) budgeted for 2026, according to Le Challenger.

The deepest cut hits the rural support programme, which loses about 26.67 billion CFA francs (about US$46 million). Within it, transfers and subsidies shrink from 54.54 billion CFA francs (about US$93 million) to 24.29 billion CFA francs (about US$41 million).

Spending moves instead to rural land development and equipment, which rises about 24.7% to 69.87 billion CFA francs (about US$119 million). That programme is now the largest line in the agriculture ministry’s budget, ahead of rural support.

General administration grows about 30.2% to 15.42 billion CFA francs (about US$26 million). Research and training edges up from 4.29 billion CFA francs (about US$7 million) to 5.28 billion CFA francs (about US$9 million).

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why the Cut to Farm Transfers Draws Questions

In public budgets, transfers and subsidies are money the state passes on to others, rather than spending on its own projects and staff. In the 2027 draft, that line in the rural support programme falls by more than half.

Le Challenger wrote that this shift “raises questions about the nature of the spending concerned.” The paper also cautioned that it would be premature to conclude that aid to producers will automatically fall.

The rise in land development and equipment, about 13.83 billion CFA francs (about US$24 million), offsets about half of the fall in rural support. The ministry’s total still shrinks by about 8.66 billion CFA francs (about US$15 million).

A Bigger Budget Under Military Rule

Mali’s Council of Ministers adopted the 2027 draft finance law on Friday 18 September, the Beninese news site La Nouvelle Tribune reported. It plans spending of 4,462.6 billion CFA francs (about US$7.6 billion), up 11.75% on the revised 2026 budget.

Revenue is forecast at 3,866.6 billion CFA francs (about US$6.6 billion), up 14.64% on 2026. That leaves a deficit of about 596 billion CFA francs (about US$1.0 billion), slightly smaller than this year’s.

The CFA franc is the currency Mali shares with seven other West African countries, and it is pegged to the euro. Amounts here are converted at about 585.5 CFA francs to the US dollar on 12 October 2026.

Mali is led by its transitional president, General Assimi Goïta, who took power in coups in 2020 and 2021. His government works with Russian military partners and formed the Alliance of Sahel States with Burkina Faso and Niger.

Local Authorities Receive 15.84% of State Resources

The farm figures follow an announcement on Thursday 8 October by General Issa Ousmane Coulibaly, minister of territorial administration and decentralisation, and government spokesperson. He said the state had allocated about 433 billion CFA francs (about US$740 million) to local authorities in 2026, Maliweb reported.

The minister said the sum equals 15.84% of state budget resources, and Maliweb cited budget ministry data for earlier years. Decentralised credits stood at 459.9 billion CFA francs (about US$785 million) in 2021 and 440.09 billion CFA francs (about US$752 million) in 2024.

Coulibaly spoke at a three-day meeting in Bamako on decrees that transfer state powers to local authorities. He said field audits would check how the funds are used.

What It Means for US Readers

The US State Department tells Americans not to travel to Mali, its highest Level 4 warning, in an advisory last updated on 2 July 2026. It bars US government employees in Mali from travelling outside the capital, Bamako, and warns of a high threat of kidnapping.

For investors, aid groups and businesses watching the Sahel, the budget is a public guide to the military government’s choices. It shows farm money moving away from transfers to the rural world and toward equipment and administration.

The government says the army, backed by Russian partners, consolidated its presence in the northern town of Kidal on 6 October. That war has shaped Mali’s politics, gold industry and public spending since the military took power.

What Is Not Known

Le Challenger’s report covers only the agriculture ministry, not defence, security or the other large spending lines in the 2027 draft. The budget document does not list the equipment projects, where they will be built or how many farmers they will reach, the paper noted.

The National Transitional Council (CNT), the appointed assembly that acts as Mali’s parliament under military rule, is now examining the draft. Until it votes, the figures remain proposals, and Mali’s budget year begins on 1 January.

More: Mali news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Mali’s 2027 draft budget cut?

It cuts the agriculture ministry’s Rural Support Programme by about 41%, to 37.73 billion CFA francs (about US$64 million). The ministry’s total budget falls about 6.3%, according to Le Challenger.

How big is Mali’s 2027 budget?

The Mali draft budget adopted on Friday 18 September plans spending of 4,462.6 billion CFA francs (about US$7.6 billion). Revenue is forecast at 3,866.6 billion CFA francs (about US$6.6 billion).

Who governs Mali?

General Assimi Goïta, the transitional president, leads a military government that took power in coups in 2020 and 2021. Mali formed the Alliance of Sahel States with Burkina Faso and Niger.

Can Americans travel to Mali?

The US State Department advises Americans not to travel to Mali, its highest Level 4 warning. It cites terrorism, kidnapping, crime and unrest.

Is the Mali draft budget final?

No. The National Transitional Council, Mali’s appointed parliament, must still examine and vote on the draft before the budget year starts.

Sources: Le Challenger via Maliweb, 12 October 2026; Maliweb, 12 October 2026; La Nouvelle Tribune, 19 September 2026; L’Aube via Maliweb, 12 October 2026; US Department of State, Mali Travel Advisory, 2 July 2026.

RWANDA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Rwanda is a small, landlocked East African country of about 14 million people, known for fast growth and heavy reliance on aid and loans.

— Why now Inflation rose to 17.2% in September from 15.7% in August, more than three times the central bank’s 5% medium-term target.

— What happened On Monday, 12 October, Rwanda’s central bank governor and finance officials met the IMF’s Africa director in Bangkok.

— The setting The talks took place on the first day of the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings, which run in Bangkok until 18 October.

— The numbers The IMF expects 7.8% growth in 2026 and 7.0% in 2027, after 9.7% growth in the first half of this year.

— Still open No new commitments from the meeting have been announced, and the IMF board vote on Rwanda’s next payout has no date yet.

Rwanda IMF talks in Bangkok on Monday, 12 October, came as prices rise at more than three times the central bank’s target. The National Bank of Rwanda’s governor and finance ministry officials met the International Monetary Fund’s director for Africa, Taarifa Rwanda reported.

For US investors, lenders and aid groups, the meeting shows how one of Africa’s fastest-growing economies plans to cool prices without stalling growth. It came two days after official data showed inflation reaching 17.2% in September.

Who Met in Bangkok and What They Discussed

Soraya Hakuziyaremye, governor of the National Bank of Rwanda, joined officials from the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning for the Rwanda IMF talks. The central bank sets interest rates, while the ministry runs the budget and negotiates loans.

Across the table sat Zeine Zeidane, who took over as director of the IMF’s African Department in 2026. His department oversees the fund’s work and lending programmes in sub-Saharan Africa.

According to Taarifa Rwanda, a Kigali news site, the talks covered the economy’s resilience, inflationary pressures and policy priorities for macroeconomic stability. The outlet described price stability as a central concern for policymakers in Kigali.

The meeting took place on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings, held from 12 to 18 October in Bangkok, Thailand. Finance ministers and central bank governors from around the world use the week for one-on-one talks with lenders.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why 17.2% Inflation Puts Prices at the Centre

The National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda, the official data agency, said prices rose 17.2% year on year in September. That was up from 15.7% in August and more than three times the central bank’s 5% target.

For households in Rwanda’s towns, the same basket of goods and services now costs about a sixth more than a year ago. The urban price index stood at 223.7 points in September, against 190.9 in September 2025.

The central bank raised its benchmark rate by half a percentage point to 8.75% after its 26 August meeting, KT Press reported. A higher rate makes borrowing dearer, which is meant to slow spending and ease pressure on prices.

The September figure arrived after that hike and just before the Rwanda IMF talks, so the bank faces a choice at its next meeting. It can raise rates again, or hold and give earlier increases more time to work.

Where Rwanda’s IMF Programme Stands

The Rwanda IMF talks build on a 38-month loan approved in June under the Extended Credit Facility, the fund’s cheap-loan tool for low-income countries. Last week, the IMF said its staff had reached agreement on the first review of that programme.

Once the IMF’s Executive Board approves the review, Rwanda can draw about US$35.7 million, the IMF said. The fund put growth at 9.7% in the first half of 2026 and forecast 7.8% for the full year.

In that statement, the IMF noted that the central bank has tightened monetary policy as inflation climbed. Because inflation broke through the range agreed in the programme, the board must discuss it under a special consultation clause.

That clause is a built-in check in IMF programmes that set inflation targets. It requires the board to discuss the government’s response before it completes the review.

What It Means for US Readers

The Rwanda IMF talks matter in Washington because the United States is the fund’s largest shareholder, with a vote on Rwanda’s review. A smooth review reassures donors and investors at a time when aid budgets are under pressure.

For US companies and investors in Rwanda, double-digit inflation pushes up wages, rents and import costs, while higher interest rates make local loans dearer. The Rwandan franc traded at about 1,476 to the US dollar on 12 October 2026.

For American visitors, faster price rises can show up in hotel, transport and restaurant bills. Travellers should check current prices rather than rely on older guidebook figures.

What Is Not Known

Officials have not said whether the Rwanda IMF talks produced any new commitments, such as tighter spending or further rate rises. It is also unclear how the IMF judges the central bank’s August rate rise against September’s jump in prices.

The date of the IMF board vote on Rwanda’s first review has not been announced. Nor is it clear whether the central bank will raise rates again when it next meets.

More: Rwanda news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who took part in the Rwanda IMF talks in Bangkok?

Central bank governor Soraya Hakuziyaremye and Rwandan finance ministry officials met Zeine Zeidane, director of the IMF’s African Department. The Rwanda IMF talks took place on Monday, 12 October, at the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings.

How high is inflation in Rwanda?

Prices rose 17.2% in the year to September 2026, up from 15.7% in August, according to the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda. The central bank’s medium-term target is 5%.

Does Rwanda have an IMF loan?

Yes, Rwanda has a 38-month Extended Credit Facility arrangement approved in June 2026. IMF staff agreed the first review in early October, which would release about US$35.7 million once the board approves it.

What is Rwanda’s central bank interest rate?

The National Bank of Rwanda raised its benchmark rate to 8.75% from 8.25% after its meeting on 26 August 2026. It has not said whether it will raise rates again.

Is Rwanda’s economy still growing?

Yes, the IMF says the economy grew 9.7% in the first half of 2026 and expects 7.8% growth for the full year. It expects growth to slow to 7.0% in 2027.

Sources: Taarifa Rwanda, 12 October 2026; International Monetary Fund, 6 October 2026; National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda, 10 October 2026; KT Press, 27 August 2026; International Monetary Fund, Annual Meetings 2026, 12 October 2026.

SOMALIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Somalia is a federal Horn of Africa nation where al-Shabaab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, still fights the government in Mogadishu.

— What happened A Somali Future Council statement published Monday 12 October warned the president over troops near ex-president Sharif Sheikh Ahmed’s home.

— The trigger On Sunday 11 October, Somalia’s intelligence agency accused Sharif’s guards of attacking its forces, and Sharif’s office denied it the same day.

— Who is involved The council unites the states of Puntland and Jubaland with the Salvation Forum, a Mogadishu opposition coalition that includes Sharif.

— The US link US Africa Command strikes al-Shabaab together with Somalia’s federal government, including a strike on 17 September near Bosaso.

— Still open It is unclear whether the government will try to disarm Sharif and other opposition figures, as local media have reported.

Somalia opposition leaders warned in a statement published on Monday 12 October that troops posted near a former president’s home in Mogadishu could spark clashes. The Somali Future Council, an alliance of Puntland, Jubaland and the Salvation Forum, said President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud would bear responsibility for the consequences.

The standoff matters beyond Somalia because Washington works with the federal government on airstrikes against al-Shabaab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group. A gunfight in the capital would pit federal forces against opposition guards, days after US officials warned of a possible Houthi presence in the north.

What the Opposition Council Said

Puntland Post and Horseed Media published the Somalia opposition council’s statement in Somali early on Monday. It said forces had been deployed at the Mogadishu home of Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, who led Somalia from 2009 to 2012.

The council accused Hassan Sheikh of a path that would legitimise shedding his critics’ blood, instead of real talks on an agreed election. It said the president would bear responsibility for whatever the deployment leads to.

Horseed Media reported that the council voiced strong concern over reports of planned action against the compounds of opposition politicians. It urged federal leaders to stop what it called provocations, so that Somalia can face its elections peacefully.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Africa Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How the Standoff Began on Sunday

The warning followed a public exchange of statements on Sunday 11 October between Sharif and the National Intelligence and Security Agency. The agency, known as NISA, is the federal government’s intelligence and security service.

NISA said armed militias under Sharif’s command attacked its Public Protection Forces in the General Da’ud section of Wadajir district, Somali Guardian reported. It said men with AK-47 rifles, machine guns and rocket-propelled grenades forced their way into homes in the Tiintiinley neighbourhood.

The agency also accused the same militias of abducting one of its officers on 24 June and obstructing an operation on 27 June. It said its own forces showed restraint to avoid civilian casualties.

Sharif’s office rejected the account the same day, Hiiraan Online reported in Somali. It said troops had been deployed near his residence, some staff had been abducted and roadblocks had restricted deliveries of food and water.

Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi answered for the federal government in a Facebook post, Hiiraan Online reported in Somali on Monday. He accused some opposition groups of mobilising armed militias and said the government would not allow armed movements that threaten Mogadishu.

Who the Main Players Are

Somalia opposition figures now call President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud the outgoing president, as the country argues over how to hold its next vote. Former prime minister Hassan Ali Khaire, who served from 2017 to 2020, used that term in a post on X on Sunday.

Khaire wrote that the military movements around former leaders’ homes were reckless and risked plunging the capital into insecurity, Hiiraan Online reported. He said force, threats and intimidation cannot resolve Somalia’s political crisis, and called for a political agreement on the elections.

Puntland is a semi-autonomous state in the northeast with its capital in Garowe, and Jubaland is a southern state bordering Kenya. Puntland’s ties with Mogadishu are tense, and its forces seized a federal-aligned base in Galkayo in August.

The third member, the Salvation Forum, is a Mogadishu coalition of opposition politicians that counts Sharif among its leading figures, Somali Guardian reported in 2025. Like the rest of the opposition, it wants a negotiated election deal, while the government pushes for direct voting through political parties.

What It Means for US Readers

The United States works with Somalia’s federal government and army against al-Shabaab. On 17 September, US Africa Command (AFRICOM) struck an al-Shabaab weapons store about 80 kilometres southwest of Bosaso, Horseed Media reported in Somali.

AFRICOM said that strike was carried out in coordination with the federal government, the same government now facing the Somalia opposition alliance. In a report published on 9 October, Horseed Media said AFRICOM believes Houthi fighters from Yemen may already operate in northern Somalia alongside al-Shabaab.

Horseed noted that a larger Houthi presence could complicate efforts to protect commercial shipping in the Gulf of Aden. Any armed clash in Mogadishu would test the security forces on which those US operations depend.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the government plans an operation to disarm Sharif and other opposition figures, as local media cited by Somali Guardian reported. No independent body has confirmed either side’s account of the incidents in Wadajir.

Somalia opposition leaders did not say how the alliance would respond if troops move on Sharif’s home. It is also unclear when, or whether, talks on an agreed election process will resume.

More: Africa news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Somali Future Council?

It is a Somalia opposition alliance that unites the states of Puntland and Jubaland with the Salvation Forum, a Mogadishu coalition that includes Sharif. It wants an election process agreed by all sides before Somalia votes.

Who is Sharif Sheikh Ahmed?

He was Somalia’s president from 2009 to 2012 and is now an opposition leader in Mogadishu. Somali Guardian says his residence lies close to the city’s airport.

What did Somalia’s intelligence agency accuse him of?

On Sunday 11 October, the agency said militias under his command attacked its forces in Wadajir district and entered homes with heavy weapons. Sharif’s office denied the account and accused government forces of abducting his staff.

Why does the Somalia opposition standoff matter to the United States?

US Africa Command carries out airstrikes on al-Shabaab in coordination with Somalia’s federal government. Fighting in Mogadishu would strain the Somali forces that US counterterrorism operations rely on.

Sources: Puntland Post (Somali), 12 October 2026; Horseed Media (Somali), 12 October 2026; Somali Guardian, 12 October 2026; Hiiraan Online (Somali), 12 October 2026; Hiiraan Online (Somali), defence minister’s warning, 12 October 2026; Hiiraan Online, 12 October 2026; Horseed Media (Somali), AFRICOM strike in Sanaag, 19 September 2026; Horseed Media, AFRICOM warning on the Houthis, 9 October 2026; Somali Guardian, Galkayo base, 5 August 2026; Somali Guardian, Salvation Forum, 1 September 2025.

World.title: Dominican Republic, Venezuela Weigh Direct Fuel Sales
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

DOMINICAN REPUBLIC · ENERGY

Key Facts — The country The Dominican Republic, a close US partner, imports the fuel it uses.

— What happened Abinader and Rodríguez met at FAO headquarters in Rome on Monday.

— The products Refidomsa and PDVSA will discuss direct AC30 asphalt and LPG sales.

— Consulates A Dominican consulate will open in Venezuela; Caracas will appoint a consul.

— US angle A US Treasury licence authorises certain Venezuelan-origin oil dealings since January.

— Still open No volumes, prices, timeline or signed agreement were announced.

Santo Domingo and Caracas will explore direct sales of petroleum products between their state oil companies. Their presidents also announced new consular steps after meeting in Rome.

The Dominican Republic and Venezuela will explore direct purchases of petroleum products after their presidents met in Rome on Monday, 12 October. Luis Abinader’s office said state refiner Refidomsa and Venezuela’s PDVSA will work out the details for both governments.

The talks matter in Washington because dealings in Venezuelan oil remain subject to US sanctions rules and Treasury licences. Any Refidomsa deal with PDVSA would test those rules in a close US partner in the Caribbean.

What the Two Presidents Agreed

Abinader and acting president Delcy Rodríguez discussed direct purchases of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and AC30 paving asphalt. El Día and Acento reported the same products and the same hand-off to Refidomsa and PDVSA.

Abinader announced the opening of a Dominican consulate in Venezuela to serve citizens of both countries, the presidency said. Rodríguez said Venezuela’s consular office in Santo Domingo will soon have a designated consul, El Día and Acento also reported.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on the Dominican Republic energy Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Meeting on the Sidelines of the FAO Forum

The meeting took place at the headquarters of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) during the World Food Forum 2026. Both presidents brought delegations and answered questions from reporters afterwards, according to the presidency and N Digital.

Rodríguez congratulated Abinader on his FAO speech, in which he highlighted the Dominican Republic’s official exit from the FAO Hunger Map. She also thanked Dominican rescuers and doctors who, she said, were among the first to arrive after Venezuela’s recent earthquake.

N Digital called the meeting a new high-level rapprochement after the diplomatic tensions that followed Venezuela’s July 2024 presidential election. It said the talks come amid steps announced during 2026 toward a gradual normalisation of relations.

Rodríguez was in Rome to launch a national food plan at the FAO the same day. Abinader is presenting his government’s record on farming and hunger at the forum.

Why It Matters for the US

The US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control issued General License 46 on 29 January 2026, authorising certain activities involving Venezuelan-origin oil. OFAC also removed Rodríguez herself from its Specially Designated Nationals list on 1 April 2026.

The Dominican Republic is one of Washington’s closest partners in the Caribbean and relies on imported fuel. A new supply channel from Venezuela would touch both its energy bill and its standing with US regulators.

What It Means for You

For US fuel exporters, a Venezuelan supply line into the Dominican market could mean new competition close to home. For now, it is a plan for talks between two state companies, not a contract.

For Venezuelans living in the Dominican Republic, a designated consul in Santo Domingo would mean a working office for papers and requests. Dominicans in Venezuela would gain the same once their country’s consulate there opens.

What Is Not Known

The presidency gave no volumes, prices, terms or timeline for the purchases, and Acento noted the same gap. It also gave no opening date for the Dominican consulate.

No joint declaration or signed agreement was released, N Digital reported. Venezuela’s Foreign Ministry readout omitted fuel, and neither side said how a PDVSA deal would fit US sanctions rules.

What Comes Next

Refidomsa and PDVSA are next in line, as both governments told them to carry the purchase talks forward. Venezuela still has to name its consul in Santo Domingo, and Rodríguez said only that this would happen soon.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Dominican Republic and Venezuela agree in Rome?

Their presidents said the state firms Refidomsa and PDVSA will discuss direct purchases of AC30 asphalt and liquefied petroleum gas. They also announced a Dominican consulate in Venezuela and a Venezuelan consul for Santo Domingo.

Where did the two presidents meet?

They met at FAO headquarters in Rome during the World Food Forum 2026. Both brought delegations and took questions from reporters afterwards.

Is there a signed fuel deal?

No, the presidency announced only talks, with no volumes, prices or timetable. No joint declaration or signed agreement was released.

Why does the US matter here?

Venezuelan oil trade is shaped by US sanctions, and a Treasury general licence has authorised certain Venezuelan-origin oil activities since 29 January. Neither government explained how a sale by PDVSA would fit those rules.

Sources: Presidencia de la República Dominicana; US Treasury, OFAC General License 46; OFAC, Venezuela-related designation removal; Venezuelan Foreign Ministry; El Día; Acento; N Digital (all accessed 12 October 2026).

World.title: Bolivia Orders Arrest of Marset’s Sister on 12 October
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

BOLIVIA · COURTS

Key Facts — The country Bolivia, where the case is heard in Santa Cruz de la Sierra.

— What happened A sentencing court declared Tatiana Marset in contempt and ordered her arrest.

— Why She missed a Monday appeal hearing on revoking her house arrest.

— Her defence Her lawyer says she is in a clinic with internal bleeding.

— US link Her brother Sebastián Marset faces narcoterrorism charges in a US court.

A Santa Cruz sentencing court declared Tatiana Marset in contempt after she missed a hearing on Monday, 12 October. Her brother, alleged drug lord Sebastián Marset, awaits trial in the United States.

A Bolivian court on Monday ordered the arrest of Tatiana Marset, the sister of alleged Uruguayan drug trafficker Sebastián Marset. Her brother faces money-laundering, drug-trafficking and narcoterrorism charges before a US federal court in Virginia.

Santa Cruz Sentencing Court 2 declared her in contempt for missing an appeal hearing, El Deber and Unitel reported. The court then issued a warrant for her arrest, according to both outlets.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 with 28.4 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (13). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.2%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Why the Court Declared Marset in Contempt

Prosecutors had appealed to overturn her house arrest and send her back to Palmasola prison in Santa Cruz, both outlets reported. Marset did not appear at the Monday hearing, according to both outlets.

Her defence said she could not attend because she is in a clinic with internal bleeding, El Deber and Unitel reported. Unitel reported that the judge found the justifications repetitive and ordered police and prosecutors to execute the warrant.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Bolivia Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Defence Seeks to Keep Marset Out of Palmasola

Defence lawyer Mónica Terrazas said she would ask the court to lift the contempt finding, El Deber and Unitel reported. Her aim is to keep her client in the proceedings and out of Palmasola, according to both outlets.

Unitel quoted Terrazas as saying her client “will be at her new hearing.” No time has yet been set for that hearing, according to Unitel.

Police Guard the Clinic Over Flight Risk

A strong police contingent guarded the clinic where Marset is being treated on Monday, Unitel reported. El Deber also published a photo of police officers outside the clinic.

The case prosecutor cited a police intelligence report at the hearing alleging a risk that she might flee, Unitel reported. El Deber did not report the flight-risk claim, which could not be independently confirmed.

The Case Against Tatiana Marset

Unitel reported that she is under investigation for criminal organisation, a charge El Deber did not specify. Unitel said police arrested her in Santa Cruz in March, in the same operation that captured her brother.

A court later moved her from Palmasola to house arrest in July, Unitel reported. Prosecutors now want that decision reversed, both outlets reported.

Sebastián Marset Faces Trial in the United States

Sebastián Marset was captured in Bolivia in March and sent to the United States the same day, Unitel and OCCRP reported. He was first indicted in the US on money-laundering charges, the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) reported.

A superseding indictment added drug-trafficking and narcoterrorism charges, according to OCCRP. US District Judge Rossie Alston set his trial for 11 January 2027, OCCRP reported on 1 July.

What It Means for You

For US readers, the ruling touches the family of a man facing a US narcoterrorism trial in January 2027. Bolivia handed him to US authorities on the day of his capture, according to Unitel and OCCRP.

President Rodrigo Paz recalled Marset’s capture on Monday while describing death threats against him, El Deber and Unitel reported. Bolivia’s police also received US riot-control equipment on 9 October.

What Is Not Known

The written ruling and the prosecutors’ appeal could not be opened, as the prosecutor’s office website blocks automated access. This report rests on what El Deber and Unitel reported.

Her medical condition has not been independently confirmed, and it is unclear when police will execute the warrant. Whether the defence filing will succeed, and when the new hearing will take place, is also unknown.

What Comes Next

After the warrant is executed, the court will rule on her legal situation and on revoking house arrest, Unitel reported. Until a final judgment, she is presumed innocent.

Sebastián Marset’s US trial is due to open on 11 January 2027, as The Rio Times reported on 4 October. He is also presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did a Bolivian court order Tatiana Marset’s arrest?

The court declared her in contempt after she missed an appeal hearing on Monday, 12 October. Prosecutors want her house arrest revoked and her return to Palmasola prison.

Who is Tatiana Marset?

She is the sister of alleged Uruguayan drug trafficker Sebastián Marset, El Deber and Unitel reported. Unitel says she is under investigation for criminal organisation.

Where is Sebastián Marset now?

He was sent to the United States after his capture in Bolivia in March. He faces charges before a federal court in Virginia, OCCRP reported.

What does her defence say?

Her lawyer says she is in a clinic with internal bleeding and could not attend. The defence plans to ask the court to lift the contempt finding.

World.title: Paraguay Evacuates 60 Families as Paraná River Rises
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

PARAGUAY · FLOODS

Key Facts — What happened At least 60 families left San Rafael, Ciudad del Este, by Monday.

— River level Itaipú measured 109.47 metres under the Friendship Bridge.

— Forecast Itaipú expects about 115 metres there in the coming days.

— Downstream Yacyretá’s operator expects 24,000 to 28,000 cubic metres per second.

— Other areas Evacuations began in Ayolas, and water is rising at Cerrito.

— Sources La Nación, ABC Color and Última Hora, citing Itaipú and the EBY.

The Paraná River is rising along Paraguay’s borders with Brazil and Argentina after heavy rain upstream. Families have left their homes, and the Yacyretá dam downstream has issued an alert.

At least 60 families have left their homes in Ciudad del Este, Paraguay, as the Paraná River swells after heavy rain upstream. La Nación and ABC Color, two Asunción dailies, reported the evacuations on Sunday, 11 October, and Monday, 12 October.

Ciudad del Este faces Foz do Iguaçu across the Friendship Bridge, the Brazilian base for visitors to Iguaçu Falls. Itaipú, the giant hydroelectric dam that Paraguay and Brazil own together, is monitoring the river and helping the families.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 with 36.0 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (55); weakest: future resources (13). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Families Leave the Low-Lying San Rafael District

The families come from San Rafael, a riverside district where La Nación reported several flooded homes on Sunday. The daily Última Hora put the number moved to safety at about 60 families, in line with La Nación.

Itaipú Binacional, which runs the dam, is coordinating the work with the city, volunteer firefighters and the military, all three papers reported. The daily Última Hora named the navy and the army’s 3rd Infantry Division among the units helping.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Paraguay Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Itaipú Expects the River to Reach About 115 Metres

Itaipú’s special flood committee measured the river at 109.47 metres under the Friendship Bridge, La Nación and Última Hora reported. Itaipú expects the level there to climb to about 115 metres in the coming days, according to Última Hora and ABC Color.

La Nación said the river could keep rising, and Última Hora quoted Itaipú as warning that the level “will keep increasing.” The same paper said the outcome depends on how much rain falls over the next few days.

Yacyretá Issues an Alert as Water Moves South

Downstream, the operator of the Yacyretá dam, shared with Argentina, issued a hydrological alert on Sunday, La Nación and ABC Color reported. Both said the Entidad Binacional Yacyretá (EBY) expects 24,000 to 28,000 cubic metres per second, after heavy rain in Brazil.

In Ayolas, the Paraguayan town beside Yacyretá, the evacuation of families at risk had begun by Sunday, La Nación reported. ABC Color published a photo on Monday showing naval prefecture staff carrying out evacuations in the Ayolas area.

Further south, both La Nación and ABC Color reported the river rising at Cerrito, a riverside community in Ñeembucú department. ABC Color said water had begun entering low-lying homes there, while La Nación said residents were moving cattle by boat.

What It Means for You

US travellers heading to Iguaçu Falls or Ciudad del Este should check local closures before they go. The Rio Times reported that Brazil shut the Iguaçu Falls walkway on Sunday as the Iguaçu River surged.

The Paraná is also the barge route for Paraguay’s soybean exports, which compete with US soybeans on world markets. Paraguay co-owns Itaipú with Brazil and Yacyretá with Argentina, both on the Paraná.

What Is Not Known

No official statement from Itaipú, the EBY or Paraguay’s National Emergency Secretariat (SEN) could be opened for this report. The facts here rest on La Nación, ABC Color and Última Hora, which cite those bodies and local officials.

The papers gave differing totals for people in shelters and for homes at risk, so those figures are left out. No outlet has reported a total number of evacuees for Ayolas or for Paraguay as a whole.

Reports differ on whether families in Ñeembucú have already been evacuated. It is also unclear whether the flood will disrupt barge traffic, since none of the papers reported shipping restrictions.

What Comes Next

Itaipú’s forecast points to about 115 metres under the Friendship Bridge in the coming days. The daily Última Hora said local institutions are preparing to help more residents who may have to leave their homes.

The EBY’s forecast of higher flows means towns such as Ayolas and Cerrito face further rises as the water moves south. La Nación reported that the EBY said its forecasts could change with the weather.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where Is the Paraná River Flooding in Paraguay?

Families have been evacuated in the San Rafael district of Ciudad del Este and in Ayolas. The river is also rising at Cerrito, in Ñeembucú department.

How Many People Have Been Evacuated?

At least 60 families have left their homes in Ciudad del Este, according to local papers. No confirmed total for Ayolas or the rest of the country has been published.

How High Will the River Get?

Itaipú expects about 115 metres under the Friendship Bridge in the coming days, according to Última Hora and ABC Color. Its flood committee had measured 109.47 metres, according to La Nación and Última Hora.

Who Is Running the Evacuations?

Itaipú, the city government, volunteer firefighters and the military are leading the work. Naval prefecture staff are evacuating families near Ayolas.

Sources: La Nación, evacuations in Ciudad del Este, Cerrito and Ayolas; Última Hora, Ciudad del Este; ABC Color, Itaipú; ABC Color, Ñeembucú; ABC Color, Ayolas evacuations (all accessed 12 October 2026).

World.content:

TANZANIA · MARKETS

Key Facts — The country Tanzania is a large East African nation whose Dar es Salaam port serves landlocked neighbours such as Zambia and Rwanda.

— What happened On Monday 12 October, Finance Minister Khamis Mussa Omar met World Bank Vice President Ndiame Diop in Bangkok, the Swahili daily Mwananchi reported.

— The numbers Omar put 33 World Bank projects at US$8.8 billion; the bank’s website lists US$8.4 billion across 33 active operations.

— The IMF Tanzania drew about US$1.7 billion from the International Monetary Fund from 2022, and the fund completed its final programme reviews in July 2026.

— The economy Official data show 6.1% growth in the first quarter of 2026 and 4.3% inflation in September, inside the 3% to 5% target.

— Still open Tanzania has not said whether or when it will ask the IMF for a new programme, and no new World Bank loan was announced.

Tanzania has 33 World Bank projects worth US$8.8 billion, Finance Minister Khamis Mussa Omar told the bank’s regional vice president on Monday 12 October. They met in Bangkok, Thailand, at the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, the Swahili-language daily Mwananchi reported.

For US investors and contractors, the talks show where the money in one of East Africa’s main trade corridors is coming from. They also came as Tanzania weighs a new IMF programme after its last programmes with the fund ended this year.

What the Minister and the World Bank Discussed

Khamis Mussa Omar, who carries the title of ambassador, is finance minister in President Samia Suluhu Hassan’s government. He also represents Tanzania as its governor at the IMF and the World Bank, his ministry says.

He met Ndiame Diop, a Senegalese economist who is the World Bank’s vice president for Eastern and Southern Africa. Diop oversees the bank’s work across 26 countries, according to his official World Bank profile.

The World Bank is the Washington-based lender that funds roads, power and schools in poorer countries, and the United States is its largest shareholder. Its annual meetings with the IMF, held in Bangkok from 12 to 18 October, gather finance ministers and central bankers.

According to Mwananchi, Diop said the World Bank would remain an important partner in financing Tanzania’s strategic and regional projects. He named energy, education, rail, especially the Central Line from Dar es Salaam to Lake Tanganyika, and cash transfers for poor households.

Omar told the bank that revenue collection and spending were on track, with inflation inside the 3% to 5% target band. Figures from the National Bureau of Statistics show growth of 6.1% in the first quarter of 2026 and inflation of 4.3% in September.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the 33 World Bank Projects Cover

Omar valued the 33 World Bank projects at 23.2 trillion Tanzanian shillings (about US$8.8 billion), at 2,635 shillings to the dollar on 12 October 2026. They span industry, education, health, farming and social protection, Mwananchi reported.

The World Bank’s own country page lists a slightly smaller active portfolio of US$8.4 billion across 33 operations, as of 31 August 2026. These come from its International Development Association, the arm that lends to the poorest countries on soft terms.

Omar listed work on Dar es Salaam port, the Central Line and the new electric Standard Gauge Railway among the strategic projects under the partnership. He also named power lines to link Tanzania’s national grid with Zambia’s.

Dar es Salaam port is a main sea gateway for Zambia, Malawi, Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda and eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Faster railways and a bigger port can cut the cost of moving copper, cobalt and farm goods to the coast.

Social spending is part of the World Bank projects too, through the Tanzania Social Action Fund (TASAF). That state fund pays small cash transfers to poor households and hires villagers for public works.

Why the IMF Question Matters

The International Monetary Fund is the Washington-based lender that helps governments short of foreign currency, and the United States is also its largest shareholder. Its programmes come with targets on deficits, debt and reforms that investors watch closely.

Tanzania drew about US$1.7 billion from the IMF between 2022 and 2026, Omar said, according to Mwananchi. About US$1.063 billion came through the Extended Credit Facility, a low-cost loan for countries with long-running shortages of foreign currency.

Another US$636.5 million came through the Resilience and Sustainability Facility, which funds climate-related reforms and ended in August 2026, he said. The IMF board completed the final reviews of both programmes in July, releasing about US$443.8 million, The Citizen reported at the time.

Omar said Tanzania is now running an internal assessment of its needs before entering any new agreement with the fund. He gave no date for a decision.

Rating Agencies and a New World Bank Round

At a preparatory session of the Tanzanian delegation, Omar said Tanzania has sent a preliminary list of proposed World Bank projects for IDA21. That is the current funding round of the International Development Association, the bank’s fund for the poorest countries.

The Ministry of Finance also said Tanzania is in talks with the credit rating agencies Moody’s and Fitch and is courting new lenders. It added that the government may seek general budget support where needed to fund development programmes.

What It Means for US Readers

For US investors, the World Bank projects and the IMF decision show how Tanzania plans to pay for its railway, port and power plans. A new IMF deal would add outside checks on the budget, while going without one would test confidence in the country’s own plans.

For US bond investors, the talks with Moody’s and Fitch matter because credit ratings shape what Tanzania pays to borrow. Better ratings would also widen the pool of foreign lenders that the ministry says it is courting.

For US engineering, equipment and consulting firms, large contracts on World Bank projects are generally open to international bidding under the bank’s procurement rules. Ports, railways and power lines are the kind of work where such tenders appear.

For US companies trading with Zambia and eastern Congo, the port and rail upgrades matter as much as Tanzania’s own economy. Copper and cobalt from the region, used in batteries and wiring, can move to the sea through Tanzania.

What Is Not Known

The World Bank has not published its own account of Monday’s meeting, and no new loan figure was announced. The ministry has not explained why its US$8.8 billion figure for World Bank projects is higher than the US$8.4 billion the bank lists.

Tanzania has not said when its internal review of IMF needs will end, or how large a new programme might be. The fund has not commented on whether talks on a fresh arrangement have begun.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does the World Bank fund in Tanzania?

Finance Minister Khamis Mussa Omar says 33 World Bank projects in Tanzania are worth US$8.8 billion. The bank’s own website lists US$8.4 billion in 33 active operations as of 31 August 2026.

Who met in Bangkok on 12 October?

Tanzania’s Finance Minister Khamis Mussa Omar met Ndiame Diop, the World Bank’s vice president for Eastern and Southern Africa. They spoke on the sidelines of the World Bank and IMF annual meetings in Thailand.

Does Tanzania have an IMF programme now?

No. The IMF completed the final reviews of Tanzania’s two programmes in July 2026, after about US$1.7 billion in lending since 2022. The government is assessing its needs before any new agreement.

Which World Bank projects matter most for trade?

Omar listed Dar es Salaam port, the Central Line, the electric Standard Gauge Railway and a power link with Zambia. These routes carry goods for Zambia, Burundi, Rwanda and eastern Congo.

Why should US investors care?

The United States is the largest shareholder in both the World Bank and the IMF. Their lending shapes Tanzania’s debt, its budget and the contracts open to American firms.
