World.title: Costa Rica Raises Mandatory Vehicle Insurance Rates for 2027
World.content:
Anyone owning a car in Costa Rica will face higher mandatory insurance costs in 2027, with private vehicles, motorcycles and buses among the categories affected by increases approved today. The General Insurance Superintendency (Sugese) authorized an average 4.03% increase in mandatory automobile insurance premiums, citing a growing number of traffic accidents, more serious injuries and rising medical expenses.

The insurance, known here in Costa Rica as the Seguro Obligatorio de Automóviles (SOA), is included in the annual marchamo payment that vehicle owners must make to legally drive on public roads. For private passenger vehicles, the insurance premium will increase from ₡30,238 in 2026 to ₡31,881 in 2027, an increase of ₡1,643, or 5.43%.

Motorcycle owners will pay considerably more. Their mandatory insurance premium will rise from ₡99,623 to ₡104,110, an increase of ₡4,487, or 4.5%. Bus operators face the largest percentage increase, with premiums climbing 12.4%, from ₡81,060 to ₡91,108. Not every vehicle category will see higher insurance costs. Light commercial vehicles will receive an 8.9% reduction, bringing their premiums to ₡17,134, while heavy cargo vehicles will pay ₡34,170, a decrease of 2.4%.

Taxi insurance premiums will fall 7.5% to ₡67,799, while special equipment vehicles will receive a 9.6% reduction. The changes come as Costa Rica continues to struggle with a high number of traffic accidents, particularly those involving motorcycles. According to insurance figures, the country recorded 46,949 traffic accidents covered by mandatory insurance in 2025, compared with 40,590 the previous year.

The number of people injured in those accidents increased from 45,570 in 2024 to 52,269 in 2025, a rise of nearly 15%. The cost of providing insurance benefits also increased substantially, climbing from approximately ₡52 billion in 2024 to ₡60.2 billion in 2025. Those expenses include medical treatment, disability payments and other benefits provided to people injured in traffic accidents.

Motorcyclists continue to account for a disproportionate share of Costa Rica’s road casualties. In 2025, motorcycle riders represented 64% of people injured in traffic accidents and 52.4% of road fatalities. During the first eight months of 2026, they accounted for 58% of traffic deaths.

Despite the higher premiums, the amount of insurance coverage available to accident victims will remain unchanged. The mandatory policy provides a basic coverage limit of ₡6 million per injured person, a figure that has remained in place since 2016. The coverage applies to medical expenses, disability benefits and death-related compensation, subject to the policy’s legal conditions.

Insurance regulators have raised concerns that the existing coverage may no longer be sufficient to meet the growing cost of treating serious accident injuries. Sugese estimates that coverage of approximately ₡15 million would be needed to pay 90% of the total costs associated with traffic accidents, more than twice the current basic limit.

For now, however, no increase in the coverage limit has been approved for 2027. Another change awaiting motorists next year is the introduction of Costa Rica’s digital marchamo. The new system will use an electronic sticker designed to last up to 10 years, replacing the traditional annual windshield identification for vehicles included in the rollout.

The cost of the electronic device will be charged separately and is not included in the newly approved insurance premiums. For car owners, it is important to understand that the insurance premium represents only one part of the annual marchamo bill. The total payment also includes the vehicle ownership tax, road safety contributions, applicable municipal charges and any outstanding traffic fines.

As a result, a 5.43% increase in mandatory insurance for private cars does not necessarily mean the overall marchamo payment will rise by the same percentage. Likewise, owners of taxis and cargo vehicles who benefit from lower insurance premiums could still face different total marchamo charges depending on their vehicle’s value and other applicable fees.

The final amount each vehicle owner must pay will depend on the complete 2027 marchamo assessment, not just the insurance rates announced this week.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Lesser-Known Juan Castro Blanco Park Prepares for Tourists
World.content:
Construction is underway on new visitor facilities at Juan Castro Blanco National Park, a lesser-known protected area in northern Costa Rica, as officials work toward opening part of the park to tourists for the first time under a formal visitor program. The project is taking shape in the Volcán Viejo area, near in the canton of Sarchí. Plans include a visitor entrance, ticket office, cafeteria, souvenir shop, parking area and a nature trail designed to accommodate people with disabilities.

Recent photographs show work underway on the foundations of visitor facilities and improvements to the planned trail, as the construction marks another step in a project intended to make one of Costa Rica’s less accessible national parks available to a wider range of visitors.

The centerpiece of the project is a sensory nature trail that will allow visitors to experience the forest through sounds, scents and touch. The idea is to create an outdoor experience that children, older adults and people with disabilities can enjoy without facing many of the obstacles found on traditional hiking trails.

Plans call for an approximately 80-meter (262-foot) accessible walkway, five sensory viewing and rest areas, a lookout overlooking a river, safety railings, benches and signs designed for visitors with different accessibility needs. The nonprofit organization ProParques has been working with private companies and local partners to develop the project.

Part of that effort involves collecting discarded plastic bottle caps and recycling them into durable plastic lumber for accessible walkways and other facilities. The initiative is part of a broader effort to make Costa Rica’s national parks more inclusive while reducing plastic waste. The work is expected to create a new attraction in Bajos del Toro, an area already known for its waterfalls, mountains and nature tourism.

Much of the region’s tourism activity takes place on privately owned land, making the planned national park facilities a potentially important addition for travelers interested in exploring public protected areas. Juan Castro Blanco National Park covers approximately 14,308 hectares (35,356 acres) and forms part of the Arenal Huetar Norte Conservation Area.

The park protects mountain forests, rivers and natural springs that supply water to communities across northern and western Costa Rica.

Water conservation is one of the park’s principal purposes. Its forests also provide habitat for wildlife, including pumas, jaguars and numerous other species. The park’s management plan, updated last year, calls for expanding sustainable tourism while maintaining protection of its forests and water resources.

Work on the sensory trail was already progressing in September, when park staff, ProParques and Café Britt collaborated on improvements that included drainage work, stone placement and adjustments to the trail’s route. For travelers hoping to visit, however, an important distinction remains: the park is not yet officially open for regular tourism.

Costa Rica’s National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC) continues to list Juan Castro Blanco as closed to tourist visitation. Although earlier project announcements had suggested a September 2026 opening, that date has passed without the facilities opening to the public.

No new official opening date has been announced, and visitors should not assume the park is accessible simply because construction is underway.

Once the work is completed and the Volcán Viejo area formally opens, Juan Castro Blanco could give travelers another way to explore Costa Rica’s mountain forests while making a national park experience available to people who cannot easily use conventional hiking trails.

World.title: Court Vacancies Stall Second Immunity Request Against Rodrigo Chaves
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Supreme Court cannot send lawmakers a new request to lift the immunity of former President Rodrigo Chaves because it lacks the alternate justice needed to form a quorum, Constitutional Chamber Justice Jorge Araya told legislators Friday. The same day, the ruling party voted in committee against his reelection.

Araya made the remarks before the Legislative Assembly’s Appointments Committee in response to a question from Frente Amplio legislator Antonio Trejos about the risk of impunity. He described the situation as very serious and said the lack of an alternate had kept the court from sending its second accusation against Chaves to the Assembly.

The pending request concerns alleged electoral crimes tied to the use of a parallel financing structure in Chaves’s 2022 presidential campaign. Chaves, who now serves as Minister of the Presidency and Minister of Finance, holds immunity from prosecution unless the Assembly votes to lift it.

When the full Supreme Court acts as a tribunal, it must sit with a complete bench. Justice Paul Rueda asked to step aside from the case and his recusal was accepted, so an alternate justice must take his seat before the court can decide whether to forward the request. The Constitutional Chamber has had no alternate justices since mid-December 2025, when the terms of the 12 judges who held those posts expired. Votes in both the previous and current legislatures failed to fill the seats.

In late July, the Constitutional Chamber upheld a legal challenge against the Assembly and ordered it to put the appointments to a vote. The vote was never opened, and the list of 18 candidates was sent back to the Appointments Committee. The shortage has affected the processing of nearly 150 case files.

The appointments have been stalled for months by political disagreements within the committee, which the ruling Pueblo Soberano party controls. At the same session, the committee voted 4-3 against reelecting Araya to a second term as a full justice. Pueblo Soberano legislators Marta Esquivel, Yara Jiménez, Antonio Barzuna and Gerald Bogantes voted against him. Trejos and National Liberation Party (PLN) legislators Janice Sandí and Salvador Padilla voted in favor.

Barzuna said Araya had completed his term and should make way for new people and argued that the justice showed a political leaning toward the PLN. Esquivel pointed to Araya’s past posts in PLN governments. Trejos backed the reelection while saying he disagrees with many of Araya’s rulings, citing his work ethic and his defense of judicial independence. Padilla said past political involvement is not a crime and that no concrete evidence of bias had been presented.

The committee vote is not final. Under Article 158 of the Constitution, Supreme Court justices are automatically reelected unless at least 38 of the Assembly’s 57 legislators vote against them. Pueblo Soberano holds 31 seats, short of that threshold without opposition support.

Lawmakers have already turned down two earlier requests involving Chaves. In late September, the Assembly rejected a Supreme Court request to lift his immunity over an accusation of alleged extortion by a public official in the BCIE-Cariñitos case. Legislators later rejected a request from the Supreme Electoral Tribunal to investigate 15 complaints of alleged political interference.

The new request would be the second from the Supreme Court and the third overall to reach lawmakers. Patricia Solano, president of the court’s Third Chamber, warned of the alternate shortage in July. On Sunday, Solano formally announced her candidacy to preside over the Supreme Court.

Until the Assembly fills the alternate seats, the full court cannot rule on whether to send the electoral case to lawmakers, leaving the accusation against Chaves on hold.

World.title: Prosecutors Probe Clearing on Protected Land Beside Montezuma Waterfall
World.content:
Costa Rican prosecutors and the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) are investigating tree cutting and earthworks on a hillside facing the Montezuma waterfall, one of the best-known natural attractions on the southern Nicoya Peninsula. Inspectors from the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC) found that trees had been cut, undergrowth stripped and the slope terraced and filled near the Montezuma River and the falls, according to a SINAC technical report dated Sept. 11. The agency said its Cóbano office had no record of any permit for the tree cutting it observed.

The report puts the affected area at about 6,564 square meters (70,656 square feet), or roughly 1.6 acres. Of that, 554 square meters (5,963 square feet) is State Natural Heritage land, which is public property under special protection. The rest is private land. Within it, another 827 square meters (8,905 square feet) lies inside the river’s legally protected buffer zone.

On one property, inspectors documented a cleared strip 10 to 20 meters (33 to 66 feet) wide and about 70 meters (230 feet) long on steep ground directly facing the waterfall. Neighboring lots showed terraces and surface changes consistent with the use of heavy machinery.

The criminal case remains open and SINAC has sent additional information to the Public Prosecutor’s Office unit that handles agrarian and environmental crimes. No one has been charged, and authorities have not publicly identified the property owner or anyone responsible for the work.

The case began with a complaint from residents. In a letter dated July 21, the Montezuma Integral Development Association and about 200 neighbors asked SINAC and local authorities whether work carried out on the hillside since 2025 had the required environmental and municipal permits. Several other community and environmental groups from the Cóbano area later joined the complaint.

Residents said trucks hauled gravel, fill and stone to the site last year between August and November, with about 200 loads reportedly planned, to build gabion retaining walls and raise the ground. They said the property’s manager reacted with verbal hostility when they asked about the work.

According to the complaint, a municipal inspector told residents at the time that the work had permits and caused no environmental damage. That account has not been confirmed by the Cóbano District Council, which did not respond to press inquiries in August. Residents also reported rocks falling onto the riverbank below the retaining walls, near the trail that leads to the waterfall, partly blocking the path. Authorities have not announced any restriction on access to the falls.

SINAC first inspected the site on July 2 and it found about one hectare (2.5 acres) of altered land and no one on the property and referred the case to the OIJ. After a second visit on Aug. 12, Nelson Marín, regional director of the Tempisque Conservation Area, said the environmental violations were continuing and announced a halt to the work. SINAC later confirmed it had ordered a precautionary stop on one of the properties.

A follow-up inspection on Sept. 8 found no new tree cutting, only soil added to plant grass on an existing terrace. SINAC has said it still needs to establish what the land looked like before the work began and whether its vegetation met the legal definition of forest, which will determine whether an illegal change in land use occurred.

The waterfall, reached by a riverside trail from Montezuma village, is a major draw for visitors to the area. The Montezuma River received an ecological Blue Flag award in 2024. Montezuma’s laid-back village and nearby beaches are a frequent stop on Nicoya Peninsula itineraries. Legislator Norjelens Lobo Vargas has requested a certified copy of the conservation area’s case file. Authorities have not said when SINAC’s technical assessment will be completed or when prosecutors will decide whether to file charges.

World.title: National Kriol Council condemns ‘degrading racial caricatures’ on cover of Assad Shoman’s new history book
World.content:
National Kriol Council condemns ‘degrading racial caricatures’ on cover of Assad Shoman’s new history book

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The National Kriol Council (NKC) has strongly condemned what it describes as exaggerated and degrading racial imagery on the cover of historian Assad Shoman’s newly released A History of Belize in Thirteen Chapters, calling on the author and publisher to explain the controversial artwork.

In a statement issued on October 9, during Kriol Heritage Month, the Council said the depiction of Black figures on the cover evokes racist caricatures historically used to ridicule and dehumanize people of African descent.

The controversy surrounds the book’s Sapphire Edition, launched on October 9 at Angelus Press. The publication is the third edition of Shoman’s influential historical work, first published in 1994 and widely used in Belizean educational institutions. The latest edition includes updated material addressing the environment, economy, Guatemala’s territorial claim, and human rights.

While acknowledging the historical significance of Belize’s Coat of Arms, which features two woodcutters, the NKC argues that historical symbolism does not excuse imagery it considers offensive.

“Our ancestors were not caricatures. They were people whose labour, resilience, resistance, knowledge, and cultural contributions helped shape Belize,” the Council declared.

The organization called on Shoman and the publisher to explain the selection of the cover and reconsider whether it appropriately reflects the dignity of the people depicted. It also urged cultural authorities to ensure greater recognition of Kriol identity and Maroon heritage in official historical documentation.

The controversy had already attracted public criticism following the book’s release, with members of the Kriol cultural heritage community questioning whether the artwork resembles blackface caricatures. Love FM

The Council maintained that preserving historical records should not mean perpetuating the indignities of the colonial past.

“Our ancestors deserve dignity. Our history deserves truth. Our heritage deserves protection. Our identity deserves respect,” the statement declared.

The NKC concluded with a forceful message: “WE WILL NOT ACCEPT ERASURE.”

World.title: Taiwan thanks Belize, praises Francis Fonseca and blasts China’s sanctions as political intimidation
World.content:
Taiwan thanks Belize, praises Francis Fonseca and blasts China’s sanctions as political intimidation

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Taiwan has strongly condemned China’s decision to sanction Belize’s Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca, describing Beijing’s actions as political intimidation and an unacceptable interference in the sovereignty and foreign policies of independent nations.

In a statement issued Monday, October 12, Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the sanctions “preposterous” and accused China of attempting to coerce other countries into submitting to its political agenda through intimidation and transnational repression. The Ministry also described Beijing’s tactics as “despicable.”

The Taiwanese Embassy in Belize also publicly expressed appreciation for Belize’s continued support, posting a message thanking the government and people of Belize for standing firmly with Taiwan and fighting against what it described as oppression and intimidation from authoritarianism.

“We also wish to extend our utmost respect for Minister Hon. Francis Fonseca,” the Embassy stated in a message published on its official Facebook page.

Taiwan further maintained that it is a sovereign, independent country and that China has no right to interfere in its diplomatic relationships. It reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening cooperation with Belize and Paraguay, emphasizing that its partnerships are built on equality, mutual respect and shared democratic values.

China announced sanctions against Fonseca and Paraguay’s Communications Minister Gustavo Villate earlier Monday, imposing travel bans, restrictions on business dealings with Chinese entities and the freezing of any assets they may hold in China. Beijing accused both officials of undermining its sovereignty through their support for Taiwan.

The Government of Belize has also rejected the sanctions, declaring that the measures will not alter its foreign policy or deter it from maintaining diplomatic relations with Taiwan. Belize’s Foreign Ministry emphasized that Fonseca was carrying out his official duties in the national interest.

The diplomatic confrontation comes just weeks after Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung visited Belize and signed new cooperation agreements with Fonseca. Belize and Taiwan established diplomatic relations in 1989 and marked their 37th anniversary on October 11, just one day before China announced the sanctions.

World.title: Caribbean Court of Justice stops brother from evicting man who built and lived in home for decades
World.content:
Caribbean Court of Justice stops brother from evicting man who built and lived in home for decades

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Belizean man who built and lived in his family home for more than three decades has won the right to stay there, after a ruling by the Caribbean Court of Justice.

On October 8, a five judge panel of the CCJ ruled in favour of Ewart Leroy Robateau in a property dispute with his brother, Allen Robateau.

The court overturned earlier decisions by Belize’s Supreme Court and Court of Appeal, which had granted Allen possession of the property.

The CCJ found that the evidence clearly showed Ewart alone developed the property, built the house with his own money and paid for its construction, improvements and upkeep for about 34 years. The court said that family arrangement was known.

Allen obtained title to the property in 2017. The CCJ held that he did so with full knowledge of his brother’s long occupation and claim, and therefore could not use that title to force him out.

Justice Barrow said the lower courts “got it plainly wrong,” and that it would be “unconscionable” to allow Allen to evict his brother.

World.title: Taiwan condemns China’s sanctions on Fonseca
World.content:
Taiwan condemns China’s sanctions on Fonseca

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Taiwan has strongly condemned China’s decision to sanction Belize’s Foreign Minister, Francis Fonseca.

In a statement issued through its Embassy in Belize on Monday, October 12, Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it firmly rejects China’s announcement of sanctions against Fonseca and Paraguay’s Minister of Information and Communication Technologies, Gustavo Villate.

Taiwan described China’s announcement as absurd and said it amounts to open interference in the sovereignty and foreign policy of other countries, in violation of the principles of international law.

The Ministry said the move shows China’s attempt to use political intimidation and transnational repression to pressure other countries and undermine Taiwan’s longstanding friendships with Belize and Paraguay.

Taiwan also extended its sincere appreciation to the Government and people of Belize for standing firmly with Taiwan against oppression and intimidation.

“We also wish to extend our utmost respect for Minister Hon. Francis Fonseca,” the statement said.

World.title: Michel Chebat begins National Security work in the south with Punta Gorda police visit
World.content:
Michel Chebat begins National Security work in the south with Punta Gorda police visit

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Days into his new role, Minister of National Security Michel Chebat is making the rounds.

On Friday, he travelled to Toledo, where he and Dr. Osmond Martinez met with officers at the Punta Gorda Police Station.

The visit came on the same day Chebat attended the Belize Defence Force’s annual Senior Officers’ Conference in Belize City, where he introduced himself to the BDF leadership and shared his vision for the Force.

Chebat has said he plans to meet with leadership and personnel across his portfolio as he settles into the job, which now covers the Police, the BDF and the Coast Guard, as well as Energy and Ports.

His visit to Toledo also comes as the district grapples with security concerns in the south, including reported Guatemalan military activity near the Sarstoon.

Chebat says building trust and supporting officers on the front lines will be key to keeping communities safe.

World.title: Orlando Habet blames Town Council for empty El Cayo Boardwalk kiosks
World.content:
Orlando Habet blames Town Council for empty El Cayo Boardwalk kiosks

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Cayo Northeast Area Representative Orlando Habet says the El Cayo Boardwalk’s kiosks remain empty because the San Ignacio Santa Elena Town Council will not issue trade licences to prospective tenants.

In a statement responding to public criticism, Habet said there are four kiosks available for rent at the Boardwalk, and rental agreements have already been signed.

But according to Habet, when those tenants applied for the trade licences needed to begin operating, the Town Council refused to issue them, leaving them unable to open despite their willingness to invest.

Habet said he shares the public’s frustration over the empty kiosks and recognizes the economic opportunity they represent for local entrepreneurs.

He said he hopes the issue can be resolved through dialogue and cooperation with the Town Council.

“Its success should not be defined by political differences,” the statement said.

The San Ignacio Santa Elena Town Council, led by UDP Mayor Earl Trapp, has not yet publicly responded.

World.title: Belize rejects China’s sanctions against Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca, vows to maintain ties with Taiwan
World.content:
Belize rejects China’s sanctions against Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca, vows to maintain ties with Taiwan

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Government of Belize has firmly rejected sanctions imposed by the People’s Republic of China against Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca, declaring that the measures will neither influence Belize’s foreign policy nor weaken its longstanding diplomatic relationship with Taiwan.

In an official statement issued at 11:40 a.m. on Monday, October 12, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs defended Belize’s sovereign right to determine its international relationships without external interference or pressure.

The Ministry emphasized that Belize’s diplomatic relationship with Taiwan was established through an independent national decision and has delivered significant benefits in healthcare, education, infrastructure, agriculture, environmental protection and development.

It further stressed that Fonseca was carrying out his official responsibilities under the instructions of the Government of Belize and in the country’s national interest.

“Measures directed at an individual for carrying out the lawful duties of his office are unwarranted, and we reject them,” the Ministry declared.

China announced the sanctions earlier Monday, ordering the freezing of any assets Fonseca may hold in China, prohibiting Chinese organizations and individuals from conducting business with him, and barring him from entering mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau.

Beijing accused Fonseca of supporting Taiwan and undermining China’s sovereignty and national interests. Similar sanctions were imposed against Paraguay’s Communications Minister Gustavo Villate. Both countries are among Taiwan’s remaining 12 diplomatic allies.

The diplomatic confrontation follows a recent visit to Belize by Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung, during which the two countries signed new cooperation agreements aimed at strengthening bilateral relations.

Despite Beijing’s actions, Belize has made clear that its foreign policy will remain unchanged.

“The Government of Belize continues to stand fully behind Minister Fonseca,” the Ministry stated.

Belize also reaffirmed its commitment to peaceful international relations and dialogue, while calling on countries to refrain from unilateral coercive measures against foreign officials.

The Ministry indicated that Belize will consult with regional and international partners regarding the development and keep the Belizean public informed.

World.title: Police seeking Lequan Thomas for questioning
World.content:
Police seeking Lequan Thomas for questioning

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police are looking for Lequan Thomas, a 27 year old Belizean of Belize City.

According to Crime Stoppers Belize, Thomas is wanted for questioning in connection with a police investigation.

Police have not released details on the investigation.

Anyone with information on his whereabouts is asked to call Crime Stoppers at 922, use the P3 app, or report to the nearest police station.

World.title: Waterhouse fine sparks questions over JC star Lyle’s eligibility in schoolboy football
World.content:
Jamaica College forward Jamone Lyle (third left) gets away from St Catherine High School’s Caiden Yen (on ground) while his teammates Jaquan Brown and Davill Jarrett (right) look on during their ISSA Manning Cup game at Ashenheim Stadium in St Andrew on Wednesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

KINGSTON, Jamaica – A major controversy has erupted around Jamaica College’s (JC) 2026 Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) schoolboy football campaign following revelations that star player Jamone Lyle has signed a professional contract, potentially rendering him ineligible for high school competition.

The issue came to a head following a disciplinary letter issued by Jamaica Premier League club Waterhouse Football Club, who Lyle represents in that competition.

The letter, dated October 9, 2026, details a disciplinary hearing where Waterhouse FC fined Lyle $60,000 for “unauthorised participation” in a Manning Cup match on October 7, 2026. According to the club, Lyle ignored explicit instructions from head coach Donovan Duckie and general secretary Richard McCallum, prohibiting him from taking the field for JC, thereby breaching his professional contract and club rules.

Under longstanding ISSA regulations, student-athletes who have signed professional contracts or actively participate in professional senior leagues are strictly prohibited from competing in schoolboy competitions like the Manning Cup and Walker Cup.

Lyle, who recently earned his senior Reggae Boyz debut against El Salvador in the Concacaf Nations League, played a pivotal role in JC’s 3–2 victory days later and again last Saturday in the Walker Cup semifinal win against Mona High, where he scored in normal time and during JC’s penalty shootout victory.

The implications of Lyle’s involvement extend well beyond an internal club fine. ISSA rules mandate severe penalties for schools fielding ineligible or professional players, although they softened the rule, allowing students – who have not signed professional contracts – to compete in both competitions five days after playing in either.

In 2019, ISSA denied Portmore United’s Lamar Walker of Clarendon College from participating in schoolboy football after he went on a tryout to Brazilian club Vaco da Gama. Similarly, he had just made his senior debut for Jamaica.

World.title: Absent witness, IT issues delay Ruel Reid and Co trial
World.content:
Former Education Minister Ruel Reid heading to court.

An absent witness meant no evidence was elicited in the trial of former Education Minister Ruel Reid, Former head of the Caribbean Maritime University (CMU) Fritz Pinnock, and their co-accused at the Kingston and St Andrew Parish Court on Monday.

The trial also started late, as when parties arrived for 10:00 am, the technology used to facilitate virtual attendance and record the trial was not ready.

It meant the matter had to be stood down while the accused, defence attorneys, and the prosecution waited almost two hours for the requisite individual, with knowledge of how to operate the system, to arrive and set up.

When proceedings eventually got underway at almost 12:00 pm, Senior Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions Ashtelle Steele indicated to presiding Judge Sanchia Burrell that the witness scheduled to take the stand on Monday was unavoidably absent due to unforeseen circumstances.

Burrell noted, however, that the prosecution ought to have multiple witnesses on standby for situations such as this.

Steele, in response, shared that the order in which witnesses are being called had been reshuffled the week prior to facilitate defence attorneys and that had affected this week as well.

“So your ability to plan and organise your witnesses is still impacted by the attendance of the attorneys,” the judge said.

More than 90 witnesses are expected to be called in the fraud trial of the five accused, which also includes Reid’s wife and daughter Sharen and Sharelle Reid, and Jamaica Labour Party Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence.

While there are 35 counts in total in the trial, the accused are charged with different counts and different witnesses are expected to affect different and sometimes multiple accused.

While Burrell lauded the conciliatory approach taken by the prosecution in how the witnesses are being called and noted she was not interfering with it, she added that there comes a time when the Crown just has to proceed.

Steele emphasised strongly that, with the testimony of one witness expected to be called later this week, all accused persons need representation present.

She also noted that testimony expected this week would be document-heavy, adding that the arrangement in which some attorneys tune in via Zoom may not be suitable for that.

“We do not recommend that counsel be online,” she said.

Brown Lawrence’s attorney Oswest Senior Smith was represented in court by a junior while listening in via Zoom were Carolyn Chuck, who represents Sharelle Reid, and Linda Wright, who represents the former education minister.

Chuck held for Shannen Clarke, who represents Sharen Reid.

Several attorneys in the fraud trial, including Hugh Wildman, who represents Pinnock, and Wright, also sit in the ongoing murder trial of six policemen occurring simultaneously in the Supreme Court in downtown Kingston.

Burrell had previously warned Pinnock he could possibly have to cross-examine a witness himself during the Monday sitting if an attorney did not turn up to represent him.

In addressing him directly on Monday, she queried whether he wished to place anything on the record regarding representation.

He indicated that his attorney had shared an email but did not share the contents with the court.

In response, Burrell indicated that an email could not be placed on the record.

“There is a way that we practise in the court; it’s not ad hoc,” she said, highlighting procedure that had shortly before taken place with other attorneys indicating absences or holding.

“There is a way that things are done and I will not, under my stewardship, be deviating from the proper way that we were all taught to do things,” she maintained.

The judge added that she had never seen it done, where emails are sent regarding matters that must be on the record.

She added that there have also been some inappropriate actions, citing emails sent to the judge, with accused persons attached to the correspondence.

Pinnock requested he be allowed to take notes on his laptop to which Burrell agreed, but noted that certain safeguards would have to be put in place.

However, without a witness, the trial adjourned until Tuesday at 2:00 pm.

Prosecutors allege that between March 2016 and October 2019 the five accused participated in a scheme with others unknown, which siphoned off more than $25 million from both the Ministry of Education and CMU.

It is alleged that this money was funnelled through transfers to various accounts either owned or controlled by the accused, or handed over in cash.

The accused have all pleaded not guilty to the charges.

– Dana Malcolm

World.title: The 20-round loophole in the Firearms Act
World.content:
Four entries were made to the Licence Management System of a firearms dealer of three individuals purchasing a total of 6,000 12-gauge bird-hunting ammunition, without the request or consent of the dealer.

Even as defence lawyers protest the rigidity of the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, calling for a review by legislators, proponents have pointed to a section that allows offenders with up to 19 rounds of illegal ammunition to evade the mandatory minimum sentences being balked at by the legal fraternity.

If convicted under Section 45 of the Act for unauthorised possession of ammunition, the Sixth Schedule outlines the penalty for an unlicensed person as ‘on summary conviction before a parish court, a fine, not exceeding five million dollars, or imprisonment, for a term not exceeding five years’.

To the chagrin of proponents of the disputed Act, attorney-at-law Ruel Gibson of Stubbs, Gibson and Associates explained that the difference lies in the number of rounds as evidenced by Sections 5 and 10.

“It appears that Section 45 allows the parish court to deal with matters of illegal possession of ammunition by an unlicensed person, providing that the amount is under 20 rounds. Being in possession of 20 rounds, or more, as per Section 10, makes the offence tantamount to that of dealing in prohibited weapons, which becomes a Gun Court matter, carrying a minimum penalty of 20 years upon conviction,” Gibson remarked.

Explaining how an increased number of illegal rounds possessed by an unlicensed person further triggers mandatory minimum sentencing, Gibson pointed to Section 6 (1) (b).

“Section 6 deems the possession of 50 rounds or more to be stockpiling of prohibited weapons, which would result in a minimum penalty of 20 years. Therefore, evidently, under 20 rounds allows sentencing flexibility in the parish court,” Gibson added.

However, proponents of the Act have lashed out at illegal possession of ammunition being tried in the parish court, pointing to the capacity of most handguns, the murder weapons of choice for criminals, carrying a maximum of 18 rounds.

Criminologist Dr Jason McKay, an active serving police officer, agreed that aspects of the Act are in need of review, suggesting there should be a separate Act, distinguishing licensed firearm holders, who could easily be in possession of an extra round for many reasons including sport-shooting but was adamant that no leeway should be afforded unlicensed persons found in possession of illegal ammunition.

“It does not take more than one round to take a life,” McKay pointed out. “Homemade firearms with one round, ‘one-pop’ guns, will kill you as instantly as the most expensive pistol on the market.

“Gunmen do not walk around with extra magazines to put themselves in the 20-or-more category. Therefore, if a premises, or person, is searched and ammunition recovered, it will rarely ever exceed 17 rounds. Does that make any of those bullets less deadlier than 20 rounds?” McKay asked.

However, he shared concerns with the legal fraternity about the treatment of imitation firearms under the Act.

“Possession of imitation firearms should come down to a matter of circumstances and intent, particularly if used in the commission of a crime,” he said.

World.title: 7 Jamaicans feature on Rolling Stone’s ‘Best Albums of 1976’ list
World.content:
Albums by seven Jamaicans made Rolling Stone magazine’s 76 Best Albums of 1976 list, which was released on Sunday.

King Tubbys Meets Rockers Uptown by Augustus Pablo and King Tubby ranks the highest for Jamaicans, coming in at #5.

World.title: Seiveright apologises to Barita over social media post, acknowledges ‘unfair impression’
World.content:
Delano Seiveright

Government Minister Delano Seiveright has expressed regret over a social media post concerning the pilot rollout of a product by the Barita Financial Group, acknowledging that his comments may have created an “unfair impression” of the initiative. The minister has also issued an apology to the board and management of Barita, and has withdrawn the post.

“Having received further clarification, I regret any unfair impression my earlier posts may have created about Barita,” Seiveright said in a subsequent post on social media. “I apologise to its Board and staff, Chairman Mark Myers, CD, & Deputy Chairman Paul Simpson, CD, and have withdrawn the posts.

“I welcome Barita’s initiative, wish it continued success and remain committed to these broader principles,” he said.

Barita Financial Group has announced the controlled pilot rollout of BPay by Barita, a digital wallet offered by Barita Merchant Bank Limited, a deposit-taking institution licensed by the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ).

In a statement Sunday, the company noted that the initiative is “focused on bringing digital financial services directly to communities, campuses and workplaces.”
