World.title: By-election breach
World.content:
In this file photo, Jamaicans wait in line to cast their ballots at a polling station in rural Jamaica.

CITIZENS Action for Free and Fair Elections (CAFFE) has joined calls for municipal corporations to hold four overdue by-elections, warning that the prolonged vacancies are leaving constituents without representation and undermining democratic accountability.

Speaking at a Jamaica Observer Press Club at CAFFE’s New Kingston offices last Thursday, former Chairman Dr Lloyd Barnett described the municipalities’ failure to fill the vacancies as a disregard of the law.

“They have completely ignored the law… There are four vacancies now. That’s a great concern to CAFFE,” Barnett argued.

CAFFE is an internationally acclaimed independent organisation that monitors voting locally and, in recent years, across the region. Its observers assess whether democratic principles are upheld, including ballot secrecy and freedom from intimidation.

The organisation has observed multiple elections since its establishment in 1997.

Barnett’s call for action follows a warning issued by the Electoral Commission of Jamaica (ECJ) in March 2026 — when it wrote to Morant Bay Mayor Louis Chin, Savanna-la-Mar Mayor Danree Delancy, and Kingston Mayor Andrew Swaby — highlighting their responsibility to fill vacancies for councillors within the stipulated time period.

The commission reminded mayors that, in accordance with the Representation of the People Act, a by-election is to be held within approximately three months of the vacancy in an electoral division being recorded in the minutes of a municipal corporation.

The vacancies arose after three sitting councillors — Yvonne Rosemarie Shaw, Dennis Gordon, and Delroy Williams — were elected Members of Parliament in the September 3, 2025 General Election, while Councillor Patrick Forrester (People’s National Party, Petersfield Division) in Westmoreland died in a motor vehicle crash on September 17 last year.

Shaw was the People’s National Party (PNP) councillor for the Morant Bay Division in St Thomas; while Gordon, the PNP represetnative for Maxfield Park Division, and the Jamaica Labour Party’s Williams, a former Kingston mayor, represented the Seivwright Gardens Division, both in the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC).

At the time, Mayor Swaby acknowledged the commission’s notice and had indicated that conversations would begin in short order to stage by-elections in the Maxfield Park and Seivwright Gardens divisions, which were represented by the People’s National Party’s Gordon and the Jamaica Labour Party’s Williams, respectively.

As Swaby delivered his statements and announcements during a monthly KSAMC meeting, he explained that the election process was delayed due to the impact of last October’s Hurricane Melissa.

According to him, conducting polls in the immediate aftermath of the Category 5 storm, which devastated Jamaica’s south- and north-western parishes, would have been distasteful.

“Councillors will recall that the by-elections to fill these vacancies were due by mid-December 2025.

However, in the aftermath of the significant destruction caused by Hurricane Melissa on October 28, 2025, I wrote the Honourable Desmond McKenzie, [minister of local government], seeking an extension of the time within which the KSAMC could complete these by-elections.

“While the parishes of Kingston and St Andrew were spared the most severe direct impact, the entire country was actively involved in helping persons affected to put their lives back in order.

I strongly believe it would have been highly insensitive to engage the residents in an election at that time,” said the mayor.

Nearly a year since Hurricane Melissa, and six months since the ECJ’s written notice, all four vacancies remain unoccupied, leaving residents unrepresented. “That, in fact, illustrates the importance of continuous vigilance.

Because here is an important part of your democracy and you have people not being represented over here because the Government and the authorities failed to act,” Barnett said, urging the municipalities to fill the vacancies as soon as possible.

World.title: Observer, NEPA launching Fi Wi Land environmental series October 19
World.content:
This video grab shows National Environment and Planning Agency Environmental Officer Damany Calder being interviewed by Jamaica Observer online reporter Carlysia Ramdeen for the first in an environmental series being launched October 19 by the State agency and the newspaper.

BATS have long been the subject of fear, folklore, and ‘duppy’ stories but these creatures we’ve spent generations running from are some of nature’s hardest-working environmental protectors.

A single insect-eating bat can consume up to 1,000 mosquitoes in an hour, providing natural pest control, while others help pollinate plants and disperse seeds, contributing to the regeneration of our forests.

Jamaica is home to an impressive 21 species of bats, including five found nowhere else in the world and eight others native to the wider Caribbean.

Yet, despite their importance, bats remain among the island’s most misunderstood creatures.

We’re putting bats in the spotlight in the premiere episode of Fi Wi Land, a brand-new environmental series from the Jamaica Observer and the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) as part of the agency’s activities in recognition of its 25th anniversary of serving the island.

Over the next 12 weeks we’ll explore the wildlife, ecosystems and natural resources that make Jamaica unique while highlighting NEPA’s work to safeguard our environment for future generations, including air and water quality management, tree reforestation, coral reef restoration, beach conservation, protection of Jamaica’s iguana population, and mangrove restoration.

The first episode of Fi Wi Land premieres October 19, 2026, on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and social media platforms.

World.title: $96 billion in missed opportunities
World.content:
NEARLY $100 billion allocated to Jamaica’s capital budget over the past decade went unspent, leaving major road, water, and health infrastructure projects severely underfunded and depriving Jamaicans across the island of critical improvements, Opposition Senator Ramon Small-Ferguson has charged.

He made the claim during his contribution to the State of the Nation Debate in the Senate on October 9, arguing that the Government’s failure to utilise the allocated funds has hampered investment in essential public infrastructure.

According to Small- Ferguson, the economic reforms that started under the Portia Simpson Miller Administration, when Dr Peter Phillips was finance minister, created the fiscal space from which the current Andrew Holness-led Government has benefited.

But, he lamented what he called “missed opportunities”.

Citing that the country’s capital budget finances roads, water systems, hospitals, and other infrastructure that improve public services and expand our capacity to grow, Small-Ferguson said, “Budgeting for that investment is a commitment.

Delivering it is the responsibility [of Government].” The Opposition senator told Parliament that over the 10 financial years from 2016/17 to 2025/26, approximately $635.7 billion was originally budgeted for capital expenditure by central government.

Of that amount, approximately $539.4 billion was actually spent.

“That is a cumulative shortfall of $96.3 billion,” he noted.

Small-Ferguson highlighted that actual expenditure fell below the original allocation in nine of the 10 years.

He said approximately $61.8 billion of the cumulative gap arose through budget reductions while another $34.5 billion remained unspent against revised allocations.

The lawmaker, who is also chief executive officer at Barita Investments Limited, outlined that in 2023/24 the Government originally budgeted $75.4 billion and spent $55.9 billion, leaving a $19.5-billion gap.

In 2024/25, delivery fell $22.5 billion short of the original allocation, while in 2025/26 it was $14.8 billion short.

Reiterating that this was a “massive missed opportunity”, Small-Ferguson stated that a $96.3-billion shortfall could fund a “massive programme of works”.

“It could fit four Cornwall Regional Hospital redevelopments; it could fit two SPARK programmes; we could build 10 Spanish Town Hospital redevelopment projects; we could do seven Rio Cobre Water Treatment projects; we could build 100 health centres with this money,” he said.

“Together, these amount to approximately $92.5 billion — still $3.8 billion below the shortfall.

This comparison illustrates the scale of roads, water systems, hospitals, and community health care that could have been advanced through more consistent investment and delivery,” he added.

Small-Ferguson argued that delay carries a cost, as transport operators pay for repairs, farmers lose time and produce reaching markets, businesses lose productive hours without reliable water, and patients wait for improved facilities.

“We pay through higher eventual costs and years of benefits foregone,” he insisted.

He also acknowledged that the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent hurricanes imposed extraordinary demands on the budget but argued that they cannot explain a delivery problem that persisted across the decade, “including in the better years when we had the opportunity to strengthen Jamaica before the next crisis”.

“Again, I say that we did not take sufficient advantage of those years.

Roads, water systems, and health facilities that could have strengthened communities and supported production remained undelivered.

We entered harder times still carrying weaknesses we should have addressed,” he argued.

“This is one reason we struggle to grow.

Businesses need reliable infrastructure to expand.

After 10 years, procurement difficulties and capacity constraints cannot remain recurring explanations without a programme to correct them.

Jamaicans should not face the next crisis still waiting for projects promised before the last one,” Small-Ferguson said.

He made several recommendations to the Government that he said could reverse the current trend.

Among them was that within six months the Government should lay before Parliament a programme identifying the principal sources of delay, the reforms required, the institution responsible for each reform, and its implementation deadline.

World.title: Northern Ireland secretary denies he ‘bent the knee’ to Sinn Féin
World.content:
Democratic Unionist leader Gavin Robinson accused Bryant of bowing to a threat of violence from Irish Republican Army militants who featured prominently within the Garvaghy Road crowd. Most IRA members have observed a cease-fire since 1997 and officially disarmed in 2005, but several small factions still plot occasional bomb and gun attacks.

Robinson said Northern Ireland’s unionists “know that this British government has bent the knee to them.”

But Bryant said his decision to bar the Orangemen — despite a decision last month by the region’s independent Parades Commission to permit a heavily restricted march by 35 Orangemen — had so far kept violence at bay.

“I utterly reject the charge that I have in any way succumbed to mob rule. The truth is, things have actually passed remarkably peacefully,” he said, adding: “I don’t think anybody seriously proposed that the police should drag people off the street.”

He spoke hours after two courts in Northern Ireland tangled with the conflict of rights stirred up by the revival of the Orange marching demands in Portadown, a sectarian dispute that triggered bloodshed and rioting across Northern Ireland in the mid-1990s.

The Court of Appeal, overseen by Northern Ireland’s highest judge, rejected a lawsuit by the Garvaghy Road protesters seeking to challenge the original Parades Commission ruling. Orange supporters said this judgment kept the door open for an eventual parade down Garvaghy Road for the first time since 1997, when police backed by British soldiers forced the parade through with the use of armored vehicles and volleys of plastic bullets.

World.title: Germany, Italy request ‘emergency brake’ power to stop new EU laws
World.content:
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz meet on the morning of a European council summit, Thursday 19 March 2026 in Brussels. | Benoit Doppagne/Belga/AFP via Getty Images

EU capitals must be able to intervene to stop new legislation from Brussels if they say it’s too burdensome for governments and businesses, the leaders of Germany, Italy and Belgium wrote on Monday.

In a letter addressed to European Council President António Costa and seen by POLITICO, the three leaders said the bloc needs an “emergency brake” mechanism to help boost its flagging economic competitiveness.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Belgian Prime Minister Bart de Wever also called to “significantly accelerate planning and approval procedures,” suspend “certain regulatory areas for a specified period” under a new “priority rule.”

World.title: Von der Leyen pitches AI as solution to reduce reporting for European businesses
World.content:
"And this is why we will introduce 'Only Once', to report data only once – and with the help of AI the administration will ensure efficient use," she said.

The speech marks the first time von der Leyen has explicitly pitched using AI specifically to reduce businesses' administrative workload.

The "only once" principle itself is not new. The Commission already included it in its EU Inc. proposal presented in March 2026, which aims to create a harmonized corporate framework allowing companies to establish and operate businesses more easily across the bloc.

Under the EU Inc. proposal, companies could submit information once through an EU-level digital interface, with relevant data automatically transmitted between authorities. However, the proposal does not specifically envisage using AI to carry out that process.

Von der Leyen did not provide details on how the AI-supported system would operate, whether it would apply to all businesses or when the Commission intends to introduce it.

In her speech, the Commission president also encouraged governments to get on board with simplification efforts by signing a pact not to add extra requirements when transposing EU-mandated legislation into national regulations.

World.title: NATO’s top general lays out plan to fight Russia — with or without America
World.content:
The rare intervention by the four-star general to discuss a military blueprint underscores NATO’s effort to deter Russia. It is also aimed at sending a message of NATO unity after a grueling year for the alliance, which was rocked by Donald Trump’s threats to annex Greenland and infighting over the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran.

Under the three-part blueprint, NATO would initially use land-based troops — buttressed by air, naval, cyber and space capabilities — to stop an assault, targeting attacking forces and preventing them from seizing territory, Grynkewich said.

NATO would then use sensors and autonomous systems among other capabilities to “overwhelm enemy formations … and their advance,” he said, before using “highly effective precision munitions” and unmanned systems if necessary to “break the [enemy] warfighting system” and “everything that supports” it.

Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said the theory laid out by Grynkewich “will send a strong message to our adversaries that we are going to defend ourselves.”

NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe said he does “not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable.” But “we will … ensure any attack against any ally proves utterly futile.”

The speech describes a more forceful response if a foe attacks, but its credibility depends on allies having the forces, infrastructure, and coordination to implement the plan.

World.title: Burnham: Iran’s IRGC ‘highly likely’ to be behind RAF Fairford terror plot
World.content:
“Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable,” they said, warning they would ensure “those responsible are held to account.”

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the Iranian ambassador to London had been summoned to the Foreign Office and warned Britain “will not tolerate threats on our soil.”

The incident near the RAF Fairford airbase — which the U.S. has used to conduct defensive strikes against Iran — took place on Sept. 27.

Seven men have been arrested as part of an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing. All have been released on bail.

The force said last week it is considering "possible foreign state involvement" as part of its enquiries.

Speaking in the House of Commons on Monday, Burnham said: "We will not tolerate these threats on our soil."

World.title: UK and EU agree to hold Brexit ‘reset’ summit on Nov. 20
World.content:
Burnham told the Commons he wanted to secure a deal on the agreements — begun by previous Prime Minister Keir Starmer — and then begin a “calm, clear-eyed, rational look” at even closer relations.

“If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have,” he said.

“Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain. Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away.”

He added: “Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.”

The prime minister also said the meeting would present an opportunity to “raise our concerns about Made In Europe” — the EU’s program of protectionism which some countries want to exclude the U.K.

Burnham has previously suggested these future options could include rejoining the single market, customs union, or even the EU wholesale.

World.title: Farage would take a ‘keen look’ at UK’s support for ‘corrupt’ Ukraine
World.content:
The Ukrainian embassy in London declined to comment.

The U.K. has committed £25 billion to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion, according to government figures published in July 2026. That includes £16 billion of military support, up to £5.6 billion in non-military support and a £3.5 billion cover limit for export finance.

Farage was answering questions at a press conference after Donald Trump deepened the gulf between Washington D.C. and Kyiv by saying he would suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports. After Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the deal, Trump said Saturday: “It’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”

Farage, an old ally of Trump who previously spoke at his campaign rallies, said he did not agree with the U.S. president’s decision to buy diesel from Russia, but criticized EU nations for “buying vast amounts of Russian petrochemicals” during the course of the war.

Farage also declined to agree with Trump’s call for regime change, saying: “I understand that Trump and Zelenskyy have a somewhat tempestuous relationship, so it’s not any particular surprise. At some point, Ukraine needs an election. That’s true if it is to be a country that aspires to have Western-style values. As to when that election comes, we’ll have to see. After all, we did have an election during World War Two.”

Asked if there is a limit to his support for Ukraine, Farage added: “No one’s support for Ukraine is limitless, is it? Is [U.K. Prime Minister] Andy Burnham’s support for Ukraine limitless? No, it’s not. But do we need to go on supporting Ukraine?

World.title: EU approves biggest Russia sanctions package since invasion began
World.content:
“This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” Kaja Kallas said.

The EU approved its biggest package of sanctions against Russia since the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, targeting the Kremlin’s ability to make missiles.

The bloc’s foreign ministers approved the package during a meeting in Luxembourg, adding 1,600 new listings “targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex,” the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas said on X.

“This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war,” she added. “More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles.”

World.title: Ceuta troops absent as Spain holds National Day parade in Madrid
World.content:
Ceuta made its presence felt at Spain's National Day parade without a single one of its soldiers setting foot on Madrid's Paseo del Prado.

 

No troops from the autonomous city took part this year, as the Spanish Ministry of Defence has kept its forces deployed there following the crisis that erupted in July, when tens of thousands of migrants crossed into the territory from Morocco.

King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, who presided over the ceremony in Madrid, will travel to Ceuta on Tuesday.

The parade took place against a tense political backdrop, after Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called an early general election for 29 November.

Sánchez arrived at the parade with parliament dissolved and was met with jeers from people gathered in the streets.

Under clear skies, 82 aircraft took part in an aerial display as part of the day's events, led by two F/A-18 jets.

On the ground, the army’s 8x8 Dragón armoured vehicles took centre stage for the first time. Marine Corps vehicles equipped with the Aracne anti-drone system also made their debut, along with two Asturcón drones from the Military Emergencies Unit - a clear sign of where the Spanish Defence Ministry is looking to invest.

A total of 3,850 men and 530 women took part in the parade.

The King and Queen then hosted a reception at the Royal Palace to mark the end of the National Day celebrations.

World.title: Portugal begins construction of high-speed rail line linking Lisbon and Porto
World.content:
Construction of a high-speed rail line (LAV) linking Lisbon and Porto began in Portugal on Monday, with work starting on the first section between Porto-Campanhã and Oiã, in the district of Aveiro.

 

Once completed, the line will enable passengers to travel between the two cities in 1 hour and 15 minutes.

According to the government, the high-speed project is a key part of the country's national airport strategy, supporting the new Lisbon airport, and will also help strengthen rail links with Spain.

The government says the project will help set up a roughly three-hour journey between Lisbon and Madrid by 2034.

“Alongside the new Lisbon airport, high-speed rail lines represent the largest infrastructure projects the country will undertake this century," Miguel Pinto Luz, Portugal's minister of infrastructure and housing, said.

"It is therefore crucial that there be - as I know there is - a strong national consensus regarding high-speed rail and, more generally, the importance of investment in the railway system," he added.

The Porto-Oirã section is to comprise 71 kilometres of high-speed railway line, including a new road-rail bridge over the Douro River, a new station at Vila Nova de Gaia-Santo Ovídio, and the expansion and redesign of the Porto-Campanhã Intermodal Station.

The concession contract for the Porto-Oiã section, signed on 29 July 2025, will cost around €2 billion, the government says, adding that it would receive €875 million in financing from the European Investment Bank and €480 million from the Connecting Europe Facility.

"This project, structured as a Public-Private Partnership (PPP), is pivotal for the public passenger transport ecosystem and serves as a key structural element for the region," the Ministry of Infrastructure and Housing says, adding that it "aligns with the European Commission's objectives of doubling passenger rail traffic, complementing conventional rail lines and fostering a multimodal, sustainable approach alongside other mobility alternatives."

World.title: French navy intercepts and boards 'shadow fleet' ship, Macron says
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron announced on Monday that the French navy had intercepted and boarded an oil tanker suspected of being involved in illegal fuel-trafficking activities.

 

The operation took place 450 nautical miles south of the island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean, according to Macron.

"Our French Navy boarded the oil tanker DF Peak, which is suspected of sailing under a false flag and of being involved in illicit fuel-trafficking activities," he wrote in a post on social media, whilst also sharing video footage appearing to show troops rappelling down onto the vessel.

He added that France remained "determined to combat the ‘shadow fleet’ wherever it may be in the world."

Catherine Vautrin, France's minister for the armed forces, congratulated those who took part in the operation and said the French military was escorting the DF Peak for further checks, under the authority of the prefect of Réunion.

Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence (GUR) says the vessel is involved in the transportation of Russian crude oil and that it is associated with the Sovcomflot shipping firm.

The ship was built in 2006 and has sailed under multiple flags, per the GUR.

In June, French forces also intercepted the Russian shadow fleet tanker "Deliver" as it was sailing off the coast of Sicily "in violation of maritime law," Macron announced at the time.

Russia's shadow fleet enables the country to evade Western sanctions on its energy sector, which prevent it from chartering or insuring oil tankers unless it complies with certain restrictions.

The shadow fleet bypasses these restrictions by making use of complex ownership structures, flags of convenience, and other tactics designed to conceal the origin of its cargo.

A number of other European countries have reported intercepting Russian shadow fleet vessels in recent months.

World.title: Citroën's iconic 2CV returns as an all-electric model
World.content:
It is one of the most eagerly awaited stars of the Paris Motor Show, which will open its doors in the French capital from 13 to 18 October: Citroën’s legendary 2CV is making a major comeback almost forty years after disappearing from the market, in a fully electric version.

 

With its V-shaped bonnet, upright windscreen and distinctive round headlights, the new city car keeps the lines of its ancestor, as well as its down-to-earth, popular DNA.

Launched in 1948 and produced until 1990, the 2CV left its mark on several generations of drivers, becoming one of the symbols of France’s post-war boom years and the first holiday getaways, with more than five million units built in all versions combined.

Simplicity, versatility and an affordable price

Just like the original model, this new 2CV is built around simplicity, versatility and an affordable price tag, at around €15,000.

"The 2CV became an icon not because of what it had, but because of what it allowed people to do. And today that spirit is back," said Citroën’s chief executive Xavier Chardon during the 2CV’s unveiling at the motor show.

To keep costs down, Stellantis is betting on a car weighing under one tonne, fitted with a small battery tailored to everyday journeys. Still at the concept-car stage, the new 2CV is expected to go on sale at the end of 2028, to coincide with the 80th anniversary of the original model, and could even be offered as a small van.

The switch to electric is being helped along by purchase incentives in France, where battery-powered vehicles reached the record level of 42% of new registrations in September. The trend is driven in particular by small electric models and by the state-backed social leasing scheme, with around 9,500 registrations over the past month.

Faced with mounting competition from Chinese brands, which are set to have a strong presence at the show, other European manufacturers are also turning to affordable electric cars, such as the new Dacia Spring or Volkswagen’s ID. Polo.

World.title: French investigators use DNA and vehicle tracking to solve stolen Renoirs case
World.content:
Investigators in France used DNA evidence and vehicle tracking to help recover two paintings worth millions of euros that were stolen from a Renoir museum last month.

 

Four men have been handed preliminary charges after the impressionist artist's "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano" and "Young Woman at the Well" works were taken from the Musée Renoir in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French riviera in a daring September heist.

The suspects are believed to have gained entry to the museum after sawing through a fence using an electric saw. They then cut clips securing four paintings before an alarm went off.

Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone told reporters on Monday that this caused the suspects to panic and that they abandoned two paintings as they fled. These were apparently later found in a protective cover.

Bessone said a breakthrough came when DNA found on an abandoned cover matched that of a 29-year-old who was already being investigated by police in a drug trafficking case, and that the man's vehicle was being tracked as part of the investigation.

Tracking data showed that the suspect and a 41-year-old man had visited the home of a third man after the theft took place, per Bessone.

Investigators believed a plot to carry out another heist was also in motion, after surveillance found the 29-year-old had visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence on 3 October. The Maeght Foundation opened in 1964 and is home to works from celebrated artists including Pierre Bonnard, Georges Braque, and Alberto Giacometti.

The suspect is then said to have met up with another man who is known to police from art theft and forgery cases in the early 2000s.

The arrests were prompted by the "very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent," Bessone said.

The third suspect hid the paintings behind a wall under a staircase following the theft, from where investigators recovered the Renoirs, he added.

World.title: Spain: National Day highlights territorial unity from Barcelona to Ceuta
World.content:
In Barcelona, about 2,000 demonstrators waved Spanish and Ceuta flags at a rally supporting Spain’s territorial integrity, under the slogan “Catalonia with Ceuta, one Spain”. Meanwhile, Vox leader Santiago Abascal travelled to Ceuta, where he laid a wreath in honour of those who died for Spain. He had chosen to mark Spain’s National Day in the North African enclave rather than attend the military parade in Madrid.

 

His visit came amid renewed focus on migration and Ceuta’s disputed status: Morocco claims sovereignty over the Spanish-administered territory. More than 70,000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July; most returned within days, but thousands remained, putting pressure on local resources.

On Sunday, police, backed by soldiers, cleared the last major migrant encampment at El Guano. More than 350 officers took part in the operation, two days before King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia were due to visit Ceuta. The royal couple are also scheduled to travel to Melilla on 14 October, their first visit to the two enclaves since 2007.

World.title: Blindsided again by Trump, Europe puts on a brave face and rallies behind Ukraine
World.content:
Europe is once again trying to save face after US President Donald Trump blindsided the continent by striking a tailored deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to release thousands of tonnes of diesel that had until now been sanctioned.

 

The news alarmed Ukraine and its European allies, who have long been wary of Trump's unpredictable diplomacy and his understanding of what a just and lasting peace means.

Tensions between the two sides of the Atlantic have never fully receded since February last year, when Trump unexpectedly called Putin and launched negotiations to end the war without consulting any European leader in advance.

That was the start of a series of unexpected developments that have rattled Europe and upended its long-held assumptions about the post-war international order. These include a hastily organised Trump-Putin summit in Alaska, a leaked 28-point plan heavily favourable to Moscow and a sanctions waiver for Russian crude oil.

The diesel deal, announced on Friday on Truth Social, added yet another chapter.

Trump then resorted to a familiar pattern: public attacks against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's legitimacy and calls for fresh elections. Ukraine's constitution bars elections in wartime, a point that Zelenskyy tends to remind Trump.

"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Trump said to Moscow's applause.

As in previous episodes, Europe finds itself scrambling to close ranks, rally behind Ukraine and make clear that, regardless of what the White House does and says, this side of the Atlantic will stay the agreed course.

"I think we need to be collectively serious. Today, I believe, we have no factual reason to change our position," French President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday.

Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Vladimir Putin. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said emulating the Trump-Putin diesel deal was "out of the question" for Europe, despite rising energy prices.

"Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, and that is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia," Merz told reporters.

A similar message echoed through Luxembourg as EU foreign ministers met and insisted that the pressure campaign on Moscow would continue unabated. Some openly decried the diesel deal, calling it regrettable and concerning.

Foreign ministers also approved a record-breaking addition of 1,600 names to the sanctions list, half of them linked to the production of ballistic missiles that fall on Ukraine. The contrast between the EU and the US could hardly have been starker.

"We showed unity today on these (1,600) listings," High Representative Kaja Kallas said at the end of the meeting.

"But, of course, it would be much stronger if we had acted together with the US. Our message to the United States is that only pressure works with Russia."

United in strain

Although the Trump-Putin deal fits a familiar pattern of erratic diplomacy that sidelines European interests, its grim context sets it apart.

The diesel deal comes at a time when Russia is rapidly escalating its attacks against Ukraine, killing scores of civilians and wrecking the levers that sustain the local economy, including power stations, data centres, warehouses and railways.

Russia's blockade in the Black Sea has left Ukrainian farmers unable to send tonnes of grain to their global clients and deprived the state of an essential revenue source.

As economic activity stagnates and material costs pile up, the EU is realising its multibillion-euro lines of support will fall short sometime next year. With the US out of the picture, the burden is set to fall on the European pocket.

The prospect of Russia selling diesel that had until now been sanctioned and making extra money to finance the bombs that rain down on Ukraine is particularly difficult to stomach for Kyiv and its allies. It also raises serious questions about how much the US can be trusted to provide security guarantees for the post-war scenario.

And yet, Europe's collective assessment remains that there is still more to lose than to gain from breaking away from the Americans.

"What we need to do is refocus and redouble our efforts in keeping pressure on Russia," Ireland's Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said on Monday.

"Our priority has to be to maintain that pressure, but also to maintain our channels with the US, because this is not going to be achievable without the support of the US."

Ukraine is bracing for a cruel winter. AP Photo

Just as news of the diesel deal broke, senior officials from Ukraine, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the European Commission and NATO were in Miami, Florida, for a round of talks hosted by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's special envoys.

The meeting was the first of its kind since the outbreak of the US-Iran war, which has absorbed the White House's foreign policy and relegated Ukraine to the second row.

"We will continue to engage with our partners and also with the US in bringing this war to a close, and the latest example of this has been the talks on Friday in Miami," the Commission's chief spokesperson said, describing the meeting as a "positive step".

Europe initially struggled to secure a seat at the negotiating table as Trump and Putin marched ahead with their private calls. It took months after European countries established the “Coalition of the Willing” for them to be brought into the US-led negotiating process.

The statements from Brussels confirm that retaining a seat at the table where Ukraine’s future as a sovereign state and Europe’s security architecture will be decided takes precedence over any diplomatic slight, however pointed or public.

Zelenskyy, whose country is already suffering blackouts ahead of a winter expected to be the harshest yet of the war, agrees that the transatlantic alliance must prevail, notwithstanding the deals that might be cut behind its back.

"An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here – in reality, not just on Truth Social," Zelenskyy said.

"We need to end Russia's war. We need to guarantee security. We need to stand together. Europe and the United States."

World.title: EU struggles to ramp up Red Sea mission as Houthis escalate attacks
World.content:
The EU’s Red Sea naval mission is struggling to attract reinforcements, with only the Netherlands and Belgium offering one extra vessel each, while the Houthis escalate their attacks on Riyadh.

 

Italy has been driving the push to bolster Aspides, the EU naval operation launched in February 2024 to secure navigation in the Red Sea. But little extra capacity has materialised, and the security situation has worsened.

"We need at least ten ships, and we are not there. But today we also heard from a few member states that the discussion is ongoing," EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas said at a press conference after the Foreign Affairs Council on Monday.

"So I hope that the ships the operation actually needs will materialise, because if we want to be a credible security provider in the region, then we need to have a credible mission," she added.

On 19 September, Kallas sent a letter to European capitals asking member states for additional naval and air assets to strengthen the EU’s presence in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical chokepoint for energy supply.

The initiative followed an Italian request, after an Italian frigate had to escort an Italian merchant vessel off Yemen’s coast. Since it became operational, Aspides has escorted hundreds of vessels in the Red Sea.

In recent days, the Houthis, a Yemeni armed group backed by Iran, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi Arabia, hitting Riyadh’s international airport and causing a total of 14 deaths and more than 300 injuries.

The mission was set up after the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas war and a surge in attacks on merchant vessels. In the past weeks, the situation in Yemen has further deteriorated, threatening vital international trade routes.

Earlier this month, Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the UAE-based outlet The National that Rome was willing to increase its contribution, but only once other EU countries showed the same commitment.

“Given that the crisis that first emerged in Hormuz and now in Bab Al Mandeb is creating major difficulties for European economies, and therefore for European citizens, I believe Europe should play a much greater role than it has so far in trying to bring about peace,” Crosetto said.

Italy, which depends heavily on Middle Eastern energy, has provided significant military support to Gulf countries, sending air-defence and radar systems to Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait in response to Iran’s airstrikes.

Italy and Greece supply the mission’s three core ships, while Germany, France, Spain, the Netherlands and Belgium contribute with vessels that drop in and out on a rotation basis, meaning that the number of operational warships constantly changes.

The Hague has committed to adding a frigate, but only in an associate role focused on awareness and information gathering. Belgium will add one of its two frigates, the Leopold I, but the warship is facing technical problems and is not expected to join the mission until next year.

Other member states have preferred to keep their ships in the Baltic and Black Seas, hotspots for Russia's hybrid attacks, a sign of how thinly the EU’s defence capabilities are stretched.

According to the Annual Defence Readiness Report 2026, a confidential assessment of the bloc’s military needs seen by Euronews, maritime capabilities face critical gaps that current investments are expected to fill only after 2030.

"I welcome the addition of ships recently offered by the member states, but it's also clear that we need more to keep the Red Sea open. It's in Europe's strategic interest," Kallas said.

World.title: 'Breaking Bad' actor and disability advocate RJ Mitte dies
World.content:
RJ Mitte said his lived experience with cerebral palsy was an asset for his role as Walter White's son Flynn on "Breaking Bad."

American actor RJ Mitte, whose lived experience with cerebral palsy was channeled into a key role in "Breaking Bad," died on Monday at the age of 34.

"It is with profound ​sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights ​advocate RJ Mitte," his management agency said in a statement.

No other details about the circumstances of his death were given.

In addition to his breakout role in in "Breaking Bad" and later credits including "Switched at Birth" and "Guardians of Justice," Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Hospitals for Children.

An 'authentic' breakout role

In "Breaking Bad," Mitte played Walter White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston's character, chemistry teacher-turned-meth dealer Walter White. Mitte's character used crutches and spoke with a slur, and gained greater prominence as the series progressed.

"Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built ​a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," the statement said.

"Breaking Bad" ran from 2008 until 2023. With 16 Emmy awards, it's often cited by critics as one of the best television dramas of all time.

Shortly after the series wrapped up, Mitte told the Associated Press that his disability and the surrounding struggles with physical therapy, family problems and exorbitant medical bills — all of which featured in the show — made him better in his role.

"You develop a different mentality and you develop a different look at how the world sees you and how you see the world," he said in 2024.

"You're able to use that. And I think it's an asset instead of something that would hinder," Mitte added.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: UK: Iran 'highly likely' to be behind RAF Fairford incident
World.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told parliament there were "strong indications" of Iranian involvement. The government summoned Iran's ambassador. The scare at RAF Fairford led to the withdrawal of USAF B-1 heavy bombers.

The British government has accused Iran of involvement in a security alert outside a UK/US airbase in southern England last month, summoning the ambassador and announcing sanctions against two individuals.

Five British nationals were arrested in the vicinity of the RAF Fairford airbase on September 27 on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses. They were later released on bail under strict conditions, and another arrest followed days later.

Police had already said they were considering the possibility of a foreign state actor's involvement, not least given RAF Fairford's importance to the US Air Force as one of the European bases that handles heavy bombers like B-1's and B-52's, with ample range to reach Iran.

Some of the more advanced US bombers at RAF Fairford were ordered home after the incident [FILE: September 29, 2026] Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

What did Prime Minister Andy Burnham tell parliament?

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers in the House of Commons on Monday that the UK might yet put further sanctions on Iran in response.

He said there were indications of Iran coordinating the potential plot.

"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC)," he said. "We will not tolerate these threats on our soil."

The degree of competence exhibited and the threat posed by the group of young British nationals from London is not entirely clear but seems potentially limited.

Preliminary reports suggest that despite a widespread security alert and bomb squad deployment, investigators ultimately did not find viable explosives in the vans. They did, however, find accelerants like petroleum.

"We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm," Burnham said.

Burnham told the Commons that Iran could potentially face further sanctions Image: House of Commons/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

Foreign Secretary Miliband says Iranian ambassador summoned

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that his department had summoned Iran's ambassador to "reiterate" the message that Britain "will not tolerate attacks on our soil."

Iran's state news agency IRNA reported Ambassador Ali Moussavi as "categorically rejecting the accusations" and calling on the British government "to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."

Miliband said that two individuals would be subject to an immediate asset freeze, travel ban and director disqualification.

He named Ruhollah Bazghandi, head of counterespionage operations in the IRGC and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, an alleged facilitator for the Zindashti criminal network.

Miliband said they were being sanctioned for "their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas."

How viable or dangerous the attack plot really was remains something of an open question, what's certain is that the young men were able to cause a major disturbance and an international incident [FILE: September 27, 2026] Image: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

Joint statement from 29 countries condemns 'Iran's use of violent attacks'

Shortly afterwards, a total of 29 countries issued a joint statement denouncing "in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks."

It said these included "the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."

All of the so-called "Five Eyes" alliance and most European NATO members were listed among the signatories, including but not limited to the US, Britain, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Spain and Ireland.

In the aftermath of the September 27 incident at Fairford, the high-tech US B-1 bombers left the airbase. The older and larger contingent of B-52's remained there.

RAF Fairford is one of several airbases in southern England with a large US usage footprint. It's located around two hours' drive west of London, in a rural area north of Swindon.

As with most such bases, it can trace its roots back to the second World War when Nazi Germany occupied most of mainland Europe and Allied powers were operating air raids and preparing for the D-Day landings out of Britain.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Hundreds of French supermarkets hit by a cyberattack that  defrosted refrigeration systems
World.content:
Hundreds of French supermarkets saw their refrigeration systems defrosted, spoiling tons of frozen food. The unprecedented attack has raised serious questions about food security across Europe.

Hundreds of French supermarkets were forced to throw away perishable goods on Monday after hackers commandeered refrigeration systems across the country, spoiling stock at major chains in a sophisticated overnight cyberattack.

Hackers destroyed the food by taking control of refrigeration systems at Cooperative U, Leclerc, Les Mousquetaires, and Intermarche stores across the country and then defrosting thousands of freezer and refrigeration units.

During the overnight attack, in some cases, fully-stocked fridges were heated up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for more than six hours.

Over 400 stores were hit according to retailers.

Prosecutors in Paris confirmed the attacks and said fires had been reported at some locations.

Intermarche said impacted stores had no choice but to "throw away all fresh and frozen products."

Leclerc told French news agency AFP that "a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers," triggering "repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores."

Supermarkets say they had no choice but to throw away fresh and frozen food that was heated to over 50 degrees Celsius for several hours overnight Image: AFP

How were the refrigeration systems accessed?

The refrigeration systems targeted were reportedly from Danish supplier Danfoss, something suggested by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office, which reportedly identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor."

Danfoss said ​it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems," adding that the units in question "were running outdated firmware."

Danfoss said it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions."

Prime Minister Lecornu's office has tasked the French cybersecurity agency ANSSI with investigating the attack and is "liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected."

"Security issues" were also reported in Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, with Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize saying it had taken refrigeration systems offline to protect them, though the company added that it saw no connection to the French attacks.

Attacks on food supply now 'a reality'

It is currently unclear who could have been responsible for the cyberattack, and no group or individual has yet to claim responsibility.

The incident comes amid growing concern over vulnerabilities related to industrial ransomware and cyberattacks by malign actors in general, as well as heightened sensitivity toward Russian hybrid attacks in the midst of rising tensions over the war in Ukraine.

Last month, French President Emmanuel Macron — a strong supporter of Kyiv's self-defense against Russia — ordered measures put in place to protect France's critical infrastructure from Kremlin "hybrid attacks."

Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher, wrote on X: "Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable."

"Food security requires more attention at all levels," wrote EU Food and Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, who condemned the attack, adding that the "exploitation of food" is now a "reality."

World.title: Poland reports arrests of 2 Turkish citizens in Germany in connection with Starlink station fire last month
World.content:
Polish authorities have reported the arrests of two Turkish citizens in Germany in connection with alleged sabotage of a Starlink station last month. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the fire an act of "hybrid warfare."

Polish officials on Monday said that two Turkish citizens have been detained in Germany in connection with a fire last month at a Starlink station in Poland.

The satellite-based Starlink internet service is widely used by the military of Poland's neighbor Ukraine amid the Russian invasion.

Officials from several EU countries have been warning of mounting Russian sabotage, cyber and hybrid attacks across Europe aiming either to erode support for Ukraine or to impact Ukraine directly.

Polish officials did not specify exactly where or when the two men were allegedly detained in Germany.

What did Poland say about the arrests and the case?

Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski reported the arrests on Monday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk following soon after.

"On behalf of Polish services, German police detained two Turkish citizens suspected of setting fire to a Starlink station in Masovia," he said on social media. "This is another act of hybrid warfare. The perpetrators of the sabotage will answer before the Polish justice system."

Masovia is the province that includes the Polish capital Warsaw, not that far from Poland's eastern borders to Belarus and Ukraine.

Poland blames Russia for incident

Poland's Special Services Minister Tomasz Siemoniak alleged that Russia was behind the incident.

He also told a press conference that, "​it is worth adding that Russian services are increasingly turning ​to individuals linked ‌to the criminal underworld" for such attacks.

World.title: Fact check: Viral videos falsely linked to Riyadh airport attacks
World.content:
Many videos claiming to show an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport have gone viral online. DW Fact check analyzes some of the most-shared footage and finds evidence it was created using AI.

Yemen's Houthi rebels have claimed responsibility for a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in recent days. At least 16 people have been killed since last Thursday, according to Saudi authorities.

As news of the attacks spreads, social media users have been sharing videos that they claim show the strikes. While some authentic footage of the attacks and their aftermath has circulated online, DW Fact check found that several viral videos are not genuine and show signs of being AI-generated.

This AI-generated video has been circulating since March and contains several inconsistencies Image: X

Claim: This post with 1.7 million views on X, claims it shows the moment of an attack on the airport.

DW Fact check: Fake

The video has been online since March 2026 and could not show the most recent attacks on the airport.

Hectic camera movements and blurry footage help conceal glitches that often point to AI-generated content. However, our frame-by-frame analysis identified several inconsistencies. That suggests the video was AI-generated.

In the video, people run toward an exit as an explosion occurs outside. Despite the apparent danger, they continue moving toward the blast, seemingly through a glass door. This reaction is implausible.

Around 10 seconds into the video, an image of a hand holding a smartphone appears on the side of a man's head.

At 12 seconds, one man first appears not to have a hand, then miraculously has one.

A side-by-side comparison shows a hand appear out of nowhere Image: X

Meta's AI identification tool finds AI signatures in the video and concludes it was created using generative AI.

Many shared the video as authentic, including the Times of Israel – its post had more than 256,000 views at the time of writing.

The video has appeared in many languages, including Arabic , English , Russian , Spanish , Turkish , Nepali , and it has been shared on YouTube , Instagram , TikTok , Facebook and other platforms.

AI generates video from real photograph

Claim: In this post on X with 2.9 million views, a user claims it shows "new video footage of the moment King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh was targeted."

AI can generate videos from still photographs Image: X

DW Fact check: Fake

The video is AI-generated and contains several inconsistencies when compared with the real airport. Using a reverse image search, we found the photograph used to generate the fake video.

The original image was uploaded to stock photo database Shutterstock in 2016. Although it was taken from a slightly different angle it shows many visual cues that overlap with the video, including the white triangular geometric patterns of the airport building roof, the dome to the left, the luggage transport vehicles and the open and closed doors of the plane.

Other elements are missing. In the video, the light pole to the left of the aircraft appears without any lamps attached. The video is grainy and contains some visual glitches where parts of the image suddenly become blurry.

When the supposed missile strikes the plane, a nearby vehicle significantly changes its shape as it is thrown into the air. Another inconsistency is that, despite the missile's massive explosion and a resulting fireball, nearby objects do not cast corresponding shadows.

The account that shared the video has repeatedly posted AI-generated content in the past.

Whereas the October 8 attack at King Khalid International Airport did reportedly badly damage a plane , this video does not show the moment of attack.

Video predates attack and shows people move through objects

Claim: This TikTok post with more than 301,000 views claims that the footage was recorded "just now from the heart of Riyadh Airport."

AI-generated videos often contain impossible scenarios, like people walking through objects Image: Tik Tok

DW Fact check: Fake

This video had already circulated online in March 2026 , months before the attack. We found the video was shared in Greek , Albanian , Turkish and Russian .

The footage contains several visual anomalies. Parts of the image appear blurry, and some people seem to merge into one another. In addition, a row of red lights in the terminal switches on one second before the supposed explosion becomes visible through the window.

The clearest indication that the video is AI-generated is the way people move through the queue barriers. At the beginning of the video, several people appear to walk directly through them. After the supposed explosion, some individuals run straight through barriers that appear to end mid-air and are connected on only one side.

Video contains Google AI watermarks

Claim: This TikTok post , which has garnered more than 500,000 views, reports on the attacks on the airports in Riyadh and Abha and includes a compilation of videos. We examined the first video.

Since August 2026, the EU's AI Act requires AI-generated content to carry machine-readable markings Image: Tik Tok

DW Fact check: Fake

Analysis using Google Gemini detected that the video was generated, at least in part, with Google AI tools. The clip contains a SynthID watermark in both the images and the audio.

The same video also circulated on Facebook , where it has received more than 157,000 views. On Facebook it has been posted by an account that only shares AI-generated videos, and it is clearly labeled as "AI-content."

All four videos examined by DW Fact check are very short. Two are between six and ten seconds long, while the other two last 13 and 15 seconds, respectively. Such brief videos are easier to create with AI and often contain very little visual information, making it difficult for viewers to verify their authenticity.

Daniel Ebertz contributed to this research.

Edited by: Chiponda Chimbelu

World.title: Germany: Labor Minister's resignation puts a spotlight on cracks within the government
World.content:
Following the sudden resignation of Bärbel Bas as Labor Minister and co-chair of the Social Democratic Party, accusations are flying in Chancellor Merz's coalition government.

The week kicked off with a bang: On Monday morning, Bärbel Bas announced her resignation as Labor Minister and as Co-Chair of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD). "Following the death of my stepdaughter, I realized that I need time to come to terms with my grief," Bärbel Bas wrote in a personal statement to party members.

However, she also cited "the public attacks against me — unfortunately, including some from within the ranks of our coalition partner" as reasons for her resignation. In fact, the pressure on Bas increased significantly in recent days. The centrist coalition government is urgently awaiting key legislative proposals from the Ministry of Labor.

Before the summer recess in July, a commission had already presented comprehensive proposals for reforming Germany's statutory pension system. The coalition partners of SPD and the center-right Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) wanted these proposals to be quickly turned into legislation. To date, however, no finalized drafts have been presented.

What are the German government's pension, labor reforms? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There had been calls for Bas' resignation

"The minister is no longer tenable. For months, she has been blocking the reforms our country so urgently needs," railed Christian von Stetten, head of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group's caucus representing medium-sized enterprises, said in reference to Bas in September.

In early October, such criticism was echoed by CDU Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, who demanded that the pension reform be passed by the end of the year. Bas had to submit the bill "promptly," Reiche said, although it was known at the time what a difficult personal situation her cabinet colleague was in at the time.

SPD co-leader, Finance Minister and Vice-Chancellor Lars Klingbeil reacted sharply on Monday, saying the political attacks against Bas had been "disgraceful." Following a meeting of the SPD leadership, he told journalists in Berlin: "This poisons the political discourse, and — in the interest of preserving our political culture — I hope that everyone will take a step back and reflect on what has actually happened over the past few weeks." He called on all centrist politicians to be careful "that we don't destroy the good people in politics by attacking one another."

Such accusations carry significant weight at a time when the coalition is already mired in a deep crisis.

Adding to this is the new vacancy at the top of the SPD. Without Bas, Klingbeil will lead the SPD alone. A party convention will be scheduled for December or January to elect new leadership for the Social Democrats. It is not certain whether Klingbeil will run again. He received a very poor result during his last reelection as party leader.

What's behind the rising polarization in German politics? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Swift replacement of Labor Minister

Alexander Schweitzer is to succeed Bärbel Bas as Federal Minister of Labor. The former state premier of the state of Rhineland-Palatinate had previously served as that state's Minister of Labor and Social Affairs. Chancellor Friedrich Merz expressed confidence that Schweitzer's experience would ensure " good cooperation within the federal government," adding that he hoped that the pending legislative proposals "will now be quickly approved by the cabinet and can be introduced into the parliamentary process."

The chancellor refuted the accusations leveled by Bas, saying that he had never discussed personal matters with her. Friedrich Merz said he had explicitly advised Bas to take the time she needed to grieve.

Merz promises change

Mistrust between the coalition partners has increased significantly, with SPD lawmakers speaking of an increasingly toxic political climate.

For months, the CDU and SPD have been grappling with low poll numbers, disappointing election results, and disputes over key reform projects. Plans for changes to the electricity tax, the introduction of a sugar tax, the pension and the labor market reform — hardly any initiative has been able to proceed without public controversy.

Adding to this is the crisis within the chancellor's party, the CDU, which saw a historic election defeat in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in September, when it even lost representation in a state parliament for the first time in history.

On Sunday and Monday, the party leadership met for a closed-door session to discuss the way forward.

They produced a four-page document which indicated a shift in priorities, putting more emphasis on social issues: affordable housing, lower electricity prices, better health care, and greater respect for citizens' lifetime achievements are mentioned in the paper. This is seen as a response to criticism that the CDU had been focusing too much on economic and regulatory issues.

Why Germany's political center is losing ground To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The chancellor admitted that voters feel that politicians are not taking their hardships and fears of social decline seriously enough. "We have to work our way out of this slump — and get out of a crisis of confidence," Merz said. "You can't just reinvent a party overnight over a weekend, but we want to show that we're ready for change... and we have to be, given the election results."

The chancellor announced that he would lower the electricity tax for everyone — a promise he had made before the general election in 2025 but had not kept.

With the closed-door meeting paper, the CDU is also sending a signal to the SPD. Instead of a programmatic shift further to the right, it is emphasizing its traditional social values — a stance that resonates well within the Social Democrats.

The chancellor made an effort to emphasize his intention to continue with the current coalition government: "The personnel changes will not call into question the basis of the coalition agreement." He then repeated what he had recently said during a visit to Ukraine: "We need a stable federal government right now in order to remain capable of acting on the international stage."

Both CDU/CSU and SPD know that calling early elections could primarily benefit the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is leading in the polls nationwide. So despite the deep rifts, Klingbeil and Merz currently see no alternative to their coalition.

This article was originally published in German.

10/12/2026 October 12, 2026 Söder: Those who voted for AfD speaker should show 'backbone'

"Do you want to go somewhere else? Then just say so," Bavarian leader Markus Söder said during an interview with public broadcaster ARD.

As a member of the CSU, the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), Söder was referencing bloc members in the state of Saxony-Anhalt who are believed to have voted for a member of the far-right in a secret ballot.

Last week, Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — whose chapter in Saxony-Anhalt is classified as right-wing extremist — was elected state parliamentary speaker.

This marked the first time the AfD has seen a member elected to such a position, and the first time in postwar Germany that a right-wing extremist has risen to this rank.

AfD lawmaker elected speaker in Saxony-Anhalt To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The populist BSW party had declared their intention to support Rausch's nomination alongside the AfD, but his win with 48 votes means that other lawmakers must have voted for him too. It is strongly suspected that these were members of the conservative CDU.

Rausch's election prompted outrage across Germany, including from CDU members who have accused their colleagues of abandoning the so-called "firewall" — the agreement amongst the country's mainstream parties not to support the AfD.

Söder called it "pretty poor form," from the CDU members in Saxony-Anhalt, saying they should "at least have the backbone" to make their decision public.

World.title: US federal agents search home of Trump critic Ilhan Omar
World.content:
Justice Department officials said the Washington residence of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, an outspoken opponent of President Trump, was raided as "part of an ongoing federal investigation."

US federal agents searched the home of a Democratic congresswoman and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump on Monday, the Department of Justice (DoJ) confirmed.

Officials from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of US immigration enforcement, were seen early on Monday morning outside the Washington home of Ilhan Omar.

"Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice," a DoJ spokesperson told the Reuters news agency in a statement which didn't specifically name Omar.

"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation."

Who is Ilhan Omar?

Omar, who came to the United States from Somalia as a child, was first elected to Congress in 2018 and is a member of the group of left-wing Democratic lawmakers known as "The Squad," who have been among Trump's most vocal opponents.

Omar represents a district including Minneapolis, home to one of the largest Somali communities in the US – a community which Trump has frequently targeted in racist outbursts.

Omar has said Trump has a 'creepy obsession' with her Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

He ​previously called Somalis "garbage" and said in February that Omar and Democratic Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan should be "institutionalized" and sent back to "where they came from."

Last ​week, Trump called Democratic candidate for US Senate from Michigan Abdul El Sayed a "RADICAL Extremist" and "Terrorist Sympathizer" while offering support for the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers

Democrats decry 'abuse of power'

House Democratic leaders condemned the search as an "abuse of power" by the Trump administration.

Omar said she will “not be silenced” and called the search of her home the “latest escalation” in President Donald Trump’s '‘intimidation" campaign.

Trump has been accused of weaponizing US agenices to go after his political opponents Image: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance

Omar has called Trump's focus on her an "unhealthy and creepy obsession" said she and her family have faced death threats, which she attributes ⁠to "hateful political rhetoric" especially ​from Trump.

On Monday, Omar said she will "not be silenced" and called the search of her home the "latest escalation" in Trump's "intimidation" campaign.

No charges against Omar were announced in connection with Monday's search, but US media reported that the operation was linked to a criminal fraud investigation into immigration paperwork submitted on her behalf by her late father when she was a child.

The search comes just three weeks before midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans will be trying to defend their thin majorities in the US.
