World.title: Czech Local Elections Deliver Warning to Babis’s Governing Coalition
World.content:
With all the votes counted by Sunday midday and on a relatively strong 48 per cent turnout, Czechia’s municipal elections of October 9-10 did not bring any major upheavals of the political scene, yet indicate some changes in voting preferences, less than a year after the coalition government of Prime Minister Andrej Babis took office.

Contrary to national elections, identifying a clear winner is difficult, especially so early after voting day: once again, the largest share of votes went to a network of local associations and independent candidates, who secured over 50,000 seats this year out of 62,000, and post-election coalition talks across Czech towns and cities can take weeks, if not months.

Czech voters also cast their ballot for a third of the Senate’s seats over the weekend, with 22 out of 27 mandates needing a second round on October 16-17.

With close to 1,500 council seats, Prime Minister Babis said the municipal elections confirmed that his ANO party “is the strongest political force at all levels”, except for the Senate. ANO emerged first in six out of 13 regional capitals, compared with eight in 2022, including in Karlovy Vary, Pilsen, Ostrava and Olomouc.

Despite the boast, most analysts point out that ANO underperformed compared to four years ago in terms of both municipal seats and the popular vote. It also recorded its worst-ever result in Prague and suffered a surprising setback in the northern city of Usti nad Labem, a long-time stronghold.

Meanwhile, ANO’s two junior partners in government also failed to mobilise their voters or reach their campaign goals. This includes the conservative Motorists for Themselves who, although focusing their campaign on larger cities, managed to break through only in Ostrava while suffering poor results in the country’s two largest cities of Prague and Brno. “I’m not happy about it, I’m not pleased,” admitted party leader and Foreign Minister Petr Macinka.

On top of that, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) party of House Speaker Tomio Okamura came out of the elections with less than 170 municipal council seats. “We have to think about what we will have to change and how we will behave until the next elections,” SPD vice-chairman Radim Fiala said as the party prepares to hold a national conference to reflect on its poor results.

Released on Sunday, a national poll put this weekend’s local ballot into national perspective. ANO remains the strongest party by a large margin but slightly weakened from six months ago, winning over 31 per cent of the vote if a general election was held today. STAN would come second in any general election with close to 17 per cent of the vote, well ahead of ODS (11 per cent), the far-right SPD (7.5 per cent) and the liberal Pirates (7 per cent). Both the Motorists and KDU-CSL would not pass the 5 per cent threshold needed to enter the lower house.

STAN in the opposition lead

Among the opposition ranks, both the centre-right STAN movement and the Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL) have been described as the main winners.

Far less prominent at the national level but known for its strong local networks at the municipal level, KDU-CSL once again secured the highest number of council seats out of all the parliamentary parties, close to 2,000. The first-round victory in the Senate of their chairman Jan Grolich can also be seen as a key achievement in strengthening the party’s clout and legitimacy.

But in line with the opinion polls from the past few months, it’s the STAN movement that stands out in this weekend’s ballot with the strongest momentum.

The party racked up the second highest number of municipal council seats and secured two senatorial mandates in the first round, with all its other candidates advancing to the second. Crucially, STAN also conquered Prague – edging out the current-ruling ODS by 1 percentage point – and their mayoral candidate Petr Hlavacek is widely expected to hold the keys to the capital following post-election talks.

Additionally, the coalition between STAN and KDU-CSL also emerged as the clear winner of the elections in Brno, the country’s second largest city. “We are the strongest opposition party, the results say so,” celebrated STAN chairman and former Interior Minister Vit Rakusan.

ODS, the largest opposition party in the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of parliament, is coming out of the weekend significantly weakened, underperforming in most regional capitals compared to 2022 on top of losing Prague and suffering a few unexpected first round senatorial defeats as well.

World.title: Greek Singer’s Death Throws Spotlight on Private Doctors’ ‘Wellness’ Claims
World.content:
When popular Greek singer Giorgos Mazonakis passed away suddenly at a private clinic in the upscale central Athens neighbourhood of Kolonaki last month, his fans were shocked.

Just 54 years old, Mazonakis was undergoing plasmapheresis, a medical procedure that removes plasma from the blood and replaces it with new plasma fluid. He suffered a heart attack and was pronounced dead on September 9.

Known officially as Therapeutic Plasma Exchange, or TPE, plasmapheresis can be used to treat a range of conditions, including myeloma, multiple sclerosis, and some leukaemias, by removing plasma from the patient’s blood and replacing it with fresh donor plasma or bottled human albumin solution.

The procedure, however, has also gained popularity as supposedly promoting ‘longevity’, ‘anti-ageing’, ‘mental clarity’ and ‘resilience’.

World.title: Minor Says Croatian Priest Abused Her in 2021, Bozanić Allegedly Did Not Report Him
World.content:
October the 13th, 2026 – A minor said she was physically abused by a Croatian priest in 2021, yet Bozanić allegedly failed to ever report him.

Index has reported that the Zagreb Archdiocese reported a priest accused of abusing a minor to the police allegedly only five years after receiving the complaint. This occurred only after Dnevnik.hr sent an inquiry about the case. A minor female person accused the priest of abuse back in 2021. The Archdiocese submitted the report to the Zagreb police only on the 9th of October this year, two days after Dnevnik.hr sent them an inquiry about the entire case. They have refused to answer any further questions about the case.

Zagreb police confirmed their receipt of the report. “The police received a report from a church legal entity, following which it has begun a criminal investigation,” they stated in their response. They added that, in accordance with the law, the inquiries are confidential and that they cannot disclose any specific details. According to unofficial information, after the 2021 complaint the priest was relieved of his duties as administrator of one Zagreb parish and banned from public activity. The Archdiocese then appointed a new administrator. It seemed that the priest had indeed been withdrawn from public life for several years.

the case should have been reported immediately – it was not

However, by decision of Archbishop Dražen Kutleša in September 2024 he was appointed parish vicar in one parish, and in August this year as a chaplain in an institution on the territory of the Zagreb Archdiocese. It is interesting that neither the decision on his relief from duties in 2021 nor the later appointments were published in the annual reviews of appointments and dismissals of priests in the Archdiocese. Information about his new duties was found in the parish’s posts on social networks and in the media. The case arose during the term of Cardinal Josip Bozanić, who was Archbishop of Zagreb from 1997 until April 2023, when he was succeeded by Dražen Kutleša.

One priest, who wished to remain anonymous, explained that Bozanić should have been the first to report the case to the police. Since he did not do so, the obligation was taken over by Kutleša, because the new archbishop is at the beginning of his term informed about all open cases, especially accusations of abuse of minors.

whether or not the vatican has been notified is unknown

The guidelines of the Croatian Bishops’ Conference for the protection of minors oblige reporting to the competent state authorities. They state that the church authority, when it receives a report, must inform the victim or parents that they are obliged to report everything to the state authorities. If, after a preliminary investigation it is established that the accusation is credible, the church authority has the obligation to forward the report to the state authorities. Given that the Archdiocese ultimately did submit a report, this suggests that it considers the accusations credible.

According to church laws, the Archbishop of Zagreb, after the preliminary investigation, should also have informed the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith about everything. It is not known whether Bozanić or Kutleša did so. Independently of church regulations, according to Croatian laws everyone is obliged to report suspicion of a criminal offence.

World.title: Environmentalist: Every Country Has a Mafia, in Croatia, the Mafia Has a  Country
World.content:
October the 13th, 2026 – An environmentalist has issued a damning message that while every country has a mafia, in Croatia, the mafia has a country. He added that people are “lobotomised by football” as Croatia slowly disappears into oblivion.

Environmentalist Vjeran Piršić recently spoke about pollution, waste management and habits that harm nature. Index reports that the well known mathematician and computer scientist who has been involved with environmental protection for decades assessed that Croatia is, as a nation, merely turning into a geographical concept and that the Croats will simply disappear as a people if the attitude towards resources does not change. He said that in Croatia, the mafia has the country and that people must wake up, reports HRT.

from maths to ecology…

Piršić’s story about ecology began back in 1980 on the island of Krk, where during the winter holidays in a cold house, he started thinking about energy efficiency. “It was absolutely freezing. I realised I couldn’t heat the house. I was under two blankets for seventeen days, listening to Pink Floyd and dreaming of living in an energy-efficient house, that the bura wouldn’t blow through and that I would be able to produce my own energy,” he said. Four decades later, he realised that idea and today lives in an energy-renovated house that produces more electricity than it consumes. At the beginning of the 2000s, his interest turned into a concrete struggle. The turning point was the Družba Adria project in 2002, which planned the export of Russian oil via Omišalj. Piršić, together with a group of like-minded people, decided to oppose it and founded the association Eko Kvarner.

“That would’ve been five million tonnes of muddy waters, with a heap of dangerous microorganisms and invasive species. A small group of us met at my home and we realised we had three options. The first was to move away, the second was to ignore the problem, but then it would only explode later. Or, we could try to fight. And us six lunatics decided to put up resistance to a project behind which stood Bush and Putin and Mesić and everyone else,” he said. After four years of struggle, with the help of other associations and people, the project was stopped.

“people in croatia are totally lobotomised”

Piršić warned about a system in which environmental impact studies, he claims, often serve to justify projects instead of objective assessment. As one of the hardest examples he cited Vranjic and the remediation of asbestos waste. “Vranjic is the evil of evils. That is the bottom of the bottom. I cried there many times,” he said. He was particularly affected by the absence of a wider public reaction to a problem that directly endangers people’s health. “One hero, Grgo Mandić, stands in front of a truck to stop a vehicle that is not for hazardous waste and is transporting it to a landfill that is not intended for that. And the police arrest him. There were maybe ten citizens, five activists. At the same time, a few kilometres away, at Poljud, thousands of Split residents were celebrating Niko Kranjčar’s transfer from Dinamo to Hajduk. I have nothing against Niko Kranjčar or Hajduk. But that is the madness. What matters is that Kranjčar came to Hajduk,” Piršić said.

Such a disproportion led him to the conclusion that citizens are reacting less and less to important problems, for which he also holds the media responsible. “People in Croatia are completely lobotomised. They are lobotomised by football, Turkish soap operas, Big Brother, by who anointed whom,” he said.

“this poison must be removed from the land”

He also spoke about the waste scandal from Gospić and explained that the proposal for temporary relocation to the area of Udbina arose after consultations with Swedish experts. He believes the first step is to remove the waste from the existing location, and then separate it and seek a long-term solution.

“You have poison under your skin. Those 35,000 tonnes of waste is poisoning this land. And believe me, it is poisoning everything,” he said. According to his proposal, the waste would be moved into appropriate bags and temporarily placed in the area of abandoned military infrastructure in Udbina. After that separation would be carried out, and as one of the options for storing the remainder he mentioned a protected part of the Željava tunnel complex, with appropriate protection and controls.

Piršić said that thermal treatment of waste is often presented as a simple solution, although its effectiveness depends on the whole system. “I don’t understand incinerators, but I have seen that in all countries where a proper waste management system has been set up, incinerators have nothing to burn. Those are huge and expensive facilities,” he said. He emphasised that even after incineration slag and ash remain which also need to be disposed of, and he warned about the importance of technology and supervision, mentioning reports of irregularities in Croatian cement plants. “So an incinerator is not the Joker so that we’ve solved everything,” he concluded.

“croats seem unable to understand very basic, elementary concepts”

He also commented on the problem of illegal dumps. He assessed that such a state shows serious shortcomings of the system, but also insufficient awareness of the general public. “That we are barbarians. That we are heavy barbarians who don’t even understand very basic, elementary things. Secondly, this is the crowning proof of my thesis that the environmental protection system has collapsed,” he said. As key steps he highlighted the education of young people, reduction of consumption, repairing of devices and proper waste separation. “If we really separate waste and teach children that the environment must be protected, then such ‘filth’ will not exist after some time. And there is no other way,” he said.

He also spoke about food waste. He said that this problem can be significantly reduced by better meal planning, thoughtful shopping and proper separation of biowaste. He explained that organic residues in landfills create methane, a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change. He also shared his own experience, where his family by planning weekly meals and shopping according to a list significantly saves money and reduces waste. He considers food waste an environmental, ethical and financial problem.

“croats will simply disappear as a people”

Using the example of plans for the construction of large poultry farms, Piršić asked the question of who such projects benefit. He believes that development must not be based on megaprojects that neglect small producers, but on the preservation of space and domestic agriculture.

“Every country has a mafia. In Croatia, the mafia has an entire country. The key question is: who needs this? For whom was this Croatia created? Is this country intended for ordinary people with family farms or for big players with mega-projects that will wipe everything and everyone out? Croatia is disappearing. It is turning into a geographical concept. Croatian agriculture is destroyed, even though billions have been invested in it. Now, they will destroy Dalmatia and the Adriatic as well by seizing space and mega resorts. And the Croats will disappear as a people. Demographically, we’re already broken,” he said.

He was asked whether or not there is hope for Croatia, given the clear statement that in Croatia, the mafia has the entire country. Piršić drew a parallel with historical periods of national awakening. “People in Croatia tend to wake up every 100 years. For the protest in Gospić, we gathered in the square where the monument to Ban Jelačić is. So… the Croatian revival did something good. A hundred years after that there was Stjepan Radić. Maybe the time has come for us to finally wake up and realise that the point is not football, Turkish soap operas or Big Brother,” he concluded.

World.title: Air Quality Monitoring Station Installed at Gospić Waste Site
World.content:
October the 13th, 2026 – A new air quality monitoring station has been installed at the shameful Gospić waste site which will assess the potential harmful impacts on the environment above the soil itself.

A measuring station has been installed at the location of PPK Velebit in Gospić, where the scandalous illegally disposed waste is currently located. Index reports that the new station will monitor concentrations of particulate matter PM2.5 and PM10 as well as the presence of metals in the air. Lika-Senj County has revealed that measurements will be carried out during the remediation in order to monitor the state of air quality and the possible impact of the entire situation there on the environment.

The station was installed at the request of the administration in Gospić by experts from the Teaching Institute for Public Health of Split-Dalmatia County. Also involved in the project are Lika-Senj County and the Environmental Protection and Energy Efficiency Fund, which are expected to continue financing air-quality monitoring in the Gospić area.

the station will measure pm2.5 and pm10 levels

The station will measure particulate matter PM2.5 and PM10, and the presence of metals will also be analysed in the collected samples. Two sedimentators have also been installed for collecting total deposited matter, in which the presence of heavy metals will likewise be determined. One sedimentator has been placed next to the measuring station and the other in a nearby settlement. The Institute states that wind directions were taken into account when selecting the sampling sites so that any possible spread of dust and particles can be monitored. Measurements and analyses should be carried out in accordance with regulations on air protection and quality. The County states that the goal is to provide citizens with expert data on the state of the air at a time of increased concern due to the waste at the PPK Velebit location.

the measuring station will remain in place throughout the duration of the large-scale clean up

Deputy Director of the Environmental Protection and Energy Efficiency Fund Mirko Budiša said that air-quality monitoring is part of the process of remediating the illegal landfill. According to him, the station should remain at the location throughout the entire remediation so that its possible impact on the environment and people’s health can be monitored. County Prefect of Lika-Senj County Ernest Petry said that the devices were installed at the invitation of the City of Gospić for an initial period of one month. He announced that the County, in cooperation with the Fund, will ensure the continuation of measurements over the next year, and longer if necessary. Petry stated that the County, the City of Gospić, the Fund and the competent ministries are participating in the monitoring. He highlighted as the goal of the cooperation the enabling of reliable monitoring of air-quality data in the area where waste has been illegally disposed.

daily data

Deputy Mayor of Gospić Ivica Kovačević said that this is a reference measuring station installed by a team from the Teaching Institute for Public Health of Split-Dalmatia County, led by Nenad Periš. He announced daily air-quality monitoring and the availability of relevant data to citizens on an almost daily basis. The measurement results should show the concentrations of particulate matter and metals at the location and serve for monitoring the situation during the remediation of the illegally disposed waste.

World.title: Rent in Croatia Rose 40% in One Year, Only Romania is Worse in EU
World.content:
October the 13th, 2026 – Rent in Croatia rose by a staggering 40% in one single year, with only Romania being worse in this regard in the entire EU.

Rent costs for apartments have risen noticeably across all of Europe, and in the most recent period Romania and Croatia have been hit the hardest. Index reports that in an analysis published by Euronews, the annual growth in rents and the specific reasons for such trends in these two countries were examined. Rents in many European countries are rising faster than the general inflation rate, reports N1.

From the second quarter of 2025 to the same period in 2026, actual expenditure on residential rents in the European Union rose by three percent. According to Eurostat data, annual growth ranged from zero percent in Finland to as much as 43.5 percent in Romania. Croatia is immediately behind it with growth of 40.1 percent. In the same period overall inflation in Romania was 9.5 percent and in Croatia 4.8 percent, which means that rents in both countries rose in real terms by more than 30 percent. The third-largest increase in the EU was recorded by Slovenia, at 10 percent, or a little more than six percent after adjustment for inflation.

The institutions that supply data to Eurostat explained to Euronews Business the reasons for such increases. According to the Romanian government, the main cause is “the increase in administratively determined rents,” i.e. those for apartments owned by the state or local units. However, Dr Adriana M. Soaita of the University of Glasgow doubts that explanation.

“Public rental apartments make up a negligible share of the total housing stock,” she told Euronews Business. She noted that rents in such apartments are so much lower than those on the private market that even tripling them would not significantly affect the average.

“If even after adjustment for inflation, Eurostat’s methodology and the informal sector we still record a large increase in rents, the cause could be the entry of newly built or completely renovated properties onto the market,” Soaita believes.

“a significant part of croatia’s housing stock has become the subject of financial investment”

In Croatia, the sharp rise in rent costs, according to the institution that supplies the data, is “a consequence of the decision of the local authorities in Zagreb to increase rents in the social-rental category.” Professor Gojko Bežovan of the University of Zagreb pointed out that a significant part of the Croatian housing stock has become the subject of financial investments. Investments in apartments and real estate for tourism have become the dominant form of saving.

Because of this, a large share of apartments in new buildings are not bought for living in but as an investment, and they often remain empty. Bežovan emphasised that Croatia introduced a tax on empty apartments from 2025, after which during 2025 and 2026 the number of rental contracts reported to the Tax Administration increased significantly. “As a primary result of that, a larger number of higher-quality residential units entered the rental market in larger cities, with rents that significantly exceed the average,” he told Euronews Business. When candidate countries for EU membership and EFTA states are included in the analysis, the largest rent increase is recorded by Turkey, where the annual rise amounted to 49.6 percent.

croatia is among the worst examples of this

Unlike Romania and Croatia, in Turkey there was no sudden jump; prices rose gradually. With inflation that exceeded 30 percent, the real growth in rents was smaller than in Romania and Croatia. Double-digit growth was also recorded in Serbia, where rents rose by 12.5 percent. Growth of more than five percent was also recorded in Bulgaria (9.9 percent), North Macedonia (9.2 percent), Iceland (8.6 percent), Greece (7.5 percent), Czechia (6.2 percent), Albania (6 percent), Slovakia (5.3 percent), Lithuania (5.3 percent) and Portugal (5.2 percent).

Among the four largest economies of the European Union, only Italy with growth of 3.5 percent was above the EU average. In Spain the growth amounted to 2.5 percent, in Germany 2.1 percent and in France 1.6 percent. In those three countries, as well as in Belgium, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg, rents did not rise in real terms when inflation is taken into account.

Emma Rosser, director of residential market research at the company JLL, pointed out that overall Eurostat data do not show extremely large increases. Nevertheless, it appears that the growth in rents for newly concluded leases remains high and is accelerating, which could indicate future problems. “Strong competition for a limited number of rental apartments in European cities is driving strong price growth for new rental contracts,” she told Euronews Business. She added that the imbalance between supply and demand is present across Europe.

housing as a financial asset and not as a social good

Dr Nóra Teller, a researcher at the Metropolitan Research Institute in Budapest, said that rent growth is driven by economic and demographic factors, but also by constraints on the supply side. “A long period of low interest rates until a few years ago encouraged borrowing in order to buy property. However, back in 2022, the costs of borrowing rose sharply, which directed many who intended to buy property for the first time towards the private rental market,” she said. She also emphasised that the financialisation of the housing market encourages price growth, because institutional investors and other owners increasingly view housing as a financial asset rather than a social good.

World.title: Spartan Takes Over Hvar with 3,600 Competitors from 63 Countries
World.content:
October 12, 2026 – The third edition of Spartan 100m & Sprint World Championship took place this weekend, cementing an important relationship between the world-renowned obstacle race and Croatia’s premier island.

One of the pleasures of covering life and tourism on Hvar for more than 15 years now (and with almost 10,000 articles on the island written) is that I have been able to watch the island evolve and to see how longer-term strategies play out. Fames for its sun, nightlife, beaches, lavender and UNESCO culture, Hvar does not have to work too hard to attract tourists, but there has been plenty of effort to diversity and prolong the tourist season over the years.

https://www.facebook.com/reel/2526211701200292

One area which the island has encountered particular success in over the last decade has been in the area of adventure tourism, with a successful partnership between the town authorities, tourist board, and Suncani Hvar hotels.

Various eye-catching events and arrivals over the years highlighted Hvar’s shoulder-season credentials as an excellent adventure tourism destination. These included hosting one of the world’s leading cycling teams, Bahrain Merida for three years as the headquarters for their winter training, as well as the world-famous Othillo Swimrun for several years.

A very welcome addition to the Hvar calendar for the last three Octobers has been Spartan, the world-famous obstacle course race, attracting athletes from all over the world. The timing of the event, just as the shoulder season is starting to die down, injects new life into the town, as well as bringing some much-appreciated late-season revenue for the hospitality providers. There is a wonderful and very youthful energy around the town over those four days, and you don’t have to be competing to join in the fun.

This year’s event was no exception, and it was a pleasure to see how this chameleon of a destination which offers everything transforms its focus to summer and the beach into showcasing its beauty and terrain for hardened athletes. And it will change again later this week, as the inaugural HVARMONY gathering – focused on the original attraction of Hvar tourism back in 1868, wellbeing.

A full report on the event was covered below by Slobodna Dalmacija, all photos by Samir Kurtagic/Spartan Hvar:

More than 3,500 athletes from 63 countries participated in the third edition of the Spartan event on Hvar, held from October 8 to 11, 2026. The four-day program featured world championships in the 100m and Sprint 5K disciplines, the Beast 21K and Super 10K races, and the Spartan Kids event. A total prize purse of $100,000 was provided for the two world championships, while the Hvar Beast also served as the second stop of the regional National Adriatic Series.

The competition took place along the Hvar waterfront and on courses connecting the coast, city streets, and the ascent to the Fortica fortress. The short course, featuring head-to-head finishes, captivated the audience during the 100m championship, while the longer races took competitors beyond the city center onto terrain that demanded not only obstacle-clearing skills but also endurance on the climbs.

Alongside athletes arriving from all over the world, a large number of locals also competed on the courses. Šime Ravlić, the Mayor of Hvar, highlighted both the participation and the organizational challenges posed by the adverse weather conditions:

“This year’s Spartan weekend presented a unique challenge for both competitors and organizers, and we are delighted that it exceeded all expectations. Adverse weather was an additional hurdle that the organizers successfully overcame; we sincerely congratulate everyone on the ground who saw this demanding project through to the end. In just three years of the Spartan event in Hvar, the number of participating countries has grown from 35 to 63—a clear indicator of the rising interest in this sport and in Hvar as a host destination. There is no need to elaborate on the global promotion generated by enthusiastic competitors alongside the organizers’ official channels. We are particularly pleased with the response from the islanders: 59 locals participated in the 5km, 10km, and 21km races—with some successfully completing all three—while 246 of the 530 competitors in the children’s race were from the island. The message conveyed to young people and islanders through the energy, perseverance, and spirit of these exceptional athletes—whom we hosted for nearly a week—is unmistakable. The Spartan event in Hvar is a success story; we therefore extend our thanks once again to the organization’s founder and leader, Joe De Sena, for his trust; to the local organizer for excellent cooperation; to the Ministry of Tourism and Sport of the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian National Tourist Board for their support; and to all local…” …participants and collaborators. Together, we made this edition of Spartan spectacular.”

100M World Championship: a world title decided in mere seconds

Oliver Addy from England won the 100-meter world championship title. In the final, he clocked a time of 32.574 seconds, defeating Caleb Riley, who finished the course in 36.477 seconds. Third place went to Tommy Matthews, who recorded a time of 31.746 seconds in the bronze-medal race.

For Addy, who has been competing in OCR for four years, the victory in Hvar capped off a successful season, and he is already thinking about returning.

“I can’t believe this sport has brought me here. I’ve had a great season and can’t wait to see what’s next. I definitely want to come back next year and defend my title. I’m ready—I can’t wait!” said Addy.

In the women’s final, Poland’s Kasia Jonaczyk triumphed with a time of 40.882 seconds. May Yahalom from Israel took the silver with a time of 1:05.297, while the bronze went to American Jaleesa Himka, who clocked 32.740 seconds in the race for third place. Jonaczyk described what the title means to her immediately after the final:

“I can’t stop smiling; I still can’t believe it. Spartan was the most important race of the year for me. This title was the one thing I was missing. Honestly, for half the year I didn’t believe I could win it, and now here I am, talking to you. I feel like I’m in heaven,” said Jonaczyk.

In the final rounds of the 100m championship, placement is determined by head-to-head duels, meaning the times recorded by the finalists and bronze medalists were achieved in separate races.

The awards were presented by Josip Pavić, State Secretary at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport; Rob Stull, President of the International Modern Pentathlon Union (UIPM); and Šime Ravlić, Mayor of Hvar.

The prize fund for this discipline totaled $70,000, split equally between the men’s and women’s competitions. The winners received $18,000 each, the runners-up $10,000, the third-place finishers $5,500, and the fourth-place finishers $1,500.

Sprint 5K World Championship: a fast start isn’t enough for gold

At the Sprint 5K World Championship—which featured a five-kilometer course and 20 obstacles—the fastest of the 56 competitors in the men’s field was the Dutchman Frank Oosterom. He won gold with a time of 39:54, ahead of Frenchman Gregory Basilic, who finished in 40:26, and Czech Richard Hynek, with a time of 40:39.

In the women’s competition, Zuzana Kocumova won the world champion title with a time of 47:35. The silver medal went to Sabrina Daolio, who finished the race in 48:00, while Henriette Bardrum took the bronze with a result of 48:43.

A prize fund of $30,000 was secured for the Sprint Championship, also split equally between the two categories. First place earned $7,000; second, $4,000; third, $2,000; fourth, $1,500; and fifth, $500.

The Beast race held on October 10 held additional significance for competitors in the Adriatic Series. Following the initial Super race in Sveta Nedelja, athletes gathered points on Hvar—over a 21-kilometer course featuring 30 obstacles—ahead of the series finale at Krvavec on October 17.

Italian athlete Claudia Bongiovanni won the women’s race on Hvar with a time of 2:41:37, while Norwegian Espen Berget triumphed in the men’s category with a time of 2:13:53.

The Adriatic Series combines three races into a single ranking for the Elite and Age Group categories. Points are awarded based on placement, with a victory earning 300 points. The final tally counts the two best results, meaning that even competitors for whom Hvar was their first race in the series can contend for the overall ranking by participating in the final Beast race at Krvavec. A Great Race and Over 500 Children on the Course

The Super 10K—featuring a 10-kilometer course and 25 obstacles—brought together competitors of varying experience levels, ranging from those for whom Hvar was their first Spartan race to seasoned participants with numerous races under their belts. At the starting line, the pre-race atmosphere was filled with dancing and laughter, as the group warm-up quickly turned into a social gathering before hitting the course.

The youngest participants had their own races, too; over 500 children took part in the Spartan Kids events. The shortest course, spanning one kilometer, was recommended for children aged four to six. The 1.5-kilometer race was open to children aged seven to 14, while the three-kilometer race was for those aged nine to 14.

Age-appropriate obstacles included climbing, crawling, and jumping, and every finisher was awarded a medal. Parents and friends cheered the children on from the sidelines, meaning the program for the youngest participants also brought together many families.

Over 300 Team Members and 143 Volunteers

More than 300 team members and 143 volunteers took part in executing the four-day program. Organization and production crews, race officials, and security teams managed the race operations, while volunteers assisted competitors and provided support on the ground. The arrival of athletes, along with their families and teams, generated additional demand for accommodation, hospitality services, and transport in October—well after the peak summer season. Josip Pavić, State Secretary at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport, highlighted the event’s contribution to extending the tourist season:

“The Spartan World Championship Hvar is an excellent example of how major international sports events can contribute to the development of year-round tourism and create added value for a destination outside the main tourist season. We are particularly pleased that, in mid-October, Hvar once again brought together thousands of participants and their supporters from over 60 countries, confirming the event’s strong international character and Croatia’s status as a sports-tourism destination. This year, the Government of the Republic of Croatia and the Ministry of Tourism and Sport recognized the project’s significance and provided €1,350,000 in co-financing. We are proud of this year’s results, as well as the growth the Spartan World Championship Hvar has achieved over the past three years.”

Hvar and Spartan to Continue Partnership in 2027

Spartan returns to Hvar from October 7 to 10, 2027. The fourth edition will offer an opportunity to experience the island from a new perspective. Organizers invite past participants to return and aim for a new personal best, and encourage those who watched the races from the sidelines this year to step up to the starting line themselves next autumn.

World.title: Hvar Tourism Returns to Its Wellbeing Roots with HVARMONY Gathering
World.content:
October 12, 2026 – Croatia’s premier island of Hvar prepares to mark 158 years of organised tourism in Europe by returning to its roots – meet HVARMONY.

Long before “wellbeing” had a name, Hvar was already living it.

Carl Honoré, Kristina Kuzmič, and Ivana Paradžiković are among the headliners of HVARMONY, a four-day gathering focused on how to live better, longer, and happier lives, taking place in Hvar from October 15 to 18.

From October 15 to 18, Hvar becomes a venue for discussing a seemingly simple yet increasingly important question: how can we live better, longer, and happier lives?

HVARMONY – The Art of Living is a new four-day event that bridges modern insights into health, longevity, movement, nutrition, mental resilience, and quality of life with the Mediterranean’s generations-old wisdom on the good life.

The idea behind HVARMONY is not to offer yet another list of rules for becoming a “better version of yourself.” Quite the opposite. In an era where wellbeing and longevity have evolved into global trends and massive industries, HVARMONY shifts the focus back to a simpler question: what do we truly need to live well?

The answers won’t be sought solely on stage. Over the course of four days, lectures and discussions will alternate with movement, workshops, outdoor activities, the sea, food, sound, and experiences that transform Hvar from a mere backdrop into an active participant in the event.

Among the headliners of this inaugural edition is Carl Honoré—the internationally acclaimed author of the bestseller In Praise of Slowness and a leading figure of the Slow Movement—who will speak about the value of slowing down in a world that constantly pressures us to speed up. Kristina Kuzmič—an international speaker and author followed by millions for her open and direct approach to topics such as parenting, mental health, life challenges, and self-relationship—is also coming to Hvar.

Joining the program alongside her are Ivana Paradžiković and a host of domestic and international authors, experts, and facilitators specializing in nutrition, movement, mental resilience, longevity, and quality of life.

Among them are Maja Brekalo, Dalibor Petrinić, Andrea Solomun, Goran Sajko, Mirela Anić, Mia Šoškić, Miriam Mack, Sebastian Orlić, Petra Hisinger, Mirta Primorac Šejić, TLEX Institute experts Neringa Thariani and Aleksandra Jovanić-Sinko, Nina Kraljić, and other program participants.

Hvar returns to its original tourism roots—in October.

The choice of Hvar and the timing is no coincidence.

Hvar’s organized tourism story began back in 1868 with the founding of the Hygienic Society, at a time when the island’s greatest assets were highlighted as its mild Mediterranean climate, sunshine, clean air, sea, and opportunities for rest and recovery.

The Hygienic Society’s first hotel opened on October 15, 1868—the very same date that, 158 years later, marks the start of the inaugural edition of HVARMONY. “Hvar began its organized tourism journey during the very time of year we would today call the off-season. The Sanitary Society’s first hotel opened on October 15, 1868, and Hvar’s comparative advantage back then was precisely its Mediterranean climate—sun, sea, clean air, rest, and recovery. That is why, for us, HVARMONY is not merely a reminder of the beginnings of tourism nearly 160 years ago, but also a message that Hvar is just as beautiful—and perhaps, in a unique way, even more so—outside the peak summer months, when its natural rhythm comes to the fore once again.

We did not envision HVARMONY as just another conference on well-being or longevity, but rather as a reminder that the art of living often lies in simple things: time spent with loved ones, good food, physical activity, being in nature, quality sleep, and the ability to simply slow down from time to time. The island teaches you this almost naturally. And perhaps that is precisely the link between a quality life and quality tourism: neither should be a race to accumulate more, but rather a quest for better balance.

I am particularly delighted that this idea was recognized right from its inaugural edition and that we will be joined in Hvar by a host of fascinating local and international authors, speakers, and experts—including Carl Honoré, Kristina Kuzmič, and Ivana Paradžiković. Their diverse perspectives embody exactly what we want HVARMONY to be: a place for exchanging ideas and experiences, and for finding simpler answers to the question of how to live better.” Director of the Hvar Town Tourist Board

A program that does not require following a strict schedule

HVARMONY does not follow a traditional conference format. Visitors can attend a single lecture, participate in a workshop, start the day with movement by the sea, discover Hvar through the story of its origins in health tourism, join a discussion in the historic Hvar Theatre, or simply take a few hours for themselves.

The program takes place at various locations across the town, including the Arsenal and Hvar Theatre, Bonj, and open-air seaside spaces. Each visitor can experience HVARMONY in their own way—whether by attending a single lecture or practice session, or by participating throughout all four days.

The event is organized by the Hvar Town Tourist Board as an initiative open to the general public. Most of the program is free of charge, though registration is required, as is advance sign-up for specific workshops and sessions with limited capacity.

HVARMONY aims to open up a conversation about health and longevity—without adding the pressure to live a perfect life. Because perhaps the art of living isn’t about constantly doing more. Perhaps it means recognizing what is enough for us, what is worth holding onto, and the pace at which we want to live. HVARMONY – The Art of Living October 15–18, 2026

For more info, visit www.hvarmony.com

World.title: Ryanair Expands Dubrovnik Flight Network, Adding Warsaw Route in 2027
World.content:
October the 12th, 2026 – Ryanair is expanding its Dubrovnik flight network as of next year, with a brand new Warsaw route operating four times per week in 2027.

Ryanair has announced a brand new route between Dubrovnik and Warsaw Modlin as part of the first package of new routes for the summer 2027 flight schedule. As stated in its media release, it is one of a total of 29 new routes presented ahead of the next summer season, as reported by both Dubrovnik Insider and Croatian Aviation.

Traffic on the new route will begin on the very first day of the summer schedule, the 29th of March 2027, and flights will operate until the 2nd of October 2027. Ryanair plans four weekly flights, every Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday. Boeing 737-800 aircraft have been announced for the route; in Ryanair’s fleet these have a capacity of 189 passengers. With four flights a week announced throughout practically the entire summer schedule, Ryanair will offer almost 42,000 seats in both directions, assuming that all planned flights are operated and that aircraft of the stated capacity are used on them.

The new route will further and better connect Dubrovnik with the Polish market during the busy summer season. Warsaw Modlin will therefore join the increasing network of destinations available from Dubrovnik, with the additional possibility of travel between the extreme south of Dalmatia and Poland.

World.title: Croatian Government Proposes Abolition of Pension Tax
World.content:
October the 12th, 2026 – The Croatian Government has proposed the abolition of pension tax, with around 541,000 people affected by the decision.

The Croatian Government has sent to Parliament a proposal for amendments to the Income Tax Act that proposes the complete abolition of tax on pensions. Poslovni reports that according to the proposal, the current reduction of the tax liability on a pension would be increased from 50 to 100 percent for the part of the pension on which income tax is calculated at the lower rate. In practice this means that income tax on such pensions would amount to zero euros.

The Government cited the example of a pensioner who receives a pension of 800 euros. With a personal allowance of 600 euros, the tax base amounts to 200 euros. If a tax rate of 20 percent is applied to it, the tax liability amounts to 40 euros, but under the current system it is reduced by 50 percent so the pensioner pays 20 euros in tax. Under the new proposal that tax would amount to zero euros.

It is estimated that the abolition of tax on pensions will reduce the revenues of local self-government units by around 180 million euros. Finance Minister Tomislav Ćorić earlier stated that around 541,000 pensioners would be covered by this change. The Government plans for the amendments to enter into force at the beginning of 2027.

World.title: Gallery: Ülle Madise sworn in as president of Estonia
World.content:
Former justice chancellor Ülle Madise was sworn in as the next president of Estonia on Monday, taking the oath of office in the Session Hall of the Riigikogu.

On Monday afternoon, President-elect Ülle Madise and her husband Lauri Madise arrived at the Office of the President in Kadriorg, where they were welcomed by President Alar Karis and his wife Sirje Karis.

From there, they traveled together to Toompea Hill, where the outgoing president greeted the Guard Battalion honor guard assembled in Lossi Square before Madise and Karis entered Toompea Castle.

At the ceremony, which began at 3 p.m., Karis delivered a final speech as head of state before President-elect Ülle Madise took the oath of office and delivered her first address as president of the Republic of Estonia.

The ceremony and speeches were broadcast live on ERR channels.

Ülle Madise's swearing in as Estonia's next president. October 12, 2026. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

Born and educated in Tartu, 51-year-old Ülle Madise is a lawyer by training. She has previously worked at the Ministry of Justice, on the Riigikogu's Constitutional Committee, as chief auditor at the National Audit Office, as legal adviser to the president and, since 2015, as chancellor of justice. She was reappointed to the latter position for a second term in late 2021.

Ülle Madise is married to Lauri Madise, who works as a judge at the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg. The couple have no children. Ülle Madise's father is former politician and Supreme Court justice Tõnu Anton.

Madise was nominated as a presidential candidate by 75 members of the Riigikogu. Representatives of the Reform Party, Eesti 200, Isamaa, the Social Democrats and unaffiliated MPs submitted the relevant documents to the National Electoral Committee.

The Riigikogu elected Madise president in a secret ballot with 71 votes.

President-elect Ülle Madise, President Alar Karis and their spouses at Kadriorg ahead of Ülle Madise's inauguration. October 12, 2026. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

World.title: Estonian grain farmers have reason to be happy with the summer
World.content:
This past summer was the best in years for grain growers, but a good harvest does not necessarily translate into strong financial results. The outlook for grain prices remains uncertain.

According to the Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture's food security report, grain quality was poor last year due to excessive rainfall. Low prices also weighed on producers' profits. This year, however, was one of the strongest harvest years in recent memory for Estonian grain growers.

According to Statistics Estonia, the total grain harvest reached nearly 1.55 million tons this year, while wheat yields were the highest in 14 years. Ants-Hannes Viira, head of agricultural policy at the Estonian Chamber of Agriculture and Commerce, said that when grain, pulses, rapeseed and turnip rape harvests are combined, this summer was the third most productive in Estonia's history.

"We were lucky with the weather this time. In the spring, there were fears that it would be a very dry year. There was very little rainfall until May, but after that, precipitation was above average. The grain will be sold, of course. Fortunately, prices are better this year than last year," Viira said.

Viira added that the grain sector's financial results are positive. Looking ahead to next year, the key factors will be the same as this year.

"We don't know what the weather will be like. Fertilizer prices will remain high next year, just as they have been this year, and there is uncertainty about grain prices. It depends on the situation in the Black Sea and whether the Ukrainian and Russian grain harvests, which have also been good this year, can reach the global market," Viira said.

The difficulties Ukrainian and Russian grain face in reaching global markets are helping support grain exports and prices elsewhere, but that may not be the case next year.

Estonian grain is exported to the Middle East and North Africa, while peas are shipped to Spain and Norway for use in animal and fish feed. Grain growers would welcome the opportunity to expand their farmland, but subsidy policies limit their ability to do so.

"For more than 20 years, we've been in a situation where permanent grassland must remain permanent grassland and arable crops cannot be grown on it. This has prevented the expansion of grain-growing areas. Ultimately, the soils and fields suitable for grain production are already being used for that purpose. There isn't much room for a major expansion in cultivated land. Arable crops cover around 400,000 to 500,000 hectares. The area has gradually increased, yes, but not significantly," Viira explained.

The more difficult years have also affected investment. According to Bank of Estonia statistics, the agricultural sector's leasing portfolio has fallen from approximately €370 million in September 2023 to around €305 million today. Marjan Savtšenko, head of business banking at Luminor, said farmers should avoid drawing up overly optimistic budgets for next year based on a single exceptionally good year. There are already signs that purchases of new machinery, for example, have declined.

"Farmers would be wise to remain conservative and build up financial reserves. Most investments go into machinery because it is essential for harvesting crops. If a neighboring property comes up for sale, farmers take the opportunity to expand their farmland," Savtšenko said.

World.title: Estonian tennis player Elena Malõgina reaches new career-high ranking
World.content:
Estonia's top-ranked tennis player Elena Malõgina hit a new career high, rising three spots to 265th in the latest Women's Tennis Association (WTA) rankings.

Malõgina (Malygina), 26, is scheduled to compete this week at an ITF W35 tournament in Birmingham. She achieved her previous record high ranking of 322nd in 2023.

Fellow Estonian tennis player Maileen Nuudi, 26, rose 16 places to rank 968th, with another 15 ranking points to be reflected in next week's update following her ITF W15 tournament victory.

Elizabeth Jürna, 20, climbed to 1,429th and Carol Plakk, 24, to 1,504th.

Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina and Belarusian Aryna Sabalenka remain first and second in the WTA rankings. Mirra Andreeva, competing as a neutral athlete, reached a career-high third place, pushing Americans Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff down to fourth and fifth, respectively.

Ukraine's Elina Svitolina rose to sixth and Czech player Karolina Muchova to seventh, while compatriot Linda Noskova fell to eighth. Poland's Iga Swiatek remained ninth and Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk 10th.

China's Zheng Qinwen, who won the WTA 1000 tournament in Beijing, climbed 31 places to No. 23.

World.title: Education ministry wants schools to teach more local dialects
World.content:
The Ministry of Education wants to make it easier to study regional varieties of Estonian in schools. Students would be able to replace their second foreign language classes with lessons in a regional variety of Estonian.

According to the Ministry of Education, regional varieties of Estonian are currently taught in around 15 to 20 general education schools in Estonia, most of them small rural schools, with just a couple of lessons a week.

However, a draft regulation has now been completed that would significantly expand opportunities to study regional varieties of Estonian starting next school year. Under the proposal, parents would have the right to request such instruction from a school if at least 10 children want to learn their local language variety. Parents at schools that already offer such instruction would not need to submit new requests.

Under the proposal, local language and culture could be studied as an elective. It would also give regional varieties of Estonian equal status with foreign languages in the curriculum, allowing students to study them more extensively as their second foreign language. The specific conditions would be established after the legislation is adopted.

Minister of Education Kristina Kallas told ERR that the change is necessary because children whose native language is Russian or Ukrainian, for example, already have the right to request two hours of instruction a week in their native language, while children who speak Võru, Setu or Mulgi at home do not have the same right.

"In the interests of children's linguistic development and the development of Estonian culture, we need to ensure equal rights so that Setu, Võru and other regional language varieties have similar rights within the education system," Kallas said.

The explanatory memorandum accompanying the draft legislation states that the change was initiated primarily by speakers of South Estonian regional varieties as the protection afforded to regional varieties of Estonian under the Language Act has proved insufficient. The proposed legislation would send a clear message to society that teaching regional varieties of Estonian and local culture is valued and protected through education.

The ministry also noted that demographic changes have led to a decline in the number of small schools, with children increasingly attending larger schools in regional centers. At these schools, instruction in regional language varieties tends to get lost among other interests and activities, making it difficult for those who want to study them to have their needs recognized.

The change would therefore give parents the right to request instruction in a regional variety of Estonian without having to reach agreements that take into account the interests of all parents at the school.

Principal supports the initiative

Jaak Israel, principal of August Kitzberg High School in Viljandi County, said the initiative is worthwhile.

"Everything helps enrich our understanding of language. After all, people need to learn the basics somewhere, including where the Estonian language originated and how it developed," he said.

The school offers an elective course in Mulgi language and culture at the upper secondary level and has also applied for funding under a support program launched by the Ministry of Education this year to help schools teach local language varieties. The application round is still underway, but Israel said the school hopes to use the funding to introduce Mulgi language instruction in the lower grades, replacing one Estonian language lesson a week.

Regarding the Mulgi language elective offered at the upper secondary level, Israel said three students are currently enrolled, although enrollment has been higher in the past. In one year, however, the school ran the course with just a single student.

Kaare Lill, principal of Võru City Center School, said Võru language instruction has only a very limited presence at her school. It is offered as part of extracurricular activities for younger students, with parents able to choose one activity lesson per week from a wide range of options. A child might therefore study Võru for one trimester, robotics for another and something related to art for the third.

Regarding families' interest, Lill noted that if grandparents have not spoken Võru at home and parents themselves have not grown up in a Võru-speaking environment, they may question the point of learning it. More aware parents, however, want their children to have the opportunity. Enrollment in the Võru language club tends to be modest rather than filling up quickly.

Lill therefore believes the proposed change is both necessary and positive in helping keep the Võru language alive, although exactly how it will be implemented remains unclear.

"We may run into some difficulties because we don't have enough teachers who feel confident and have the skills to pass on the Võru language and use it in their lessons. Teachers often come to schools from all over Estonia and they don't have that background," she said.

The principal of August Kitzberg High School in Viljandi County, however, believes finding teachers will not be a problem at his school. Israel said they have an Estonian language teacher who has completed relevant courses and he welcomed the idea of offering Mulgi as a second foreign language.

Israel believes that greater coverage of the issue could also increase parental interest, adding that there is certainly already a group of families interested in the opportunity. However, the change would also need to be accompanied by adequate funding.

Schools to receive support for teaching dialects

According to Kristina Kallas, the change concerns the possibility of teaching regional varieties of Estonian in basic schools. Although upper secondary schools would not be subject to the same requirement, they would still have the option of offering such instruction, as they do with other foreign languages.

"We know that Setomaa High School, for example, already offers Setu language instruction. But this is limited to regions where these language varieties are spoken. Foreign language instruction can be offered uniformly across Estonia, while the teaching of regional language varieties is limited to the areas where they are used," Kallas explained.

To help ensure there are enough teachers, a support program for teaching regional varieties of Estonian is available to fund the publication of textbooks and the development of teaching materials.

Under the draft legislation, responsibility for coordinating the teaching of regional varieties of Estonian and supporting schools would be transferred to the Institute of the Estonian Language, so that individual schools would not have to deal separately with issues such as teaching materials and teacher training.

Instruction in regional varieties of Estonian should not increase students' workloads. However, if a school has no room in its existing timetable, it would be allowed to increase the maximum permitted weekly workload for students by one lesson.

The change would primarily affect schools in the historical areas where the Võru, Setu, Mulgi, Tartu, Saare, Kihnu, Muhu, Hiiu, Kodavere, Kuusalu, Lüganuse and Jõhvi varieties of Estonian are spoken. There are approximately 155 basic schools in these regions.

The requirement would apply only to schools located in areas where distinct regional varieties of Estonian have historically developed.

According to the latest census, 23 percent of people aged 65 and older speak a regional variety of Estonian, compared with just 3 percent of children aged 14 and younger. In total, approximately 160,000 people in Estonia speak a regional variety of the language.

The Ministry of Education has sent the draft amendments to the Basic Schools and Upper Secondary Schools Act to stakeholders for feedback. Under the current plan, the changes would take effect as early as next school year.

World.title: Ülle Madise: Attempts to reeducate people have delivered a setback to trust
World.content:
The attempts of the past decade to remake people, to prescribe how they should live, think, feel or speak have inevitably undermined mutual trust. We have learned that lesson. Now we must rebuild trust, Ülle Madise said in her first speech as president.

On September 2, I spoke about how Estonia's greatest treasure is its people. And so it is. We must do everything possible to ensure that there are many people to carry on the Estonian language and culture. To make Estonia the best place to raise children and grow old, to invent and create, to pursue science and do business. To ensure that our children are among the smartest, most well-balanced and happiest in the world. And that the joy of living does not fade later in life, amid the responsibilities of work and family or because of age or health.

Pristine nature, rustling forests. The sea, lakes and rivers. Birds and animals. Plants, mushrooms and bees. Fish and dragonflies. Just one generation from now, the natural world here will be an even greater wonder than it is today. If only we know how to preserve it. Estonia is already one of the most pleasant places in the world to live. Mosquitoes, puddles, good and bad skiing weather included.

Everyone here in Estonia must be able to feel that they themselves, as well as their lives, work and creations, are valuable. That there is plenty of room for all of us, different as we are. With our own interests, views, lifestyles, tastes and native languages.

High culture and pop culture, alternative culture and the underground, the whole colorful spectrum. Rehearsing for the Song and Dance Celebration does not interfere with hip-hop or a midnight rave and vice versa! Estonia is free, exciting, vibrant, evolving and diverse.

Can we preserve such an Estonia and continue building it? I believe that depends on trust, hope for the future and courage.

Perhaps we do not notice it every day or have forgotten, but in most parts of Estonia, kindness, honest work, common sense and helping one another are still held in high regard. A neighbor helps pull a car out of the snow, an elderly person shivering at a bus stop is offered a ride and gets where they need to go, someone else's children get a ride home from practice along with one's own, fresh cucumbers and tomatoes are hung on a neighbor's door handle or apples are left out for anyone to take. Let us notice these things, appreciate them and do our part.

Unfortunately, in my work as chancellor of justice, I saw far too often how someone gives their best, dedicates themselves to helping others, but does not receive the same consideration in return. Yet they could. They should.

Take, for example, a mother who, through circumstances beyond her control, is raising a child alone, working, studying for a profession that society badly needs and volunteering wherever she can. Yet when she herself needs help, she all too often encounters bureaucratic obstruction and cold arrogance in seeking support.

My colleagues and I at the Office of the Chancellor of Justice always stood against soulless bureaucratic procedures wherever we encountered them. What is the point of a system in which officials can shrug their shoulders and coldly declare that "clients did not receive the service," rather than recognize that a child and their mother were left without help?

Fortunately, there are people who find solutions. But do we know how to recognize and appreciate them for it?

Take a police officer who saves the life of a child speeding along on a battery-powered scooter, only to hear the parent respond with ... I will not even repeat it. How can anyone believe that a highly trained officer leaves their family to go to work in the evening simply to harass law-abiding people?

Or a teacher who cares deeply about their students, looks for opportunities to help them spread their wings, comes home in the evening, opens their computer — and there it is! No, not messages of gratitude.

We need much more trust and warm appreciation. Doctors, journalists, police officers, teachers, farmers — each of us, in our respective professions, is a trained specialist doing our best. And trust really must be earned. By genuinely doing our best. All of us, in our lives and work.

The attempts of the past decade to remake people, to prescribe how they should live, think, feel or speak have inevitably undermined mutual trust. We have learned that lesson. Now we must rebuild trust.

For people who have experienced occupation, ideological propaganda of any kind provokes contempt, which can drive even the best of people to write or do things they would otherwise never even consider. And to vote against everything simply for the sake of it. Eventually, resentment translates into election results.

Everyone has the right to vote exactly as they see fit. That is what elections are for. What matters most is that people do not stop voting altogether, that they do not fall silent, become indifferent or withdraw from life entirely.

Indifference is an enemy of a free democratic society, as are the loss of hope for the future and sheer noise. The rule of law rests not only on legislation but also on trust and the knowledge that the rules apply to everyone and that people are treated fairly. Let us not allow ourselves to be turned against one another here in our own corner of the world, among our own people. There should be as few people as possible who feel so bad — perhaps with good reason — that they are prepared to tear things down, because we need to build the future.

If you want peace, prepare for ... you know the rest. Peace must be preserved. Everyone can play a part in that.

The first step is to maintain peace of mind. There is far too much fear of war in the air. Whenever I come away from a discussion of the actual security situation, assessed on the basis of facts, I feel much calmer than I do after reading deliberate fearmongering. Of course, I know that politics or business interests lie behind it. But still.

Yes, the world around us is unpredictable and dangerous. Of course it is. I understand the concern and I worry too. A global crisis of trust? That is true as well. Ukraine must be supported in every conceivable way so that the war of aggression against it ends and a lasting, just peace is achieved. So that war criminals are punished and the aggressor pays for the damage. We must convincingly demonstrate around the world that international law, a rules-based international order and the protection of human rights benefit most countries and all people.

Estonia has worked diligently to make itself stronger. The Estonian Defense Forces, the Estonian Defense League, the Women's Voluntary Defense Organization. Our entire system of comprehensive national defense. Our committed neighbors in the Baltic and Nordic countries. Poland. All our allies in Europe and NATO. All of this is what makes us secure.

Please, let us not allow fear or hopelessness into our hearts. Fear paralyzes us or drives us to do foolish things. We must act wisely. And everyone has an opportunity to do so. I dare to assure you that the future is neither bleak nor predetermined. We are building it ourselves. In times of uncertainty, we must recognize the great opportunities before us and make skillful use of them.

We also need more humor and lightness in general. And something to sustain our spirits.

Culture cannot be treated as something that comes after everything else. Culture sustains and supports us, comforts us, broadens our horizons, warns us, cleanses the dark corners of the human soul and helps us become better people. Let us not miss out on cultural events close to home. Let us make them inviting and accessible to children and young people, as well as to those who have little money or difficulty getting around.

Let us appreciate our writers, filmmakers, theater professionals, artists, designers and museums — both new creations and our heritage. Let us always take an interest in how other peoples live and in their cultures. When I am abroad, I try to visit a museum or church, even if only briefly.

And let us make ourselves visible: exhibitions by Estonian artists around the world, our magnificent orchestras and choirs, theatrical performances, novels, medals won at sporting competitions — all of it matters. So do scientific research and inventions that make their way into production, as well as collaborative projects. Bold and trustworthy entrepreneurship. Technology companies, startups, agricultural businesses and the defense industry, of course. But not only those!

These days, it is a major achievement when an entrepreneur can produce something distinctive and of very high quality, at a reasonable price and in an environmentally responsible way and deliver the products on time. Not just here in Estonia, but anywhere in the world.

Estonia's trump card is education. We know it ourselves and so does the entire educated world, but we must work harder to ensure that every child in Estonia receives a good education and has ample opportunities. This must not depend on whether a child attends a small rural school or one in Tallinn's residential districts, whether they live with their parents, a foster family or in a children's home or whether they are still learning Estonian. Estonia's future depends on a good education for all its children.

The AI Leap initiative in schools, launched under the leadership of President Alar Karis, deserves recognition and continuation. The future belongs to those who know how to use artificial intelligence wisely while remaining free and capable as human beings. The leap that has begun must aim as far as possible. And always in such a way that AI does not become an "ow!"

Technology must not make us forget that people also need to be able to manage on their own. Excessive dependence on technology and electricity is dangerous for everyone, everywhere. All it takes is a storm or a thief to land us in serious trouble. Let us remain resilient.

Estonia's Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs Liisa Pakosta is leading an international discussion on establishing regulations for artificial intelligence. Estonia is exactly the country that should be taking the lead. We have extensive experience as a digital state and a complicated history. We know how to understand other peoples and countries around the world and perhaps they can understand us as well.

The digital divide does not exist or deepen only within societies, where in some places it is causing ever greater poverty, suffering and resentment with each passing year or even month. That is why we need an agreement that artificial intelligence must also be accessible to smaller and poorer countries and that AI must serve humanity, not the other way around.

To protect the Estonian language and culture, and all small nations and cultures, we must ensure that they are properly and accurately represented in artificial intelligence models.

Armies of bots serving the interests of an aggressor state are vigorously spreading falsehoods and teaching artificial intelligence to lie and ultimately those lies will harm everyone. Countries that wish to remain sovereign and independent should have a vital interest in combating hostile propaganda.

The president cannot and must not take the place of the popularly elected Riigikogu, the government or the courts. The separation and balance of powers is of great value. The president has an important role in maintaining that balance.

The date for a meeting of the National Defense Council, as provided for in the Constitution, has already been set. I would take the saying "Train hard, fight easy" a step further: If the training is exceptionally rigorous, there will be no battle at all. And that, after all, is our goal.

We could begin combating a lack of ideas and growing uniformity here at home by encouraging bold thinking and dreaming. The president's think tank is one place for that. Thinking together, debating and sharing humor bring out the best in people, from academics to schoolchildren. That is how new ideas are born.

The president can recognize and support everyone working to ensure that families have places to live and raise children, that the birth of a child does not lead to financial hardship and that someone who wants to build a home in the countryside can also obtain a loan. Let making Estonia a child- and family-friendly country become an issue in the upcoming elections and every election thereafter. Not by backing anyone into a corner or putting them on the defensive, but by cheerfully showing how well things can be done.

Perhaps we also need a Tiger Leap in mental health. Yes, of course we need more psychologists and psychiatrists, greater recognition of individual differences and more consideration for them. But we also need to eliminate unnecessary pressures that are breaking more and more people.

Excessive and destructive competitiveness, pulling one another down, noise, harassment, injustice, loneliness, overwhelming fear and anxiety and hopelessness are not inevitable features of life. I will do my best to help us find the courage. Because why be unhappy and lose when it is possible to be happy and win?

The president can help make the voices of people heard more clearly — what troubles them, what they expect and what they hope for — in Võrumaa and Virumaa, Mehikoorma and Häädemeeste, Saaremaa and Hiiumaa, Paide and Põltsamaa and everywhere that local communities are working hard to keep life from moving away, to ensure that farms flourish, that tourism and business in general develop and that it remains worthwhile for successive generations to make an effort.

The money needed to sustain our free Estonian state can come only from a strong and adaptable economy. So let us give entrepreneurs the freedom to act. We do not need all-encompassing convenience that makes people lazy and helpless. We do not need orders, prohibitions, unnecessary bureaucracy or overseers everywhere, stifling creativity and initiative. The head of state can remind people of that, too. In the form of a veto, if necessary.

I will take time to meet people from different walks of life in different parts of Estonia. To listen to them, share their concerns and joys and try to understand. And then to carry their message forward. My colleagues and I will be seen in gardens, factories, barns, company brainstorming spaces, schools, nursing homes, village squares, hospitals, city streets and other places where everyday life unfolds. I am afraid I will not be able to attend ceremonial events as often as I should and I ask for your understanding.

I hope to maintain regular contact with members of the Riigikogu, the prime minister and ministers and the heads of constitutional institutions, understanding and respecting their respective roles. Here, too, trust, respect for one another's dignity and working together for Estonia's future and the benefit of everyone living here are what matter.

I have said repeatedly and I will say it again: All our previous heads of state have been the right people in the right place at the right time and have made Estonia better and greater. Thank you very much! Thank you, President Alar Karis. I would also like to thank Mrs. Sirje Karis in particular. Her work for Ukrainian children alone deserves the highest recognition.

As I continue the work of my predecessors, I feel a profound sense of humility and responsibility.

If we trust one another, value freedom, responsibility and clear communication, have the courage to be good people, trust in life, believe in Estonia and maintain a hopeful outlook, all good things are possible.

Long live Estonia!
