World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019103/Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.title: Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019103/Two Chinese Books Shortlisted for US National Translation Awards
World.content:
Two books translated into English from Chinese have been shortlisted for the 2026 U.S. National Translation Awards, which recognize excellence in both original and translated literary works.

The shortlist, announced Tuesday by the American Literary Translators Association, includes two originally written in Chinese: Chinese author Shuang Xuetao’s short story collection “Hunter,” translated by Jeremy Tiang, and Hong Kong writer Hon Lai Chu’s “Mending Bodies,” translated by Jacqueline Leung, among a total of 11 poetry and prose works translated from nine languages.

“The Ruins,” an anthology by Chinese poet Ye Hui and translated by Li Dong, was longlisted among 23 works across prose and poetry on Sept. 3 but did not make the shortlist. Ye is known for his spare, understated poems that draw on everyday life and nature and explore questions of time, memory, and existence.

Established in 1998, the awards rank among the world’s top professional accolades for literary translation. Winning translators in both categories — poetry and prose — each receive a $4,000 prize. Translations of Chinese works have previously been listed for the prize, including works by contemporary writers Xu Zechen and Yan Lianke, as well as Qing dynasty (1644–1911) novelist and playwright Li Yu.

Shuang Xuetao, author of “Hunter,” one of the two shortlisted Chinese works, was born in 1983 in Shenyang, capital of the northeastern Liaoning province. He is widely considered a leading figure in the “Dongbei Renaissance,” a cultural movement emerging from northeast China, or Dongbei. Known for his use of local dialect, Shuang often portrays the lives of ordinary people in the region, long dismissed as a cultural backwater and rust belt. Several of his works have been adapted into films.

“Hunter” features 11 standalone stories, some of which were originally written in Dongbei dialect: from provincial ambulance drivers searching for a hospital in the middle of the night, to a legendary knife fighter working in a factory. In a note about their selection published alongside the announcement, the competition’s judges wrote that Shuang’s stories “paint a portrait of a region marked by gritty pragmatism, dark humor, and magical realism.”

The work was translated by Shuang’s long-term collaborator Jeremy Tiang — a novelist in his own right. The judges wrote that Tiang “expertly translated Shuang’s often inventive, utterly unique description; his English texts are layered and witty.”

The second book nominated for the prize, “Mending Bodies” by Hong Kong writer Hon Lai Chu, is a work of speculative fiction and follows a young woman adjusting to life after surgically binding her body to a partner, in a future where people are encouraged to do so. Hon has previously drawn praise for her surreal, introspective fiction, which often explores the fragility of the body, memory, and human relationships.

According to the judges, Jacqueline Leung, the book’s Hong Kong-based translator, “flawlessly translates the between-the-lines subtleties of the languages.”

“The shortlisting of these works carries substantial significance for the overseas circulation of Sinophone literature and its greater visibility within global professional literary circuits, representing, in a sense, a multifaceted retelling of Chinese stories across fiction and poetry,” Shao Dong, an assistant professor of creative writing at Hong Kong Metropolitan University, told Sixth Tone.

The overall award winners will be announced on Oct. 23 as part of the American Literary Translators Association’s annual conference.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Covers of “Hunter,” “Mending Bodies,” and “The Ruins,” by Shuang Xuetao, Hon Lai Chu, and Ye Hui, respectively. Reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019087/‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.title: ‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019087/‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.content:
The thieves came in the dead of night in late August — seven ghostly figures illuminated only by the glow of their flashlights and burning cigarettes. When they left, tucked under their arms were 10 chickens and two geese.

The next day, watching footage of the theft recorded by a security camera, Xu Lingni’s heart sank. It was the end of a dream.

The poultry had been kept overnight in a hilltop coop at the bucolic Huxi campus of the Sichuan Fine Arts Institute (SCFAI), in the southwestern megacity of Chongqing, and belonged to the Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative, a student-led club aimed at rebuilding the bonds between humans and nature.

The group had intended to use the project to promote interest across campus and beyond in food-waste conversion, community-supported agriculture, plastics consumption, and other sustainability issues.

For Xu, the club’s leader, those plans vanished along with those 12 birds. Yet worse was to come.

After a brief investigation, the Chongqing police discovered that several workers hired by SCFAI for a summer construction project had taken the poultry and eaten them. Their crew manager agreed to pay 7,000 yuan ($1,040) to compensate for the financial loss and the students’ emotional distress.

However, the theft drew widespread attention and sparked fresh criticism over raising animals on campus. Facing mounting pressure, the school’s leadership decided to ban the practice. The cooperative was over.

Hatching a plan

The Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative was a key part of the Healing Garden Project, which inhabits a patch of land on campus once piled high with construction waste. Seven years ago, Jin Lipeng, an associate professor in SCFAI’s School of Experimental Art, led students in repurposing the debris to pave paths and build planting beds. He envisioned an area that could restore nature and nurture people.

At the time, the campus cafeteria was sending hundreds of kilograms of food scraps — often mixed with unsorted plastic waste — to an incinerator dozens of kilometers away. Jin and his students began to use these leftovers as compost, converting roughly 40 tons of food waste into fertilizer over the years.

The idea for the cooperative stemmed from a graduate student’s thesis project in spring 2025 that looked at permaculture and the role of foraging chickens in loosening soil, eating pests, clearing weeds, and providing eggs. To test a theory, the student purchased five chickens of a local breed with red combs and black skin. They were allowed to roam freely through campus and returned at night to their hilltop coop.

Xu, an undergraduate majoring in sculpture, was already involved in the garden project and began informally caring for the chickens, buying them grain and taking them to the veterinarian.

In summer last year, as temperatures soared above 40 degrees Celsius, one bird died of heatstroke, and three others disappeared. Fearing that the sole survivor would get lonely, Xu bought a new one from the market. Then one of the escapees returned.

A few days later, Xu found six new adolescent chickens in the coop. A school janitor, who had bought them to raise for their meat, agreed to sell the birds to the students. These were soon joined by a common chicken brought from a roadside stall, a Plymouth Rock chicken, a new hatchling, and a wuhei black-boned chicken. (Two birds died before the theft — one from hypothermia, the other from a wild animal attack. The wuhei chicken was the only one left behind by the thieves; its dark plumage likely made it hard to spot at night.)

As the flock grew, the birds began producing more eggs than the students could eat. Jin, whose research area includes labor issues, proposed creating the cooperative as a student club and asked Xu to lead it. Soon, the students were dividing up their responsibilities: caring for the animals, sourcing and selling merchandise, writing articles, and managing social media channels. In June this year, several attended an international conference to introduce the cooperative’s work.

Those who joined the project felt that caring for the chickens brought them “healing energy.” Xu recalls one classmate who would often hold the birds and cry. “The theft this summer hit her especially hard, and she wasn’t the only one,” Xu says, adding that the cooperative not only fostered friendships but also helped some members find meaning.

While she doesn’t exactly share Jin’s grand ideals, Xu believes that through her work she came to understand seemingly distant but deeply personal issues such as permaculture and climate change.

“Most university students have no idea where eggs come from, what happens to food waste, or why rubbish gets incinerated,” she said in a speech at a climate change forum in May. “Dorm rooms are piled with takeout plastic. Delivery workers risk heatstroke in extreme temperatures. Yet few students have enough awareness to connect these to drought, heat, and carbon emissions.

“Our work lets people feel the pressure and causes of climate change firsthand,” she added, “and shows that through campus community-supported agriculture we can mount a small resistance.”

Making a mess

The cooperative began selling eggs for about 2 yuan each to residents on and around campus this March. The chickens laid two to eight eggs a day. Xu stored them in her apartment’s refrigerator, took orders through an online group chat, and delivered them to customers on her electric bike. She calculates that this brought in just over 500 yuan in total.

Fans of the project were kept up to date through the club’s channel on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, which has more than 6,300 followers. In addition, the cooperative sold themed merchandise including fridge magnets, tote bags, and silk scarves, which brought in about 2,000 yuan.

Not everyone was supportive, though. The most common complaint was that the free-roaming chickens often defecated on the pathways and at the entrance to the student dormitories. To prevent this, this summer the birds were fenced in on the hillside.

In 2022, Chongqing introduced regulations prohibiting the raising of livestock and poultry in urban areas. However, the restrictions apply only to commercial-scale farming, while exceptions can be made for educational purposes and scientific research.

While the number of chickens at SCFAI was far below commercial scale, the activity fell outside the definition of “backyard rearing,” putting it in a gray area. As such, the school took an open-minded approach, requiring only proper fencing and separation, despite repeated objections from others in the campus community.

The cooperative used old bamboo posts and tall netting to enclose the poultry on the hilltop. But the gate was never locked. “This is a public welfare project. Anyone was welcome to come in to spend time with the chickens,” Xu explains.

For security, the group installed an infrared camera to watch the flock at night and raised two goslings to guard the coop. “Geese bite hard. Once I went up the hill in a raincoat, and they didn’t recognize me, so they bit me,” Xu adds. “We’d thought the intruders would be stray cats or weasels — never thieves.”

Ruffling feathers

The theft sparked an outpouring of grief online. “Come home, little ones” and “My babies are gone” were typical comments posted by students in the aftermath.

In the coming weeks and months, Xu and her classmates had planned to step up marketing and sales, offer egg-based food delivery services, and write a handbook on community supported agriculture that could inspire other schools and universities.

That’s now all been scrapped. This fall, the school’s leadership announced a ban on keeping poultry on campus.

In a statement, it also said that officials had learned during mediation that the maintenance workers who took the birds had endured long hours of intense labor in hot weather, with limited food and lodging. Some students strongly objected to this version of events, arguing that chicken meat is cheap and widely available — and that the workers weren’t “desperate,” they just wanted to taste free-range birds.

“Pioneering ecological practice is inherently accompanied by trial and error and waiting,” the statement read. “We will review and consolidate, continue deepening our existing work, and wait for the right conditions to restart explorations.”

The cooperative maintained that its activities “filled a gap” in the school’s labor education by giving students hands-on experience as well as teaching responsibility and empathy. But there was no overturning the decision.

The sole survivor of the theft, the wuhei chicken, was moved to a student’s home for safekeeping and has quickly adapted to her new environment. Xu says the bird is even laying eggs again.

(Due to privacy concerns, Xu Lingni is a pseudonym.)

Reported by Kong Lingyu.

A version of this article originally appeared in FoodThink. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.title: China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.content:
DeepZang, China’s first Tibetan-language large language model, is being upgraded to better adapt to Tibetan dialects, enable real-time translation between Tibetan and Mandarin Chinese, and support offline use.

At a Monday seminar in Hohhot, capital of northern China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, the model’s developer unveiled a series of upgrades scheduled between October and December. The seminar featured representatives from companies, research institutions, and universities.

DeepZang, developed by local technology company Choknor, was launched in March in Lhasa, capital of the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region. Its app supports AI-powered conversations, translation, and speech transcription in Tibetan, Mandarin Chinese, and English.

At the model’s launch, organizations including the Xizang branches of China Mobile and the People’s Insurance Company of China, as well as Sichuan Minzu Publishing House, signed agreements with Choknor to promote its adoption.

According to Choknor, DeepZang has attracted nearly 400,000 users across Xizang, the northwestern Qinghai and Gansu provinces, and southwestern Sichuan province, where most of China’s Tibetan speakers reside.

The company has said the model has cut the time needed for some Tibetan-Chinese translation tasks involving two or three people from 40 minutes to just over 10 minutes for one person. It also reported that the model has been used in such varied settings as helping non-Tibetan-speaking doctors communicate with local patients, generating Tibetan-language contracts for yak sales, and assisting grassroots officials in drafting Tibetan work reports.

The model has been trained on nearly 70 million pairs of standardized Tibetan and Chinese texts, along with more than 30,500 hours of Tibetan speech covering its three major dialect groups — Ü-Tsang, Kham, and Amdo. The team collected the data from libraries, medical institutions, and monasteries, among other settings.

At Monday’s seminar, Choknor unveiled plans to develop offline language packages for Tibetan, Chinese, and English, allowing the app to function with limited or no internet access. The company also plans to pilot 50 simultaneous interpretation devices among at least 300 participants in Lhasa this December.

Tenzin Norbu, Choknor’s founder, said the company aims to bring DeepZang into “pastoral tents, tourist service counters, and grassroots hospitals,” enabling Tibetan speakers to “enjoy the benefits of artificial intelligence on an equal footing.”

Choknor said on Sunday that beyond fostering exchanges and integration among ethnic groups, DeepZang could help ensure the accuracy of Tibetan-language information and contribute to social stability and long-term security.

Founded in 2016, Choknor specializes in Tibetan-Chinese bilingual speech technology, scanning and translation tools, and optical character recognition. Its products include smart computer mice, scanning and translation pens, and an AI-powered Tibetan subtitling system.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.title: The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.content:
With hundreds of concerts scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, some fans found the cheapest way to upgrade a seat was to rent a better camera phone.

For about 100 to 200 yuan ($15 to $30) a day, concertgoers can rent flagship smartphones with powerful telephoto cameras that pull distant performers into clearer view, a useful option when high demand leaves fans seated far from the stage and professional cameras and long lenses are often barred from venues.

On Chinese rental platform Renrenzu and Xianyu, a secondhand marketplace owned by Chinese tech giant Alibaba, some flagship phones are listed as “concert essentials.”

One Renrenzu ad touted a “200-megapixel telephoto, crystal clear — even the nosebleed seats feel VIP,” while the platform has also offered concert ticket reimbursements through prize draws.

The phones on offer are among the latest flagships from Chinese smartphone makers such as vivo and OPPO, with high-resolution telephoto cameras, image stabilization, and, in some cases, detachable lens kits that extend their reach.

A vivo X300 Ultra bundled with a telephoto lens, for example, rents for about 215 yuan for one day, while a two-day rental brings the average daily cost down to about 125 yuan. Other popular models include OPPO’s Find X10 Pro Max, which packs three 200-megapixel rear cameras and is advertised as supporting up to “20x lossless zoom” with its official telephoto kit.

Such high-end models typically sell for about 5,000 to 8,000 yuan, while official telephoto lens kits can add another 1,000 to 2,000 yuan, making a short rental far cheaper for fans who only want the extra reach for one concert.

Online, concertgoers are comparing phones and lens attachments, posting photos from the stands, and swapping tips on which setups work best from distant seats.

Liu Hang, who attended Taiwan singer Steve Chou’s concert at Beijing Workers’ Stadium, told Time Finance that he brought a Ruiying Z10 camera module and telephoto attachment made by Chinese tech giant Huawei into the venue. “I had a 580-yuan ticket, but with the ‘Huawei cannon,’ it felt like a 1,680-yuan seat,” he said.

Another social media user, who said he had attended nearly 100 concerts, compared several phones and camera setups for live shows. He said such phones were easy to carry, worked well for close-up shots, and had a dedicated stage mode that automatically adjusted exposure, though adding a telephoto attachment made it tiring to hold through an entire concert.

Renrenzu said orders for concert-related equipment jumped 388% year on year over the summer, far outpacing a 67% rise in short-term rentals overall. A total of 257 concerts were scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, according to Alibaba’s entertainment data platform Lighthouse.

Chen Shenyu, a manager at consulting firm China Insights Consultancy, told Time Finance that smartphone photography was becoming less about simply recording daily life and more about performing well in specific situations. Concerts are especially challenging because fans may be seated far from the stage, lighting changes constantly, and they are often shooting handheld photos and video.

That also makes concerts a natural showcase for smartphone makers, Chen said. If consumers increasingly reach for telephoto cameras at sporting events, on trips, and during family activities, demand for the same high-end imaging features could extend well beyond concerts.

(Header image: Posts show concertgoers using flagship camera phones with telephoto attachments to capture performers from the stands. From Xiaohongshu)

World.title: China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.content:
Chinese travelers are increasingly stringing together multiple destinations during the weeklong National Day holiday, boosting mid-holiday air travel and drawing more visitors to smaller cities and counties.

More than 20% of air travelers booked flights to two or more destinations during the holiday, which runs from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, according to online travel platform Tongcheng Travel. Demand for flights in the middle of the holiday rose 35% from a year earlier.

Smaller destinations were among the biggest beneficiaries of the holiday travel boom, with data from travel platform Qunar showing that its 10 top trending scenic spots were all in county-level destinations.

In Qilian County in northwestern Qinghai province, which has a population of about 50,000, more than 100,000 tourists arrived on Oct. 3, filling local hotels and prompting authorities to house nearly 500 stranded visitors in school dormitories as temperatures fell to minus 4 degrees Celsius and snow covered nearby mountaintops.

The county’s culture and tourism department received more than 400 calls for help in seven hours, according to local authorities. Posts on Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, showed tourists searching for rooms as hotels across the county filled up.

One traveler told domestic outlet Jimu News that he spent the afternoon and evening searching major booking platforms after arriving in Qilian from Xi’an but could not find a room. After seeing a notice from local tourism authorities, he called for help and was assigned a school dormitory room shared by four people, with new bedding provided.

Wansui Mountain Martial Arts City in central Henan province also struggled with heavy crowds, repeatedly capping admissions and suspending same-day ticket sales after interest surged 22-fold from a year earlier.

Many travelers were also going farther and staying away longer. According to Tongcheng Travel, people on multi-city trips visited an average of 1.2 more cities than in 2025, with Chengdu, Suzhou, and Wuhan among the busiest transfer hubs.

More than 70% of multi-city travelers booked both natural and cultural attractions, suggesting that many were combining different types of destinations within a single itinerary.

Interest in six- to 10-day groups and customized tours to destinations including Xinjiang, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou rose more than 60% on Tongcheng from a year earlier. Couples and families accounted for more than half of those bookings.

(Header image: Tourists visit the Zhuo’er Mountain Scenic Area in Qilian County, Qinghai province, Oct. 1, 2026. VCG)

World.title: Saudi capital’s airport to remain shut this week as airlines cancel services
World.content:
ROAD TO AIRPORT. General view of the highway leading to the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 12, 2026.

Lufthansa Group canceled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a suspension to and from Riyadh until the end of October

Authorities have extended the closure of Riyadh’s international airport until Saturday, October 17, and airlines scrapped flights after continuing attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis emptied the skies over Saudi Arabia’s capital.

Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to “allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport’s facilities,” the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.

Late on Monday, the Houthis said they had attacked the airport with a ballistic missile, shortly after Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the group towards Riyadh.

The Houthis also said in a statement that they targeted an airbase in Khamis Mushait in the kingdom’s southwest with a drone. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.

A Notice to Airmen issued on Monday showed King Khalid International Airport will stay closed until 2100 GMT on October 17.

The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East and with higher jet fuel prices that are eating into profits.

They have also raised worries over civil aviation becoming a target in armed conflict.

“This level of sustained intense attack on civil aviation is unprecedented,” said Mark Zee, founder of OPSGROUP, a membership-based organization that provides aviation safety advice.

“I think this requires us to rethink how we view the current risk picture, and tread very carefully,” he said.

Air traffic tracker Flightradar24 showed planes avoiding the city on Monday, though jets were crossing Saudi airspace and landing at top hub Jeddah on the country’s west coast.

Cancellations across all Saudi airports reached 46.4%, aviation analytics firm Cirium said.

Crisis overshadows Saudi business outlook

The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia. EU aviation body EASA widened a Saudi airspace warning on Friday, citing missile and drone attacks.

“The impact goes beyond Saudi Arabia to the wider region and to its global connections,” said aviation analyst John Strickland.

OPSGROUP advised airlines to avoid the southern aviation corridor over the Middle East altogether, and take a route from Europe to Asia over central Asia.

That adds “extensive distance” for some routes and “closes off options for getting into Dubai, Abu Dhabi for most western carriers,” Zee said.

Lufthansa Group canceled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a suspension to and from Riyadh until the end of the month.

Etihad Airways said it had canceled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to “regional disruption,” adding that all flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh would be canceled until October 19.

Qatar Airways said on Monday it had temporarily suspended flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam due to the “current situation.”

Delta Air Lines said it was delaying planned services from Atlanta to Riyadh, initially due to start on October 23, until March 2027.

The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia’s real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6% this year, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity.

The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the program. – Rappler.com

World.title: Selma Blair arrested, accused of abusing flight attendants
World.content:
Two flight attendants report injuries and one of them is taken to a hospital

LOS ANGELES, USA – Actor Selma Blair has been arrested after flight attendants reported a “physically abusive passenger” on a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey’s police department said on Monday, October 12.

Police identified Blair, known for roles in the movies “Cruel Intentions” and “Hellboy,” as the suspect in an incident on Sunday evening, October 11.

She was taken into custody at New York’s John F. Kennedy Airport and transported to a hospital for evaluation, police said in a statement. Two flight attendants reported injuries and one of them was taken to a hospital, according to the statement.

A representative for 54-year-old Blair said she had a medical emergency during the flight.

“Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct,” Blair’s representative said. “Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition.”

Blair has spoken publicly about her battle with multiple sclerosis. She was diagnosed with the autoimmune disorder in 2018. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Breaking Bad’ actor and disability rights activist RJ Mitte dead at 34
World.content:
IN MEMORIAM. Actor RJ Mitte poses at the premiere for "El Camino: A Breaking Bad Movie" in Los Angeles, California, US, October 7, 2019.

Mitte was best known for his breakout role on the AMC cable TV series 'Breaking Bad,' playing the only son of the lead character, Walter White, a terminally ill high school teacher who descends into a secret life of crime cooking crystal meth

LOS ANGELES, USA – Actor RJ Mitte, whose personal experience living with cerebral palsy informed his role as Walter White Jr, the physically disabled son of a methamphetamine kingpin in the landmark television show “Breaking Bad,” died on Monday, October 12, at age 34.

News of Mitte’s death in Brownsville, Texas, was confirmed in a statement released through the talent management agency that represented the actor. No other details about the circumstances of his death were given.

“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” the statement said.

Drawing from his real-life experience with cerebral palsy, Mitte was best known for his breakout role on the AMC cable TV series “Breaking Bad,” playing the only son of the lead character, Walter White, a terminally ill high school teacher who descends into a secret life of crime cooking crystal meth.

Mitte’s character, who adopted the nickname Flynn, used crutches and spoke with a slur, gains greater prominence as the story arc of the series progressed. He starts out as a carefree teenager who largely admires his father but later struggles to reckon with the family’s disintegration as the truth about Walter White’s “Heisenberg” alter ego emerges.

“Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion,” the statement said, noting that the actor was active in a number of philanthropic organizations devoted to fundraising and awareness for cerebral palsy and other muscle-control disorders.

The acclaimed series, often cited by critics as one of the best television dramas of all time, ran from 2008-2013, garnering 16 Emmy awards, including two for best drama series.

He later played a high school wrestler with cerebral palsy in the 2021 coming-of-age drama “Triumph.” He was a Screen Actors Guild spokesman for performers with disabilities, and a celebrity ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy. – Rappler.com

World.title: Pope Leo to enter hospital for surgery on lung nodule
World.content:
THE POPE. Pope Leo XIV attends a meeting with university students and professors at the Catholic University of Central Africa in Yaounde, Cameroon, April 17, 2026.

The Vatican says the Pope's recovery is expected to take about a week. All his public events have been canceled until October 20.

VATICAN – Pope Leo was due to be hospitalized in Rome on Tuesday, October 13, ahead of surgery to remove a small growth on one of his lungs, in the first major health issue of his 17-month tenure.

Leo, 71, said on Sunday, October 11, that a small nodule had been found on a checkup, was “well-contained” and had been spotted early.

He was expected to leave the Vatican for Rome’s Gemelli hospital late morning, the Vatican press office said, without specifying when the actual operation would take place.

Leo, elected by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had health issues previously.

The Vatican has said his recovery is expected to take about a week. All his public events have been canceled until October 20.

A nodule on the lung is a small, localized lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors such as smoking.

Dr. Federico Venuto, chief of thoracic surgery at Rome’s Policlinico Umberto I hospital, said procedures to remove lung nodules are usually minimally invasive, and can sometimes involve use of a thin camera tube called a thoracoscope.

“The complication rate is extremely low,” he told Reuters.

The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, died at age 88 in April 2025 and was hospitalized several times as he grew frail in his later years.

Leo, who spoke in a firm, clear voice at his only public event on Monday, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17.

In the same address on Sunday when the pope announced his need for surgery, Leo pledged he would go forward with the trip. – Rappler.com

World.title: Scam or legit? Banks launch checker website, Google-backed game to learn
World.content:
Even Google Philippines country manager Prep Palacios fell victim to a costly online scam: 'I'm a tech executive, and I was still fooled'

MANILA, Philippines – That urgent message asking you to transfer money for an emergency may look convincing, but before you open up your bank app, you can now use tools to get a second opinion or practice spotting scams.

A scam-checking website and an interactive game are among the tools being promoted as banks, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), and technology partners step up efforts to help Filipinos recognize fraud before sending money.

At ScamCheck.ph, users can paste suspicious text messages or upload screenshots for an AI-assisted assessment of whether they might be fraudulent. The website also provides information on common scams, allows victims to share their experiences, and offers guidance on reporting fraud.

The website was initially developed by Metrobank and civic technology group BetterGov.ph in late 2025, but is now being promoted more widely through the Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines’ (BMAP) campaign.

Jennifer Ng, BMAP director and program lead for the Scam Check Movement, said banks, government agencies, telecommunications companies, and other organizations are being encouraged to feed their legitimate messages, promotional materials, and communications to train the tool in better distinguishing authentic messages from those impersonating banks and government offices.

For those who want to practice, Google’s Be Scam Ready game puts players through scenarios based on scam tactics. Players follow a character’s story, making decisions and getting feedback on their ability to detect scams.

Not even Google PH’s boss was safe from scams

The initiatives come as regulators acknowledge that repeatedly warning Filipinos about scams has done little to stop people from falling victim.

“We keep coming up with the same messages over and over again and yet people are still scammed,” BSP Deputy Governor Bernadette Romulo-Puyat told reporters on Monday, October 12. “It’s not enough to come up with social media [posts that say] don’t share personal information, don’t press on links.”

She said the BSP is working with BMAP and behavioral science specialists to improve how scam warnings are communicated, with the goal of getting consumers to act on them before making transactions.

Even Google Philippines country manager Prep Palacios knows how easily someone can fall for a scam.

A couple of years ago, she was making an online purchase and had what seemed like a professional exchange with the seller. But after she sent her payment, the seller’s account disappeared, along with their messages. She lost P90,000.

“It wasn’t really just about the money. It was the realization of how easily I got manipulated,” Palacios said. “I’m a tech executive, and I was still fooled.”

A 2026 report by the Global Anti-Scam Alliance (GASA) found that 84% of Filipino adults surveyed encountered a scam attempt in the past year.

Some 15% reported losing money directly or through stolen personal information that resulted in financial losses, even as more than half of the respondents expressed confidence in their ability to recognize scams.

The study, based on a survey of 1,160 adults, estimated that Filipinos lost P121.8 billion to scams annually, averaging P10,427 per victim.

Meanwhile, Google.org, Google’s philanthropic arm, has committed $5 million to the ASEAN Foundation’s Scam Ready ASEAN program, which runs from 2025 to 2027. The funding covers regional scam-prevention activities, including interactive learning tools and the training of 2,000 master trainers who are expected to educate at least 550,000 people across Southeast Asia.

Locally, BMAP programs director Catherine “Peewee” Villanueva said the training effort aims to reach one million Filipinos through schools and communities.

An initial 105 master trainers, mostly from banks and other financial institutions, have been mobilized. They will train others within their organizations, while banks plan to incorporate scam prevention into existing financial literacy programs. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIST: The Marcos administration’s cybersecurity efforts
World.content:
The Marcos administration details its initiatives aimed to be completed by 2028 under the second National Cybersecurity Plan

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s administration developed the second iteration of the National Cybersecurity Plan (NCSP).

This plan aims to address the country’s growing vulnerability to cyber threats and achieve the following outcomes by the end of Marcos’ term in 2028:

Proactive protection and security of national cyberspace

Increased workforce capability

Strengthened policy framework

According to the DICT, the plan aligns with the country’s Development Plan, National Security Strategy, National Cybercrime Strategy, and other cybersecurity strategies by national government agencies. On April 6, 2024, Marcos officially gave the green light to carry out the plan and adopted it through Executive Order No. 58.

Below are the government efforts listed under the NCSP.

Protection and Programs

1. National Fiber Backbone (NFB): A high-speed, government-owned nationwide broadband network. This allows the recalibration of Government Network (GovNet) infrastructure security and unites all national and local government agencies into one Wide Area Network (WAN).

The initiative began rolling out its initial phase in 2023 and launched Phase 1 of the Mindanao Integrated Government Network last June.

2. National government cloud platform: It will be used for storing confidential government data in close coordination with the Department of National Defense (DND), Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), and Philippine National Police (PNP) to secure the physical internetwork of GovNet and the NFB. It also includes the landing stations and submarine cable systems.

The DICT kickstarted its Cloud First Policy in 2017 and has built on it ever since. In 2024, the e-GovCloud initiative hosted 1,277 government systems.

3. Strengthened National Computer Emergency Response Team (NCERT) and Modernized National Security Operations Center (NSOC): On April 7, 60 more agencies were onboarded as part of the national plan. This expands the operation’s coverage nationwide.

These teams would handle incident response, investigation, government Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT) services, threat monitoring and hunting, malware analysis, and threat advisories. A centralized system accessible by other agencies would also be in place to delegate incident tickets for monitoring.

4. National cybersecurity threat database: An accessible database that categorizes threats and is uploadable to cybersecurity defense systems. In 2024, the DICT said NSOC monitors over two million cyber threats per day. However, as of writing, the database is not yet publicly accessible.

5. Partnerships with Public Telecommunication Entities (PTEs) and Internet Service Providers (ISPs): The DICT, National Telecommunications Commission (NTC), and telecom providers would establish reporting protocols to assist in security countermeasures to detect threats and malicious activities early and combat malware outbreaks.

Major telecommunications companies, such as Globe Telecom, Smart Communications, PLDT, Converge ICT Solutions Incorporated, Infinivan, and PT&T, have begun their partnership with the DICT in 2025. This laid the groundwork for the nationwide rollout of the Protective Domain Name System (PDNS), which scans DNS queries in real time and blocks access to dangerous websites, including those used for phishing, malware, and the spread of fake news.

6. Misinformation combat: On April 14, the DICT partnered with the Presidential Communications Office and the Department of Justice to launch “Oplan Kontra Fake News,” an inter-agency framework designed to curb the spread of disinformation and AI-generated deepfakes.

7. National Cybersecurity Intelligence Fusion Center: The plan looks to establish a nationwide network of CERTs with clearly defined roles and a new incident response model. The NCSP detailed a new workflow and hierarchical model, with the DICT NCERT and the Defense CERT as top command.

As of July, the DICT partnered with the Korea International Cooperation Agency to build a physical cybersecurity center in Valenzuela.

8. Securing submarine cable infrastructure: The DICT will coordinate with government agencies such as the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) to develop a map of all cables and them to prevent damage due to theft, anchorage, earthquakes, and major climate disturbances.

Earlier this year, the DICT partnered with Australia’s Cable Connectivity and Resilience Centre to develop a framework to protect the country’s subsea cables and submitted the analysis to Marcos. Telco companies PLDT, Globe, and Converge also joined the agency to plan a cable system that will loop around the country, which may be completed in 24 months.

9. Bilateral and multilateral international cooperation: The plan looks to expand existing agreements with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the United Nations, Interpol, and other bilateral agreements with other countries.

The country has partnered with Korea to build a cybersecurity center. It also had a Cyber-Digital Policy dialogue with the United States in 2024 to strengthen both countries’ ICT, their resilience to cybersecurity threats, and the growth of the digital economy.

Workforce and Education

1. October as Cybersecurity Awareness Month: On October 2, 2023, Marcos signed Proclamation No. 353, changing the commemoration of Cybersecurity Awareness Month from September to October. This coincides with the international cybersecurity month celebrations.

2. ICT Academy: The ICT Literacy and Competency Development Bureau (ILCDB) was upgraded to ICT Academy on October 1 to develop a highly skilled workforce capable of addressing cybersecurity challenges. It would also engage with research initiatives and collaborate with industry partners, government agencies, and international bodies to ensure a globally accepted approach.

3. Cybersecurity jobs in government: The DICT would collaborate with the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) and the Civil Service Commission (CSC) to create official job titles, hiring qualifications, and specialized exams for cybersecurity career service positions in the government.

Under the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of Republic Act No. 12254, signed on March 24, the three agencies were required to develop guidelines establishing specialized cybersecurity positions across all national agencies, including local governments, state universities and colleges (SUCs), and government-owned or controlled corporations.

4. Partnerships with local and international training providers: The department would work with private industry leaders to create online short courses that would be internationally recognized and certified.

It has already secured a multi-year deal with Google to enhance the country’s cybersecurity defense. The partnership would train public servants to use Gemini Enterprise and Google Workspace, with the end goal of training 200,000 people nationwide over the next 18 months.

5. Cybersecurity programs and scholarships: The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) and SUCs are encouraged to develop cybersecurity degree programs. The DICT would also partner with TESDA in creating National Certification in various cybersecurity skills. These programs would also be included in partial and full scholarships.

In 2019, CHED has already listed cybersecurity as one of the priority courses for scholarship programs under Memorandum Order No. 5, s. 2019. As of writing, some universities offer cybersecurity programs, including Mapúa University, De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde, and Lyceum of the Philippines University.

6. National and international hacking competitions: The DICT would organize regional and national hacking competitions where winners would take part in international competitions. The agency would also build a network of experts, resource persons, and trainers.

The DICT kicked off HackForGov in 2019, an annual nationwide cybersecurity competition. It has become an annual competition since then, with different regions hosting the event. Winners would eventually represent the country in the annual Cyber SEA Game.

Policies

1. Strengthening National Cybersecurity Inter-Agency Committee: Marcos has reinforced the established committee, created under E.O. 189, s. 2015. The committee would serve as a convergence hub of different government agencies and the main forum for information sharing, planning, and ensuring policies don’t conflict with other interests.

The President has then mandated the DICT to submit biannual implementation reports on national cyber policies.

2. Executive Order on Critical Infrastructure and Critical Information Infrastructure: E.O. 119, s. 2026 updated government data classification, and the framework for data security. This covers all digital or hybrid government-owned data, including private service providers that handle government data.

3. Mandatory security labelling of devices: The plan looks to require routers and switches sold in the market to be labeled to inform the public about the security of the products.

4. Revision on VAPT service providers’ accreditation: The DICT revised the existing accreditation of VAPT service providers last January under Department Circular No. HRA-001, s. 2026. The revisions would add customer feedback through complaint mechanisms and train service providers on managing them.

5. Establish policies, guidelines, and procedures on network security systems: The DICT would partner with the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), Department of Science and Technology, the academe, and industry partners to develop network security system protocols.

The agency has already released Department Circular No. 003, s. 2024, mandating all government agencies to adhere to security measures and response protocols. This also includes rerouting internet traffic to DICT-managed PDNS, automated vulnerability scans, and sharing information with the NSOC.

6. Minimum cybersecurity standards: Under Republic Act NO. 12254, the DICT was prescribed to implement minimum information security standards for government systems. In March 2026, an IRR was issued requiring all government agencies to comply.

7. Legislative Agenda and Enactments: The DICT would endorse key legislative measures to Congress to resolve economic challenges, information asymmetry, and establish legal cybersecurity protections. In 2026, the House of Representatives approved on third and final reading House Bill No. 9605, or the proposed “National Cybersecurity and Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Act of 2026.”

The bill is aligned with the administration’s Digital Transformation Framework and seeks to establish mandatory cybersecurity standards and certification systems, ensuring consistent defense protocols for public and private sectors. – Rappler.com

World.title: Quorum scare stalls Day 38 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial
World.content:
Senate President Win Gatchalian and presiding officer Chiz Escudero listen to the proceedings on Day 24 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 14, 2026.

The trial finally reached quorum past 10 am following the arrival of senator-judges Robin Padilla and Camille Villar

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday, October 12, encountered a hiccup.

Shortly after the opening prayer of Senator-judge Mark Villar, the trial paused for several minutes, over what could be a scare on the lack of quorum of the Senate impeachment court.

Only 11 senator-judges were present in the proceedings at 10 am. The court reached quorum with 13 senator-judges present at around 10:08 am, following the arrival of senator-judges Camille Villar and Robin Padilla.

Senator-judges Imee Marcos, Alan Peter Cayetano, Bong Go, and Pia Cayetano — all minority-allied — were absent during the roll call. However, Go and Pia Cayetano were present in the afternoon proceedings.

This is the second time since last week the court proceeded with only 13 senator-judges present. Usually, at least 14 to 15 senator-judges participate in the proceedings.

The initial lack of quorum comes amid questions over the minority bloc’s participation in the trial. Over the weekend, Padilla said members of the Senate minority bloc may skip the impeachment proceedings over what they call is “distortion” of the Constitution.

Padilla and Go previously filed a petition with the Supreme Court (SC) challenging the September 23 decision of the impeachment court that lowered the conviction threshold.

Padilla also claimed last weekend that there was “disregard for law” in the impeachment proceedings, despite the general impression that presiding officer Chiz Escudero had been doing fairly well in managing the trial.

Padilla’s comment that did not sit well with his colleagues, including Senator-judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson.

“I don’t know what Sen. Padilla meant by ‘disregard for law’ or if he was referring to the entire impeachment court na member din naman siya. If so, hindi kaya maituturing na direct assault sa integridad ng korte ang mga bibitiwan niyang pananalita?” he said.

(I don’t know what Sen. Padilla meant by “disregard for law” or if he was referring to the entire impeachment court where he is a member. If so, won’t his remark be taken as a direct assault on the integrity of the impeachment court?)

Lacson added that if Padilla was referring to individual senators, then he should just go and name them.

On Monday, Padilla did not only attend the trial but was also among those who made interjections following the testimony of foreign financial analyst Alexander Cabrera, who had pegged the Vice President’s undeclared wealth at P817 million from 2022 to 2025. This amount, Cabrera testified before the court, could even reach as high as P1.5 billion.

With the defense expected to present evidence after the trial break, or from November 9 onwards, will there no longer be any quorum issues? – Rappler.com
