World.title: Man dies at popular Qld swimming spot
World.content:
A man has died at a popular waterfall and swimming spot in Far North Queensland.

Emergency services recovered the man's body from Millaa Millaa Falls about 5pm on Monday, two hours after they were called to the area, 100 kilometres south-west of Cairns.

Police have not provided any further details about the man's death or where he was from.

A report would be prepared for the coroner, police said.

Millaa Millaa Falls is prominently featured in tourism promotional material and is heavily frequented by visitors during the dry season.

The falls are on a popular circuit of waterfalls in the southern Atherton Tablelands.

Andrew Broadbent, who runs a nearby caravan park, said the area had "been a lot quieter" in recent weeks as the peak tourist season had passed.

Millaa Millaa Falls is widely regarded as one of the safer waterfalls in Far North Queensland, although two men died at the site in July 2024.

"It's not a high-flow waterfall. It's just a curtain waterfall straight down into a little pond and it's quite shallow," Mr Broadbent said.

"There are hundreds of people who go swimming there."

Mr Broadbent, who moved to the area about 10 months ago from north Brisbane, said conditions in the past fortnight had been "absolutely beautiful [with] no rain".

"Prior to that, we've had a lot of rain this dry season but, again, it's not a high-flow waterfall," he said.

"Even when it pours down with rain, you can still go swimming in it. It's not a dangerous waterfall to swim in."

World.title: Police close first suspected illicit tobacco stores under Victoria's new powers
World.content:
The first stores suspected of selling illicit tobacco in country Victoria have been closed under new powers designed to curtail the sector.

Victoria Police's Viper Taskforce, alongside Tobacco Licensing Victoria, raided the stores yesterday, posting yellow stickers on the door advising of the closures.

New powers that came into effect on September 9 allow authorities to inspect stores suspected of selling illicit tobacco and close them for 90 days.

More than 60 stores have now been closed, including at least four in Gippsland yesterday.

The authority closed three stores across Moe and Newborough in the Latrobe Valley and one in Yarram.

The closures are the first outside Melbourne and Geelong.

Shops shut by the Viper Taskforce have a yellow short-term closure notice slapped on their front door. (ABC News: Jarrod Whittaker)

Tobacco Licensing Victoria chief operating officer Bree Oliver told ABC Gippsland Breakfast the authority chose the Latrobe Valley as its first country target because of tip-offs suggesting a high concentration of illicit tobacco.

"We verify that intelligence and obviously use that intelligence to identify where are our priorities, where are the targets, where does it make the most sense," Ms Oliver said.

"Where will we have the biggest impact and clearly the Latrobe Valley is a site where the supply of illicit tobacco is considerable."

The yellow notices posted to the stores' entrance give a reopening date and state that no one can enter the premises unless an exemption is granted.

"We will be monitoring those premises should they open up again and we'll take action," Ms Oliver said.

Ms Oliver said the authority could issue an additional short-term closure notice or apply to the Magistrates' Court for a long-term order.

Cigarettes sold illegally usually retail for about $20 a pack and have not been taxed, compared with about $50 for legal cigarettes.

In recent years, many illicit tobacco shops have been linked to organised crime, often with offshore leaders.

World.title: Suspected arson attack destroys four cars at prison carpark
World.content:
Four cars have been destroyed by fire at the Yatala Labour Prison car park in Adelaide's north, in what is being investigated as a suspected arson attack.

The early morning incident has prompted renewed calls for enhanced safety at the site from the union representing prison staff, which said its members felt "absolutely outraged" by what had occurred.

The Public Service Association (PSA) also said two staff had encountered a person wearing a balaclava when they arrived for work this morning, but that the person fled the scene.

"We've got major security concerns and safety concerns for the Yatala carpark being wide open like it is," PSA SA vice-president Craig Bates told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"We have been calling on the department to erect a fence."

Police are investigating the incident and have described it as "suspicious", and said emergency services were called to the site on Peter Brown Drive at Northfield about 4am.

They said two Mitsubishi station wagons and two Toyota sedans were completely destroyed.

Police have asked anyone who witnessed suspicious behaviour in the area or has relevant dash cam footage to contact Crime Stoppers.

Department for Correctional Services chief executive David Brown said there was CCTV of the incident, but said he would not go into the details of what it showed.

But he said he had met with management at the site this morning.

"We've had a critical incident at the site," Mr Brown said.

"It's obviously a live and very active police investigation and we are always looking at ways we can enhance safety for our staff, including the safety of the carpark area.

" It was an outrageous incident this morning — four government vehicles were set alight and have been written off by this act of arson. I'm very concerned about the nature of the incident. "

The incident has been described by police as suspicious. (891 ABC Adelaide: Bobby Macumber)

The PSA said it had raised concerns five months ago, saying that "inadequate security was putting staff at risk".

The union said it wrote to the department in May urging security improvements including "an extension of the perimeter fence and 24-hour protective security officers", but that those requests were rejected.

"Only a number of months ago, a stolen vehicle was driven through that car park with people wearing masks and they were later found to have a firearm," Mr Bates said.

"There have been other issues with vehicles being damaged and stuff like that too.

"A fence is a bit of a no-brainer and it's high time it happened. To be honest it should have happened ages ago."

The department CEO said the incident would be reviewed, and did not rule out the installation of a new fence.

"Every option is on the table including whether we can partition or fence off access to the car park, but also recognising that Yatala Labour Prison is a large prison and it has a lot of interface with the public," Mr Brown said.

World.title: Breaking: Charges laid after baby found dead at Adelaide motel
World.content:
South Australia's police minister says charges have been laid following the death of an infant, who was found by police at the Tollgate Motel on Saturday.

At a press conference this morning, SA Police Minister Michael Brown confirmed charges had been laid, but did not confirm what the charges were or who they had been laid against.

"I've been advised that charges have been laid, but at this time I don't have any other information I can give you unfortunately," he said.

Mr Brown said he had "not had the chance to be fully briefed yet" about the matter.

Yesterday, SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said the parents of the child were not known to the state's child protection agency.

Police and ambulances were called to the motel, which is adjacent to the South Eastern Freeway, five kilometres south-east of the Adelaide CBD, on Saturday morning.

Some witnesses in the area estimated about 20 officers were present at the scene, before establishing a cordon and leaving by mid-afternoon.

At the time, police said an investigation was ongoing and a report would be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: Alice Springs bracing for more storms after 'worst in 40 years'
World.content:
A wind-lashed Alice Springs is bracing for another storm even as residents have not yet finished clearing up downed tree branches, knocked over fences, leaking roofs and restoring power from "the worst storm in 40 years" on Monday afternoon.

Bureau of Meteorology duty forecaster Ruby Cuthbertson said wind speeds of up to 96 kilometres per hour were recorded at the Alice Springs airport on Monday afternoon — the ninth-highest October wind speed in 75 years.

The damage was widespread across Alice Springs. (ABC Alice Springs: Xavier Martin)

"A lot of that moisture has come down from the tropics and is driving a lot of those thunderstorms in the south," she said.

Ms Cuthbertson said a south-easterly surge on Tuesday afternoon would cause thunderstorms over Alice Springs, Yulara and Ti Tree.

"The watch points today are for heavy rain, damaging winds and large hail," she said.

"Particularly just kind of north of Alice we've got some slow-moving potential for those storms, so if they do form there the main risk would be heavy rainfall and then around Yulara, the risk would be damaging winds if we see thunderstorms form up there."

NT emergency services help with cleaning up after Monday's severe storm. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Ms Cuthbertson said the thunderstorms would persist later into the week, before the weather was expected to clear next week.

Thousands of homes without power

Power And Water said electricity had been restored to 5,000 houses, but there were still about 4,000 homes without across a "widespread" area.

Executive general manager of power services Belinda Small said there had been extensive damage, but extra crews from Tennant Creek, Darwin and Katherine were travelling to Alice Springs to provide support.

"There wasn't a lot of Alice Springs that wasn't impacted," she said.

A camper trailer was flipped during Monday's storms. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"We've got multiple bays of overhead power lines on the ground, where poles are bent and damaged, and that's a full day's work to repair.

" One of our senior managers in Alice Springs described it as the worst storm in 40 years that he's been there. "

Ms Small said Power and Water was bracing for more storms and encouraged residents to be patient.

Damage widespread

Northern Territory Emergency Services Deputy Chief Officer Adam White said the service had had 50 requests for assistance from all suburbs of Alice Springs, mostly for trees on houses and cars and roof damage.

"I would ask people, if you can today, clean up any debris that's left … get it to the tip or to somewhere safe, secure it where you can, so that if we do have another storm come through, we don't have extra debris," he said.

Neighbours pitched in to help after a storm hit Alice Springs. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Alice Springs Town Council director of infrastructure Sally O'Callaghan said there was no part of town unscathed, but council had been focusing its clean-up efforts in The Gap and Gillen.

"Currently we're working through a lot of priority areas, people's access, road access and footpaths to be able to create accessibility through town," she said.

" We actually had quite a significant number of staff that saw the storm come through and stayed back last night, so we actually were ready to hit the ground as soon as it was safe to do so. "

Ms O'Callaghan said the Alice Springs tip would be open as normal today, and the library and pool would open after sustaining some damage.

Trees were down across Alice Springs after Monday's hectic storm. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Northern Territory Police senior sergeant Paula Dooley-McDonnell encouraged residents to stay informed on road closures, weather advice and emergency information through Secure NT.

She said people should drive to the conditions, avoid flooded areas and keep away from fallen powerlines.

World.title: Critical Melbourne teen's close ties with fatal stabbing victim revealed
World.content:
Some Melbourne teenagers have witnessed the deadly aftermath of Victoria's youth crime crisis from both sides of the law.

One tight-knit friendship group in the city's northern suburbs is made up of both victims and alleged offenders, as well as those in-between left dealing with the fallout when something goes wrong.

Among them is a 13-year-old boy fighting for his life in hospital after an alleged botched arson last Monday.

For three months leading up to that incident, the same boy was reeling from the alleged murder of his friend Darweish Mohamed, 15, who was allegedly stabbed to death outside a hospital in Craigieburn.

Five people have been charged over Darweish's death, including three teenagers charged with murder.

Darweish Mohamed died in July after allegedly being stabbed outside a Craigieburn hospital. (Supplied: GoFundMe)

The boy wounded in the fire kept a framed photo of Darweish on his desk at home.

Friends of both teens told the ABC they have already lost one friend from violence that got out of hand, and they are praying they do not lose a second.

"They were really close. Darweish and [the boy] were great friends," a friend of the pair said.

The 13-year-old and his associates allegedly drove a stolen car to a house in Taylors Hill in the early hours of October 5, before dousing two cars and, inadvertently, themselves, in petrol before setting the vehicles alight.

Friends of a teenager seriously injured after a botched alleged arson say he isn't "a bad kid". (ABC News: Kate Meade)

Police allege they tried to flee in the stolen car but crashed it as flames took hold of their clothing.

Two of the youths then allegedly ran away, leaving the 13-year-old screaming in the street before he collapsed from suffering burns to 90 per cent of his body.

He has remained in a critical condition at the Royal Children's Hospital, undergoing major skin graft surgery.

Allegations of WhatsApp cash promises

The group allegedly received their orders to carry out the Taylors Hill arson on WhatsApp, with a children's court hearing they were promised $3,000 for the attack.

Critically injured 13-year-old got firebombing order on WhatsApp The teenager is fighting for life after being engulfed in flames during an alleged arson attack in Melbourne's north-west on Monday.

From his bedside in hospital, the boy's family pleaded with young people to avoid the lure of quick cash and notoriety among their peers often dangled in front of them by more experienced criminals.

Echoing that plea, the boy's friends, who are not named because they, the boy and his co-accused are underage, say he did not know any better.

"He was never a bad kid," the friend said.

"[His alleged] actions are shameful yes, but it was in the wrong crowd he was involved in.

"He's just a boy who wants to be respected by his friends."

Two 16-year-old boys, including one out on bail at the time, are behind bars as they face charges over last Monday's alleged arson, while a 15-year-old boy was arrested but released without charge.

The ABC last week revealed details about how the accused teens contacted the 13-year-old's sister on Snapchat, admitting to his involvement in the alleged arson, apologising and offering his family cash.

Les Twentyman Foundation chief executive Paul Burke said teenagers were particularly vulnerable to influence from older people and should not have to deal with their friends being injured or killed by violence.

"These are kids who should be worrying about school, sport and spending time with their mates, not whether someone in their friendship group will be the next victim," he said.

A Korean barbecue restaurant on Springvale Road was set alight in the early hours of Sunday October 11. A 15-year-old boy was taken to hospital under police guard with burns. (ABC News)

"At 12 or 13, they're still finding their place in the world, and the wrong influences can have tragic consequences.

" We need to reach these kids before they're drawn into dangerous situations. "

Less than a week after the Taylors Hill incident, another teenager was treated for burns after torching a Korean barbecue restaurant in Springvale.

More than 15 separate fires have been lit across Melbourne in the past week, leaving dozens of victims, neighbours and business owners terrified.

Many of those offenders, often believed to be underage, remain on the run.

"No child should grow up believing this level of violence is normal," Mr Burke said.

World.title: Documentary explores how harmful conspiracy theories can take hold of us
World.content:
There was a time when Aftermath co-director Jared Nicholson was in a dark place, getting most of his "news" from far-right podcaster and conspiracy theorist Alex Jones.

"You're in this echo chamber," he says. "It formed my entire world view."

It's how he first encountered video footage of the late Wendy Scurr. She was a first responder during the Port Arthur massacre on April 28, 1996, which remains the worst mass shooting in modern Australian history, claiming 35 lives.

Scurr worked at the historic site's information centre. A former St John's ambulance officer, she trained many of the staff in first aid. They fought to save as many people as possible. "She was a hero," Nicholson says.

Fast facts about Aftermath What: A confronting documentary exploring the tragic grip of conspiracy theories Directed by: Jared Nicholson and Ben Lawrence When: Screening at the Adelaide Film Festival Likely to make you feel: Like pain is a difficult space in which to manoeuvre

Taking a dark turn

The event left a long shadow for survivors and those who aided them. As the news cycle moved on, Scurr felt abandoned. Suffering from PTSD and unable to work, she campaigned for proper mental health care for her and her fellow first responders.

Tragically, Scurr fell down a rabbit hole, following wildly untrue conspiracy theories that sprung up in the wake of Port Arthur. It was while in a similarly dark online space that Nicholson encountered Scurr.

"Every time there was a mass-shooting event, people would share this video of Wendy," he says.

While Scurr was offline, Nicholson managed to track her down.

" Then began this three-year process of unpicking her story, becoming close and getting lost in everything. "

Aftermath director Jared Nicholson and director of photography Nick Frayne. (Supplied: Jaz Anderson, Alejandro Carriel)

Increasingly troubling beliefs

Premiering at the Adelaide Film Festival, the often-confronting Aftermath explores how a stoic, sensible woman like Scurr could find herself believing in such astonishing untruths.

It's equally the story of how Nicholson withdrew from the abyss that threatened to swallow him too.

Nicholson's parents split when he was three. His father was an evangelical zealot who talked in tongues, filling his young son's head with the terrifying promise of the rapture alongside conspiracy theories about Y2K and 9/11.

Nicholson says "distrust of governments and the mainstream media has left a lot of people questioning nearly everything". (Supplied: Jaz Anderson and Alejandro Carri)

"I've got a son who's five years old," Nicholson says. "Had I said the same stuff to him, I could see how messed up he would be."

In documenting Scurr's story, Nicholson became increasingly troubled by her unfounded beliefs, pulling him deeper into a paranoid quagmire.

And then Scurr fell ill. "I just had this belief that Wendy f***ing survived everything, she's going to survive whatever's next," he says. "Then you get the call saying that she's passed."

Telling tricky stories

Mourning Scurr and feeling increasingly lost, Nicholson turned inwards, examining his own fraught childhood and experiencing mental health issues.

" I had my mental reckoning, a year or so after Wendy's passing, and that was when I started to reflect on my own childhood and go, 'Wow.' "

He reached out to seasoned documentarian Ben Lawrence (Ithaka, The People vs Robodebt) for help in shaping Aftermath.

"Ben was that person to try to help me make sense of what the hell this thing could be."

Lawrence was cautious, at first. "When Jared first approached me, the story kind of scared me," he says. "I certainly went in thinking this was going to be a really difficult story to tell."

But difficult does not equal unworthy. "It's critical that we, as filmmakers, tell stories that frighten us," Lawrence says.

His grappling with the Robodebt scandal was one such challenge. While that was a very different scenario from that shown in Aftermath, some of the harm caused has parallels, particularly around what some people feeling the lack of sufficient support.

"When something like this happens, you need society to be able to rush in and take care of the most vulnerable," Lawrence says.

When that doesn't happen, otherwise sensible people can find themselves warped by disturbing conspiracy theories that can bend them out of shape.

"It consumed Wendy," Lawrence says. "And then Jared tells me about his childhood, so you have these two characters in freefall."

Difficult conversations

Providing no easy answers, Aftermath acknowledges that the trying times we live in are seeing more and more people turn to conspiracies.

Nicholson insists it's vital we talk about this disenfranchisement, and what happens when people get lost in that dark space.

" Distrust of governments and the mainstream media has left a lot of people questioning nearly everything," Nicholson says. "And that's before you get to AI, which twists what we perceive to be reality. "

Nicholson's glad the Adelaide Film Festival was willing to get into the weeds with him. "They're risk-takers that back bold stories," he says. "For me, it's about telling the story from the inside, with understanding and empathy."

Lawrence agrees, suggesting we need to be better at having difficult conversations, especially around the most confronting issues.

"Talk to someone that has a different belief than you," he says. "Try to understand them. That's what Jared's done in this film, is he really tried to understand Wendy, to humanise her and his own journey.

"At the end of the day, that's what we're encouraging people to do. That's the only way we're going to navigate our way out of all of this."

Aftermath screens at the Adelaide Film Festival

World.title: Ministers and Aboriginal custodians divided over Darwin housing development
World.content:
The federal government ministers responsible for new housing estates being built at Darwin's Lee Point are coming under more intense pressure to stop the controversial development from cabinet colleagues.

Defence Housing Australia is building 200 defence homes and 600 housing lots for private sale on the site in the city's northern suburbs, in a development that has attracted large public protests and dozens of arrests over the past four years.

The cabinet pressure and lobbying from Territory Labor has exposed deep divisions within Darwin's Larrakia Indigenous community about whether concerns about sacred sites should kill the project.

While many Larrakia people oppose the development, custodian Helen Secretary has now spoken out to support it.

Helen Secretary said Defence Housing Australia has worked closely with her to consult about local cultural heritage. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

Ms Secretary has accused opponents of the Lee Point development of unfairly trying to kill the project on the basis of protecting sacred sites.

"The sacred and recorded site Binybara is a reef at the tip of Lee Point," she said, pointing out to sea.

"The story of Binybara is that that was Dariba Nunggalinya, Old Man Rock's wife.

"Where Defence is doing the clearing, there are no sacred sites within that area of land, so don't use sacred sites to stop development."

Ms Secretary said she and other Larrakia people have been working with Defence Housing Australia to ensure no culturally important places are interfered with.

The DHA development at Lee Point has sparked years of protests and debate. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"Why I'm speaking out is that Defence have been consulting with Larrakia people, we've been working well together under the cultural heritage monitoring," she said.

The 2024 Country Liberal Party candidate said she was also concerned to see the NT Labor Opposition change its position to oppose the Lee Point development, after supporting it while in government.

"I'm for development, we need more housing. Darwin is a city now, we don't live in a time capsule and development is going to happen," she said.

The custodian said she hopes her work with Defence Housing could eventually help deliver benefits to her community.

Defence Housing Australia told the ABC it has "undertaken extensive consultation" with Larrakia people and would "continue to do so as the project progresses".

Ms Secretary's view is diametrically opposed by Larrakia custodian Lorraine Juwayning Williams, who said the development would impact a sacred area.

Lorraine Juwayning Williams says her people have long claimed the Lee Point area as culturally significant. (Supplied: Lorraine Williams)

"This entire area is actually sacred to us, this area of land is a women's site, and I haven't even spoken about it to the Aboriginal Areas Protection Authority, because even in giving that information, culturally, we're in conflict," she said.

"I feel really sad that Larrakia now, they're almost pushed into being pro-development."

Another Larrakia custodian Tibby Quall forced a pause on the clearing for several months this year by arguing in the NTCAT tribunal that Indigenous stone tools should not have been removed during land clearing.

Defence Housing Australia told the ABC the stop work order has since been lifted.

Lorraine Juwayning Williams says the DHA development will interfere with a sacred area. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

After four years of protesting at Lee Point, Ms Williams said she has lobbied Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy by telling her the bush site's secret story.

"I said: 'One on one, Aboriginal woman to Aboriginal woman, I'm going to tell you what this is about, you need to understand it, and then make a decision based on that'," Ms Williams said.

Complaints about environmental offsets

The Friends of Lee Point community group has also increased its campaign to stop the development on environment grounds.

Ian Redmond has asked the national EPA to investigate the black-footed tree-rat to ensure the DHA development does not violate biodiversity laws. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

The group's convenor Ian Redmond wrote to the National Environment Protection Agency complaining that the federal government's plan to ensure it does not break biodiversity law by threatening the endangered black-footed tree-rat population appeared inadequate.

He said the plan to provide the animals with another adjacent area nearby to live in appears to have offered inferior alternative habitat.

"Nearly 14 out of the 22 hectares is monsoon forest without large trees for den hollows, so it doesn't work, the black footed tree rat would be worse off," he said.

The Friends of Lee Point community group believe the offset site provided for the black-footed tree-rat is inferior. (Supplied: Daniel Brown)

Defence Housing Australia said: "The nominated site for protection of black-footed tree-rat habitat associated with the 2CRU development site was accepted through the Commonwealth's environmental approvals."

Bird researcher Dr Amanda Lilleyman said she doubts there will be enough suitable land for a similar endangered Gouldian finch.

"We have not seen the Gouldian finch offset plan and we have questions about whether it will provide appropriate habitat," she said.

Amanda Lilleyman is worried there may not be suitable alternative habitat available for Gouldian finches if Lee Point is developed. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

Defence Housing Australia said it has lodged a Gouldian finch offset plan with the federal environment department which will be published once approved.

Political lobbying steps up

Last month, Northern Territory Labor Opposition MLA Ed Smelt joined the lobbying effort to stop the development by taking one of the federal government ministers responsible, Katy Gallagher, out to see Lee Point.

Labor flips on Lee Point development During its eight years in government, Territory Labor supported an 800-home defence development in Darwin, but just before the Nightcliff by-election its candidate reveals the party's position has changed.

"I pointed out the issues about outstanding cultural and environmental heritage; she accepted what I was saying and she understood the concerns that constituents have," he said.

He and other opponents have appealed to the federal government to build its contested 110-hectare Lee Point housing estate on the 123 hectares of surplus land that it plans to sell off for development at Defence Berrimah.

"The Defence Establishment Berrimah is a fantastic site and a terrific opportunity," Mr Smelt said.

Asked by the ABC whether she thought the housing estates should be built at Berrimah instead of Lee Point last week, Ms McCarthy said that question was one for Senator Gallagher to decide.

Defence Housing Australia said it has presented a plan to protect the Gouldian finch to the federal government. (Supplied: Tobia Aakesson)

"But … I have advocated as the senator for the Northern Territory for Senator Gallagher to look at all of those issues," she said.

Ms Secretary said she hoped some Defence Berrimah land could go to the Larrakia.

"There's certain areas of land that Defence have been discussing with us to give back to the Larrakia people in the future; this isn't about that at the moment," she said.

Ms Gallagher's office did not answer questions about whether the government would consider stopping or moving the Lee Point development.

World.title: Australia facing biggest jobless rate spike of developed world
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAustralian economy Australia facing biggest jobless rate spike of developed world Shane Wright October 13, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia faces the biggest increase in unemployment in the developed world next year – even as the country’s economy remains one of the globe’s fastest growing and inflation cools – with warnings the AI boom and soaring government debt is a growing risk to all nations. The International Monetary Fund (IMF), in its six-monthly updated economic outlook, on Tuesday warned that the good luck that had helped the world economy overcome the turmoil caused by the US-Israel war against Iran could soon run out. The number of Australians out of work could soar close to 800,000 by 2027. Louie Douvis The monetary fund is forecasting the global economy to expand by 3.1 per cent this year before accelerating by 3.4 per cent in 2027. Inflation is expected to hit 4.7 per cent this year, largely due to a surge in prices for commodities including oil and food, before easing slightly to 4.1 per cent. Australia’s economy is tipped to grow by 1.9 per cent this year and 1.6 per cent in 2027. Both forecasts are 0.1 of a percentage point lower than what the IMF forecast in April.



At that level of growth, only the United States, Spain, Singapore and New Zealand are expected to expand faster than Australia. But unemployment in Australia is expected to climb by 0.3 of a percentage point, from 4.4 per cent this year to 4.7 per cent in 2027. Almost all other developed nations are expected to enjoy either no change in unemployment or a small fall between this year and next. Loading At 4.7 per cent, the number of Australians out of work would approach 800,000. Despite the increase, Australia’s jobless rate remains lower than most other rich nations: it is 5.3 per cent in Britain, 8.1 per cent in Sweden and 6.3 per cent in Canada.



The lift in unemployment is expected to help reduce Australia’s inflation rate, which is forecast to fall from 3.9 per cent this year to 3.1 per cent in 2027. At that level, only a small number of nations would have face price pressures higher than Australia, including Austria and Greece. Related Article Inflation Inflation jumps to four-month high a day after RBA rate rise International Monetary Fund chief economist Silvana Tenreyro said the global economy had aced an “exceptional sequence of events” over the past seven years including the pandemic, the disruption to global supply chains, the wars in Ukraine and Iran and challenges to the world’s trading system. She said the economy had got through all of this. The recent surge in oil prices, for instance, would have ordinarily hurt the global economy, but a rundown in inventories, re-routing of new supplies, plus a sharp lift in renewable energy sources had all helped to offset the expected macroeconomic fallout. But Tenreyro said the way the world had responded to the lift in oil prices, on top of the economic boost produced by the AI construction boom, was now under threat.



“This resilience is under strain. Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing policy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience,” Tenreyro said. “With gains clustered in a small number of firms, sectors and economies, global expansion is heavily reliant on a narrow set of technological and financial conditions. “More generally, resilience has been uneven, varying noticeably with economies’ exposure to the war and the AI boom, and causing divergent outcomes.” Tenreyro said the lift in government borrowing costs, which have pushed interest rates on public debt to their highest levels in more than a decade, meant governments had to find ways to reduce their debt levels. “The interaction of higher financing costs with elevated debt levels exposes a key margin of vulnerability,” she said.





“We are not immune from these global factors, but we are better placed than many others. We are well positioned to benefit from the global AI investment boom and our efforts to strengthen supply chains are helping to buffer us in a fragmenting world.” Chalmers said the government was already undertaking many of the IMF’s recommendations, including by making cuts in spending and investing in energy security policies. World.title: One person killed, several injured in US roller coaster incident
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTragedy One person killed, several injured in US roller coaster incident Updated October 13, 2026 — 12:54pm ,first published October 13, 2026 — 10:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Georgia, USA: One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a roller coaster in Georgia, according to police. The tragedy occurred on Monday afternoon (US time) on the Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia amusement park, about 25 kilometres north-west of Atlanta, according to the Cobb County Police Department. Loading Detectives with the department’s major crimes unit will investigate the incident. Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured.



Witnesses who spoke to NBC affiliate WXIA of Atlanta said they saw a man fall from the Goliath roller coaster, with at least two saying they saw him strike parts of the ride multiple times before hitting the ground. “He fell and hit the car three different times,” one said, NBC reported. A patron died on the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday (US time). CNN Passengers are evacuated from the roller coaster after the incident in Georgia. ABC7 “The man started levitating in the air sideways,” said another witness, Logan Conner, who was on the ride at the time. “We made direct eye contact with him.”



A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they were fully cooperating with investigations into the incident. “We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said. The Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. Six Flags Over Georgia Authorities and Six Flags did not identify the roller coaster. However, local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster. The roller coaster, which was opened in 2006, goes as fast as about 110km/h and reaches heights of 61 metres, the park’s website reports. During about 3½ minutes, riders “navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills,” according to the website.



This death would be at least the seventh at the Georgia park, including one in 2006 in which a man had a likely heart attack on the Goliath coaster, according to the Doan Law Firm, whose practice areas include amusement park accidents. Last month, Six Flags Magic Mountain, in southern California, announced that it was retiring its famous X2 roller coaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. Six Flags recently settled a wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022. Three more lawsuits alleging traumatic brain injuries were filed last week. Last year, a 32-year-old man died after riding a high-speed roller coaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. He died from blunt impact injuries and his death was ruled accidental. World.title: ‘Inhumane act’: Homicide investigation launched after beloved grandmother found dead in stock dip
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime ‘Inhumane act’: Homicide investigation launched after beloved grandmother found dead in stock dip Daniel Lo Surdo and Riley Walter Updated October 13, 2026 — 12:42pm ,first published 11:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A homicide investigation has been launched after the body of a beloved grandmother was found partially submerged in a stock dip on a rural NSW property, as her family demands answers for the “callous, inhumane act”. The body of Yvonne Whear, a 73-year-old last seen in the Northern Rivers almost eight months ago, was severely decomposed when it was discovered partially submerged in half a metre of water at a property 20 kilometres south of Murwillumbah last week. Two bike riders spotted the remains in the stock dip while using a popular track running past the property. Yvonne Whear was last seen on February 19. NSW Police A post-mortem examination on Monday identified the remains and sparked a homicide investigation under Strike Force Milera, which will deploy officers from the State Crime Command’s homicide squad, along with other specialised units, to the Northern Rivers. Whear’s three children, in a statement released on behalf of the family, said they were “devastated and horrified” by the development.



“We are left facing a future without her, carrying unimaginable grief and unanswered questions,” the family said. Yvonne Whear, captured on CCTV in a Murwillumbah service station the day she disappeared. Tweed-Byron Police District “Not only has she been robbed of her life, her children and grandchildren now all face the horrific trauma of this callous inhumane act. While whoever is responsible for this is still out there in the community … Yvonne deserves justice, our family deserves answers.” The family were told of the tragic news on Tuesday morning, as detectives prepared to return to Whear’s hobby farm on the outskirts of Dungay, near the Queensland border. Further forensic testing and searches are expected at the residence.



Tweed/Byron Police District Commander Matt Zimmer said the state’s detectives would deliver justice for Whear, as they investigate the circumstances ahead of her death. “There are still significant questions about what happened to her and how she came to be where she was found,” he said.



“Someone knows what happened to Yvonne. Whether you have previously spoken to police or have information you have not yet shared, we need you to come forward.” Whear was last seen on February 19, when security cameras captured her driving north on Queensland Road at Murwillumbah towards her farm about 3.20pm. Mobile phone data shows she watched YouTube videos that afternoon, and just before 5pm, checked her voicemail. Whear’s body was found in an unused stock dip. NSW Police First responders at the rural property in Terragon last week, after the body was discovered. Nine Her phone was last detected by a phone tower near Dungay at 10am on February 20, and hasn’t been seen since.



Whear lived on her farm surrounded by her animals, including ducks, chickens, dogs, rabbits and cats. She kept in regular touch with her family, which includes three children, 10 grandchildren, and one great-grandchild. Whear’s daughter Gillian Hallac grew concerned for her mother’s welfare after she failed to make contact for two days. Detectives initially suspected Whear met with misadventure while driving on snaking roads through the Northern Rivers, though concerns grew as police searches uncovered no signs of the woman or her gold Ford Escape SUV. Gillian Hallac, pictured with daughter Amelia, 8, believes her mother was taken from her home. Steven Siewert Drones and helicopters searched from the air, while police divers scoured the Rous and Tweed rivers.



There was a breakthrough in the search last month, when investigators found the woman’s car in the Rous River less than 10 kilometres from her property. The SUV was recovered from the water, and forensically and mechanically examined. Personal belongings believed to be Whear’s were also recovered. Whear’s Ford Escape was recovered in September, one month before her body was found. NSW Police Whear was engaged in a long-running dispute involving the lease agreement over the farm she rented for 23 years. She was due to appear in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal the week after she vanished. There is no suggestion the proceedings are related to Whear’s disappearance, nor is anyone involved in them accused of any wrongdoing.



Hallac, speaking to this publication in August, said despite the legal proceedings, Whear had no reason to leave her life behind. Her mother was employed as a disability support worker, and was undertaking an art course at TAFE. “She had a life with plans and responsibilities and people who loved her,” Hallac said. “We don’t believe she had any ordinary reasons to leave the property that evening.” Anyone with information that could assist police is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. World.title: Ruthless Roos leap towards relevance with Blakey blockbuster
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Ruthless Roos leap towards relevance with Blakey blockbuster Marc McGowan Sports reporter October 13, 2026 — 12:32pm

October 13, 2026 — 12:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

North Melbourne finally reeled in their big fish. Or, “Lizard” in this case. Nick Blakey is not a gun midfielder or a Coleman Medal-winning spearhead, but he is a legitimate star with an All-Australian honour and two grand final appearances on his resume. Nick Blakey has played his final game in the famous red and white of Sydney. Sam Mooy He grew up in Sydney and chose to start with the Swans instead of being a father-son selection at the Kangaroos, where his father John was a dual premiership player, and flirted with a move to Geelong before eventually choosing North. But who cares? Blakey will be at the Roos in 2027, and for at least the next eight seasons.



The trade is a victory for list boss Brady Rawlings and co. after falling short in these types of pursuits so many times across the years. Related Article Live

AFL 2026 AFL trade period LIVE updates: Roos complete blockbuster Blakey deal, and they’re not done yet; Blues, Giants at Whitfield impasse The Roos were viewed as nothing more than a stalking horse two years ago when Dan Houston left Port Adelaide and was considering his options en route to Collingwood. Richmond legend Dustin Martin gave up about $2 million to stay a Tiger for life after the Kangaroos audaciously offered him $11 million across seven years in 2017 to try to lure him as a restricted free agent to Arden Street. North also swung and missed on the likes of Isaac Heeney (in 2016), Josh Kelly (2017 and 2021), Jordan De Goey (2018) and Andrew Gaff (2018) despite their willingness to give them all at least, and in some cases more than, $1 million annually on long-term deals.



For so long, the Roos’ failed recruiting missions made them the butt of jokes. Instead, they had to overpay for B- and C-graders, or hunt in the bargain bin to bring in players from other clubs. Blakey’s family connection clearly helped this time, as did the enormous money on offer, but very likely North Melbourne’s improving on-field fortunes as well. There is still work to be done, evidenced by them ruthlessly sacking Alastair Clarkson and turning to Jaymie Graham, but the arrow is pointing up, even if it has taken far longer than hoped. Dustin Martin was one of a list of A-grade talents who spurned the Roos. Getty Images After a ninth-placed finish in 2018, the Kangaroos since placed 12th, 17th, 18th, 18th, 17th – when they infamously beat Gold Coast in the last round to “lose” the No.1 pick and first access to Harley Reid) – 17th, 16th and then 14th this past season.



There were priority picks, major player turnover, a bunch of fired coaches and a lot of pain in between. The expectation will be for North Melbourne to take a leap next year, and it is not unreasonable to think they could be in wildcard calculations with the new top-10 ladder format. Loading The Blakey coup happened quickly once the disgruntled 26-year-old, who was contracted for five more seasons at Sydney, decided his relationship with the Swans was irreparable after the fallout from the events in the early hours of August 17 at the Pullman in East Melbourne. It helped the Roos’ cause that Geelong’s assets dried up from trading for Jordan Ridley and Rowan Marshall, leaving little to no hope for them to also bring in Blakey.



Rivals no longer: Paul Curtis and Blakey will both be part of the puzzle for North Melbourne moving forward. Getty Images What follows with Blakey and North Melbourne will be significant in whether the Roos have truly turned the corner, on and off the field. Blakey will be under more pressure to perform than ever before, from the monster contract to playing in Melbourne and even the Pullman scandal. The Roos’ board, headed by president Sonja Hood, signed off on a $12 million offer for Blakey, who was one of five players handed season-ending suspensions by the Swans for his involvement in a night of wild partying at the Pullman. A separate Victoria Police investigation is ongoing after three women, working as exotic dancers, variously alleged they were sexually assaulted and touched inappropriately without consent.



No charges have been laid, and all five Sydney players who served the bans denied criminal wrongdoing. One of those players, Riley Bice, is no longer a subject of the investigation and is being treated as a witness. How the Roos utilise Blakey will be fascinating, given what they are paying him and what they gave up at the trade table, headlined by pick six this year and a first-rounder in 2028. Related Article AFL 2026 Blues to investigate Cowan, Hayward incidents and pass results to AFL Will Blakey simply reprise his Swans role as a dashing defender, or will North Melbourne ask for more? They plan to also secure Adelaide’s contracted key defender Nick Murray before tomorrow’s trade deadline, so Blakey should be spared from that type of responsibility. The success of this move will be crucial to whether the Kangaroos take the next step in their goal to one day be contending for premierships again, as well as if they become a destination club for more big-name recruits.



No one expects North to suddenly rival Geelong, Collingwood and Hawthorn in that department, but the Brisbane Lions have shown how quickly things can change when the wins and flags start stacking up. We also just saw Zak Butters choose the Western Bulldogs over the Cats, so anything is possible. The Kangaroos might only be getting started. They sure hope so. World.title: Queensland parliament updates: Labor leader and Child Safety minister in question time firing line
World.content:
The Opposition has taken aim at freshly returned minister Amanda Camm over child safety data, while the government used question time to unload on Labor leader Steven Miles citing a fresh internal criticism finding its way to the media.

Asked to guarantee no child who harmed or died due to departmental delays, or how many of the 91 children known to the child safety system who died last year were waiting for an assessment, Camm did not give a direct response.

“Any loss of a child’s life, of any age, whether they are known to the Child Safety Department or just a Queensland or Australian child, or any child, is a tragedy,“ Camm said.

Several government backbenchers lobbed softball questions to Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie, allowing him to tee-off against Miles using quotes in recent media reports critical of his leadership but noting the lack of a clear replacement.

“The Leader of the Opposition’s position is untenable,” Bleijie said. “His front bench – look to the left, look to the right. They are leaking against you.”

Independent Noosa MP Sandy Bolton quizzed Premier David Crisafulli about whether he still intended to change the state’s voting system back to an optional preference scheme before the 2028 election.

Crisafulli said he would, and claimed it would have benefited the LNP to have done so already, noting Labor’s win in the Stafford byelection.

“The primary vote [there] on this side was far higher than Labor, and the only reason that the member of Stafford [Luke Richmond] sits there is because of preferences from the Greens and the Socialists,” Crisafulli said.

“I think it’s very very safe to say, under that [optional preferential] voting system, the member for Stafford wouldn’t be here, and the Leader of the Opposition wouldn’t be there.”

World.title: Don’t blame Ukraine: Prices go up and up, thanks to Trump’s wars
World.content:
BusinessThe economyInflation Opinion Don’t blame Ukraine: Prices go up and up, thanks to Trump’s wars Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 13, 2026 — 12:08pm

October 13, 2026 — 12:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Donald Trump’s “diesel-for-sanctions” deal with Vladimir Putin is an indication of how desperate he has become in the lead-up to next month’s midterm elections. Rather than seeking to shift blame for his polling woes to Ukraine, he should look in the mirror. When the latest inflation data is released on Wednesday morning in the US, it is expected to show that the inflation rate in the world’s largest economy rose again in September, adding to the cost-of-living pressures that are the key issue in the midterms. Donald Trump has blamed Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky for the rise in energy costs, which could cost him the midterm elections. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The consensus among US economists is that headline inflation will have risen from August’s 3.4 per cent to 3.6 per cent or 3.7 per cent, with “core” inflation (excluding energy and food costs) either steady or edging up from 2.5 per cent to 2.4 per cent. That disparity between headline and core rates points to the major factor in the persistently high US inflation rate – the surge in gasoline and diesel prices that has occurred as a result of Trump’s decision to go to war in the Middle East.



The day before the February attacks by the US and Israel on Iran, oil was trading at $US70 a barrel. Today it is above $US106 a barrel. US gasoline prices average $US2.28 ($3.27) a gallon on the eve of the attacks. Today, they average $US4.35 ($6.24) a gallon. Diesel cost, on average, about $3.80 a gallon on February 27. Today, it is $US6.27 a gallon. As has often been the case with Trump, his ego and impulses – in this case the desire to bend the Fed to his will, or in the war with Iran, his expectations of an easy and glorious victory – undermine his ambitions. Those increased costs not only feed directly into households’ costs of living, but they also, over time, bleed into the wider economy as the delayed impact on transport costs and agricultural production flows through and impacts consumer prices and corporate margins.



When the members of the Federal Reserve Bank’s Open Market Committee meet in a fortnight to decide whether to raise their policy rate for a second successive meeting, however, they won’t just be considering the direct and indirect costs of energy. Related Article Opinion

Russia-Ukraine war The Putin ‘solution’: Donald Trump’s strange deal is destined to fail Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The focus on energy costs has tended to relegate the other major Trump-inspired source of inflation to the sidelines of discussion but – as with fuel prices – the impact of his tariffs is still working its way through the US economy. The New York Fed produced a research paper last year that concluded that about 90 per cent of Trump’s 2025 tariffs were passed through to US import prices and were absorbed by domestic businesses and consumers. Last week, the Fed researchers produced an update. They found that for every percentage point increase in average tariffs, consumer prices increased by about a quarter of 1 per cent after one year.



About two-thirds of the effect arose because tariffs raised the prices of imported goods, while the rest arose indirectly as US companies paid more for imported parts and materials and because US producers raised their prices when competing imports cost more. A good illustration of the second-round effects of the tariffs is steel, where Trump imposed a 50 per cent tariff on imports in February last year. US steel prices have risen faster than anywhere else in the world, with hot-rolled coil prices up more than half. US steel prices have risen faster than anywhere else in the world, with hot-rolled coil prices up more than half. AP That’s great and immensely profitable for the handful of US domestic steel mills, but not so great for downstream manufacturers and, ultimately, US consumers. The Fed analysis found that the direct effect of higher import prices flowed through quite quickly. About half the increased costs were in place after three months and all of them by six months, with retailers taking a few months to lift their prices.



The indirect effects – the increased input costs to US manufacturers – took longer to surface. In the first six months, US producer prices rose slightly, but the response then builds and roughly doubles over the next six months, they said. Most of Trump’s baseline tariffs on the rest of the world were implemented, with delays, in the middle of last year. Having been deemed illegal by the Supreme Court in February, those “Liberation Day” tariffs were quickly replaced by interim tariffs with a uniform rate of 10 per cent, until they were in turn displaced by the “forced-labour” tariffs of either 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent on 60 economies that Trump announced in July this year. Pricey consequences: Trump as he announced his “Liberation Day” tariffs on April 2, 2025. Getty Images There are, of course, other sector-specific tariffs that Trump imposed last year on “national security” and other grounds, like those on steel and aluminium, but the significant point here is that the tariffs have been a moving feast and that the delay before their full impact on end-prices is felt means they are still feeding into the inflation rate.



The Fed researchers said that, in a scenario where a 10 per cent tariff is imposed on all imports (which is the base case for Trump’s forced-labour tariffs) consumer goods prices would be 2.6 per cent higher after 12 months, or about a quarter of the tariff increase. Related Article Opinion

US politics When Trump gets a thrashing at the midterms, four words will come back to haunt him Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Thus, the impact of both higher energy costs as a result of the war on Iran and higher consumer goods prices due to Trump’s tariffs is still flowing through the US economy. The inflation rate also isn’t being helped by the massive investments being made in artificial intelligence and its flow-on effects to the prices of capital, semiconductors, construction costs and electricity and water. AI companies are spending about $US750 billion ($1.1 trillion) this year and are forecast to spend at least another $US2 trillion (if the boom in the sector lasts) over the next two years. In the long run, AI may (or may not) increase productivity and decrease inflation rates but, in the near term, the frenzy adds to inflation.



Trump’s deal with Putin will have a minor impact on US diesel prices, if any. The volumes of diesel are too small to have a material effect. If the war in Iran ended tomorrow, it would have a much greater impact, even though it might take months and, in some instances years, for the damage done to infrastructure in the Middle East and confidence in passing through the Strait of Hormuz to be fully remedied and supplies of oil and refined products to be fully restored. Similarly, if Trump stopped announcing new tariffs, or better still withdrew all those he’s put in place or has announced, the inflation rate would subside and probably be very close to the Fed’s 2 per cent target. Prices would still be higher than before the Iran war and his trade wars, but stable. Loading Unless there is an increase in the inflation rate above expectations this week, the Fed is likely to sit on its hands later this month rather that raise rates again days before the midterms.



Market expectations have fallen back from a near-certainty of another 25-basis-point increase following Fed chairman Kevin Warsh’s hawkish commentary after last month’s meeting. They are now pricing in a less than 20 per cent chance that the Fed will move again this month. A rate rise is fully priced in for December. In any event, a cut in interest rates to the 1 per cent or less that Trump consistently calls for aren’t going to happen while the inflation rate remains pumped up by his war and tariffs – unless he can find another solution. Related Article US election With a month to go, Republicans’ midterm prospects are ‘catastrophically bad’ And he thinks he has one. The administration is again targeting Fed governor Lisa Cook, with Trump setting up a “committee of inquiry” staffed by three Trump loyalists, including his key economic adviser, the obsequious Kevin Hassett, into allegations made by another fiercely loyal Trump appointee that Cook committed mortgage fraud by making false statements on a loan application. The inquiry came after the Supreme Court ruled that Cook had been denied procedural fairness when Trump sought to fire her “for cause” from the Fed’s board. Should the “kangaroo court,” as it is being described by Cook supporters, do what Trump wants, the matter will inevitably end up before the Supreme Court again.



The unintended consequences of the campaign against Cook is that another Trump target, former Fed chair Jerome Powell, will probably continue to defy convention and remain on the Fed’s board until his term ends in January 2028 rather than risk the damage to the Fed’s independence that could arise if Trump were able to stack the board. Other Fed governors – including Warsh – might also be emboldened, if only to protect their own reputations. As has often been the case with Trump, his ego and impulses – in this case the desire to bend the Fed to his will or, in the war in Iran, his expectations of an easy and glorious victory – undermine his ambitions. World.content:
PoliticsFederalAustralian economy Australia facing biggest jobless rate spike of developed world Shane Wright October 13, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australia faces the biggest increase in unemployment in the developed world next year – even as the country’s economy remains one of the globe’s fastest growing and inflation cools – with warnings the AI boom and soaring government debt is a growing risk to all nations. The International Monetary Fund (IMF), in its six-monthly updated economic outlook, on Tuesday warned that the good luck that had helped the world economy overcome the turmoil caused by the US-Israel war against Iran could soon run out. The number of Australians out of work could soar close to 800,000 by 2027. Louie Douvis The monetary fund is forecasting the global economy to expand by 3.1 per cent this year before accelerating by 3.4 per cent in 2027. Inflation is expected to hit 4.7 per cent this year, largely due to a surge in prices for commodities including oil and food, before easing slightly to 4.1 per cent. Australia’s economy is tipped to grow by 1.9 per cent this year and 1.6 per cent in 2027. Both forecasts are 0.1 of a percentage point lower than what the IMF forecast in April.



At that level of growth, only the United States, Spain, Singapore and New Zealand are expected to expand faster than Australia. But unemployment in Australia is expected to climb by 0.3 of a percentage point, from 4.4 per cent this year to 4.7 per cent in 2027. Almost all other developed nations are expected to enjoy either no change in unemployment or a small fall between this year and next. Loading At 4.7 per cent, the number of Australians out of work would approach 800,000. Despite the increase, Australia’s jobless rate remains lower than most other rich nations: it is 5.3 per cent in Britain, 8.1 per cent in Sweden and 6.3 per cent in Canada.



The lift in unemployment is expected to help reduce Australia’s inflation rate, which is forecast to fall from 3.9 per cent this year to 3.1 per cent in 2027. At that level, only a small number of nations would have face price pressures higher than Australia, including Austria and Greece. Related Article Inflation Inflation jumps to four-month high a day after RBA rate rise International Monetary Fund chief economist Silvana Tenreyro said the global economy had aced an “exceptional sequence of events” over the past seven years including the pandemic, the disruption to global supply chains, the wars in Ukraine and Iran and challenges to the world’s trading system. She said the economy had got through all of this. The recent surge in oil prices, for instance, would have ordinarily hurt the global economy, but a rundown in inventories, re-routing of new supplies, plus a sharp lift in renewable energy sources had all helped to offset the expected macroeconomic fallout. But Tenreyro said the way the world had responded to the lift in oil prices, on top of the economic boost produced by the AI construction boom, was now under threat.



“This resilience is under strain. Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing policy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience,” Tenreyro said. “With gains clustered in a small number of firms, sectors and economies, global expansion is heavily reliant on a narrow set of technological and financial conditions. “More generally, resilience has been uneven, varying noticeably with economies’ exposure to the war and the AI boom, and causing divergent outcomes.” Tenreyro said the lift in government borrowing costs, which have pushed interest rates on public debt to their highest levels in more than a decade, meant governments had to find ways to reduce their debt levels. “The interaction of higher financing costs with elevated debt levels exposes a key margin of vulnerability,” she said.





“We are not immune from these global factors, but we are better placed than many others. We are well positioned to benefit from the global AI investment boom and our efforts to strengthen supply chains are helping to buffer us in a fragmenting world.” Chalmers said the government was already undertaking many of the IMF’s recommendations, including by making cuts in spending and investing in energy security policies. Georgia, USA: One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a roller coaster in Georgia, according to police. The tragedy occurred on Monday afternoon (US time) on the Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia amusement park, about 25 kilometres north-west of Atlanta, according to the Cobb County Police Department. Loading Detectives with the department’s major crimes unit will investigate the incident. Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured.



Witnesses who spoke to NBC affiliate WXIA of Atlanta said they saw a man fall from the Goliath roller coaster, with at least two saying they saw him strike parts of the ride multiple times before hitting the ground. “He fell and hit the car three different times,” one said, NBC reported. A patron died on the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday (US time). CNN Passengers are evacuated from the roller coaster after the incident in Georgia. ABC7 “The man started levitating in the air sideways,” said another witness, Logan Conner, who was on the ride at the time. “We made direct eye contact with him.”



A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they were fully cooperating with investigations into the incident. “We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said. The Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. Six Flags Over Georgia Authorities and Six Flags did not identify the roller coaster. However, local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster. The roller coaster, which was opened in 2006, goes as fast as about 110km/h and reaches heights of 61 metres, the park’s website reports. During about 3½ minutes, riders “navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills,” according to the website.



This death would be at least the seventh at the Georgia park, including one in 2006 in which a man had a likely heart attack on the Goliath coaster, according to the Doan Law Firm, whose practice areas include amusement park accidents. Last month, Six Flags Magic Mountain, in southern California, announced that it was retiring its famous X2 roller coaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. Six Flags recently settled a wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022. Three more lawsuits alleging traumatic brain injuries were filed last week. Last year, a 32-year-old man died after riding a high-speed roller coaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. He died from blunt impact injuries and his death was ruled accidental. World.title: ‘Inhumane act’: Homicide investigation launched after beloved grandmother found dead in stock dip
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime ‘Inhumane act’: Homicide investigation launched after beloved grandmother found dead in stock dip Daniel Lo Surdo and Riley Walter Updated October 13, 2026 — 12:42pm ,first published 11:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A homicide investigation has been launched after the body of a beloved grandmother was found partially submerged in a stock dip on a rural NSW property, as her family demands answers for the “callous, inhumane act”. The body of Yvonne Whear, a 73-year-old last seen in the Northern Rivers almost eight months ago, was severely decomposed when it was discovered partially submerged in half a metre of water at a property 20 kilometres south of Murwillumbah last week. Two bike riders spotted the remains in the stock dip while using a popular track running past the property. Yvonne Whear was last seen on February 19. NSW Police A post-mortem examination on Monday identified the remains and sparked a homicide investigation under Strike Force Milera, which will deploy officers from the State Crime Command’s homicide squad, along with other specialised units, to the Northern Rivers. Whear’s three children, in a statement released on behalf of the family, said they were “devastated and horrified” by the development.



“We are left facing a future without her, carrying unimaginable grief and unanswered questions,” the family said. Yvonne Whear, captured on CCTV in a Murwillumbah service station the day she disappeared. Tweed-Byron Police District “Not only has she been robbed of her life, her children and grandchildren now all face the horrific trauma of this callous inhumane act. While whoever is responsible for this is still out there in the community … Yvonne deserves justice, our family deserves answers.” The family were told of the tragic news on Tuesday morning, as detectives prepared to return to Whear’s hobby farm on the outskirts of Dungay, near the Queensland border. Further forensic testing and searches are expected at the residence.



Tweed/Byron Police District Commander Matt Zimmer said the state’s detectives would deliver justice for Whear, as they investigate the circumstances ahead of her death. “There are still significant questions about what happened to her and how she came to be where she was found,” he said.



“Someone knows what happened to Yvonne. Whether you have previously spoken to police or have information you have not yet shared, we need you to come forward.” Whear was last seen on February 19, when security cameras captured her driving north on Queensland Road at Murwillumbah towards her farm about 3.20pm. Mobile phone data shows she watched YouTube videos that afternoon, and just before 5pm, checked her voicemail. Whear’s body was found in an unused stock dip. NSW Police First responders at the rural property in Terragon last week, after the body was discovered. Nine Her phone was last detected by a phone tower near Dungay at 10am on February 20, and hasn’t been seen since.



Whear lived on her farm surrounded by her animals, including ducks, chickens, dogs, rabbits and cats. She kept in regular touch with her family, which includes three children, 10 grandchildren, and one great-grandchild. Whear’s daughter Gillian Hallac grew concerned for her mother’s welfare after she failed to make contact for two days. Detectives initially suspected Whear met with misadventure while driving on snaking roads through the Northern Rivers, though concerns grew as police searches uncovered no signs of the woman or her gold Ford Escape SUV. Gillian Hallac, pictured with daughter Amelia, 8, believes her mother was taken from her home. Steven Siewert Drones and helicopters searched from the air, while police divers scoured the Rous and Tweed rivers.



There was a breakthrough in the search last month, when investigators found the woman’s car in the Rous River less than 10 kilometres from her property. The SUV was recovered from the water, and forensically and mechanically examined. Personal belongings believed to be Whear’s were also recovered. Whear’s Ford Escape was recovered in September, one month before her body was found. NSW Police Whear was engaged in a long-running dispute involving the lease agreement over the farm she rented for 23 years. She was due to appear in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal the week after she vanished. There is no suggestion the proceedings are related to Whear’s disappearance, nor is anyone involved in them accused of any wrongdoing.



Hallac, speaking to this publication in August, said despite the legal proceedings, Whear had no reason to leave her life behind. Her mother was employed as a disability support worker, and was undertaking an art course at TAFE. “She had a life with plans and responsibilities and people who loved her,” Hallac said. “We don’t believe she had any ordinary reasons to leave the property that evening.” Anyone with information that could assist police is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. World.title: Ruthless Roos leap towards relevance with Blakey blockbuster
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Ruthless Roos leap towards relevance with Blakey blockbuster Marc McGowan Sports reporter October 13, 2026 — 12:32pm

October 13, 2026 — 12:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

North Melbourne finally reeled in their big fish. Or, “Lizard” in this case. Nick Blakey is not a gun midfielder or a Coleman Medal-winning spearhead, but he is a legitimate star with an All-Australian honour and two grand final appearances on his resume. Nick Blakey has played his final game in the famous red and white of Sydney. Sam Mooy He grew up in Sydney and chose to start with the Swans instead of being a father-son selection at the Kangaroos, where his father John was a dual premiership player, and flirted with a move to Geelong before eventually choosing North. But who cares? Blakey will be at the Roos in 2027, and for at least the next eight seasons.



The trade is a victory for list boss Brady Rawlings and co. after falling short in these types of pursuits so many times across the years. Related Article Live

AFL 2026 AFL trade period LIVE updates: Roos complete blockbuster Blakey deal, and they’re not done yet; Blues, Giants at Whitfield impasse The Roos were viewed as nothing more than a stalking horse two years ago when Dan Houston left Port Adelaide and was considering his options en route to Collingwood. Richmond legend Dustin Martin gave up about $2 million to stay a Tiger for life after the Kangaroos audaciously offered him $11 million across seven years in 2017 to try to lure him as a restricted free agent to Arden Street. North also swung and missed on the likes of Isaac Heeney (in 2016), Josh Kelly (2017 and 2021), Jordan De Goey (2018) and Andrew Gaff (2018) despite their willingness to give them all at least, and in some cases more than, $1 million annually on long-term deals.



For so long, the Roos’ failed recruiting missions made them the butt of jokes. Instead, they had to overpay for B- and C-graders, or hunt in the bargain bin to bring in players from other clubs. Blakey’s family connection clearly helped this time, as did the enormous money on offer, but very likely North Melbourne’s improving on-field fortunes as well. There is still work to be done, evidenced by them ruthlessly sacking Alastair Clarkson and turning to Jaymie Graham, but the arrow is pointing up, even if it has taken far longer than hoped. Dustin Martin was one of a list of A-grade talents who spurned the Roos. Getty Images After a ninth-placed finish in 2018, the Kangaroos since placed 12th, 17th, 18th, 18th, 17th – when they infamously beat Gold Coast in the last round to “lose” the No.1 pick and first access to Harley Reid) – 17th, 16th and then 14th this past season.



There were priority picks, major player turnover, a bunch of fired coaches and a lot of pain in between. The expectation will be for North Melbourne to take a leap next year, and it is not unreasonable to think they could be in wildcard calculations with the new top-10 ladder format. Loading The Blakey coup happened quickly once the disgruntled 26-year-old, who was contracted for five more seasons at Sydney, decided his relationship with the Swans was irreparable after the fallout from the events in the early hours of August 17 at the Pullman in East Melbourne. It helped the Roos’ cause that Geelong’s assets dried up from trading for Jordan Ridley and Rowan Marshall, leaving little to no hope for them to also bring in Blakey.



Rivals no longer: Paul Curtis and Blakey will both be part of the puzzle for North Melbourne moving forward. Getty Images What follows with Blakey and North Melbourne will be significant in whether the Roos have truly turned the corner, on and off the field. Blakey will be under more pressure to perform than ever before, from the monster contract to playing in Melbourne and even the Pullman scandal. The Roos’ board, headed by president Sonja Hood, signed off on a $12 million offer for Blakey, who was one of five players handed season-ending suspensions by the Swans for his involvement in a night of wild partying at the Pullman. A separate Victoria Police investigation is ongoing after three women, working as exotic dancers, variously alleged they were sexually assaulted and touched inappropriately without consent.



No charges have been laid, and all five Sydney players who served the bans denied criminal wrongdoing. One of those players, Riley Bice, is no longer a subject of the investigation and is being treated as a witness. How the Roos utilise Blakey will be fascinating, given what they are paying him and what they gave up at the trade table, headlined by pick six this year and a first-rounder in 2028. Related Article AFL 2026 Blues to investigate Cowan, Hayward incidents and pass results to AFL Will Blakey simply reprise his Swans role as a dashing defender, or will North Melbourne ask for more? They plan to also secure Adelaide’s contracted key defender Nick Murray before tomorrow’s trade deadline, so Blakey should be spared from that type of responsibility. The success of this move will be crucial to whether the Kangaroos take the next step in their goal to one day be contending for premierships again, as well as if they become a destination club for more big-name recruits.



No one expects North to suddenly rival Geelong, Collingwood and Hawthorn in that department, but the Brisbane Lions have shown how quickly things can change when the wins and flags start stacking up. We also just saw Zak Butters choose the Western Bulldogs over the Cats, so anything is possible. The Kangaroos might only be getting started. They sure hope so.
