World.title: Queensland parliament updates: Labor leader and Child Safety minister in question time firing line
World.content:
The Opposition has taken aim at freshly returned minister Amanda Camm over child safety data, while the government used question time to unload on Labor leader Steven Miles citing a fresh internal criticism finding its way to the media.

Asked to guarantee no child who harmed or died due to departmental delays, or how many of the 91 children known to the child safety system who died last year were waiting for an assessment, Camm did not give a direct response.

“Any loss of a child’s life, of any age, whether they are known to the Child Safety Department or just a Queensland or Australian child, or any child, is a tragedy,“ Camm said.

Several government backbenchers lobbed softball questions to Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie, allowing him to tee-off against Miles using quotes in recent media reports critical of his leadership but noting the lack of a clear replacement.

“The Leader of the Opposition’s position is untenable,” Bleijie said. “His front bench – look to the left, look to the right. They are leaking against you.”

Independent Noosa MP Sandy Bolton quizzed Premier David Crisafulli about whether he still intended to change the state’s voting system back to an optional preference scheme before the 2028 election.

Crisafulli said he would, and claimed it would have benefited the LNP to have done so already, noting Labor’s win in the Stafford byelection.

“The primary vote [there] on this side was far higher than Labor, and the only reason that the member of Stafford [Luke Richmond] sits there is because of preferences from the Greens and the Socialists,” Crisafulli said.

“I think it’s very very safe to say, under that [optional preferential] voting system, the member for Stafford wouldn’t be here, and the Leader of the Opposition wouldn’t be there.”

That disparity between headline and core rates points to the major factor in the persistently high US inflation rate – the surge in gasoline and diesel prices that has occurred as a result of Trump’s decision to go to war in the Middle East.

Having been deemed illegal by the Supreme Court in February, those “Liberation Day” tariffs were quickly replaced by interim tariffs with a uniform rate of 10 per cent, until they were in turn displaced by the “forced-labour” tariffs of either 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent on 60 economies that Trump announced in July this year. Pricey consequences: Trump as he announced his “Liberation Day” tariffs on April 2, 2025. Getty Images There are, of course, other sector-specific tariffs that Trump imposed last year on “national security” and other grounds, like those on steel and aluminium, but the significant point here is that the tariffs have been a moving feast and that the delay before their full impact on end-prices is felt means they are still feeding into the inflation rate.



The Fed researchers said that, in a scenario where a 10 per cent tariff is imposed on all imports (which is the base case for Trump’s forced-labour tariffs) consumer goods prices would be 2.6 per cent higher after 12 months, or about a quarter of the tariff increase. Related Article Opinion

US politics When Trump gets a thrashing at the midterms, four words will come back to haunt him Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Thus, the impact of both higher energy costs as a result of the war on Iran and higher consumer goods prices due to Trump’s tariffs is still flowing through the US economy. The inflation rate also isn’t being helped by the massive investments being made in artificial intelligence and its flow-on effects to the prices of capital, semiconductors, construction costs and electricity and water. AI companies are spending about $US750 billion ($1.1 trillion) this year and are forecast to spend at least another $US2 trillion (if the boom in the sector lasts) over the next two years. In the long run, AI may (or may not) increase productivity and decrease inflation rates but, in the near term, the frenzy adds to inflation.



Trump’s deal with Putin will have a minor impact on US diesel prices, if any. The volumes of diesel are too small to have a material effect. If the war in Iran ended tomorrow, it would have a much greater impact, even though it might take months and, in some instances years, for the damage done to infrastructure in the Middle East and confidence in passing through the Strait of Hormuz to be fully remedied and supplies of oil and refined products to be fully restored. Similarly, if Trump stopped announcing new tariffs, or better still withdrew all those he’s put in place or has announced, the inflation rate would subside and probably be very close to the Fed’s 2 per cent target. Prices would still be higher than before the Iran war and his trade wars, but stable. Loading Unless there is an increase in the inflation rate above expectations this week, the Fed is likely to sit on its hands later this month rather that raise rates again days before the midterms.



Market expectations have fallen back from a near-certainty of another 25-basis-point increase following Fed chairman Kevin Warsh’s hawkish commentary after last month’s meeting. They are now pricing in a less than 20 per cent chance that the Fed will move again this month. A rate rise is fully priced in for December. In any event, a cut in interest rates to the 1 per cent or less that Trump consistently calls for aren’t going to happen while the inflation rate remains pumped up by his war and tariffs – unless he can find another solution. Related Article US election With a month to go, Republicans’ midterm prospects are ‘catastrophically bad’ And he thinks he has one. The administration is again targeting Fed governor Lisa Cook, with Trump setting up a “committee of inquiry” staffed by three Trump loyalists, including his key economic adviser, the obsequious Kevin Hassett, into allegations made by another fiercely loyal Trump appointee that Cook committed mortgage fraud by making false statements on a loan application. The inquiry came after the Supreme Court ruled that Cook had been denied procedural fairness when Trump sought to fire her “for cause” from the Fed’s board. Should the “kangaroo court,” as it is being described by Cook supporters, do what Trump wants, the matter will inevitably end up before the Supreme Court again.



The unintended consequences of the campaign against Cook is that another Trump target, former Fed chair Jerome Powell, will probably continue to defy convention and remain on the Fed’s board until his term ends in January 2028 rather than risk the damage to the Fed’s independence that could arise if Trump were able to stack the board. Other Fed governors – including Warsh – might also be emboldened, if only to protect their own reputations. As has often been the case with Trump, his ego and impulses – in this case the desire to bend the Fed to his will or, in the war in Iran, his expectations of an easy and glorious victory – undermine his ambitions. World.title: Pacific news in brief for 13 October
World.content:
Samoa

World Rugby says Samoa's national teams will continue to participate in regional and international events under Lakapi Samoa.

A spokesperson said current discussions on the future of the sport's management in the country will not affect the national teams.

The spokesperson said work on confirming the way forward for the sport in Samoa continues, following the setting up of a new rival union three months ago.

World Rugby said Manu Samoa will compete at the Nations Cup in November as per the schedule.

Samoa

Maota Airport in Samoa has officially reopened, more than two decades after regular flights were discontinued in 2000.

Samoa Global News reported that the restored services will connect Maota with Fagali'i and Faleolo.

Samoa Airport Authority CEO Faaofonuu Tumanuvao Evile Falefatu described the reopening as "a new start for Savai'i."

Prime Minister La'aulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt signalled plans for more aviation development.

He said Asau is being considered as an alternative international airport for Samoa, as if Faleolo was faced with an emergency situation, there would be no alternative access into and out of Samoa.

Naoero

The Asian Development Bank has signed a US$15 million package with a subsidiary of the Naoero Air Corporation.

The money - part loans and part reimbursable grant - will help Naoero Airlines' acquisition of a preowned Boeing 737-800, to replace an aging aircraft.

Naoero Air Corporation board chair Charleston Deiye said that the fleet modernisation marks an important step in strengthening the reliability and resilience of air connectivity across the Pacific.

Cook Islands

The Cook Islands government has been getting precise, three-dimensional measurement of the shape of its land and near-shore environment.

The Prime Minister's Office said that the data provided a new evidence base for decision-making in areas like flooding, coastal hazards, and land use.

Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) uses laser pulses from an aircraft to measure the shape and elevation of land and the near-shore seabed in fine detail.

Prime Minister Mark Brown said the data will also be useful in climate advocacy, saying good data is a form of leverage.

He said it is the difference between asking to be believed, and being able to provide an evidentiary base that cannot be ignored.

Marhsall Islands

The Marshall Islands has opened its new permanent mission to the United Nations in New York, establishing a permanent, government-owned home for the island's diplomatic representation.

The mission reflects the Marshall Islands' long history with the United Nations, beginning 75 years ago during its time as a United Nations Trust Territory and continuing with its membership in the organization since 1991.

In a release, the President's Office said the acquisition of the mission building represents a significant investment in the Republic's diplomatic engagement with the United States, Pacific partners, and the broader international community.

Solomon Islands

Solomon Islands Prime Minister Mathew Wale says his country will continue to speak up for West Papua, noting that it is an issue of justice and human rights.

His and other leaders' recent comments at the United Nations drew a response from Indonesia which rejected allegations of systematic human rights violations in Papua.

Wale told local media that reducing the local indigenous Melanesian population to become a minority in their own land is not right.

World.title: Thousands of Kiwis could live longer with continuous glucose monitoring - study
World.content:
Thousands of Kiwis needing intensive insulin therapy (rIIT) could live longer with wider use of real-time continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) technology, a new study has found.

The study - led by Associate Professor Ryan Paul (Ngāti Maru, Hauraki), an endocrinologist at the University of Waikato and Health New Zealand, alongside researchers in the US and the United Kingdom - compared the use of real-time CGM devices with traditional finger-prick testing for people with type 2 diabetes.

The study estimated that people with type 2 diabetes rIIT using the technology were expected to live longer, gaining around three additional months of life on average, and spend more years in better health, with fewer complications.

"The whole idea is how can we intervene early in diabetes so we can keep people with diabetes well and not developing complications and dying from their diabetes and that is what CGM allows us to do," Paul told RNZ.

The study found that continuous glucose monitoring was very cost-effective for those on multiple injections of insulin a day, he said.

Particularly for Māori and Pacific people, who were at least two and a half times more likely to develop diabetes, to develop complications from their diabetes and to die from their diabetes, he said.

"We are now also seeing the intergenerational cycle of type 2 diabetes, and what I mean by that is that babies born to mums that have diabetes during their pregnancy will now have a very high chance of developing type 2 diabetes themselves by the time they become 30 years of age, and then subsequently potentially increasing the risk of their children and that's both fathers and mothers."

The technology could also be cost effective for young people with type 2 diabetes, which when it did start at an earlier age was much more aggressive, he said.

"In fact, for our young Maori and Pacific people, they're actually dying up to 20 to 25 years earlier than European people without diabetes. Now, they are not small numbers, and that's why we're really passionate to try and do all that we can in this space to try and improve care. Part of it is getting access to technology that we know that works and is cost-effective."

Associate Professor Ryan Paul, an endocrinologist at the University of Waikato and Health New Zealand. Supplied

Paul said CGMs involved a small sensor which sat under the skin and tracked glucose levels throughout the day and night, sending that information to a receiver, usually a smartphone.

"So people in real time can know what's happening to their glucose levels, that means they can change their treatment, they can see the effects of kai or food or physical activity, and they know what needs changing, and it really empowers people to manage their diabetes."

It was much less invasive than traditional finger-prick testing, with the sensor lasting at least 10 days it meant one finger prick every two weeks rather than up to four a day, he said.

Paul said he encouraged patients with a CGM to experiment with how different types of kai and exercise affected their glucose levels.

"That real-time positive reinforcement provides exponentially more information than what fingerpricks do. Because fingerpricks are only a snapshot but what CGM shows is the complete trends and will actually alarm whenever glucose levels get too low or get too high and that enables whānau to act there and then to correct their glucose levels rather than waiting at least hours till their next fingerprick is due."

An example of a real time glucose monitoring patch with a smartphone as the receiver. Supplied

Paul said the price of CGMs were dropping as more competitors came onto the market. The sensor involved in this study cost about $50-55 per week for people that were self-funding, he said.

That was still a lot of money, but there were other sensors on the market, the cheapest one available was $25 per week, he said.

"Test strips to do fingerpricks aren't cheap and even though these sensors may cost $50-55 per week, they still end up to downstream savings on the health system and that is because how expensive the complications of diabetes are for Health New Zealand.

"So Health New Zealand spends over 2 billion per year on diabetes care and a vast majority of that, well over 80 percent of that is actually managing complications of diabetes."

Complications included laser treatment or surgery for eye disease, dialysis or transplant for kidney disease and amputations for foot disease, he said.

Paul said it should be celebrated that New Zealand had arguably the best access in the world to CGM technology for people with type 1 diabetes but, those with type 2 diabetes on multiple injections of insulin per day would also greatly benefit from this technology.

"I'll be honest, people think that [type 2 diabetes] is all self-induced and that since it's self-induced, people shouldn't be allowed to have access to technology but what people often forget or aren't aware of is that in terms of obesity and diabetes, at least 50 to 70 percent of that is genetic and we're in what I describe as a perfect storm for an obesogenic environment in terms of the cost of living and how expensive healthy kai and food is and we know that rates of physical activity are reducing."

World.title: RLWC2026: Toa Samoa banks on Luai
World.content:
Toa Samoa's head coach and co-captain both believe veteran Jarome Luai will be the key man in their campaign at the 2026 Rugby League World Cup.

Coach Ben Gardiner and co-captain Junior Paulo told NRL.com in Australia they both believe Luai is the man to guide them.

Luai has been instrumental in either the number six or seven jersey for the Samoans in the past, having led the side to the final at the 2022 event.

Gardiner said there are a number of options for his halves partner, with Chanel Harris-Tavita, Clayton Faulalo and Ronald Volkman all in the squad.

The coach believes his star playmaker will flourish in the team's style and playing pattern.

"He's played seven a number of times for us," Gardiner told NRL.com.

"There's that type of game where he's required to manage the game for us as a seven. He's our most experienced player in that area and he'll handle it well.

"We play a style of football that's a powerful style of football, a go-forward style of football that requires a lot of support, which opens up his running game.

"We all know he's at his best when he runs the ball so we'll be encouraging him to do that."

Luai's co-captain Paulo said they will wrap their support around the PNG Chiefs bound player.

"He's able to brush everything off his shoulders and he's ready to play some footy," Paulo said.

"This is what Jarome has been looking forward to, playing once more for Samoa, but I think he's a bit misunderstood by many people.

"Towards the back end of the year I think people were very opinionated about him. For Romy he's locked into putting his best foot forward and representing Samoa. He clearly enjoys being in these camps.

I've been lucky enough to see Romy evolve as a leader and grow into being the leader he is now

"All the boys will be backing him and luckily nothing fazes Romy too much."

Paulo said the team's presence at home in Apia last week with their Fetu Samoa women's team had reminded the players of what their heritage meant to them.

He said the welcome by the people and the support they received lifted the players' spirits.

"The biggest thing was seeing the smiles on kids' faces and them striving to want to be play for Samoa one day," he said.

"The inspiration we can generate is why we represent Samoa so proudly."

Meanwhile, Gardiner told NRL.com the team they have is the strongest they have been able to put together since the last World Cup.

Despite missing powerhouse forward Payne Haas and Terrell May, Gardiner is confident he has a squad capable of taking out the tournament.

"We've got a real balance of experience and youth and some guys that are in great form so it's a great opportunity for us, our fans and our people," he said.

"Our aim over the last four years was to build experience into our team, grow out key positions and bring guys along so that when we hit Rugby League World Cup 26, we were ready with our best team available."

Gardiner has backed the former Penrith Panthers combination of Spencer Leniu, Luai, Brian To'o and Stephen Crichton to spearhead their performances.

The quartet combined to win three premierships from 2021-2023 for the Panthers, before Crichton joined the Bulldogs and Leniu moved to the Roosters.

Luai and To'o stayed on at the Panthers in 2024 to help the club claim a fourth NRL title.

Gardiner believes his warriors will be ready to dismantle France at the CommBank Stadium in their opening game on Friday.

World.title: Reserve Bank puts digital cash on hold
World.content:
Audio player for " Can my landlord put a political billboard on my home? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/1872050%2Freserve-bank-puts-digital-cash-on-hold

Can my landlord put a political billboard on my home? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 9m

The Reserve Bank has paused the development of its digital cash proposal.

It had been planning to have a government-backed digital currency in place by 2030.

University of Otago economist Murat Ungor has previously described it as a way that New Zealand could shore up monetary sovereignty.

"Right now, when you check your bank balance, you are looking at a promise from your bank to pay you," Ungor told RNZ.

"With a central bank digital currency, that money would be a direct claim on the Reserve Bank itself, the safest form of money possible."

The Reserve Bank said it was focused on a broader work programme exploring how to modernise the payment system and implement a real-time retail payment solution.

"This is an important area of focus for the Reserve Bank due to the essential nature of payment systems as a core economic infrastructure that supports the whole economy. While the system remains reliable for many users, there is an opportunity to maximise its contribution to a digital economy and prepare it for an increasingly uncertain future. Modern payments infrastructure would be able to support emerging new forms of payment including digital central bank money along with the private money in your banking account."

Ungor said the pause was not a concern as long as it did not turn into a drift.

"The Reserve Bank treats the two strands of its Future of Money and Payments work, digital cash and payments modernisation, as closely connected. Getting the underlying payments infrastructure right first makes sense. There is little value in introducing a new form of digital money without considering how it would fit into a modern payments system.

"The Reserve Bank has identified potential benefits from modernisation, including lower transaction costs, less fraud and scam activity, and opportunities for new products and services. Addressing the practical limitations of the current system and modernising the infrastructure is a sensible priority.

"At the same time, the reasons for exploring digital cash have not disappeared. Cash use and acceptance are declining, while private forms of digital money, including stablecoins, are developing. This raises important longer-term questions about access to central bank money in digital form and New Zealand's monetary sovereignty. There is a legitimate debate about how significant these risks are, and whether digital cash is the right response. But those questions deserve a considered answer, even if the eventual conclusion is that New Zealand does not need to introduce it."

He said the Reserve Bank should algin its work on payments modernisation with its assessment of digital cash rather than allowing digital cash to fall off the agenda.

"I would like to see it maintain the policy work, explain clearly what criteria would trigger a resumption or a decision not to proceed, and continue engaging with the public.

"Public concerns also need to be taken seriously. In its consultation, the Reserve Bank found substantial concern about the possibility that digital cash could replace physical cash. It has stated that digital cash would not replace physical cash, and it is important that this distinction is communicated clearly."

World.title: Mystery of large pool of blood found in Wellington pedestrian tunnel solved
World.content:
The mystery of the large pool of blood found in a Wellington pedestrian tunnel has been solved, with the woman involved left bemused at how the community feared the worst.

The woman - who did not want to be named - said a sudden scooter crash saw her "faceplant" in the pedestrian tunnel beneath Wellington Airport.

Her comments came as police confirmed they were concluding their investigation, having identified the source of the blood.

"There's lots of conspiracy theorists that want to think someone's got vampire blood or it's a Covid thing," she told RNZ.

"I've heard all sorts. I've no time for the gossip side of things. Let's crack on doing life," she said.

Police had appealed to the public for information after they were called to Coutts Street in Rongotai on 4 October after the large pool of blood was found in the tunnel linking Miramar and Rongotai.

Detective Senior Sergeant Steve Wescott said testing showed the blood was human blood but, as of Friday last week, they were yet to locate anybody in the nearby area.

The woman involved said she was a regular user of the tunnel on her e-scooter, but while heading home the week before the discovery, she accidentally caught the edge of the footpath.

"It was just clip a curb and you're standing up on a scooter that goes at 16 kph and you don't have a chance to stop your face breaking the concrete.

"Contusions to the forehead and nose with a substantial amount of blood," she said.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The woman said she was very grateful for two men who helped her at the scene, one who was equipped with a first aid kit.

She said she was able to make her way home and after seeing her GP the next day was directed to Accident and Emergency in Wellington where she underwent tests and spent a night under observation.

She was alerted to media reports of the discovery her blood and told RNZ she contacted police via 105 and was interviewed by officers last week.

"I thought 'that sounds like it could be a me thing'," she said.

A spokesperson for Wellington police said they had identified the source of the blood.

"We can confirm the matter is not of a suspicious nature, and no further Police involvement is required.
