World.title: Man in court charged with stealing EV charging cables worth more than $57,000
World.content:
A man has appeared in court charged with stealing more than $57,000 worth of EV car charging cables in Canterbury.

Gabriel Verry, 26, is accused of using garden loppers to remove cables from five locations including BP Dallington, BP Redcliffs and Pak'nSave Wainoni between 2 October and 12 October.

He appeared at the Christchurch District Court on Tuesday charged with five counts of dishonestly taking EV charging cables, possession of a methamphetamine pipe and failing to assist police in a search.

Verry was remanded on bail to a Mackenzie District address on a 24-hour curfew ahead of a second court appearance in November.

The cables are stolen for the scrap metal, including copper.

Canterbury Rural Area Commander Inspector Peter Cooper said police had received reports of 23 charging stations being targeted by thieves since July, with 62 cables damaged across the Waimakariri and Selwyn districts and Christchurch.

"The offending has caused significant disruption to EV users and substantial costs to charging network providers through damage and replacement of infrastructure," he said.

"Police have been working closely with victims and industry partners to identify and locate those responsible to hold them to account. While an arrest has been made, our enquiries are ongoing and we are not ruling out further arrests.

"This activity is extremely dangerous and you put yourself at risk of severe harm when tampering with these cables. Police continue to work closely alongside scrap metal dealers around the regions and remind them that receiving stolen goods is also a crime."

Rewiring Aotearoa chief executive Mike Casey said about 80 percent of EV charging was done at home but damage to public charging stations inconvenienced people on longer trips.

He said copper from the cables was valuable.

World.title: Michael Jordan Last Dance jersey sells for record $20m
World.content:
The jersey Michael Jordan wore during Game 2 of the 1998 NBA Finals, featured in the Last Dance documentary, has sold for a record $US14 million ($20 million).

Hunt Auctions announced yesterday that the game-worn, autographed Chicago Bulls jersey was purchased by Miami real estate investor Ron Firman in a private sale.

It is the highest price ever paid for a piece of basketball memorabilia, and according to the auction house, the newly sold Jordan jersey ranks as the second-largest sale in history among game-worn sports jerseys.

The New York Yankees jersey worn by Babe Ruth in Game 3 of the 1932 World Series — during which Ruth called his shot ahead of a home run — went for $US24.12 million in 2024.

Jordan and the Bulls defeated the Utah Jazz in six games to win the 1998 championship, the sixth and final title of his career in Chicago.

Game 2, played on June 5, 1998, in Salt Lake City, saw Chicago even the series 1-1 in large part due to a dominant performance from its superstar guard.

Jordan put up 37 points, five rebounds, and three assists in a 93-88 victory. He would go on to collect his sixth and final Finals MVP award, two more than anyone else in NBA history, nine days later.

The wildly popular Last Dance documentary, released in 2020, was centred around that 1997-98 Bulls season.

"The record-setting price achieved for the related Michael Jordan jersey is yet another corroborative result as to the significance of Jordan within the industry and popular culture. This remarkable garment bore witness to one of Jordan's most hallowed NBA Finals appearances as part of his 'Last Dance' season to complete his illustrious career," David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions, said in a statement.

"While Michael Jordan's importance within the sports memorabilia marketplace has long been established, it has now escalated to an elite asset class more typically reserved for iconic works of art."

The previous record for a basketball memorabilia item was $US12.26 million for the home jersey worn by Jordan in Game 3 of the 1998 Finals, which was sold via auction in September.

Reuters

World.title: European Tour gives LIV golfers ultimatum and shuts door on playing both
World.content:
The European Tour has delivered an ultimatum to players contemplating the new version of LIV Golf, saying anyone who joins will not be allowed to remain a tour member.

"Players need to make a choice," Guy Kinnings, chief executive of the European Tour, said in a statement yesterday first reported by the BBC.

The tour previously let LIV players keep their European membership as long as they paid fines for playing LIV events that conflicted with the tour.

LIV Golf files for bankruptcy LIV Golf files for bankruptcy, flagging a restructure with a massive loan from the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia.

Australian golfers Cameron Smith, Lucas Herbert, Elvius Smylie and Marc Leishman all played in the LIV league in 2026.

It extended an olive branch earlier this year to nine players, allowing them to play LIV events without sanctions provided they settled all previous fines and agreed to add European Tour events to their 2026 schedules.

Kinnings delivered a much stronger message — us or them — as LIV tries to emerge from bankruptcy after Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund cut off financial support.

LIV has up to $300 million from BC Partners as it leans into a 10-tournament season focusing on team competition and players owning equity in LIV 2.0. Players have until October 25 to decide whether to stick with LIV, which could determine whether the beleaguered circuit can move forward out of bankruptcy.

The European Tour, however, is requiring anyone seeking to join to disclose where they intend to play in 2027. The tour said it would terminate membership if the disclosures prove false.

"As we have said for many years, we have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by," Kinnings said. "Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour."

Players must be European Tour members to compete in the Ryder Cup next September, adding pressure to the likes of Tyrrell Hatton of England, Tom McKibbin of Northern Ireland, Adrian Meronk of Poland and Thomas Detry of Belgium.

A lawyer for Jon Rahm said last week in a bankruptcy hearing for LIV that the former number one wanted to terminate his LIV contract. The question for Rahm, a two-time major champion, is how he works his way back to the PGA Tour.

Sergio Garcia also asked to end his LIV contract, and David Puig of Spain has indicated he is ready to take on a European Tour schedule.

The European Tour is negotiating a renewed alliance with the PGA Tour, which involves commercial opportunities and a path for the 10 leading players on the Race to Dubai to get PGA Tour cards.

Patrick Reed and Eugenio Chacarra, who both previously played for LIV Golf, are a lock to earn PGA Tour cards this year off the European Tour points list. Bernd Wiesberger of Austria, another player who signed early with LIV, also has a chance at a tour card.

The plan of LIV 2.0 is to have such a streamlined schedule to allow players to compete elsewhere. But the PGA Tour bans LIV players for at least one year dating to their last LIV appearance, and now the European tour is demanding them to pick a tour.

AP

World.title: Smith monitored for concussion after hit to helmet while batting
World.content:
Australia will continue to test Steve Smith for a delayed concussion, after the vice-captain's blow to the head added further questions around the side for the second Test.

Smith did not take the field on day four in Durban, after being struck on the side of the helmet by a short ball from South African speedster Anrich Nortje while batting in the morning session.

The 37-year-old was assessed on the field and passed a test, appearing unfazed as he reached 27 in Australia's pursuit of quick runs.

Steve Smith copped a blow on the helmet early in his innings. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

However, Australia opted to keep him off the field in case there had been a concussion, and conduct further tests. As of stumps, Smith had not failed any.

He is expected to be tested again on Tuesday morning in Durban, and will continue to be assessed for as long as Australia sees fit.

Smith has previously battled concussions, most famously when he was struck in the head by Jofra Archer during the 2019 Ashes.

While the early signs are good, any concussion would leave Smith in serious doubt for Sunday's second Test in Gqeberha given the tiered-return protocols.

It would also add to the quandary around the make-up of Australia's side for that match.

Josh Inglis is back in South Africa after his fractured finger, batting in the nets wearing a splint on Monday and offering every sign he will be available for Sunday.

Cameron Green is also recovering from an abdominal strain, and not yet ruled out of the second Test.

Either of the pair would likely have batted at number five in this Test if fit, but Matt Renshaw's scores of 190 and 82 have made the case for him to stay there.

AAP

World.title: Live: Kangaroos swing second trade after landing Blakey in blockbuster
World.content:
Regardless of Tassie concessions, what's the vibe on the talent level of next years draft class? - Luke

(Getty Images)

It's actually shaping up as a really strong draft next year. Which makes it all the more frustrating at how obliterated it is going to be with Tasmania, father-son and academy picks.

First of all, Tassie have already signed seven players who otherwise would have been top draft prospects. They include Baxter Sruk (pictured), Axel Walsh and Jake Miller, all of whom would have been right at the very top of most club's boards.

Then you've got the likes of Louis Salopek and Zemes Pilot, two more guns who are tied to Port Adelaide through academy or father-son systems. Then there's Koby Bewick, another top prospect tied to Essendon via father-son.

So you take a strong crop, remove seven of the best players from it 12 months out, take another three or four out to academy and father-son bidding, then give Tasmania seven of the top 13 picks, with only a few to be traded away.

Clubs are running scared.

World.title: Cyclist who ditched Australia withdrawn from world champs over allegations
World.content:
British track cyclist Matthew Richardson, who defected from Australian cycling at the end of the Paris Games, has been withdrawn from this week's UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai

Richardson had been earlier named in the British squad for the championships, which run from October 14 to 18, before British Cycling confirmed he had been withdrawn.

"British Cycling can confirm that Matt Richardson has been withdrawn from the Great Britain Cycling Team squad for the upcoming 2026 Tissot UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai, China," a spokesperson said in a statement provided to Reuters.

The governing body did not give a reason for Richardson's withdrawal.

The Times reported that Richardson had been removed from the team amid an investigation into "alleged discriminatory posts and behaviour".

Reuters has not independently verified the allegations, and has contacted Rocket Sports, Richardson's management agency, for comment from the rider.

Richardson was injured in a crash during the World Series keirin event in Japan and was ruled out from making his highly anticipated England debut at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow in July.

Richardson was born in Maidstone, England, and moved to Australia at the age of nine.

A week after the closing ceremony of the Paris Games — where Richardson won silver medals in the individual sprint and men's keirin and a bronze in the team sprint — he stunned Australia by announcing his defection.

In 2025, Richardson became the first rider to break nine seconds for the "flying 200m", setting a new time of 8.941 seconds.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Refusing to yield momentum, ruthless Australia is perfectly set for victory
World.content:
Momentum, most agree, is among the most elusive psychological phenomena in professional sport. How to obtain and maintain the positive kind? How exactly to halt and reverse its opposite?

For three and a half days of this Durban Test, since Matt Renshaw began calmly pulling Australia's first innings out of the fire and seizing the game's initiative, Australia has stubbornly maintained control. South Africa, haphazardly, has failed to regain it.

Renshaw's dream Test continues Matt Renshaw claims his maiden Test wicket to help Australia reduce South Africa to 4-102 at stumps on day four of the first Test in Durban.

Early on day four, Renshaw made a further mockery of the difficulties that have curtailed the progress of every other batter in this game — so far, none from either team has managed so much as a half-century — and belted 82 more precious runs in even time.

More absurdly still, as shadows covered the Kingsmead pitch late on day four, the burly Queenslander ripped one of his unheralded off-spinners out of the rough and removed Temba Bavuma, capping a horror game in which the Proteas skipper has been unable to buy a run and incapable of engineering the moments of inspiration his opposite number constantly pulls from his hat.

Could Bavuma have done much to drastically alter what has transpired here? Other than by contributing his usual runs, probably not.

He certainly can't grab the ball himself and rip through a middle-order batsman, as Pat Cummins did to Tristan Stubbs within sight of stumps.

Nor can Bavuma and his teammates always play out of their skins, above expectations, beyond their limitations, which has been the impossible task South Africa has pulled off, to the betterment of Test cricket, in the last two years.

That the home side enters the final day 319 runs in arrears with six wickets in hand is a testament to the chain of events a single player can set in motion, as Renshaw has in this game.

Only a few forced errors prevented Australia calling it a perfect day: looking less like a Test opener by the day, Travis Head fell cheaply again; thanks to a fast, frightful bouncer from the indefatigable Anrich Nortje, Steve Smith is being assessed under concussion protocols, which may imperil his selection for the second Test, although it did not stop him from using an iPad to assess the catching chances he missed out on as he sat in the pavilion.

Steve Smith copped a blow on the helmet early in his innings. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Basically everything else about Australia's gung-ho approach worked out. To set a target as imposing as 421, they rattled along at 4.65 runs an over in the first session and a spirit-sapping 6.36 in the second, each batsman more enthusiastic than the last to attack at all costs.

Nic Maddinson clubbed an entertaining 46 to establish the launching pad. Smith and Marnus Labuschagne wound back the clock with a typically hyperactive partnership, the latter reaffirming the sense he has turned the corner, towards big runs. Renshaw reprised his peak Matthew Hayden routine, toying with the South African bowlers. Even Beau Webster, previously out of sorts, made fluent runs too and could be permitted some frustration that the declaration halted his spree.

Cummins, in a contrasting cameo to his first innings vigil, hammered 32 from 12 deliveries, bombing Simon Harmer for a string of sixes that left South Africa dejected and dashed any remaining hope the off-spinner held of selection in the second Test.

The final effect of the Australian batting effort was something like a WCW tag team taking turns flying off the ropes with elbows extended.

All that now stands between Australia and certain victory is the solitary excellence of Aiden Markram, who always saves his best for Australia and finished the day undefeated on 45.

In the corresponding Test eight years ago, when the Cape Town fiasco was still on the horizon, Markram's epic century delayed Australia's victory in almost identical circumstances.

If the day was characterised by one team doing a bunch of things far better than its opponent, special mention must go to Josh Hazlewood for not just the most classically Hazlewoodian stat line — eight overs, three maidens, 2-20 — but for nipping out David Bedingham for 46, thus ending a 66-run second-wicket partnership with Markram that shaped as South Africa's last realistic chance of getting close.

Are Australians complacent about the unassuming New South Welshman and his mountains of wickets? Do we underestimate the problem it poses to batsmen when a 196cm giant releases a heavy ball from that kind of stratospheric trajectory, lifting length balls into their ribs? How much harder is that to handle when, at the other end, the skipper skids it through lower, attacking the off stump from a different angle?

Probably it is the closest thing in the present era to what batsmen encountered four decades ago when Malcolm Marshall and Joel Garner combined to devastating effect for the golden-era West Indies.

Another good thing South Africa has given Test cricket in recent years is the guarantee of a result: not a single encounter there in the past decade has ended in a draw. Long may it be so.

World.title: Quick hits: Cummins goes big as Maddinson makes manic cameo
World.content:
Pat Cummins's explosive knock pushes Australia clear, Keshav Maharaj produces some magic in his follow-through and Steve Smith doesn't join his teammates in the field.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Maddinson's manic start

Maddinson picked up where he left off. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Nic Maddinson hooked the first ball of the innings for four, so it was no surprise that he got a move on when day four began with Australia needing quick runs to set up a victory.

He hit two boundaries in his first three balls faced, but both were off the edge. Then, after watching opening partner Travis Head chip a tame shot to mid-on, Maddinson decided to force the issue.

Through cover, down to third man, back over the bowler … the controversially selected 34-year-old made a real statement as he raced to within one shot of a maiden half-century.

But it came to an end on 48 off 38 balls when Anrich Nortje uprooted his middle and leg stumps with a searing yorker.

A famous Test inning? Perhaps not, but a career high likely to earn him another chance to prolong his strange Test career.

2. Maharaj's bizarre juggling take

Maharaj surprised himself with his bizarre juggling effort. (Fox Cricket)

With Matt Rensaw having pushed into the 80s and looking destined for a second century for the match, it felt like the South Africans were in need of something extraordinary to dismiss the Queenslander.

And although not quite a work of art, Keshav Maharaj's diving return catch was certainly out of the ordinary.

With Renshaw having chipped one back towards the bowler, the finger spinner did well to get down in his follow-through, before juggling the ball once, twice, taking his eye of the cherry, and ultimately securing it in his palm while lying on the turf.

He looked as surprised as anyone to have taken the catch, which was confirmed after a lengthy review by the TV umpire.

3. Cummins's late cameo

Pat Cummins made a quickfire cameo. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Australia was surprisingly circumspect during the middle session, with Matt Renshaw and Beau Webster doing little more than keeping the scoreboard ticking over.

Pat Cummins clearly had no plans to declare on Renshaw when he had a second ton for the match in the offing, but when Renshaw was caught out, the captain took it on himself to up the tempo.

He wasted little time attacking the spin of Simon Harmer, smacking his fourth ball for six over long-on and adding three more in his next four deliveries from the off-spinner before declaring on 6-314 having clattered 32 off 12 to take his team to a 420-run lead.

4. Smith sidelined

Steve Smith injured his finger as he took a catch on day three and copped a blow to the helmet on day four. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Steve Smith's slips catching changed the game on day three but soon after Cummins's declaration it became clear he would not have the same impact on day four.

Smith stayed in the pavilion when the Australian team took to the field for South Africa's run chase on account of a sharp blow he copped to the helmet from an Anrich Nortje bouncer while batting.

He carried on to 27 before holing out, but the after-effects of that head knock appeared to keep him sidelined.

He also hurt his finger taking the catch that ended South Africa's first innings, which could have caused issues in the slips.

5. Renshaw's dream Test continues

Comfortably the top scorer in the match, Matt Renshaw added his maiden Test wicket late on day four. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Matt Renshaw couldn't have dreamt it better.

With shadows lengthening in Durban, and with South Africa's innings threatening to steady, Australia's freshly minted golden boy was thrown the ball.

South Africa captain Temba Bavuma had faced 18 balls for his one run and was set on seeing his team to stumps, but he was unable to contend with the drift and turn of Renshaw's part-time off spin, the Queenslander drawing the batter forward and having him caught at short leg by a diving Maddinson.

Renshaw was mobbed by his teammates as he celebrated his maiden Test wicket and Australia marched on to be six wickets from victory at stumps on day four.

That came after the southpaw had once again led Australia's efforts with the bat, peeling off 82 to add to the 190 he made in the first innings.

Remarkably, Renshaw remains the only player to pass 50 in the match.

World.title: Wallabies admit they 'faced the music' after harrowing All Blacks loss
World.content:
It was brutal, but the Wallabies knew they had to confront the reality of Saturday night's defeat to the All Blacks sooner rather than later.

"The group came together Sunday morning, faced the music a little bit," Wallabies fullback Tom Wright said in Sydney on Monday.

By "music", Wright was referring to the 50-19 scoreline dished out by the All Blacks at Eden Park, which meant their hold of the Bledisloe Cup will stretch into a 24th consecutive year.

Having made a promising start to narrowly trail 17-14 at half-time, the Wallabies were blown away in the second term.

Wallabies thrashed by All Blacks The Wallabies are outclassed by a rampant All Blacks outfit at Eden Park, with the home side retaining the Bledisloe Cup for yet another year.

The All Blacks shifted gears after the break, scoring five tries to one as they added another chapter to the Wallabies' dismal history at Eden Park.

The Wallabies have not defeated the All Blacks at their spiritual home since 1986.

The result also brought the Wallabies' six-match unbeaten run to an end, after their recent form created hope they could snap their Auckland losing streak.

"No-one wants to be on the receiving end of 50 points and no-one wants to be on the receiving end of a loss," Wright said.

"But at 17-14, we were right in the contest.

"The game was there to be taken. We squandered a couple of chances."

The All Blacks have held the Bledisloe Cup since 2003. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Among those opportunities was a line-out throw deep inside All Blacks territory early in the second half.

The All Blacks chose not to contest the line-out as they prepared to counter a driving maul.

Instead, the Wallabies wasted an ideal attacking platform and the chance to claim the lead by giving away a penalty at the set-piece, allowing the All Blacks to exit their 22.

The home side proceeded to move play down field, resulting in Cam Roigard's 48th-minute try.

"It's a game of moments," Wright said.

"We earned opportunities to get close to their line really early in the second half.

"We weren't disciplined enough to execute a play and that was right down on their try line.

"We were pleased with how we started the second half and then there was a snowball effect of moments."

Wright noted the All Blacks "physically imposed themselves" during the match while also dominating one of the key battlegrounds: contestable kicks.

The All Blacks retained possession from eight of their 11 contestable kicks, with Roigard particularly effective from scrum half.

All six of the contestable kicks he launched were retrieved.

The All Blacks dominated the aerial battle against the Wallabies. (Getty images: Fiona Goodall)

The Wallabies could not compete with the All Blacks in this part of the game, despite having aerial threats such as wingers Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Max Jorgensen.

They enjoyed the upper hand in contestable kicks when they defeated the world champion Springboks 42-38 in Perth late last month.

"We saw that the ABs were able to apply pressure the same way we've done previously," Wright said.

Back on Australian soil, the Wallabies have shifted their attention to Saturday's return Test against the All Blacks at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

The Bledisloe Cup may not be at stake, but the Wallabies' pride is on the line as they look to end a 12-Test losing run against their trans-Tasman rivals.

With the post-match review of the Eden Park defeat done and dusted, Wright maintained the Wallabies were moving forward.

"I certainly don't think there's any mental scars," Wright said.

Tech.title: The Social Reckoning is flopping at the box office
Tech.content:
As important as some of the messages in The Social Reckoning are, the movie has been drastically underperforming at the box office. Per Variety , Aaron’s Sorkin’s follow up to The Social Network only grossed a measly $5.5 million this past weekend against a budget that’s somewhere within the $30–42 million range. That would make it a certifiable flop that’s costing Columbia Pictures (and Sony) quite a bit of money — especially when you compare it to The Social Network’s $22 million opening.

This isn’t entirely surprising given how middling reviews for the film have been. It’s currently got a 55% rating on Rotten Tomatoes and has widely been trashed on social media. All of this might be reflective of audiences hoping for a proper sequel to The Social Network, which won three Oscars for its screenplay (written by Sorkin), editing, and score. But it might speak to people not fully clicking with Mikey Madison’s performance as whistleblower Frances Haugen or Jeremy Allen White’s turn as Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz. (Madison, for her part, indicated to The Hollywood Reporter that it was Sorkin’s vision as director that kept from “authentically and faithfully represent[ing] a real person,” which she hopes to do in the future.) It also probably didn’t help that Jesse Eisenberg — who portrayed Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network — had no interest in being in the film, according to Sorkin himself.

Tech.title: Meta has some Wonder Full new AI models
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta is making up for lost time in the AI race. After launching Muse Spark, the first model from its revamped Superintelligence Labs division, and buzzy AI agent Muse, it’s now launching two new models it claims can go toe-to-toe with the industry’s best.

The new models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, are available for Muse Code subscribers starting today. Wonder can also be accessed through the Meta Model API, Meta said.

Meta says it eventually plans to power its Muse AI agent with Wonder, starting with subscribers, and will develop specialized models it “can bring to everyone using Muse.” It hasn’t shared specifics or provided a timeline for either.

The company says its new models can rival leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, including GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1, pointing to results from internal testing on several industry benchmarks. It’s unclear how they stack up against Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, whose capabilities are still coming into focus.

The launches are part of Meta’s aggressive push to reestablish itself as a major force in AI. The company has poured billions into talent and infrastructure and has been steadily expanding its AI lineup, including with image model Muse Image and a heavy focus on bringing useful AI agents to the masses through Muse.

Tech.title: Elon Musk has donated over $276 million to Republican midterm efforts
Tech.content:
is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Elon Musk has handed out at least $276 million to Republican groups since July, The New York Times reports, making him both the party’s top known donor and the biggest established midterm donor. $158 million of that money — one of the largest political donations in American history — has been funneled into the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC that aims to secure and maintain a Republican Senate majority. Among others, it’s fighting to retain the party’s Senate seat in Texas, which serves as a major hub for Musk’s business empire.

He’s also donated over $76 million to America PAC, a super PAC Musk founded in 2024 that canvasses for hard-to-reach Republican voters. Smaller amounts have also been given to other conservative groups, including:

$20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund super PAC for House Republicans

$10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, supporting Ken Paxton’s Senate Seat bid in Texas

$10 million to the Republican Governors Association

$2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association

The roughly $366 million that Musk has donated to federal committees over the entire 2025-26 election cycle is significantly higher than the $290 million he gave out in 2024 to help President Trump return to office, when he pledged to spend “around $45 million a month.” That’s despite Musk announcing in May last year that “In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future.” He’s consistently failed to stick to that promise so far.

Tech.title: The Yandex outage probably didn’t blitz Russian bots
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Multiple Ukrainian drone strikes over the last week have taken Russian data centers offline and reportedly caused online bot traffic to plummet — but in reality it’s probably not the kind of bot activity most people associate with Russia.

A chart citing Cloudflare data has been circulating around social media platforms, showing a sharp decline in bot traffic following attacks on Yandex servers — a technology company often described as “Russia’s Google.” While many people are inferring that the chart refers to bot farms that push disinformation, conspiracy theories, and other harmful content across online platforms, reputed troll farm exposer antibot4navalny says the data “has nothing to do with social media.”

Many of the charts are sourcing from this Cloudflare data, which is specific to Yandex service activity. Image: Cloudflare

In a thread on X, antibot4navalny says the chart is actually measuring requests from automated Yandex web crawlers. These bots have broad uses, so while they can be used maliciously to hack user accounts and target people with spam, they’re also very commonly used to index websites for search engines and provide customer service support. The chart is also specific to Yandex-based traffic, and not bot activity from Russia at large — which remains largely unchanged around the data center attacks, according to Cloudflare.

Other charts have also been shared that show the same alleged decline in Russian disinformation bot activity. One such diagram was shared on X by European Parliament member Tomáš Zdechovský, who claimed that online activity around the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) political party plummeted following the Russian data center attacks.

Computer scientist Raphael Wimmer says he suspects the source diagram shared by Zdechovský is AI-generated, pointing out several inconsistencies with the activity timeline it’s supposedly tracking, including a data point logged for a future date: October 15th. The image appears to have first been posted by Threads user Robin Schlingheider. The data’s source isn’t established, and the original doesn’t include any reference to Germany’s AfD party. Wimmer says Schlingheider has evaded his questions about where the image originated.

“Could we (and especially politicians, journalists and scientists who should know better) please stop sharing unverified images?” Wimmer said.

Meanwhile, the vast majority of Yandex-operated systems still appear to be offline following the latest drone strike, including the Yandex Pay digital payment service, leaving users unable to transfer funds, check balances, or make purchases. Yandex Fintech head Dima Pirogov said in a statement (translated via Google) that “we can’t yet give you a precise restoration timeline, but we promise: we won’t stop until the service is restored.”

Tech.title: Mechanism’s first Switch 2 case is as awesome as I hoped it would be
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Most companies have slowed down releasing new Switch 2 cases, but one of my favorite accessory makers recently debuted its first, after a few delays. The $49 Basecase from Mechanism is a snap-on shell for the console that taps into the company’s modular lineup of mounts. You could already mount the Switch 2 in numerous ways with its $19 Basegrip (to your wall, to its Gaming Pillow, to a monitor arm, etc.). The difference is that this new product protects your console, makes its Joy-Con more comfortable to use, and has some interesting modularity.

The console shell allows for the full range of the Switch 2’s kickstand, and access to all of the ports, buttons, and fan vents. Notably, it fits more snugly than others I’ve tried because it clamps on near the console’s bottom USB-C port. This is a good thing. You can unlock its rear plate and replace it with a custom 3D-printed version for more fun and/or more utility. Mechanism sent over a couple of printed examples that hint at the possibilities — one that has Lego pegs on it for sticking on some minifigures, and another that has crannies for game cartridges.

The Basecase clips securely to prevent the rear plate from flexing when you mount and unmount it from Mechanism’s accessories. Each of the four included grips has a storage slot for a Switch game cartridge, which is a lovely touch.

The grips that slide onto the back of the Joy-Con protectors are modular, too. The set includes two sizes that add varying degrees of bulk, both of which make them more comfortable to use. Remove any of the grips, and there’s a spot for a game cartridge. It’s a fun way to bring extra physical games. Mechanism included some extra grip types that aren’t for sale to show what’s possible with a 3D printer. I really liked the pair that has a little shelf on each side to let your middle or ring fingers rest.

You can’t use the Switch 2 in its dock with the Basecase. So, Mechanism includes a dock adapter that takes a different approach — not necessarily better or worse — than Dbrand did with its Killswitch. Instead of cradling the Switch 2, it’s simply a female-to-male USB-C cable that you have to maneuver onto the dock’s video-out port. Installing it isn’t quite as easy as its marketing indicates, but I eventually got it working. Those who use a third-party USB-C dock from Jsaux or Genki won’t need to use this component.

This 3D-printed grip that Mechanism sent over made a night-and-day difference with my comfort while using the Switch 2 in handheld mode. Even though this looks precarious, the games are pretty snug in their storage section in this printed rear plate.

The Basecase seems designed to address multiple points of failure in earlier Switch 2 cases released by Dbrand, Genki, and others that unfortunately let some quality control issues slip in an effort to launch cases first when the Swtich 2 first debuted.

For instance, the Basecase’s Joy-Con grips have a little rubber lip that fits around the top of the controller’s inner colored section. Dbrand revised its comfy Killswitch grip to add this after some users noted their consoles tumbling to the ground when they grabbed it by the controller without supporting the Switch 2’s weight. The Basecase does a good job of preventing this issue.

Also important: the swappable Joy-Con grips attach easily, requiring almost no effort to line up the latch pins to snap on. I could never quite get the feel for the ones included with Genki’s Attack Vector case (we’ll see how Genki’s upcoming Grips fare). Also, while most thin, plastic cases from competitors exhibit ill-fitting sections or flex, the Basecase feels tougher.

If you’re bought into Mechanism’s ecosystem of mounts and have a Switch 2, there’s a good chance that you’ve been waiting for this release (and, perhaps, you already own this case). For gamers who haven’t yet tried out the company’s system of mounts, this is a really good place to start. You can grab all of the 3D printer files at Makerworld or Printables.

Photography by Cameron Faulkner/The Verge

Tech.title: Android is the best and worst thing about Googlebooks
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

My first week with the new Android-powered laptops has been about as rocky as anyone’s, but I’ve slowly learned to like them, even if love still feels a ways off. Every moment that’s impressed me has been thanks to Android, whether I’ve been accessing a native version of a useful app or quickly checking my phone notifications from the laptop user interface.

But man, sometimes it just sucks.

Phone connectivity is flaky, app casting is awkward, and file-sharing seems to be flat-out broken. And that’s just the interaction between a Googlebook and a phone — I have a whole other set of gripes about the limitations of native Android apps on a $1,000 laptop.

If Googlebooks ever become a success, Android is going to get the credit. But if it all goes wrong, that’s exactly where the blame will lie too. So far, success feels a lot further away than failure.

Getting started

During setup you can copy every app from your phone, or just a selection.

The Googlebook setup process is Android through-and-through. It’s similarly quick, just a few minutes from beginning to end, including time to register biometric logins, log into a Google account, and connect it to a phone to find your apps and backups. There’s a little variation in the exact setup between the Asus and HP models I’ve been testing, but mostly just whether it defaults to installing every app from your phone or only the desktop-optimized ones.

Things get janky once you’re into the OS, though. Even if you use an Android 17 phone to set up the laptop, it’s unlikely to remain connected afterwards for features like file sharing and app casting. Fully pairing either of my Googlebooks to a phone has required toggling cross-device settings on both devices, multiple restarts, and the occasional prayer, until the two devices find each other. Moving to a new Wi-Fi network broke things for me all over again, requiring a restart of the Googlebook to get the devices back talking to each other — and yes, they need to be on the same Wi-Fi network to talk, and to have Bluetooth enabled too, so the connection won’t work when you’re offline.

My Asus Googlebook has now formed a pretty reliable connection to an Oppo phone I’ve been reviewing, though it still refuses to recognize any other phones; my HP model flits between that Oppo and the Vivo X Fold 6, occasionally connecting to both at once. Yesterday, for the first time all week, it connected to my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, after both laptops had stubbornly ignored that phone for days — even though it’s Google’s own hardware.

Going native

Downloadable episodes! On a laptop! This low key might be my favorite thing about Googlebooks.

I’ve loved elements of the Googlebook experience. It’s great being able to access quick, compact, desktop versions of apps I’d normally be stuck using through a web browser on my MacBook. It’s even better that some of those apps have different functionality for being mobile versions: being able to download series from HBO Max or Netflix and watch them offline means a Googlebook could replace my Android tablet, which is mostly just a device for watching movies on planes at this point.

But many, many more apps are a headache to use on an Android laptop. Some don’t have desktop-optimized versions — the mobile version of Slack is truly unworkable in a desktop environment, and Adobe’s Android apps are pale shadows of their desktop selves. Others claim to be “Optimized for desktop” in the Play Store, but in practice that usually means they’ve stretched the UI to fit a desktop scale and included basic mouse and keyboard support — “basic” being the operative word, with most not recognizing right-clicks or occasionally shifting into a portrait view. “Made for desktop” seems to be the only Play Store tag that really counts for much, and I’ve only seen it on a handful of apps.

Some apps claim to be “Made for desktop,” everything else is likely to feel at least a little awkward.

Even Google’s own apps are often limited. Chrome is the worst offender, since you’re likely to use it so much. Google insists this is a desktop version of the browser, but it lacks feature parity with other platforms: there’s no support for switching profiles, opening tabs in a split view, or creating custom search engine shortcuts. Those are just the omissions I’ve run into from my daily MacBook workflow, and there are no doubt countless more.

And despite Google’s promise that Chromebooks offer the “entire Play Store library,” that isn’t entirely true. I’ve already run into two apps that I simply can’t install from the Play Store — Bluesky and the login authorization tool Okta. It’s not an Intel issue either, as Google alluded to on Monday: the Arm-based HP Googlebook also won’t run either app.

My laptop needs aren’t complex: I spend 90 percent of my time on my work MacBook Air inside Chrome and Slack, and most of the rest in Photoshop or Lightroom. But all four are subpar on a Googlebook right now, and it’s all because they’re fundamentally Android apps that can’t compete with true desktop alternatives.

Casting confusion

If Android apps on your laptop aren’t enough, Googlebooks also let you cast the Android apps on your phone to your laptop.

A dedicated app drawer shows everything installed on your connected phone.

Some version of Android app casting or mirroring has been around before on both Windows and Chromebooks. The difference in Google’s implementation is that instead of mirroring the whole phone UI, you cast specific apps, either through a dedicated app drawer in the taskbar or by tapping into a synced notification from your phone. Those apps still run on the phone itself — which gets a notification that an app is casting — but are controlled via the PC.

It’s not well-suited to streaming music or video, or running multiple apps at once, but that doesn’t seem to be the intent anyway. Where casting shines is in quickly dipping into an app without reaching for your phone and unlocking it, like updating a payment in the settlement app Splitwise or sending a quick message in WhatsApp. I’ve really enjoyed being able to dive in and out of a phone task from my laptop, while minimizing the risk of getting distracted by Instagram.

Casting is clever and mostly works well, but I think I’ve found it useful because I’m new to the Googlebook and haven’t set every app up yet. Google argues it’s designed for apps you might want to use from your laptop but wouldn’t want to install there, but that’s a pretty short list, especially given that installing an Android app is generally quick, painless, and a minimal drain on storage. Long-term, I’m not sure how often I’d want to cast a mobile app when I could just install a native version, especially since you can’t copy and paste between native apps and cast versions, or access the Googlebook file system when casting.

Casting Bluesky from the phone just doesn’t work, made worse because the Bluesky app is unavailable for Googlebooks otherwise.

Even when the cross-device connection runs smoothly, some apps — especially secure ones like my authorization app or banking app — won’t run. Others try to open but don’t work: my credit card app breaks on bootup, while Bluesky renders text illegibly. Casting some apps even create rendering issues when I next open them back on the actual phone.

The rest is a mess too

Then there are the other problems.

Continue On lets you start a task on your phone and pick it up on the Googlebook. It’s great when it works, but that’s rare. Only a handful of apps are supported, and even those trigger inconsistently. It works when I open a Google Drive document, but only sporadically in Gmail, and so far never for Calendar.

Notifications are powerful, but messy, with phone and laptop notifications mixed together. Phone notifications open via app casting, but the system gets confused easily. For various reasons, right now my Slack notifications open a casted phone app rather than the native Googlebook app; WhatsApp notifications don’t come through even from my phone; and I can either get notifications for my work Gmail account or my personal one, but not both at once.

File transfer is entirely broken. While I can see my phone’s storage as a drive inside the file manager, accessing those files is near-impossible. It can take minutes to load up the file system, and minutes more to open or transfer a single 5MB photo. It’s completely unusable. This should be fixable, at least. Quick Share — Android’s equivalent to AirDrop — is also supported, and the same files that take minutes over file transfer share in seconds with Quick Share.

This is what I usually see when I try to open an image from my phone’s file system. And if I want to copy a file to the laptop, I get to watch this progress bar for a few minutes.

It’s the Googlebook in a nutshell: the idea is wonderful, the execution entirely lacking. A week in, I’m learning to work around the kinks and headaches of this odd little OS, finding ways to make the most of it and to maximize those moments when my laptop and my phone just work together. When it clicks, it feels like the payoff to a decade and a half of using Android every day.

Right now, that feeling doesn’t hit nearly as often as it needs to, and certainly not enough to make up for the countless times Android just feels broken in this form factor. The question is whether Google — a company with a deserved reputation for giving up when the going gets tough — has the commitment to see this through and turn things around. It’ll need its own teams to fix what’s broken, third-party developers to pledge support en masse, and a rethink of how to integrate native apps with casting from a phone.

When I first saw the Googlebooks a few weeks ago, I really thought one might be my next laptop. After spending a week with them, I’m not so sure. I certainly wouldn’t buy a Googlebook as they are right now, but I wouldn’t rule out an Android laptop in the future — the execution just needs to catch up to the idea.

Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

Tech.title: No Man’s Sky is coming to the iPhone and iPad
Tech.content:
The No Man’s Sky universe is about to get a little bit smaller — but in a good way. Hello Games announced that its long-running sci-fi exploration game will be coming to iOS, with versions for both the iPhone and iPad available starting on October 28th.

According to Hello’s Sean Murray, the mobile version of the game is essentially the full No Man’s Sky experience. “I guess I should say this is not No Man’s Sky Lite,” he wrote in a blog post. It includes all of the game’s many, many updates that have come out since launch — like the gigantic Voyagers expansion from last year — and the only major features missing will be multiplayer and the planetary settlements. Murray likens the iOS version to when the game initially launched on the original Switch. “On Switch we have listened to players and built from there, including with a much expanded version on Switch 2,” he says. “Based on feedback and player numbers we will support iOS in a similar way.”

The game will be playable on the iPhone 11 and 3rd generation iPad Air and above, and the studio says that the download comes in at a surprisingly scant 5GB. It also has newly-designed touch controls, as well as support for controllers, screen casting, and mouse-and-keyboard on the iPad. Murray also notes that “Perhaps most importantly we’ve put tons of work into battery life and thermodynamics, and we’re super proud that No Man’s Sky can be enjoyed for really long comfortable play sessions.” It’ll be “free to try” at launch, though it’s not clear how much the full version will cost.

It’s now been a decade since No Man’s Sky first launched, and the game has changed dramatically since its debut. iOS will be joining a huge list of supported platforms, including Mac, PC, and essentially every modern console, and there’s also a VR version available. Just as significant, Hello has continued to keep the game vibrant with a constant stream of free expansions, including the recent Cosmos update in September, which fleshed out the vast expanse of space with more things to explore.

Tech.title: The OnePlus 16 is the company’s most interesting phone in years
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Today the OnePlus 16 launched in China, the company’s first flagship phone since quitting both the US and European markets this summer. As luck would have it, it also looks like the company’s best phone in some time.

Like most OnePlus phones, the 16 is positioned around performance, with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, and up to 1TB of storage and 16GB of RAM. That’s backed up by an enormous 9,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, one of the biggest seen in any Android flagship yet. 100W wired and 50W wireless charging complete the power setup.

On the display front, the phone jumps to a 185Hz OLED panel for the first time. That’ll not only be used for 185fps gaming in compatible titles, but can also run at up to 165Hz throughout the system UI — a first for high refresh rate panels like this.

Image: OnePlus

Even the cameras, not usually OnePlus’ strong suit, have had a meaningful upgrade. The main camera has a higher resolution (200 megapixels), larger sensor (1/1.4-inch-type), and faster aperture (f/1.4) than the OnePlus 15’s. That should help, given we found that phone’s camera had frustrating “imitations in low light.” 50-megapixel ultrawide and telephoto cameras round out the rear trio, and the latter also enjoys a big bump to a 1/1.95-inch sensor.

Image: OnePlus

There’s a design flourish too, with the phone’s silver finish including LED lighting that features a big “16” and what the company claims is a set of galactic coordinates. While the shapes of the lights are fixed, they’ll reportedly flash with different rhythms to notify you of calls, messages, battery level, and more.

The OnePlus 16 is available in China starting from ¥5,699 (about $850). With OnePlus no longer in either the US or Europe, there’s no hope of a launch for the 16 in either market.

Tech.title: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder
Tech.content:
Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model.

Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.

According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

“Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads.

That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5.

Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent.

In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”

To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark, which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.

“We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch.

The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year. Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.

According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio, which came online earlier this year.

Tech.title: WindBorne wins a hefty US Air Force contract for its balloon data
Tech.content:
The U.S. Air Force will buy data collected by WindBorne Systems‘ fleet of autonomous weather balloons under a new contract that could be worth nearly $50 million to the startup.

WindBorne currently has about 700 weather balloons flying around the globe, collecting atmospheric sensor readings that the company sells to customers and also feeds into its own AI weather forecasting model. WindBorne, founded in 2015 and based in Redwood City, California, is one of the first organizations to directly feed empirical data into a deep-learning weather model.

The company has worked closely with the U.S. government, particularly the National Weather Service and the U.S. Air Force and Navy, but this is the single-largest contract the company has participated in. The contract is worth up to $49 million, but the Air Force pays only as it needs data. It can place orders for specific regions at specific times. So far, it has ordered $1.7 million worth, and executives expect more orders to follow.

“This is largely a vehicle through which continued growth of the constellation can be supported, as well as some work on research and development to continue to improve the hardware and performance of the balloons,” WindBorne co-founder and CTO Andrey Sushko told TechCrunch. He added that the contract, which was awarded without competitive bidding, is “a determination by the government that for this capability of collecting global data, we were the only company able to provide it in the way that met their needs for these operations.”

WindBorne CEO John Dean told TechCrunch in August that the company had raised a $37 million Series B round to continue scaling its business. Earlier this summer, the company released the latest version of its forecasting model, WeatherMesh 6, which it says provides more accurate forecasts than the traditional model run by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which simulates the atmosphere using the laws of physics.

Since the arrival of transformer model architectures and the ECMWF’s release of a massive weather dataset a few years ago, AI weather forecasting has become one of the more productive uses of deep-learning technology. Meteorologists previously relied on expensive supercomputers running detailed equations that approximate how the atmosphere behaves. Now, end-to-end learning can ingest decades of weather data and issue predictions more quickly.

Models built by frontier labs and government agencies are proving more accurate than traditional forecasts, although it is still a jagged frontier, with both types of forecasts required to enable useful understanding of the weather. Google DeepMind’s latest weather model offers important new capabilities, and its cyclone forecasting tools are becoming increasingly central to how the U.S. government responds to hurricane season.

In August WindBorne became the first organization to send an unpowered flight system — one with no engine — to collect data in the eye of a typhoon. The company maneuvers its balloons by adjusting their altitude, bleeding air, or dropping sand carried as ballast, to send the vehicles into winds that take them where they need to go.

“That’s a pretty novel step, and the two ingredients for that are one, having good wind and weather models, and knowing how to navigate them; and two, having a large enough constellation that you have balloons in the right places,” Sushko said. “It’s one of the first times that a deep-learning model was used for actual operational decisions.”

Tech.title: Honeyjar offers AI tools to improve PR and comms at every company
Tech.content:
Journalists, entrepreneurs, and even some public relations professionals will tell you that the PR process is broken (buy me a drink sometime, and I’ll give you my rant). But could AI actually make things better?

Honeyjar, which will be attending this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt as part of the Startup Battlefield 200, wants to use AI to make the expertise and judgment of the best PR pros available to everyone, including founders who have no idea where to start.

The startup’s founders, CEO Michelle Masek and CCO Nadia Jamshidi, certainly fit the bill when it comes to PR expertise. They’ve both spent decades in the field, doing in-house communications and working at agencies. Masek recently served as senior vice president of marketing and communications for Ev Williams’ venture firm, Obvious Ventures.

As Masek described the challenges involved in “helping with the why and when of comms and marketing for 110 portfolio companies” (the startups her firm had invested in), I flashed back to my own brief stint leading marketing at an early-stage VC firm, where founders were constantly asking for help getting into TechCrunch. So I wasn’t surprised that Masek found herself asking, “Is there a way to scale the senior-level expertise into AI [in a way] that actually helps users do the work of comms in the proactive and skilled way that we do?”

Honeyjar is her answer to that question. It automates processes like writing announcements, finding the best journalists to pitch, and identifying the most promising speaking opportunities. But Jamshidi told me in a follow-up email that Honeyjar’s vision goes beyond getting press coverage and beyond specific AI tools.

“Honeyjar can find reporters, build media lists, scan news and social, track coverage, and surface opportunities,” she said. “Those capabilities are important, but they’re just one piece of what we’re building. The bigger idea is bringing the whole communications workflow together: signals, context, strategy, judgment, timing, and execution.”

And it’s not just for founders. Masek said she’s come to realize there are “millions and millions of unassigned communicators responsible for the work of comms.”

“They don’t have the title of comms, but they’re marketers, investors, authors, creators, school superintendents, sports team leaders,” she added. “It’s incredibly horizontal, this need to nail strategic communications. It’s always passed around, but the problems are very often not solved.”

Image Credits:Honeyjar

Nor is Honeyjar trying to replace PR professionals. Masek said she and Jamshidi built the tool they wanted to use themselves. She argued that Honeyjar can make PR firms and in-house comms teams more effective, while allowing individual PR practitioners to “take on that third client without any scaling cost.”

When Honeyjar opened its waitlist, it received 10,000 signups in the first 24 hours, said Masek. Beta testers include Nextdoor, tech startup Coco Robotics, investor Bloomberg Beta, and agencies Mission North and Full Picture.

That sounds promising for companies looking to get more attention, but it could be a nightmare for journalists. We receive more pitches than we can respond to, many of them already written by AI chatbots.

When I raised my fears about getting inundated with even more PR slop, Masek noted that while Honeyjar can draft a pitch email or a social media post in the customer’s voice, the customer actually has to hit send or publish.

“We never want a world where the human is removed from the loop,” she said.

And that’s also where judgment is key. Masek said she and Jamshidi tried to “infuse and encode Honeyjar with our wisdom.” Through a broader initiative called the Comms Lab, they’re now training the product on the judgment of other PR pros as well.

“For us, judgment is knowing what to do, what not to do, when to act, and how to adapt to the situation,” Jamshidi added. “That comes from understanding a company’s goals and priorities, what’s happening inside and outside the organization, and knowing what to say, to whom, where, and when.”

In some cases, Masek said Honeyjar might even tell a founder that they’re simply not ready for coverage.

“We hear from reporters all the time who want better pitches, who want to hear from experts directly,” she said. “We actually see a future where there are more credible pitches in your inbox from sources who you actually want to hear from.”

Tech.title: Microsoft president says UK is best placed to drive AI regulation
Tech.content:
Microsoft president Brad Smith is calling for urgent regulation of AI, and his argument is that consumer products like milk and washing machines have more oversight than the companies building artificial intelligence.

On a recent BBC podcast, Smith called AI both a “weapon and a tool” that is putting the world’s cybersecurity at risk and said the “moment has arrived” to institute global safety rules.

Smith also said the U.K., and not the U.S. or European Union, is best placed to lead on global safety rules. Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI), launched in 2023, receives access to major models from U.S. frontier labs before they are deployed and has quickly become a leader in AI safety testing.

That role has been under threat in recent weeks, with U.S. president Donald Trump warning against “globalist” organizations, which he claims are interfering with American companies. Last month, he reportedly asked Anthropic and OpenAI to withhold new models from British testers, but AISI confirmed on Monday that it is able to access and test the latest models.

Despite the president’s pushback, however, Smith argued the U.K. can regulate AI in ways that the U.S. cannot.

“In Washington, D.C., people don’t look at the U.K. and they don’t look at London the way they look at Brussels,” he told the BBC. “That’s a strength.”

His comments come amid rallying cries from tech leaders, including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, to slow the pace of AI development in the wake of several incidents where AI agents went rogue.

Last month, Trump hosted tech leaders of companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, AMD, SpaceX, Meta, and Google, at the White House to discuss AI safety. They signed a “morally binding” document in which they agreed to work with “independent auditors” to assess the safety and capabilities of their AI models.

Smith says the document is a “good step,” but it stops short of the type of regulation that is necessary. The problem with voluntary self-regulation, he said, is that only the “good companies” will comply.

“It’s the companies that are not as responsible that you need to worry about,” he said.

Smith outlined several AI safety rules he’d like to see put into place, like a legal obligation to alert an organization if its system was breached by rogue AI agents. He also appears to be in favor of AI labs getting the approval of outside evaluators before an AI product is released and spoke positively about kill switches to pause or slow down AI if humans lose control of it.

“Let’s speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together,” Smith said. “I hope that’s the role we can play as a company. I hope that’s the role the U.K. can play as a country.”

Tech.title: This AI startup says it can generate permit-ready blueprints in minutes
Tech.content:
Nearly two decades ago, a young college student wrote his final thesis about software capable of generating design documents for school buildings. Al Dram was studying architecture — following in the footsteps of his parents and grandfather — but it was technology that really intrigued him.

There was just one problem: The technology his idea required didn’t exist yet.

“Then ChatGPT came along,” said Dram, recalling when OpenAI released the generative AI chatbot that uses large language models (LLMs) in November 2022.

His old idea suddenly seemed a lot more possible. Within six months, he launched the concept of Blueprints AI, a startup that uses AI to produce code-compliant and permit-ready architectural construction blueprints in minutes from a 2D sketch or PDF.

Blueprints AI, which Dram officially incorporated in 2025 in Santa Monica with co-founder Coco Cao, was selected for the 2026 Startup Battlefield 200, a cohort of promising early-stage startups that have earned a spot to exhibit at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place this week from October 13 to 15 in San Francisco.

During that 20-year lead-up to Blueprints AI, Dram earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in architecture from the University of Tehran and completed two years of PhD coursework on digital design at the European Graduate School in Switzerland. He moved to the United States and opened an architecture firm in 2018 called Drams Design-Build. Then, after obtaining a general contractor’s license, he added a construction business in 2021.

Dram should have been satisfied. He wasn’t.

“I was saying, okay, maybe I can build new projects that change people’s life in that area, but it wouldn’t be a big impact,” he said. “What makes me very excited about technology is the impact, the hours saved, the energy saved of people doing the same thing over and over and over.”

Blueprints AI will unveil a more capable second-generation version of its software at Disrupt. Dram and Cao say it will make a big impact because it takes over the repetitive drafting work that fills most of an architect’s day.

“It will make better spaces for people because now architects have the time to design,” said Dram. He said architects spend about 80% of their time on drafting and only 20% on design. “I want to flip that to be 20-80.”

Dram and Cao met at an AI conference several years ago and combined their skills to build the company. Cao, a data scientist from Hong Kong, handles sales and go-to-market strategy as chief commercial officer.

The pair trained their models using eight years of approved drawing sets from Dram’s design and construction firm, which is still in business.

Its first-generation software produces architectural construction documents and costs between $3,200 and $8,500 a month, depending on the plan. Custom pricing for enterprises is also available.

The startup’s second-generation software will deliver a considerable upgrade. Customers can start with a description or sketch of a project and create blueprints for every aspect of a building at once, including architecture, structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and interior design. Version 2 allows users to design and make changes to the project, an upgrade over the first iteration. Importantly, one design change updates the entire project and is checked against local building codes.

Early customers are already using the second version, and Dram said it will become publicly available this week. The startup is already working on a third version of its software that will add in structural analysis and electrical panel design.

The technology doesn’t replace licensed architects, according to the co-founders. Licensed professionals still review the documents and affix their seal before submitting them for permits. The judgment stays human, they say.

Blueprints AI is targeting two groups with its new software. Professional architecture, engineering, and design firms make up one group, while developers and real estate owners make up another. The startup offers its software as a subscription and may add a one-time flat-fee option for those who just want it for a single project.

To learn more about Blueprints, catch hundreds of other startups, and learn from headliners like RJ Scaringe of Rivian and Amjad Masad of Replit, join us at TechCrunch Disrupt, kicking off Tuesday in downtown San Francisco.

Tech.title: Fitbit Edge is Google’s middle ground between Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch
Tech.content:
Google’s Fitbit lineup expanded on Monday with the introduction of the Fitbit Edge, a new wearable that’s positioned between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch.

Priced at $179.99, it combines the Fitbit Air’s slim band with an OLED display for checking map directions, notifications, weather, and music controls.

Like the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, the Edge works with Google Health Coach, powered by Gemini. (You’ll need a Google Health Premium subscription to use it.) The coach can use your fitness, health, and medical information to put together weekly routines and workout plans, then adjust them around your schedule.

It also comes with Google’s Health Guardian feature, which is designed to spot notable changes in health measurements over time, including indicators related to blood pressure and insulin resistance. (The company announced these features at the Pixel Watch 5 launch in August.)

Image Credits:Google

Google says the Fitbit Edge can automatically recognize and log up to 100 activities, including runs, bike rides, and walks. The company explains it uses context from your movement to work out what you’re doing and add it to your weekly goals. Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather.

The Fitbit Edge’s built-in GPS is 40% more accurate than the previous generation, the company claims, which should make it easier to track outdoor runs. Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips.

Meanwhile, the battery is rated for up to seven days on a charge, and the wearable is water-resistant to 50 meters.

The Fitbit Edge is available to preorder through the Google Store, with store availability set for October 27.

Color choices include Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon. There’s also a Stephen Curry Special Edition, priced at $219.99.

Tech.title: Smart ring maker Ultrahuman to roll out biological-age model across UAE
Tech.content:
Ultrahuman, a Bengaluru-based health tech startup best known for its smart rings, has partnered with Abu Dhabi health authorities to develop a biological-age model that it says will eventually be made available to people across the United Arab Emirates.

On Monday, Ultrahuman announced that it had signed a two-year memorandum of understanding with the Abu Dhabi Public Health Center (ADPHC) to develop and validate the model, which will combine clinical biomarkers with data from wearable devices. The partnership aims to use these signals to estimate how quickly an individual is aging and identify factors — including sleep, activity, cardiovascular health, and metabolism — that may be accelerating or slowing that process.

The partnership marks Ultrahuman’s latest effort to go beyond selling wearable hardware and deploy its health algorithms at a much larger scale. The startup increasingly sees itself as a health-data company, with its smart ring serving as one way to collect information that can underpin algorithms spanning aging, longevity, and other areas of health, CEO Mohit Kumar said in an interview.

“If you look at Ultrahuman as a company, we obviously have the Ultrahuman Ring, which is a way to acquire data from the human body,” Kumar told TechCrunch. “But truly, what we care about is not just the form factor, the ring, but what do we do with this data?”

Working with a government gives Ultrahuman the opportunity to apply its algorithms to a far broader population than its own customer base, Kumar said. The startup has sold around 800,000 smart rings globally so far. The Abu Dhabi partnership is Ultrahuman’s first step toward deploying a health algorithm at a national scale, with the health age model eventually intended to be available to people across the UAE, according to the company.

Even though Ultrahuman is known for its smart rings, Kumar said the biological-age model is being designed to be wearable-agnostic, allowing data from rings, wrist-worn devices, straps, and patches to feed into the system alongside clinical biomarkers. Individuals will eventually be able to access their health age through government digital-health platforms including TAMM and Sahatna, the startup said.

Ultrahuman and ADPHC will spend the next two years working on research and clinical validation of the model. Kumar told TechCrunch that the broader rollout will happen in phases, but did not provide a timeline.

The UAE is already among Ultrahuman’s 10 largest markets and accounts for about 4% to 5% of its overall revenue, Kumar said. The startup has operated in the market for nearly five years and sees about 25% higher retention there compared with its other markets, he noted.

Ultrahuman’s existing customer base gives it a narrower view of the population than a government health system. Its typical users are between 25 and 43 years old, Kumar said, while deploying the model across the UAE would expose it to a much broader range of age groups.

The underlying biological-age model was developed using Ultrahuman’s existing data, combining users’ chronological ages with wearable signals and, for some users, blood-test markers, Kumar told TechCrunch. That allows the startup to track how health markers typically change with age and identify deviations from those patterns.

Kumar stressed the model will not be trained on data from the UAE. “We will deploy an algorithm on the UAE data,” he said, adding that Ultrahuman will not have access to personally identifiable information through the program.

Ultrahuman is not the only smart-ring maker working with Abu Dhabi on preventive health. In May, the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi announced a partnership with Ultrahuman arch-rival Oura to combine the company’s wearable data with the emirate’s longitudinal health data, initially focusing on women’s health and cardiometabolic risk.

Kumar told TechCrunch that Ultrahuman is not aware of another company working with Abu Dhabi authorities on the health age model specifically. While he acknowledged that the government works with multiple health-tech companies, he declined to comment on the scope of Oura’s work with Abu Dhabi.

The parallel partnerships come as Ultrahuman and Oura compete in the smart-ring market while looking to push their businesses beyond wearable hardware and deeper into preventive health. The work with the Abu Dhabi authorities also comes as Ultrahuman is looking to build a smart ring that can run software on the device and even power everything from AI interactions to games.
